title: Japanese N5
description: Japanese from your first sentences to JLPT N5. Grammar lessons cover です and polite verbs, particles, adjectives, the て form, plain forms, wanting, inviting, permission, experiences and comparisons. About 800 everyday words are learned through typed vocabulary reviews (romaji turns into kana as you type), about 100 kanji through notecards and inside words, with furigana you can turn off. Requires Japanese: Hiragana and Katakana.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Introducing yourself: は and です
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the kana course you read your first sentence, わたしは がくせいです。 This lesson turns that
one sentence into a toolkit. By the end you can say who you are, where you're from, what you
do and which language you study; ask other people the same things; say "no, I'm not"; and
answer yes or no. You'll also meet your first six **[[kanji]]**, the characters Japanese
borrowed from Chinese, and see how this course writes them.

## Kanji and furigana

Japanese is written with three scripts at once. Hiragana carries grammar (particles, endings),
katakana writes loanwords and foreign names, and kanji write most nouns and the stems of verbs
and adjectives. A kanji stands for a meaning as well as a sound: 人 means "person", whether it
is read ひと or じん.

From this lesson on, words that are normally written in kanji appear in kanji, with their
reading in small kana above them. Those small kana are called **[[furigana]]**: {学生|がくせい}
(student), {先生|せんせい} (teacher), {日本|にほん} (Japan). Japanese children's books and
manga use furigana the same way. You can turn them off with the Furigana switch once you know
a word; try it from time to time to test yourself.

Most kanji have two kinds of reading:

- an **[[on'yomi]]** ("sound reading"), based on the Chinese pronunciation the character arrived
  with, mostly used in words of two or more kanji: 学 is ガク in {学生|がくせい};
- a **[[kun'yomi]]** ("meaning reading"), a native Japanese word given to the character, often used
  when the kanji stands alone: 人 is ひと, "a person".

Dictionaries and this course write on'yomi in katakana and kun'yomi in hiragana, so you can
tell them apart at a glance. You don't need to memorize every reading of a kanji. Learn the
words, and the readings come with them.

## The basic sentence: A は B です

The most useful sentence in Japanese has three parts:

| Topic | は | Description | です |
|---|---|---|---|
| わたし | は | {学生|がくせい} | です。 |
| エマさん | は | アメリカ{人|じん} | です。 |
| {山本|やまもと}さん | は | {先生|せんせい} | です。 |

わたしは {学生|がくせい}です。 — I'm a student.
エマさんは アメリカ{人|じん}です。 — Emma is American.
{山本|やまもと}さんは {先生|せんせい}です。 — Ms Yamamoto is a teacher.

は (read "wa") is a **[[particle]]**: a short word placed after another word to show its job. This
one marks the **[[topic]]**, what the sentence is about: "As for me, …", "As for Emma, …".

です is the **[[copula]]**, the word that links the topic to what it is: "am", "is", "are". It
never changes for I, you, she or they, and it never changes for one or many. It is also
polite: it's the form you use with anyone you don't know well, which is everyone, for now.
Its final す is very light, close to "des".

Notice what isn't there: no word for "a" or "the", and no "he" or "she". Once the topic is
clear, Japanese drops it. If someone asks what you do, {学生|がくせい}です。 alone is a complete
and natural answer, "(I) am a student." Starting every sentence with わたしは sounds stiff.

## Saying "is not": じゃ ありません

To make the sentence negative, replace です with じゃ ありません:

{学生|がくせい}です。 — I'm a student.
{学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません。 — I'm not a student.

じゃ ありません is the everyday spoken form. では ありません (では read "dewa") is the same
thing, a little more formal and the usual choice in writing:

{山本|やまもと}さんは {学生|がくせい}では ありません。{先生|せんせい}です。 — Ms Yamamoto isn't a student. She's a teacher.

You will also hear じゃ ないです, which means the same and is very common in conversation.
This course uses じゃ ありません for now and comes back to じゃ ないです in Module 3.

## Asking questions with か

Put か at the end of a sentence and it becomes a yes-or-no question. か is a
**[[sentence-final particle]]**: a particle that comes at the very end and changes what kind of
sentence it is. The word order stays the same, and in writing the sentence ends with 。:

エマさんは {学生|がくせい}ですか。 — Emma, are you a student?

Answer with はい (yes) or いいえ (no), then the full sentence or a short one:

はい、{学生|がくせい}です。 — Yes, I'm a student.
いいえ、{学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません。かいしゃいんです。 — No, I'm not a student. I'm an office worker.

Two short answers are worth learning as set phrases:

- はい、そうです。 — Yes, that's right. (そう = so, that way)
- いいえ、ちがいます。 — No, that's not right. (ちがいます = it's different, it's wrong)

ちがいます is how Japanese people correct a wrong guess politely; it's softer than repeating
the whole negative sentence. And when someone tells you something, そうですか (with a falling
voice) means "I see" or "Oh, really?"

Notice that Japanese "yes" and "no" answer whether the *question* is right, not whether the
thing is. You'll see what that means for negative questions later in the course.

## Talking to people: names and さん

Put さん after other people's names: エマさん, {山本|やまもと}さん, けんさん. It works like Mr or
Ms but goes with family names and given names alike, and with men and women alike. Two firm
rules:

- **Never put さん after your own name.** わたしは エマです。 — not ~~エマさんです~~. さん is
  respect, and you don't show respect to yourself.
- **Use the person's name instead of "you".** Japanese has a word for "you", あなた, but it
  sounds distant or too direct when said to someone whose name you know. To ask Emma whether
  she is a student, say エマさんは {学生|がくせい}ですか, using her name where English says "you".

Teachers are called {先生|せんせい}, either alone or after the family name: {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}.
The honors lesson "Names, titles and seals" goes deeper into names and titles.

## Countries, nationalities and languages

Add {人|じん} (person) to a country's name to get the nationality, and ご (language) to get
the language:

| Country | Person | Language |
|---|---|---|
| {日本|にほん} Japan | {日本人|にほんじん} Japanese (person) | {日本語|にほんご} Japanese (language) |
| アメリカ the US | アメリカ{人|じん} American | えいご English |
| イギリス the UK | イギリス{人|じん} British | えいご English |
| カナダ Canada | カナダ{人|じん} Canadian | えいご, フランスご |
| {中国|ちゅうごく} China | {中国人|ちゅうごくじん} Chinese (person) | {中国語|ちゅうごくご} Chinese |
| かんこく South Korea | かんこく{人|じん} Korean | かんこくご Korean |

English is えいご, not アメリカご. Someone from abroad in general is a
{外国人|がいこくじん} ("outside-country person"). The written word for "language" here is
{語|ご}; you'll learn that kanji properly in a later lesson, but the furigana tells you how to
read it now.

## The particle の: "of" and "'s"

の joins two nouns, and the first one describes the second. It covers "'s", "of", and
the job of many English compound nouns:

- わたしの {名前|なまえ} — my name
- エマさんの {本|ほん} — Emma's book
- {日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい} — a Japanese teacher (a teacher of Japanese)
- {大学|だいがく}の {先生|せんせい} — a university teacher, a professor
- アメリカの {大学|だいがく} — an American university

The order is the reverse of English "of": the describing word comes first, the main word
last. {日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい} is about a teacher; {先生|せんせい}の {日本語|にほんご} would be "the
teacher's Japanese".

## Jobs and studies

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {学生|がくせい} | student |
| {大学生|だいがくせい} | university student |
| {高校生|こうこうせい} | high-school student |
| {先生|せんせい} | teacher |
| かいしゃいん | office worker, company employee |
| いしゃ | doctor |
| エンジニア | engineer |

かいしゃいん (company employee) is how most people with an office job describe themselves;
Japanese people usually name the company rather than the job title. いしゃ is the word for
"a doctor", but you address a doctor as {先生|せんせい}.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 人 | person | ジン, ニン | ひと | 2 | {人|ひと}, {日本人|にほんじん}, アメリカ{人|じん} |
| 日 | sun, day | ニチ, ジツ | ひ, -か | 4 | {日本|にほん}, {日本人|にほんじん} |
| 本 | book, origin | ホン | もと | 5 | {本|ほん}, {日本|にほん} |
| 学 | study, learning | ガク | まな(ぶ) | 8 | {学生|がくせい}, {大学|だいがく} |
| 生 | life, be born | セイ, ショウ | い(きる), う(まれる), なま | 5 | {学生|がくせい}, {先生|せんせい} |
| 先 | ahead, previous | セン | さき | 6 | {先生|せんせい} |

Memory notes (our own pictures, not the history of the characters):

- 人 is two legs walking: a person seen from the side.
- 日 is a sun with a line across it, drawn square; "day" follows from "sun".
- 本 is a tree (木) with a mark at the bottom: the root, the origin. Japan, {日本|にほん}, is
  "the origin of the sun", the land of the rising sun. Books are 本 too.
- 学 has a child (子) at the bottom under a roof: a child learning.
- 生 looks like a plant pushing up through the ground: life, being born.
- 先 has legs at the bottom, stepping ahead. A {先生|せんせい} is "one born ahead", someone who went
  first.

{日本|にほん} has a second reading, にっぽん, used on stamps, banknotes and at sports events. にほん is
the everyday one.

## Dialogue: meeting at the university

```dialogue
# At the international office
やまもと: はじめまして。{山本|やまもと}です。{日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい}です。
= How do you do. I'm Yamamoto. I'm a Japanese teacher.
エマ: はじめまして。エマ・ジョーンズです。よろしく おねがいします。
= How do you do. I'm Emma Jones. Pleased to meet you.
やまもと: こちらこそ、よろしく おねがいします。エマさんは イギリス{人|じん}ですか。
= Pleased to meet you too. Emma, are you British?
エマ: いいえ、ちがいます。アメリカ{人|じん}です。
= No, I'm American.
やまもと: そうですか。{大学生|だいがくせい}ですか。
= I see. Are you a university student?
エマ: はい、そうです。とうきょう{大学|だいがく}の {学生|がくせい}です。
= Yes, that's right. I'm a student at Tokyo University.
やまもと: ジョンさんも {学生|がくせい}ですか。
= Is John a student too?
エマ: いいえ、ジョンさんは {学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません。エンジニアです。
= No, John isn't a student. He's an engineer.
```

Some things to notice. エマ gives her name without さん; {山本|やまもと} adds さん to it. こちらこそ means
"I'm the one who should say so": the standard reply to よろしく おねがいします. The ・ between
エマ and ジョーンズ separates the parts of a foreign name. And も ("too, also") takes the place
of は: ジョンさんも, never ジョンさんはも. You'll practise も in the next lesson.

## A self-introduction

A Japanese self-introduction (じこしょうかい) follows a set shape. Use it as a template:

> はじめまして。
>
> ジョン・パーカーです。カナダ{人|じん}です。
>
> エンジニアです。{日本語|にほんご}の {学生|がくせい}です。
>
> よろしく おねがいします。

How do you do. I'm John Parker. I'm Canadian. I'm an engineer. I'm a student of Japanese.
Pleased to meet you. Replace the name, nationality and job with your own. Saying your name
again with よろしく at the end, or bowing slightly as you say it, is natural.

## Say it

```speak
はじめまして。エマです。
= How do you do. I'm Emma.
アメリカ{人|じん}です。
= I'm American.
{日本語|にほんご}の {学生|がくせい}です。
= I'm a student of Japanese.
{先生|せんせい}ですか。
= Are you a teacher?
いいえ、{先生|せんせい}じゃ ありません。
= No, I'm not a teacher.
こちらこそ、よろしく おねがいします。
= Pleased to meet you too.
```

## Pronunciation

- です and ありません: the final す is almost silent. Say "des", not "de-su".
- {学生|がくせい} and {先生|せんせい}: the い after せ lengthens the vowel, "gakusē", "sensē".
  Don't say "sei" with a glide.
- {日本人|にほんじん}: ん is a full beat. Count it: に・ほ・ん・じ・ん, five beats.
- じゃ ありません runs together: "ja arimasen", with a light pause at most.

## Common mistakes

- Putting さん on your own name: ~~わたしは エマさんです~~.
- Using あなた for someone whose name you know. Use the name.
- Dropping です in polite speech: ~~わたしは {学生|がくせい}~~ sounds blunt or unfinished.
- English order with の: ~~{先生|せんせい}の {日本語|にほんご}~~ for "Japanese teacher". The describing word
  comes first: {日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい}.
- アメリカご for English. The language is えいご.
- A question mark instead of か. In polite Japanese, か makes the question; ？ is optional in
  casual writing.

## Key points

- A は B です: "A is B". は (wa) marks the topic; です links it politely to what it is.
- Negative: じゃ ありません (spoken) or では ありません (more formal).
- か at the end makes a yes-or-no question; answer はい / いいえ, そうです / ちがいます.
- A の B: B of A, A's B. The describing word comes first.
- Country + {人|じん} = nationality; country + ご = language (but English is えいご).
- さん goes after other people's names, never your own; use names, not あなた.
- Kanji have on'yomi (katakana in dictionaries) and kun'yomi (hiragana); furigana show the
  reading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: This, that, which: こそあど and の
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 gave you A は B です for people. This lesson points at things. You'll learn the
Japanese words for "this", "that", "which", "here", "there" and "where", how to ask what
something is and whose it is, and the particle も ("too, also"). Along the way you'll meet a
dozen everyday objects: the things in a bag or on a desk.

## The こそあど family

Japanese has a neat system of pointing words. Every set has four members, and the first kana
tells you which is which:

| Starts with | Points to | English |
|---|---|---|
| こ | near me (the speaker) | this, here |
| そ | near you (the listener) | that, there (by you) |
| あ | over there, away from both of us | that, over there |
| ど | which one? | which, where |

Teachers call the whole system **[[こそあど]]** after those four kana. English has only "this" and
"that"; Japanese splits "that" in two. Hold up a pen and it's こ. Point at the bag in your
friend's hand and it's そ. Point across the room, or at a building down the street, and it's
あ.

## これ, それ, あれ, どれ: this one, that one

These words stand alone, like nouns, and take particles:

これは かさです。 — This is an umbrella.
それは わたしの かばんです。 — That (by you) is my bag.
あれは {先生|せんせい}の {車|くるま}です。 — That (over there) is the teacher's car.

To ask what something is, use {何|なん}ですか:

A: これは {何|なん}ですか。 — What's this?
B: それは じしょです。 — That's a dictionary.

Notice that the answer switches from こ to そ. The object is near A, so A calls it これ; for
B it's near the listener, so it's それ. If both of you are looking at something far away,
both of you say あれ.

どれ means "which one?" when there are three or more to choose from:

エマさんの かさは どれですか。 — Which one is your umbrella, Emma?
— これです。 — This one.

Question words never take は: ~~どれは~~ and ~~{何|なに}は~~ are wrong. Put the question
word in the B slot, just before です.

## この, その, あの, どの + noun

When you want to say "this umbrella" rather than just "this", use the の-forms. They can't
stand alone; a noun always follows:

この かさは わたしのです。 — This umbrella is mine.
その とけいは いくらですか。 — How much is that watch? (いくら: Lesson 3)
あの {人|ひと}は だれですか。 — Who is that person (over there)?
どの ノートが エマさんのですか。 — Which notebook is yours, Emma?

The last sentence uses が, not は, after どの ノート. A question word (だれ, {何|なに}, どれ, or
どの + noun) can't be the topic, because the topic is something both speakers already know; so
when a question word comes first, it takes が. Lesson 5 explains が. For now, the pattern
X は どれですか (which one is X?) is the easiest way to ask.

Don't mix up the two sets:

| Stands alone | Before a noun |
|---|---|
| これは {本|ほん}です。 | この {本|ほん}は わたしのです。 |
| ~~このは {本|ほん}です~~ | ~~これ {本|ほん}~~ |

## ここ, そこ, あそこ, どこ: places

The place words follow the same pattern, with one surprise: the "over there" word is あそこ, not
"あこ".

ここは {大学|だいがく}です。 — This (place) is the university. / We're at the university.
トイレは どこですか。 — Where is the toilet?
— あそこです。 — It's over there.
エマさんの かさは そこです。 — Your umbrella is there (by you), Emma.

Asking where something is with は … どこですか is one of the most useful sentences you can
know. In a shop, say すみません、トイレは どこですか。

| | こ | そ | あ | ど |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| thing | これ | それ | あれ | どれ |
| + noun | この | その | あの | どの |
| place | ここ | そこ | あそこ | どこ |

## Who and whose: だれ, だれの

だれ is "who". Add の for "whose":

あの {人|ひと}は だれですか。 — Who is that person?
— {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}です。 — That's Professor Yamamoto.
これは だれの かさですか。 — Whose umbrella is this?
— わたしのです。 — It's mine.

In the answer, わたしの stands alone: "mine". When the noun is clear, Japanese drops it after
の, so わたしの かさです shortens to わたしのです. In the same way {先生|せんせい}のです is "it's the
teacher's".

## {何|なに} and {何|なん}: two readings of "what"

The kanji 何 is read なに or なん. The rule of thumb:

- なん before です, before の, and before sounds made with t, d or n, and before counters
  (later lessons): {何|なん}ですか, {何|なん}の {本|ほん} (a book about what?).
- なに in most other places, especially before particles such as を and が, and in
  {何語|なにご} (what language?).

A: これは {何|なん}の {本|ほん}ですか。 — What's this book about? (a book of what?)
B: {日本語|にほんご}の {本|ほん}です。 — It's a Japanese book.
A: たなかさんは {何語|なにご}の {先生|せんせい}ですか。 — What language do you teach, Mr Tanaka?

If you mix them up, people still understand you, but {何|なん}ですか is the one you'll use a
hundred times, so learn it first.

## も: also, too

も replaces は (or が) when you want to say "also". It goes after the word that is "also":

わたしは {学生|がくせい}です。けんさんも {学生|がくせい}です。 — I'm a student. Ken is a student too.
これは わたしの かさです。それも わたしのです。 — This is my umbrella. That one is mine too.

も never sits next to は: ~~けんさんはも~~. In a negative sentence, も means "not … either":

エマさんは {日本人|にほんじん}じゃ ありません。ジョンさんも {日本人|にほんじん}じゃ ありません。 — Emma isn't Japanese. John isn't Japanese either.

## Things in your bag

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| かさ | umbrella |
| かばん | bag |
| とけい | watch, clock |
| えんぴつ | pencil |
| ペン | pen |
| ノート | notebook |
| さいふ | wallet, purse |
| かぎ | key |
| じしょ | dictionary |
| しんぶん / {新聞|しんぶん} | newspaper |
| ざっし | magazine |
| スマホ | smartphone |

スマホ is short for スマートフォン (smartphone); everyone says スマホ. ノート is a notebook, never a
banknote. しんぶん is written {新聞|しんぶん} ("new hearing"), with two kanji you'll learn later.
じしょ and {新聞|しんぶん} join your word list in later modules; use them freely now. とけい covers both a watch and a clock.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 何 | what | カ | なに, なん | 7 | {何|なん}ですか, {何語|なにご} |
| 名 | name, famous | メイ, ミョウ | な | 6 | {名前|なまえ} |

- 何 has a narrow, squeezed form of 人 (person) on the left, next to a box with a hook:
  picture a person holding up a box and asking "what's this?"
- 名 is a crescent-moon shape (evening) over a mouth (口): at dusk you can't see faces, so you call out
  your name.

なまえ (name) is written {名前|なまえ}. Its second kanji, 前 (before, in front), comes later in
the course; the furigana carry you until then. You already know the word from the kana
course:

わたしの {名前|なまえ}は エマです。 — My name is Emma.
お{名前|なまえ}は？ — Your name? (お makes it polite: use it for someone else's name)

## Dialogue: whose is this?

```dialogue
# After class
せんせい: すみません、これは だれの かさですか。
= Excuse me, whose umbrella is this?
けん: あ、それは わたしのです。ありがとう ございます。
= Oh, that's mine. Thank you.
せんせい: この じしょも けんさんのですか。
= Is this dictionary yours too, Ken?
けん: いいえ、ちがいます。エマさんのです。
= No, it isn't. It's Emma's.
せんせい: そうですか。エマさんは どこですか。
= I see. Where is Emma?
けん: あそこです。あの {人|ひと}です。
= Over there. That person.
せんせい: あの スマホも エマさんのですか。
= Is that smartphone over there Emma's too?
けん: いいえ、あれは {先生|せんせい}のです。
= No, that's yours, sir.
```

The last line shows the rule from Lesson 1 in action: Ken uses {先生|せんせい} where English uses
"you". And notice how the pointing words follow the objects: the umbrella in the teacher's hand
is これ to the teacher and それ to Ken; the phone across the room is あれ to both.

## Say it

```speak
これは {何|なん}ですか。
= What's this?
それは じしょです。
= That's a dictionary.
これは だれの かさですか。
= Whose umbrella is this?
わたしのです。
= It's mine.
トイレは どこですか。
= Where's the toilet?
あの {人|ひと}は だれですか。
= Who is that person?
```

## Pronunciation

- あそこ has three short beats: a-so-ko. Don't stretch the first a.
- {何|なん}ですか: the ん is a full beat, and the う of です all but disappears: "nan des ka".
- えんぴつ: four beats, え・ん・ぴ・つ; the ん sounds like m before ぴ.

## Common mistakes

- この or その alone: ~~このは {何|なん}ですか~~. Use これ / それ when no noun follows.
- これ / それ before a noun: ~~これ かさ~~. Use この かさ.
- Forgetting to switch from こ to そ in an answer about the other person's thing.
- Question word with は: ~~だれは {先生|せんせい}ですか~~. Say {先生|せんせい}は だれですか, or use が
  (Lesson 5).
- はも or もは. も replaces は.
- Saying あこ for "over there". It's あそこ.

## Key points

- こ = near me, そ = near you, あ = away from both, ど = which / where.
- これ / それ / あれ / どれ stand alone; この / その / あの / どの need a noun after them.
- ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ are places: X は どこですか — where is X?
- だれ = who; だれの = whose; わたしの = mine (the noun after の can drop).
- {何|なん} before です and の; {何|なに} before most particles and in {何語|なにご}.
- も = also, too (not … either in a negative); it replaces は.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, prices and age
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Numbers come up in your first hour in Japan: prices, phone numbers, room numbers, someone's
age. This lesson teaches the numbers from 0 to 99,999, the places where their sounds change
(the part every learner has to practise), and three things to do with them: say a price with
{円|えん}, ask "how much?" with いくら, and give an age with さい. You'll also learn the number kanji,
which you'll see on menus, price tags and calendars.

## 0 to 10

| | Number | Reading | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | ゼロ / れい | ゼロ, れい | ゼロ is the everyday one; れい in more formal use |
| 1 | {一|いち} | いち | |
| 2 | {二|に} | に | |
| 3 | {三|さん} | さん | |
| 4 | {四|よん} | よん, し | よん is the usual reading |
| 5 | {五|ご} | ご | |
| 6 | {六|ろく} | ろく | |
| 7 | {七|なな} | なな, しち | なな is the usual reading |
| 8 | {八|はち} | はち | |
| 9 | {九|きゅう} | きゅう, く | きゅう is the usual reading |
| 10 | {十|じゅう} | じゅう | |

Three numbers have two readings. Use よん, なな and きゅう when you say a number on its own or
build a bigger one. し, しち and く turn up in counting aloud (いち, に, さん, し …) and in a few
fixed words, such as the names of some months, which you'll meet in Module 2. One reason
people avoid し and く is that they sound like the words for "death" and "suffering"; the
honors lesson "Numbers in daily life" tells that story.

## 11 to 99

Japanese builds numbers the way you'd say them on a calculator: tens, then ones.

| Number | Built as | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | 10 + 1 | じゅういち |
| 15 | 10 + 5 | じゅうご |
| 20 | 2 × 10 | にじゅう |
| 24 | 2 × 10 + 4 | にじゅうよん |
| 37 | 3 × 10 + 7 | さんじゅうなな |
| 49 | 4 × 10 + 9 | よんじゅうきゅう |
| 70 | 7 × 10 | ななじゅう |
| 99 | 9 × 10 + 9 | きゅうじゅうきゅう |

There are no special words like "eleven", "twelve" or "twenty". If you know 1 to 10, you know
everything up to 99.

## Hundreds and thousands: the sound changes

ひゃく (100) and せん (1,000) work the same way, 2 × 100, 3 × 1,000 and so on. But a few
combinations change sound to be easier to say. These are worth learning by heart:

| | × 100 (ひゃく) | × 1,000 (せん) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ひゃく | せん |
| 2 | にひゃく | にせん |
| 3 | さんびゃく (changes) | さんぜん (changes) |
| 4 | よんひゃく | よんせん |
| 5 | ごひゃく | ごせん |
| 6 | ろっぴゃく (changes) | ろくせん |
| 7 | ななひゃく | ななせん |
| 8 | はっぴゃく (changes) | はっせん (changes) |
| 9 | きゅうひゃく | きゅうせん |

The pattern behind the changes:

- After さん, the next sound is voiced: ひゃく becomes びゃく, せん becomes ぜん. (よん also ends
  in ん but doesn't change: よんひゃく, よんせん.)
- ろく and はち shrink to a small っ, and ひゃく hardens to ぴゃく: ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく.
  はち + せん becomes はっせん the same way.
- 100 and 1,000 on their own are just ひゃく and せん, not "いちひゃく" or "いちせん".

Then put the parts in order, biggest first: 365 is さんびゃくろくじゅうご; 1,980 is
せんきゅうひゃくはちじゅう; 3,800 is さんぜんはっぴゃく.

## 万: counting in ten-thousands

Here Japanese and English part ways. English groups digits in threes (thousand, million).
Japanese groups them in fours, and the unit after せん is まん, 10,000:

| Number | Reading |
|---|---|
| 10,000 | いちまん |
| 20,000 | にまん |
| 35,000 | さんまんごせん |
| 60,000 | ろくまん |
| 99,999 | きゅうまんきゅうせんきゅうひゃくきゅうじゅうきゅう |

Unlike ひゃく and せん, まん always needs a number in front: 10,000 is いちまん, never just "まん".
And 10,000 is never "じゅうせん" (ten thousand). If a number has five digits, count four from
the right and put まん there: 4|8000 is よんまんはっせん.

In horizontal writing Japanese mostly uses ordinary digits: 1,980{円|えん}, 35,000{円|えん}. Kanji numbers
appear in vertical text, on some menus and signs, and inside words. Both are read the same
way.

## Prices: 円 and いくら

The currency is the yen, {円|えん}. Japanese say it "en"; the y in "yen" comes from an older way of
writing Japanese in the Latin alphabet. Put the number first: 500{円|えん} (ごひゃくえん), 1,200{円|えん}
(せんにひゃくえん), 10,000{円|えん} (いちまんえん).

One small surprise: 4 yen is よえん, not "よんえん". Bigger amounts with 4 are regular:
40{円|えん} is よんじゅうえん, 400{円|えん} よんひゃくえん.

To ask a price, use いくら (how much?):

これは いくらですか。 — How much is this?
— 380{円|えん}です。 — It's 380 yen. (さんびゃくはちじゅうえん)
この ノートは いくらですか。 — How much is this notebook?
— {百五十円|ひゃくごじゅうえん}です。 — It's 150 yen.

## Age: さい and なんさい

Age uses さい (years old) after the number. Several numbers change sound before it, like
before ひゃく:

| Age | Reading | Age | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | いっさい (changes) | 6 | ろくさい |
| 2 | にさい | 7 | ななさい |
| 3 | さんさい | 8 | はっさい (changes) |
| 4 | よんさい | 9 | きゅうさい |
| 5 | ごさい | 10 | じゅっさい (changes) |

いち, はち and じゅう shrink to small っ: いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい (じっさい is also correct, and
is the traditional form). 11, 18 and 21 do the same: じゅういっさい, じゅうはっさい, にじゅういっさい.

20 has its own word: はたち. Twenty was long the age of adulthood in Japan (it became 18 in
2022), and most towns still hold their coming-of-age ceremony for twenty-year-olds, so the age
keeps its special word. (にじゅっさい is also correct and sometimes
heard.) 30 is さんじゅっさい, 40 よんじゅっさい.

To ask someone's age:

- {何|なん}さいですか。 — How old are you? (plain and polite; fine for children and peers)
- おいくつですか。 — How old are you? (softer and more polite; use it with adults)

Many adults would rather not be asked, so ask only when it's natural, for example among
students of the same age.

## Phone numbers

Phone numbers are read digit by digit, with の for each hyphen:

090-3816-2475 → ゼロきゅうゼロの さんはちいちろくの によんななご

Two habits make phone numbers sound natural. First, 0 is ゼロ (some people say まる, "circle").
Second, the one-beat numbers に and ご are stretched to two beats, "nī" and "gō", so they
match the two-beat digits such as いち and ろく. A beat of Japanese timing is called a
**[[mora]]**: に is one mora, いち is two, and にい is two.

To ask for a number:

{電話|でんわ}ばんごうは {何|なん}ばんですか。 — What's your phone number?

ばんごう is "number" (as in phone or room number), and {何|なん}ばん is "what number?"

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 一 | one | イチ, イツ | ひと(つ) | 1 |
| 二 | two | ニ | ふた(つ) | 2 |
| 三 | three | サン | み, みっ(つ) | 3 |
| 四 | four | シ | よ, よん, よっ(つ) | 5 |
| 五 | five | ゴ | いつ(つ) | 4 |
| 六 | six | ロク | む, むっ(つ) | 4 |
| 七 | seven | シチ | なな, なな(つ) | 2 |
| 八 | eight | ハチ | や, やっ(つ) | 2 |
| 九 | nine | キュウ, ク | ここの(つ) | 2 |
| 十 | ten | ジュウ, ジッ | とお | 2 |
| 百 | hundred | ヒャク | | 6 |
| 千 | thousand | セン | ち | 3 |
| 万 | ten thousand | マン, バン | | 3 |
| 円 | yen, circle | エン | まる(い) | 4 |

The readings in brackets, such as ひと(つ), belong to the native counting words in Lesson 4.

Memory notes:

- 一, 二, 三 are one, two and three lines: the easiest kanji there are.
- 四 is a box with legs inside, like a table with four corners; 五 looks like a squashed
  "5" on a stand.
- 六 is a little person with a hat and two legs; 七 is an upside-down 7 crossed by a line.
- 八 spreads out like the two lines of a widening road, a sign of luck you'll meet in the
  honors lesson; 九 is a 9 with a long tail; 十 is a plus sign: ten fingers crossed.
- 百 is 一 (one) on top of 白 (white): one hundred is a "white" number, a fresh page.
- 千 is 十 with a slanted stroke on top: ten, raised a level.
- 万 is the kanji on the biggest banknote, the {一万円|いちまんえん} bill; its hook and sweep look
  like a ribbon unrolled for a long way.
- 円 is a window frame. It also means "circle"; the currency is named after round coins.

Large numbers in kanji line up like this: {三百|さんびゃく} (300), {八千|はっせん} (8,000),
{二万|にまん} (20,000), and {千円|せんえん} (1,000 yen) is the banknote everyone carries.

## Dialogue: swapping numbers

```dialogue
# After class
エマ: けんさん、{電話|でんわ}ばんごうは {何|なん}ばんですか。
= Ken, what's your phone number?
けん: ゼロはちゼロの いちごよんきゅうの さんななろくにです。
= It's 080-1549-3762.
エマ: すみません、もう いちど おねがいします。
= Sorry, once more, please.
けん: ゼロはちゼロの、いちごよんきゅうの、さんななろくにです。
= 080, 1549, 3762.
エマ: ありがとう ございます。けんさんは {何|なん}さいですか。
= Thank you. How old are you, Ken?
けん: はたちです。エマさんは？
= I'm twenty. And you, Emma?
エマ: じゅうきゅうさいです。
= I'm nineteen.
```

Notice エマさんは？ with a rising voice: "And you?" Japanese drops the rest of the question when
it's the same as the one just asked.

## Reading: the school cafeteria

> {学食|がくしょく} メニュー
>
> カレー 420{円|えん}　うどん 330{円|えん}　ラーメン 480{円|えん}
>
> おにぎり 150{円|えん}　コーヒー 100{円|えん}

{学食|がくしょく} is the student cafeteria. Read the prices aloud: よんひゃくにじゅうえん,
さんびゃくさんじゅうえん, よんひゃくはちじゅうえん, ひゃくごじゅうえん, ひゃくえん. Then
ask about each one: カレーは いくらですか。— 420{円|えん}です。

## Say it

```speak
これは いくらですか。
= How much is this?
さんびゃくえんです。
= It's 300 yen.
はっぴゃくえんです。
= It's 800 yen.
さんぜんえんです。
= It's 3,000 yen.
いちまんえんです。
= It's 10,000 yen.
{何|なん}さいですか。
= How old are you?
はたちです。
= I'm twenty.
```

## Common mistakes

- Regular forms where the sound changes: ~~さんひゃく~~, ~~ろくひゃく~~, ~~はちひゃく~~,
  ~~さんせん~~, ~~はちせん~~. Say さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん, はっせん.
- Saying "いちひゃく" or "いちせん", but forgetting いち in いちまん.
- Counting ten-thousands in English style: ~~じゅうせん~~ for 10,000. It's いちまん; 50,000
  is ごまん.
- Using し, しち or く for prices or ages: say よんひゃくえん, ななさい, きゅうさい.
- ~~いちさい~~, ~~はちさい~~, ~~じゅうさい~~: use いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい.
- Pronouncing 円 "yen". It's えん.

## Key points

- 0–10: ゼロ, いち, に, さん, よん, ご, ろく, なな, はち, きゅう, じゅう.
- Build bigger numbers biggest part first: 365 = さんびゃくろくじゅうご.
- Sound changes: さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく; さんぜん, はっせん.
- Japanese counts in ten-thousands: 10,000 = いちまん.
- Price: number + {円|えん}; ask with いくらですか.
- Age: number + さい, with いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい; 20 = はたち; ask {何|なん}さいですか or
  おいくつですか.
- Phone numbers digit by digit, の for the hyphen.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Shopping: を ください
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now point at things (これ, その かさ) and ask prices (いくらですか). This lesson lets you
buy them. You'll learn to ask for something with を ください, to say how many you want with the
native Japanese counting words ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ…, to ask for a total, and to name a few
colors. You'll also see the polite お in front of words like お{金|かね} and おちゃ, and learn
three kanji you'll find on every shopping street: 店, 大 and 小.

## Asking for things: N を ください

ください means "please give me". Put the thing you want in front of it, followed by を:

これを ください。 — This one, please. / I'll take this.
おちゃを ください。 — Tea, please.
その かさを ください。 — That umbrella, please.

を (read "o", as you learned in the kana course) is the particle that marks the **[[object]]**,
the thing an action is done to. Here the action is "give", and the thing given is the object.
を always comes right after the noun, and ください comes last.

In a shop or café you'll also hear and use おねがいします, from the kana course. It's a little
softer and works for services as well as things:

コーヒーを おねがいします。 — A coffee, please.

Both are polite. ください is the clearest choice when you point at something on a counter.

## How many: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ

Japanese doesn't put a plain number in front of a noun the way English says "three apples".
It uses a **[[counter]]**, a small word added to the number that depends on what you're counting.
There are dozens of counters, and you'll learn the common ones in Module 3, but one set works
for almost any thing when you shop: the native Japanese numbers ending in つ.

| | Written | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {一|ひと}つ | ひとつ |
| 2 | {二|ふた}つ | ふたつ |
| 3 | {三|みっ}つ | みっつ |
| 4 | {四|よっ}つ | よっつ |
| 5 | {五|いつ}つ | いつつ |
| 6 | {六|むっ}つ | むっつ |
| 7 | {七|なな}つ | ななつ |
| 8 | {八|やっ}つ | やっつ |
| 9 | {九|ここの}つ | ここのつ |
| 10 | {十|とお} | とお (no つ) |
| how many? | いくつ | いくつ |

These are a separate, older set of Japanese numbers, so they don't sound like いち, に, さん,
even though they're written with the same kanji ({三|みっ}つ, {三|さん}). Say them aloud until the
rhythm sticks: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ. From 11 on, people switch back to ordinary
numbers (じゅういち, じゅうに …) or to another counter.

The counted number goes after the particle and before the verb:

りんごを みっつ ください。 — Three apples, please.
おにぎりを ふたつ ください。 — Two rice balls, please.
この パンを ひとつ ください。 — One of this bread, please.

Not ~~みっつの りんご~~, which is grammatical but sounds like a written description, not an
order. The pattern is always thing を number ください.

To ask how many someone wants, use いくつ:

A: たまごは いくつですか。 — How many eggs (do you want)?
B: よっつ おねがいします。 — Four, please.

## The total: ぜんぶで

ぜんぶで means "in total, altogether" (ぜんぶ = all, and で marks the way you're counting):

ぜんぶで いくらですか。 — How much is it altogether?
— ぜんぶで 680{円|えん}です。 — 680 yen in total. (ろっぴゃくはちじゅうえん)

## Polite お

Some nouns take an お in front that makes them sound polite or gentle: おちゃ (tea),
お{金|かね} (money), おにぎり (rice ball), お{店|みせ} (shop). For some words the お has become part
of the word: a rice ball is always おにぎり (にぎり alone is a kind of sushi), and tea is almost
always おちゃ. For others it's optional and makes your speech softer: {店|みせ} and お{店|みせ} are both fine.

You'll also hear お before words about the person you're talking to: お{名前|なまえ} (your
name). Never put it on your own things in that sense.

## Colors: a first look

Four color words end in い and work like English adjectives, before a noun:

| Word | Color | Example |
|---|---|---|
| あかい | red | あかい りんご — a red apple |
| あおい | blue (also green for traffic lights) | あおい かさ — a blue umbrella |
| {白|しろ}い | white | {白|しろ}い かばん — a white bag |
| くろい | black | くろい ペン — a black pen |

They also end a sentence before です: この かさは あおいです。— This umbrella is blue. Words like
these are called い-adjectives, and Module 3 teaches all their forms.

In a shop, add の after the color to mean "the … one":

あかいのを ください。 — The red one, please.
くろいのは いくらですか。 — How much is the black one?

The の stands for the thing, like "one" in English. It's the same idea as わたしの ("mine")
from Lesson 2.

## Big and small

{大|おお}きい (big) and {小|ちい}さい (small) are two more い-adjectives, and your first words
written with a kanji followed by kana. The kana part after the kanji is called **[[okurigana]]**:
it carries the ending that changes in grammar, while the kanji carries the meaning. In
{大|おお}きい, 大 is read おお and きい is the okurigana.

{大|おお}きい かばん — a big bag
{小|ちい}さい とけい — a small watch
この セーターは {大|おお}きいです。{小|ちい}さいのは ありますか。 — This sweater is big. Do you have a small one?

The last sentence uses ありますか (do you have …?, is there …?), which Lesson 5 teaches. It's
too useful in shops to leave out.

## Food and drink

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| おちゃ | tea (usually green tea) |
| ジュース | juice, soft drink |
| ぎゅうにゅう | milk |
| パン | bread |
| りんご | apple |
| たまご | egg |
| おにぎり | rice ball |

ジュース covers fruit juice and sweet fizzy drinks; ぎゅうにゅう is the word on a milk carton
(people also say ミルク). コーヒー and {水|みず} you know from the kana course.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 店 | shop, store | テン | みせ | 8 | {店|みせ}, お{店|みせ} |
| 大 | big, great | ダイ, タイ | おお(きい) | 3 | {大|おお}きい, {大学|だいがく} |
| 小 | small, little | ショウ | ちい(さい), こ, お | 3 | {小|ちい}さい |

- 店 is a building with a roof on the left (the slanting stroke and the line at the top) and a
  counter under it: a shop.
- 大 is a person standing with arms spread wide: "this big!"
- 小 is a small thing in the middle with two little bits falling off either side.

You already know 大 from {大学|だいがく} (university, "big learning") and {大学生|だいがくせい}. There
the on'yomi ダイ is used; in {大|おお}きい the kun'yomi おお.

## Dialogue: at a fruit shop

```dialogue
# At the greengrocer's
てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome!
エマ: すみません、この りんごは いくらですか。
= Excuse me, how much are these apples?
てんいん: ひとつ 150{円|えん}です。
= 150 yen each.
エマ: じゃあ、みっつ ください。それから、その みかんも ください。
= Then three, please. And those mandarins too.
てんいん: みかんは いくつですか。
= How many mandarins?
エマ: いつつ おねがいします。ぜんぶで いくらですか。
= Five, please. How much is that altogether?
てんいん: ぜんぶで 850{円|えん}です。
= 850 yen altogether.
エマ: はい、1000{円|えん}です。
= Here's 1,000 yen.
てんいん: 150{円|えん}の おかえしです。ありがとう ございました。
= Here's your change of 150 yen. Thank you very much.
```

てんいん is a shop assistant. Notice ひとつ 150{円|えん}: "one, 150 yen", the usual way to give a
price each. じゃあ means "well then"; それから means "and also, after that". みかん is a
mandarin orange (3 × 150 = 450 yen, and the mandarins come to 400). お{金|かね} given back as
change is おかえし, and ありがとう ございました, the past form of thanks, is what shop staff say
when you leave.

## Say it

```speak
これを ください。
= I'll take this, please.
りんごを みっつ ください。
= Three apples, please.
あかいのを ください。
= The red one, please.
ぜんぶで いくらですか。
= How much is it altogether?
おちゃを ふたつ おねがいします。
= Two teas, please.
```

## Pronunciation

- みっつ, よっつ, むっつ, やっつ: the small っ is a full beat of silence. みっつ has three beats,
  み・っ・つ. Without it, みつ would be another word (honey).
- とお has two beats: the long お matters.
- ください has four short beats, く・だ・さ・い. Don't stretch any of them.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out を, or putting it after ください: ~~ください これを~~. The order is thing を
  ください.
- Putting the number before the noun, English-style: ~~みっつ りんごを ください~~. Say
  りんごを みっつ ください.
- Using いち, に, さん with things: ~~りんごを さん ください~~. Use the つ counter.
- ~~とおつ~~ for ten. Ten is just とお.
- この or その without a noun: ~~このを ください~~. Say これを ください.
- Writing {大|おお}きい without its okurigana. The きい has to be there.

## Key points

- Ask for things with N を ください (or N を おねがいします).
- を marks the object; it's written を and read "o".
- Count things with ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ, いつつ, むっつ, ななつ, やっつ, ここのつ, とお;
  ask いくつ. The number goes after を: りんごを みっつ ください.
- ぜんぶで いくらですか — how much altogether?
- お makes some nouns polite: おちゃ, お{金|かね}, お{店|みせ}.
- Color words あかい, あおい, {白|しろ}い, くろい go before nouns; あかいの = the red one.
- {大|おお}きい / {小|ちい}さい: kanji for the meaning, okurigana for the ending.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Where things are: あります, います
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far every sentence has ended in です. This lesson brings in your first two verbs, あります
and います, both meaning "there is" or "to be (somewhere)". With them you can say what's in a
room, where your keys are and who is at home. You'll also learn the particle が, which marks
the **[[subject]]**; に for "in, at, on"; a dozen words for positions such as "on", "under" and
"next to"; and や…など for "things like…".

## あります and います

Japanese has two verbs of existence, and the choice depends on what exists:

| Verb | Used for | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| あります | things that don't move by themselves: objects, plants, buildings | {本|ほん}, つくえ, {木|き}, {店|みせ} |
| います | things that move by themselves: people and animals | {人|ひと}, {先生|せんせい}, いぬ, ねこ |

{本|ほん}が あります。 — There's a book.
ねこが います。 — There's a cat.

Their negatives are ありません and いません: "there isn't".

ねこは いません。 — There's no cat. / The cat isn't here.

The ます ending marks them as polite verbs, like です. Dictionaries list them as ある and いる;
Module 2 explains verbs and their forms. Some speakers use います for a bus or taxi
waiting with its driver (タクシーが います), but objects in general, even phones, take あります.

## Saying where: N に N が あります

To say what is in a place, start with the place, mark it with に (in, at, on), then the thing
with が, then the verb:

| Place | に | Thing | が | Verb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| へや | に | テレビ | が | あります。 |
| こうえん | に | いぬ | が | います。 |

へやに テレビが あります。 — There's a TV in the room.
こうえんに いぬが います。 — There's a dog in the park. (こうえん = park)

が marks the subject: the thing that exists, here the thing the sentence tells you is there. It's
new information. That's why it's が and not は: you're introducing the TV or the dog to the
listener for the first time.

Questions use {何|なに}が and だれが:

へやに {何|なに}が ありますか。 — What's in the room?
へやに だれが いますか。 — Who's in the room?

(Lesson 2 said question words never take は; here's where が comes in.)

## Saying where a known thing is: N は N に あります

When both speakers already know the thing and the question is *where* it is, it becomes the
topic, with は, and the place comes after it:

| Topic | は | Place | に | Verb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| テレビ | は | へや | に | あります。 |
| {先生|せんせい} | は | {大学|だいがく} | に | います。 |

かぎは どこに ありますか。 — Where are the keys?
— かばんの {中|なか}に あります。 — They're in the bag.
エマさんは どこに いますか。 — Where is Emma?
— {大学|だいがく}に います。 — She's at the university.

The difference between the two patterns is the same as between "There's a dog in the park"
and "The dog is in the park". With が the thing is news; with は it's already known.

You can also ask X は どこですか, which you learned in Lesson 2. Both are natural: X は どこに
ありますか is a little more specific.

## Location words

To be precise, put a location word after the thing with の: つくえの {上|うえ}, "the top of the desk",
"on the desk". The whole phrase is the place and takes に.

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {上|うえ} | on, above, top | つくえの {上|うえ}に |
| {下|した} | under, below | いすの {下|した}に |
| {中|なか} | in, inside | かばんの {中|なか}に |
| {外|そと} | outside | まどの {外|そと}に |
| {前|まえ} | in front of | {店|みせ}の {前|まえ}に |
| {後|うし}ろ | behind | ドアの {後|うし}ろに |
| よこ | beside, at the side of | ベッドの よこに |
| となり | next to (side by side) | {大学|だいがく}の となりに |
| ちかく | near, nearby | {駅|えき}の ちかくに |
| {左|ひだり} | left | テレビの {左|ひだり}に |
| {右|みぎ} | right | テレビの {右|みぎ}に |
| あいだ | between | AとBの あいだに |

These are **[[location nouns]]**: nouns that name a position relative to something, used with
の before them and a particle after them. English uses a preposition ("under the chair");
Japanese says "the chair's underneath".

いすの {下|した}に ねこが います。 — There's a cat under the chair.
{店|みせ}の {前|まえ}に {人|ひと}が いますか。 — Are there people in front of the shop?
{駅|えき}の ちかくに {大|おお}きい {店|みせ}が あります。 — There's a big shop near the station.

Three pairs need care:

- となり vs よこ: となり is "next door, the next one in a row", usually the same kind of
  thing (two houses, two people, two shops). よこ is simply "at the side". {山本|やまもと}さんの
  となり is the person sitting next to Yamamoto; {本|ほん}だなの よこ is beside the bookcase.
- あいだ needs two things joined by と ("and"): {本|ほん}だなと まどの あいだ, "between the
  bookcase and the window". と joins nouns, only nouns.
- {前|まえ} and {後|うし}ろ are front and back of something. {後|うし}ろ has kana after the kanji, ろ,
  which you must write.

## Things like…: や and など

と lists everything: ペンと ノート, "a pen and a notebook" (and that's all). や lists examples, with
more left unsaid. Add など ("and so on") to the last item if you like:

つくえの {上|うえ}に ペンや ノートが あります。 — There are pens, notebooks and things on the desk.
へやに テレビや ベッドなどが あります。 — In the room there's a TV, a bed and so on.

など comes before the particle: ベッドなどが, not ~~ベッドがなど~~.

## Rooms and furniture

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| へや | room |
| つくえ | desk |
| いす | chair |
| ベッド | bed |
| テレビ | television |
| まど | window |
| ドア | door (Western-style) |
| {本|ほん}だな | bookcase, bookshelf |
| れいぞうこ | refrigerator |
| いぬ | dog |
| ねこ | cat |

{本|ほん}だな is {本|ほん} (book) + たな (shelf), with the sound change た → だ that often happens when two
words join.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 上 | up, above | ジョウ | うえ, あ(がる), のぼ(る) | 3 | {上|うえ} |
| 下 | down, below | カ, ゲ | した, さ(がる), お(りる) | 3 | {下|した} |
| 中 | middle, inside | チュウ | なか | 4 | {中|なか}, {中国|ちゅうごく} |
| 外 | outside | ガイ, ゲ | そと, ほか | 5 | {外|そと}, {外国人|がいこくじん} |
| 左 | left | サ | ひだり | 5 | {左|ひだり} |
| 右 | right | ウ, ユウ | みぎ | 5 | {右|みぎ} |

- 上 and 下 are mirror images: a line (the ground) with a mark pointing up from it, or down.
- 中 is a box with a line straight through the middle.
- 外 has an evening moon on the left and a fortune-teller's crack on the right: picture
  someone stepping outside at night.
- 左 and 右 share a hand on top. 左 has エ ("e") underneath, 右 has 口 (a mouth). Think "the
  right hand feeds the mouth"; the other one is left.

You met 中 and 外 in Lesson 1 already: {中国|ちゅうごく} (China, "the middle country") and
{外国人|がいこくじん} (foreigner, "outside-country person"). The kanji in {前|まえ} and {後|うし}ろ are taught
in Module 2, but you can read them with furigana now.

## Dialogue: where are my keys?

```dialogue
# Leaving the house
けん: ゆきさん、かぎは どこに ありますか。
= Yuki, where are the keys?
ゆき: つくえの {上|うえ}に ありませんか。
= Aren't they on the desk?
けん: いいえ、ありません。ペンや ノートは ありますが…。
= No. There are pens and notebooks, but…
ゆき: じゃあ、かばんの {中|なか}は？
= Then what about inside your bag?
けん: かばんの {中|なか}にも ありません。
= They're not in the bag either.
ゆき: あ、テレビの {前|まえ}に ありますよ。ねこの {下|した}です。
= Oh, they're in front of the TV. Under the cat.
けん: あ、ほんとうだ。ありがとう。
= Oh, so they are. Thanks.
```

にも is に + も: "in … too / not in … either". Particles can stack like this. ありますが
means "there are, but…"; Module 2 covers が for "but", and よ at the end of ゆき's line points
out something the listener doesn't know. ほんとうだ is casual for "it's true".

## Reading: my room

> わたしの へやは {大|おお}きくありません。でも、いい へやです。
>
> まどの {前|まえ}に つくえが あります。つくえの {上|うえ}に パソコンや {本|ほん}などが あります。
>
> つくえの {右|みぎ}に ベッドが あります。ベッドと ドアの あいだに {本|ほん}だなが あります。
>
> ベッドの {上|うえ}に ねこが います。{名前|なまえ}は ミルです。

My room isn't big. But it's a nice room. In front of the window there's a desk. On the desk
there's a computer, books and so on. To the right of the desk there's a bed. Between the bed
and the door there's a bookcase. On the bed there's a cat. Its name is Miru.

({大|おお}きくありません is the negative of {大|おお}きいです, from Module 3; でも = but; いい = good;
パソコン = computer.)

## Say it

```speak
つくえの {上|うえ}に {本|ほん}が あります。
= There's a book on the desk.
いすの {下|した}に ねこが います。
= There's a cat under the chair.
かぎは どこに ありますか。
= Where are the keys?
かばんの {中|なか}に あります。
= They're in the bag.
へやに だれが いますか。
= Who is in the room?
{大学|だいがく}の となりに {店|みせ}が あります。
= There's a shop next to the university.
```

## Common mistakes

- います for objects or あります for people and animals: ~~ねこが あります~~, ~~{先生|せんせい}が
  あります~~. Ask yourself: can it walk away by itself?
- English order: ~~{本|ほん}が あります つくえの {上|うえ}に~~. The verb comes last.
- ~~{上|うえ}の つくえに~~ for "on the desk". The thing comes first, then の, then the
  location word: つくえの {上|うえ}.
- は where the thing is new: へやに テレビは あります sounds like "As for TVs, there is one in
  the room (but maybe not other things)". Use が to introduce something.
- Using で for location with あります / います: ~~へやで ねこが います~~. Existence takes に.
  (で marks where an action happens, Module 2.)
- Using や for a complete list. や means "among other things".

## Key points

- あります for things and plants, います for people and animals; negatives ありません,
  いません.
- Place に thing が あります: what's there (new information, が marks the subject).
- Thing は place に あります: where a known thing is (the topic, with は).
- Location words follow the thing with の: つくえの {上|うえ}, かばんの {中|なか}, AとBの あいだ.
- {何|なに}が / だれが ありますか, いますか; question words take が, not は.
- A や B (など) — A, B and so on; A と B — A and B (complete).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Names, titles and seals
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 1 you learned two rules: put さん after other people's names, never your own, and use
names instead of あなた. This lesson explains the world behind those rules: how Japanese names
are built, the whole family of name suffixes (さん is only one of them), when people use a
title such as {先生|せんせい} instead of a name, how Japanese names are written in English, and the
personal seal, the はんこ, that many people still use in place of a signature.

## Family name first

A Japanese name has two parts, and the family name comes first:

| Full name | Family name (みょうじ) | Given name |
|---|---|---|
| {山本|やまもと} ゆき | {山本|やまもと} | ゆき |
| {木下|きのした} けん | {木下|きのした} | けん |
| {中川|なかがわ} はると | {中川|なかがわ} | はると |

The family name is called みょうじ. The given name is simply {名前|なまえ}, or {下|した}の
{名前|なまえ} ("the lower name", because in vertical writing it's written below the family
name). Japanese has no middle names.

Most family names are written with two kanji, often with a picture of the landscape in them:
{山本|やまもと} is "base of the mountain", {中川|なかがわ} "middle of the river", {小川|おがわ}
"little river", {木下|きのした} "under the tree". The most common family names in Japan,
さとう, すずき, たかはし and たなか, are written with kanji you haven't met yet. Given names are
much more varied, and their kanji can have unusual readings, which is why Japanese people often
ask each other how a name is written.

In everyday adult life people mostly use family names. A colleague, a neighbour or a shop
owner is {山本|やまもと}さん, not ゆきさん. Given names are for family, close friends and
children. When you meet someone, the safe choice is to use the name they give you: if they say
{山本|やまもと}です, call them {山本|やまもと}さん.

Foreign names are written in katakana and usually keep their own order, given name first:
エマ・ジョーンズ. People will often call you by your given name plus さん (エマさん), because it's
easier to say. That's normal and friendly.

## Name suffixes

さん is the all-purpose suffix, but there are others. Choosing one shows how you see your
relationship with the person. These little words are **[[honorific suffixes]]**:

| Suffix | Used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| さん | almost anyone: adults, colleagues, neighbours, shop staff | {山本|やまもと}さん |
| さま | customers, people you write to formally, people you serve | {山本|やまもと}さま |
| くん | boys and young men; also juniors at school or work | けんくん |
| ちゃん | small children, close friends, family, pets | ゆきちゃん |
| {先生|せんせい} | teachers, doctors, and some other experts | {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい} |
| (none) | family and very close friends | ゆき |

A few notes on each:

- さま is more respectful than さん. You hear it from shop and bank staff (おきゃくさま, "the
  customer"), on envelopes and in emails (ゆき さま), and when a hospital or bank calls out
  your name from the waiting room. Never use it about yourself.
- くん is for boys and for people junior to you. A teacher might call a boy けんくん; a manager
  sometimes calls younger staff, men and women, by family name + くん. Many schools now use さん
  for all pupils instead.
- ちゃん sounds cute and close. Children are ゆきちゃん; teenage girls often use ちゃん between
  themselves; a grandmother may still call her fifty-year-old son by his childhood name with
  ちゃん. Using it with an adult you don't know is too familiar.
- {先生|せんせい} replaces さん: it's {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}, never ~~{山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}さん~~.
  It's used for school and university teachers, doctors and dentists, and also for lawyers,
  politicians and well-known writers or artists. Students usually say just {先生|せんせい}
  without the name.
- No suffix at all, calling someone by the bare name, is called よびすて. It's normal in
  families and between close friends, and rude anywhere else.

## Titles instead of names

Japanese often uses a role instead of a name, where English would use a name or "you":

- In school and university clubs, juniors call seniors せんぱい ({山本|やまもと}せんぱい, or just
  せんぱい).
- At work, a manager may be called by a title: {社長|しゃちょう} (company president), ぶちょう
  (head of department).
- In families, children call their parents お{母|かあ}さん and お{父|とう}さん, and younger siblings
  call an older sister おねえさん: nobody calls their mother by her name.
- Shop staff and customers use no name at all; you'll hear すみません to get attention, and
  おきゃくさま from the staff.

So when English needs "you", Japanese reaches for the name, the title or the role. Only when
none of those fit does it use あなた, and then it sounds distant: it's common on forms, in
advertisements and in song lyrics ("you" in general), and some married couples, mostly of an
older generation, use it as a mild "dear". Said to a colleague's face, あなたは… can sound like
the start of a complaint.

## Asking someone's name

The polite way to ask is short:

お{名前|なまえ}は？ — Your name, please? / What's your name?

The お before {名前|なまえ} makes it someone else's name and shows respect; the question is left
unfinished, which softens it. The reply is just the name and です:

{山本|やまもと}です。 — I'm Yamamoto.

In formal settings you'll hear longer and more polite versions, which you only need to
recognize for now.

## Business cards

At work, a first meeting usually includes swapping business cards (めいし). Hold yours with
both hands, turned so the other person can read it, say your name and よろしく おねがいします,
and take theirs with both hands too. Look at it, then keep it on the table in front of you
during the meeting rather than putting it straight into a pocket. The card shows the company
first, then the department and title, then the name: this order (group first, person last) is
the same idea as family name first.

```dialogue
# A first meeting at work
きのした: はじめまして。みどり ぎんこうの {木下|きのした}です。
= How do you do. I'm Kinoshita, from Midori Bank.
ジョン: はじめまして。ジョン・パーカーです。よろしく おねがいします。
= How do you do. I'm John Parker. Pleased to meet you.
きのした: よろしく おねがいします。パーカーさんは エンジニアですか。
= Pleased to meet you. Mr Parker, are you an engineer?
ジョン: はい、そうです。{木下|きのした}さんは…
= Yes, that's right. And you, Ms Kinoshita…
きのした: わたしは ぶちょうの アシスタントです。
= I'm the department head's assistant.
```

Notice that きのした introduces herself with her company first (みどり ぎんこうの {木下|きのした}, "Kinoshita
of Midori Bank") and her family name only. ジョン gives his full name in the Western order,
and きのした picks the family name, パーカーさん, because that's what she would use for a
Japanese colleague. ぎんこう is a bank; アシスタント, an assistant.

## Japanese names in English

How should a Japanese name be written in the Latin alphabet: Yuki Yamamoto or Yamamoto Yuki?
For a long time the custom was to switch to English order when writing in English. In 2019
the Japanese government decided that its own official documents in English would keep the
Japanese order, family name first, from 2020 on, often with the family name in capitals to
make it clear: YAMAMOTO Yuki. Many companies, newspapers and individuals still use given name
first in English, so you'll see both. If you're unsure, ask the person which they prefer, or
write the family name in capitals.

Passports avoid the question altogether: they have separate fields for the surname and the
given name.

## はんこ: the personal seal

In Japan a small stamp often does the job of a signature. A はんこ (the formal word is いんかん)
is a little cylinder, usually of wood, plastic or stone, with a name, normally the family name,
carved on one end. You press it on an ink pad, most often red, and stamp it on a document.

There are different kinds for different jobs:

| Kind | What it's for |
|---|---|
| じついん | a seal registered at the city office, used for the biggest contracts: buying a house or a car |
| ぎんこういん | a seal registered with your bank, traditionally needed for opening an account or withdrawing money at the counter (many banks now accept a signature instead) |
| みとめいん | an everyday seal: receiving a parcel, approving an office document, school forms |

Cheap みとめいん for common family names are sold ready-made in shops, in racks sorted by name.
A registered seal is usually made to order, because it must be unique.

In the office, a document may travel from desk to desk collecting little red circles as each
person approves it. Since 2020, the government and many companies have dropped seal
requirements for most forms, and electronic signatures are spreading, but you'll still be
asked for a はんこ, or a signature (サイン) instead, for many everyday things. Foreign residents
can usually sign. Some have a seal made with their name in katakana, which many city offices accept
for registration; it also makes a popular souvenir.

At the door, a delivery driver may say:

ここに はんこか サインを おねがいします。 — A seal or a signature here, please.

か between two nouns means "or".

## Common mistakes

- Putting さん, さま or {先生|せんせい} on yourself, or on your own family members when talking
  to outsiders.
- Doubling titles: ~~{先生|せんせい}さん~~.
- Using a colleague's given name because that's what you'd do at home. Wait until they invite
  you to.
- Using ちゃん or くん for an adult you've just met.
- Calling someone あなた to their face when you know their name.

## Key points

- Family name (みょうじ) first, given name second: {山本|やまもと} ゆき. Adults mostly use family
  names.
- さん for nearly everyone, さま for customers and formal writing, くん for boys and juniors,
  ちゃん for children and close friends, {先生|せんせい} for teachers and doctors; no suffix only
  in close relationships.
- Roles and titles (せんぱい, {社長|しゃちょう}, お{母|かあ}さん) often replace names; あなた is avoided.
- Since 2020 Japanese government documents in English put the family name first: YAMAMOTO
  Yuki.
- A はんこ (いんかん) is a name seal used like a signature; みとめいん for everyday use,
  じついん for registered, important contracts.
