lessons.title: Numbers in daily life
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 3 taught you how to say numbers. This lesson is about how Japanese people live with
them: why 4 and 9 are avoided, how people count on their fingers, how phone numbers, floors
and room numbers work, how to read a price tag that shows two prices, the number puns people
use to remember things, and the five-stroke character people draw to keep a tally.

## Unlucky 4 and 9

Two of the old number readings sound like unpleasant words:

- し (4) sounds the same as し, "death".
- く (9) sounds the same as く, "suffering".

Because of this, many people avoid し and く in situations where luck matters, and this is one
common explanation for why よん and きゅう became the usual readings. You'll notice the
superstition in a few places:

- Some hospitals and hotels have no room 4, or no fourth floor, or skip rooms ending in 4 and
  9. Some car parks skip space 4.
- Gifts are rarely given in sets of four: a set of four plates or cups is avoided as a wedding
  present.

It isn't something people take very seriously in daily life (prices end in 4 and 9 all the
time), but it's polite to keep it in mind when giving presents.

## Lucky numbers

On the other side, 8 is a lucky number. The kanji {八|はち} widens towards the bottom, and people
see in its shape a road that opens out into a prosperous future. 7 is also considered lucky,
partly through the seven gods of good fortune of Japanese folk religion and partly through the
Western "lucky seven". Odd numbers in general are thought of as good for celebrations: money
gifts at weddings usually come in odd numbers of 10,000-yen notes (three is common), because an
odd number can't be divided in two.

## Counting on your fingers

Japanese people usually count on their fingers in a different way from many English speakers.
Start with an open hand, palm towards you. For 1, fold the thumb in. For 2, fold the index
finger; 3, the middle finger; 4, the ring finger; and 5, the little finger, making a fist. To
go on to 6, many people open the fingers again, starting with the little finger, until the
hand is open at 10.

When showing a number to someone else, though, people hold up fingers much as English
speakers do: one index finger for 1, the index and middle fingers for 2. A thumb and forefinger
making a circle can mean "OK", and in some contexts "money".

## Phone numbers

Japanese phone numbers start with 0. Mobile numbers begin with 090, 080 or 070 and have 11
digits; landlines start with an area code, 03 for Tokyo and 06 for Osaka. As you learned in
Lesson 3, they're read digit by digit, with の for each hyphen and に and ご stretched to two
beats.

Two short numbers every resident knows:

| Number | Reading | For |
|---|---|---|
| 110 | ひゃくとおばん | police |
| 119 | ひゃくじゅうきゅうばん | fire and ambulance |

Notice ひゃくとおばん: the 10 in 110 is read とお, the native word for ten you learned in Lesson
4, and ばん is "number". These two are read as whole numbers, not digit by digit.

## Floors and rooms

Floors are counted with かい (floor):

| Floor | Reading |
|---|---|
| 1かい | いっかい |
| 2かい | にかい |
| 3かい | さんがい (also さんかい) |
| 6かい | ろっかい |
| 8かい | はっかい (also はちかい) |
| 10かい | じゅっかい |
| {何|なん}かい | なんがい (also なんかい) |

As in American English, the ground floor is 1かい and the floor above it 2かい (British
English would call those the ground and first floors). Basement floors are ちか (underground) +
number: ちか1かい is B1.
Department store food halls are usually down there.

Room and flat numbers combine the floor and the room: room 305 is on the third floor. People
read room numbers either as one whole number, さんびゃくご, or digit by digit, さん まる ご
(with まる for 0) or さん ゼロ ご. All are understood. A Japanese address for a flat ends with
the room number: …マンション 305.

## Big numbers on price tags

Large prices are grouped in ten-thousands, as you saw in Lesson 3. Beyond 99,999:

| Amount | Japanese | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| 100,000 | {十万|じゅうまん} | じゅうまん |
| 1,000,000 | {百万|ひゃくまん} | ひゃくまん |
| 10,000,000 | {千万|せんまん} | せんまん, いっせんまん |

The trick is to move the comma in your head: 1,000,000 is 100|0000, "one hundred
ten-thousands". Car and house adverts often write prices like 250{万円|まんえん} (2.5 million yen)
for exactly this reason. Note いっせんまん: in front of まん, せん often gets いっ, though plain せんまん is common too.

Coins come in 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 and 500 yen; banknotes in 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 yen (a
2,000-yen note exists but is rare). The 5-yen and 50-yen coins have a hole in the middle. A
new series of banknotes came out in 2024, so you'll see two designs of each note.

## Prices with tax: ぜいこみ and ぜいぬき

Japan has a consumption tax of 10% on most goods and services, and 8% on food and drink
(except alcohol) bought to take away (the reduced rate also applies to newspapers delivered by subscription).
Since 2021, shops have had to show the total price including tax. Many still show the price
before tax too, often in bigger figures, which can confuse visitors:

> ぜいこみ 1,100{円|えん}（ぜいぬき 1,000{円|えん}）

ぜいこみ is "tax included", ぜいぬき "tax excluded". The number you pay is the ぜいこみ one.
Sometimes it's written with the tax as a separate word: "1,000{円|えん}＋ぜい" means 1,000 yen
plus tax.

Eating in at a restaurant is charged 10%, and taking the same food away 8%, so a fast-food
counter may ask whether you're eating in (てんない, "in the shop") or taking it away
(おもちかえり).

## Number puns: ごろあわせ

Because every digit has several readings (いち or ひと, さん or み, よん or よ or し, and also
English-style ones like ワン and ゼロ), Japanese people make words out of numbers. This kind of
pun is called ごろあわせ, and it turns up in phone numbers for businesses, in passwords people
remember, and in special days:

| Number | Read as | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 4649 | よ ろ し く | よろしく (please treat me well) |
| 39 | さん きゅう | サンキュー (thank you, from English) |
| 11{月|がつ}22{日|にち} | いい ふうふ | "good married couple" day, November 22 |
| 2{月|がつ}22{日|にち} | にゃん にゃん にゃん | cat day, February 22 (にゃん is a cat's miaow) |

So a shop's phone number may end in -4649, and November 22 is a popular day for weddings.
ろ for 6 comes from ろく, shortened, く for 9 is the old reading, and に for 2 turns into the
miaow にゃん. Puns like these are why
learning all the readings is worth it.

## Keeping a tally: {正|せい}

When Japanese people count votes on a board, keep score in a game or count people passing,
they don't draw four lines and a slash. They write the character {正|せい} ("correct"), one stroke
at a time. It has exactly five strokes, so a finished {正|せい} means 5:

| Count | What you've drawn so far |
|---|---|
| 1 | the top horizontal line |
| 2 | + a vertical line down from the middle of it |
| 3 | + a short horizontal line to the right of that vertical, halfway down |
| 4 | + a short vertical line on the lower left |
| 5 | + the long horizontal line along the bottom: {正|せい} is complete |

Then start a new {正|せい}. Three complete {正|せい} and two strokes is 17. This is also the normal
stroke order for writing the character, so tally-keeping doubles as handwriting practice. The
kanji itself isn't one you need for N5; it's here because you'll see it on whiteboards
everywhere.

## Common mistakes

- Giving four of something as a present, or choosing room 4 or 9 for a guest without thinking.
- Reading 3かい as さんかい only: さんがい is the more common reading.
- Paying attention to the big ぜいぬき number on a price tag. Look for ぜいこみ.
- Reading 110 for the police digit by digit. It's ひゃくとおばん.
- Calling the ground floor "the first floor up": in Japan the ground floor is 1かい.

## Key points

- し (4) and く (9) sound like "death" and "suffering", so よん and きゅう are preferred, and 4
  and 9 are avoided for gifts and sometimes for room numbers. 8 and 7 are lucky.
- People count on their fingers by folding them in from the thumb.
- Mobile numbers start 090/080/070; police is 110 (ひゃくとおばん), fire and ambulance 119.
- Floors with かい: いっかい, さんがい; the ground floor is 1かい; ちか1かい is B1.
- Big numbers group in ten-thousands: 100,000 = じゅうまん, 1,000,000 = ひゃくまん.
- ぜいこみ = tax included (what you pay), ぜいぬき = before tax; the tax is 10%, or 8% on take-away
  food.
- ごろあわせ: number puns such as 4649 = よろしく.
- {正|せい} is the tally sign: five strokes for five.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling time
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 gave you です, the question word なに/なん and numbers up to 99,999. This module
is about daily life: what time it is, what you do every day, where you go, which day it is
and how to invite someone. All of it starts with the clock.

By the end of this lesson you can ask and tell the time, say a.m. and p.m., give opening
hours with "from … to …" and say "about", "just after" and "to the hour". You'll also meet
seven new kanji, starting with the one you'll see on every clock and timetable: 時.

Numbers come first in a time, then a word that says what is being counted. Japanese calls
these counting words counters, and you already know a few (〜えん, 〜さい, 〜つ). Telling time
uses two more: 〜{時|じ} for the hour and 〜{分|ふん} for minutes. Like many counters, they
change the sound of some numbers, and those changes are what this lesson drills.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words in this lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 時 | time, hour | ジ | とき | 10 | {何時|なんじ}, {4時|よじ}, {時々|ときどき} (Lesson 7) |
| 分 | minute; part; understand | フン (プン), ブン | わ(かる) | 4 | {10分|じゅっぷん}, {何分|なんぷん} |
| 半 | half | ハン | なか(ば) | 5 | {半|はん}, {3時半|さんじはん} |
| 午 | noon | ゴ | — | 4 | {午前|ごぜん}, {午後|ごご} |
| 今 | now | コン | いま | 4 | {今|いま}, {今日|きょう} |
| 前 | before, front | ゼン | まえ | 9 | {午前|ごぜん}, {5分前|ごふんまえ} |
| 後 | after, behind | ゴ, コウ | あと, うし(ろ) | 9 | {午後|ごご}, {後|うし}ろ (behind) |

Memory notes (my own, not the real history of the shapes):

- 時: the sun 日 on the left, and on the right a temple's bell-tower shape that rang the
  hours. Sun plus bell: what time is it?
- 分: a knife (the bottom part) cutting something in two (the top 八). Cutting an hour into
  pieces gives minutes.
- 半: a vertical line slicing straight through the middle. Half.
- 午: a pole standing straight up at noon, when its shadow is shortest. You'll almost always
  see it in {午前|ごぜん} (before noon) and {午後|ごご} (after noon).
- 今: a roof over a single moment. Now.
- 前 and 後 come as a pair: before and after, in front and behind. Lesson 5 used まえ and
  うしろ for places; here the same idea works for time.

{今日|きょう} (today) is a special reading: the kanji mean "now" + "day", but the word is read
きょう as a whole, not こんにち. Words like this are learned whole.

## Hours: 〜{時|じ}

Put the number before {時|じ}:

| Time | Reading | Time | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| {1時|いちじ} | いちじ | {7時|しちじ} | しちじ (irregular) |
| {2時|にじ} | にじ | {8時|はちじ} | はちじ |
| {3時|さんじ} | さんじ | {9時|くじ} | くじ (irregular) |
| {4時|よじ} | よじ (irregular) | {10時|じゅうじ} | じゅうじ |
| {5時|ごじ} | ごじ | {11時|じゅういちじ} | じゅういちじ |
| {6時|ろくじ} | ろくじ | {12時|じゅうにじ} | じゅうにじ |

Three hours are irregular, and they are the ones that catch everyone:

- 4 o'clock is よじ. Not よんじ, and never しじ. (よん is the usual "four", and よ is its short
  form; し is avoided because it sounds like the word for death.)
- 7 o'clock is しちじ. You'll sometimes hear ななじ, especially when someone wants to avoid
  confusion with いちじ (1 o'clock) on a noisy phone line. Both are understood; しちじ is
  the standard one.
- 9 o'clock is くじ, not きゅうじ.

{何時|なんじ} asks "what time?": {何|なん} + {時|じ}.

{今|いま} {何時|なんじ}ですか。 — What time is it now?

{2時|にじ}です。 — It's two o'clock.

Notice how little you need. "It" and "now" are not required: {何時|なんじ}ですか。 alone is a
fine question when the meaning is clear, and the answer is just the time + です.

## Minutes: 〜{分|ふん} (ふん or ぷん)

{分|ふん} is "minute". After some numbers it becomes ぷん, and the number itself can get a small
っ. The pattern follows the sound changes you saw with ひゃく → さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく in
Lesson 3:

| Minutes | Reading | Minutes | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| {1分|いっぷん} | いっぷん | {6分|ろっぷん} | ろっぷん |
| {2分|にふん} | にふん | {7分|ななふん} | ななふん |
| {3分|さんぷん} | さんぷん | {8分|はっぷん} | はっぷん (also はちふん) |
| {4分|よんぷん} | よんぷん | {9分|きゅうふん} | きゅうふん |
| {5分|ごふん} | ごふん | {10分|じゅっぷん} | じゅっぷん (also じっぷん) |

The rule of thumb: numbers ending in 1, 6, 8 and 10 shrink and add っ (いっ, ろっ, はっ,
じゅっ) and then ぷん follows; 3 and 4 keep their shape and take ぷん; 2, 5, 7 and 9 take
plain ふん. Larger numbers follow their last part:

| Minutes | Reading |
|---|---|
| {15分|じゅうごふん} | じゅうごふん |
| {20分|にじゅっぷん} | にじゅっぷん (also にじっぷん) |
| {30分|さんじゅっぷん} | さんじゅっぷん |
| {45分|よんじゅうごふん} | よんじゅうごふん |
| {50分|ごじゅっぷん} | ごじゅっぷん |

Note that 4 minutes is よんぷん, with よん, while 4 o'clock is よじ. And 7 minutes is normally
ななふん, while 7 o'clock is しちじ. Each counter keeps its own habits, so learn whole chunks:
よじ, よんぷん.

Hours and minutes go together without anything in between, biggest unit first:

{9時10分|くじじゅっぷん}です。 — It's 9:10.

{4時45分|よじよんじゅうごふん}です。 — It's 4:45.

{何分|なんぷん} asks "how many minutes" or "what minute": {何時何分|なんじなんぷん}ですか。 — What
time exactly (what hour, what minute)?

## Half past: {半|はん}

{半|はん} means "half". After an hour it means half past:

{3時半|さんじはん}です。 — It's half past three (3:30).

{3時30分|さんじさんじゅっぷん} is also correct; {半|はん} is shorter and more common in speech.

## A.m. and p.m.: {午前|ごぜん}, {午後|ごご}

{午前|ごぜん} (a.m., before noon) and {午後|ごご} (p.m., after noon) go *before* the time, not
after it as in English:

{午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}です。 — It's 8 a.m.

{午後|ごご} {7時半|しちじはん}です。 — It's 7:30 p.m.

Most of the time people leave them out, because the situation tells you. Timetables, opening
hours and tickets often use the 24-hour clock instead: {13時|じゅうさんじ} is 1 p.m., {18時|じゅうはちじ}
is 6 p.m., {20時|にじゅうじ} is 8 p.m. You'll mostly read those, so it's enough to recognize them.

For a looser time of day, use these words:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| あさ | morning |
| ひる | noon, the middle of the day |
| ばん | evening |
| よる | night |

ばん and よる overlap: ばん is the evening, the time of dinner; よる is the dark part of the
night. あさ {7時|しちじ} is "7 in the morning", よる {11時|じゅういちじ} "11 at night".

## Before, after, about, exactly

Four small words make times more natural.

### 〜{前|まえ}: to the hour

{9時|くじ} {5分前|ごふんまえ}です。 — It's five to nine (8:55).
Literally "five minutes before nine".

### 〜すぎ: just after

{10時|じゅうじ}すぎです。 — It's just after ten. With minutes it's also
possible ({10時5分|じゅうじごふん}すぎ), but alone it means "a little after".

### 〜ごろ: about

{3時|さんじ}ごろです。 — It's about three. ごろ is only for points in time,
never for amounts.

### ちょうど: exactly

ちょうど {12時|じゅうにじ}です。 — It's exactly twelve. ちょうど usually goes before
the time; {12時|じゅうにじ}ちょうど, after it, is also common.

## From … until: から and まで

から means "from" and まで means "until, to". They go after the time, like every particle:

{店|みせ}は {10時|じゅうじ}から {8時|はちじ}までです。 — The shop is open from ten to eight.

ひるやすみは {12時|じゅうにじ}から {1時|いちじ}までです。 — Lunch break is from twelve to one.
(ひるやすみ = lunch break)

Japanese needs no verb here: "the shop is ten-from eight-until" is a complete sentence with
です. Ask with {何時|なんじ}:

{何時|なんじ}からですか。 — From what time (does it start)?

{何時|なんじ}までですか。 — Until what time (is it open)?

You can use one of them alone: {午後|ごご} {5時|ごじ}までです。 — It's until 5 p.m. And they work
for places too (Lesson 8): とうきょうから — from Tokyo.

## Pronunciation

- Make the small っ a real one-beat pause: ろっぷん is ro-p-pun, four beats (ろ っ ぷ ん).
  ろくふん is a mistake.
- くじ (9 o'clock) has two short beats; don't stretch it into くうじ.
- じゅうじ (10 o'clock) has a long う; じゅじ is not a word.
- よじ (4:00) and よんじゅう (40) both use よ/よん. Say them slowly a few times: よじ,
  よんぷん, よんじゅっぷん.

```speak
{今|いま} {何時|なんじ}ですか。
= What time is it now?
{4時|よじ}です。
= It's four o'clock.
{9時半|くじはん}です。
= It's half past nine.
{午後|ごご} {7時10分|しちじじゅっぷん}です。
= It's 7:10 p.m.
{6分|ろっぷん}です。
= Six minutes.
{10時|じゅうじ} {5分前|ごふんまえ}です。
= It's five to ten.
```

## Dialogue: what time is it?

```dialogue
# At a bus stop
エマ: すみません。{今|いま} {何時|なんじ}ですか。
= Excuse me. What time is it now?
たなか: えっと… {4時|よじ}{20分|にじゅっぷん}です。
= Um… it's 4:20.
エマ: ありがとうございます。あの、ゆうびんきょくは {何時|なんじ}までですか。
= Thank you. Um, until what time is the post office open?
たなか: {5時|ごじ}までですよ。
= Until five.
エマ: {5時|ごじ}ですか。
= Five?
たなか: ええ。でも、ゆうびんきょくの ATMは {7時|しちじ}ごろまでです。
= Yes. But the post office ATM is until about seven.
エマ: そうですか。どうも。
= I see. Thanks.
```

ゆうびんきょく is the post office (Lesson 8). よ at the end of たなか's answer adds "I'm telling
you", and ええ is a softer はい. Notice that エマ asks a yes/no question by just repeating
the information with か: {5時|ごじ}ですか。 — "Five?"

## Reading: opening hours

> みどりカフェ
>
> {午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}から {午後|ごご} {9時|くじ}まで
>
> ランチ：{11時半|じゅういちじはん}から {2時|にじ}まで
>
> {日|にち}・{月|げつ}は {6時|ろくじ}まで

Midori Café, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Lunch from 11:30 to 2. Sundays and Mondays until 6. (Days of
the week are Lesson 9: {日|にち} is short for Sunday, {月|げつ} for Monday.)

## Common mistakes

- よんじ, しじ for 4 o'clock: it's よじ. きゅうじ for 9 o'clock: it's くじ.
- ろくふん, いちふん, じゅうふん: the sound changes are not optional here. Say ろっぷん,
  いっぷん, じゅっぷん.
- Putting {午後|ごご} after the time, English-style ({3時|さんじ} {午後|ごご}). It comes first:
  {午後|ごご} {3時|さんじ}.
- ごろ for amounts: ごろ is only "about (a point in time)". "About ten minutes" uses another
  word (ぐらい), which you'll meet later.
- Forgetting that から and まで follow the word: から {10時|じゅうじ} is English order.

## Key points

- Hours: number + {時|じ}. Irregular: {4時|よじ}, {7時|しちじ}, {9時|くじ}.
- Minutes: number + {分|ふん}, which becomes ぷん after 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 (いっぷん, さんぷん,
  よんぷん, ろっぷん, はっぷん, じゅっぷん).
- {半|はん} is half past; {午前|ごぜん}/{午後|ごご} go before the time.
- 〜{前|まえ} (to the hour), 〜すぎ (just after), 〜ごろ (about), ちょうど (exactly).
- から (from) and まで (until) follow the time: {10時|じゅうじ}から {8時|はちじ}まで.
- New kanji: 時 分 半 午 今 前 後.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Verbs: ます, ません, ました
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far your sentences have ended in です ("is") or あります/います ("there is"). This lesson
gives you the rest: real actions. You'll say what you do every day, what you did yesterday
and what you didn't do, with the four polite endings ます, ません, ました and ませんでした.
You'll also learn three particles that go with actions: を for the thing you act on, に for
the time and で for the place where it happens.

You met a few verbs in the kana course, written in kana: たべる (eat), のむ (drink), よむ
(read), かく (write), いく (go) and かえる (go home). From now on most of them are written
with kanji: {食|た}べる, {飲|の}む, {行|い}く. This lesson's five kanji are all verbs.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 食 | eat, food | ショク | た(べる) | 9 | {食|た}べる |
| 飲 | drink | イン | の(む) | 12 | {飲|の}む |
| 見 | see, look | ケン | み(る) | 7 | {見|み}る |
| 行 | go | コウ, ギョウ | い(く) | 6 | {行|い}く (Lesson 8) |
| 来 | come | ライ | く(る), き(ます) | 7 | {来|く}る (Lesson 8), {来週|らいしゅう} (Lesson 9) |

The words for "food" and "a drink" are built from these verbs plus もの (thing): たべもの and
のみもの. Their last kanji is not one of this course's, so this course writes them in kana;
in Japan you'll usually see them written with two kanji each.

The hiragana after a kanji in a verb is called okurigana: {食|た}べる is the kanji 食 (た) plus
べる. The kanji stays the same while the hiragana changes: {食|た}べます, {食|た}べました.

Memory notes:

- 食: a lid (the roof at the top) over a bowl of good food. Eat.
- 飲: a squeezed version of 食 on the left, and on the right a person with a wide-open mouth.
  Food or drink going into an open mouth: drink.
- 見: an eye 目 on legs. An eye walking around: see, look.
- 行: a crossroads, split in two halves. Which way to go?
- 来: it looks like a tree (木) with two little marks and an extra branch: someone coming
  toward you through the trees. Its readings change a lot: {来|く}る, but {来|き}ます.

## What a verb is, and the ます form

A **[[verb]]** is a word for an action or a state: eat, go, sleep, be. In Japanese the verb
comes at the end of the sentence, after everything else.

Dictionaries and your word list give each verb in its basic form, the one ending in an
う-row kana (〜う, 〜く, 〜む, 〜る…): {食|た}べる, {飲|の}む, {見|み}る. This is called the
dictionary form. In polite conversation you change it to the **[[ます form]]**, which has four
endings:

| | Meaning | {食|た}べる (eat) | {飲|の}む (drink) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ます | do, will do | {食|た}べます | {飲|の}みます |
| ません | don't, won't | {食|た}べません | {飲|の}みません |
| ました | did | {食|た}べました | {飲|の}みました |
| ませんでした | didn't | {食|た}べませんでした | {飲|の}みませんでした |

Two things English speakers find surprising:

- Japanese has no separate future tense. ます covers "I do (habitually)" and "I will do",
  so it's called the **[[non-past]]**. {毎日|まいにち} コーヒーを {飲|の}みます。 is "I drink coffee
  every day"; あした {飲|の}みます。 is "I'll drink it tomorrow." The time word tells you which.
- The person doesn't change the verb. {飲|の}みます is "I drink", "you drink", "she drinks"
  and "they drink". When nobody is named, it's usually "I" in a statement and "you" in a
  question.

The ます form is polite, the normal way to speak to people you don't know well, to teachers
and at work. Friends and family use shorter forms, which you'll learn in Module 5. Polite is
never wrong with strangers, so learn it first.

### Making the ます form

Take away ます and what's left is the **[[ます stem]]**: {食|た}べ, {飲|の}み. Here's how to get
from the dictionary form to the stem. Verbs fall into three groups.

### Group 2 (る verbs)

The dictionary form ends in an い-row or え-row sound + る (〜いる, 〜きる, 〜べる, 〜ねる…).
Drop the る:

| Dictionary form | ます stem | ます form |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる (eat) | {食|た}べ | {食|た}べます |
| {見|み}る (see, watch) | {見|み} | {見|み}ます |
| おきる (get up) | おき | おきます |
| ねる (go to bed) | ね | ねます |
| あびる (take a shower) | あび | あびます |

### Group 1 (う verbs)

All the others. Change the last kana from the う row to the い row
of the same column, then add ます:

| Dictionary form | Change | ます form |
|---|---|---|
| {飲|の}む (drink) | む → み | {飲|の}みます |
| {読|よ}む (read) | む → み | {読|よ}みます |
| {書|か}く (write) | く → き | {書|か}きます |
| はたらく (work) | く → き | はたらきます |
| つくる (make) | る → り | つくります |
| {行|い}く (go) | く → き | {行|い}きます |

### Group 3 (irregular)

Only two verbs, plus the many verbs built on する:

| Dictionary form | ます form |
|---|---|
| する (do) | します |
| {来|く}る (come) | {来|き}ます |
| べんきょうする (study) | べんきょうします |

So a **[[group 1 verb]]** changes its last kana, a **[[group 2 verb]]** drops る, and a
**[[group 3 verb]]** has to be learned. べんきょうする is one of many **[[する verbs]]**: a noun (べんきょう,
study) + する. You can also say べんきょうを します.

The catch: a few verbs end in 〜いる or 〜える but are group 1 anyway. You already know one:
かえる (go home) looks like group 2, but it's group 1, so its ます form is かえります, not
かえます. Another is {入|はい}る (enter), which you'll meet later: {入|はい}ります. You can't see
it from the spelling, so your word list gives the group of every verb.

## を: the thing you act on

を (read "o", typed wo) marks what the action is done to: the thing eaten, drunk, watched,
made.

パンを {食|た}べます。 — I eat bread.

テレビを {見|み}ます。 — I watch TV.

しゅくだいを します。 — I do my homework.

Verbs that take an object with を are called **[[transitive verbs]]** ({食|た}べる, {飲|の}む,
{見|み}る, つくる, する). Verbs that don't are **[[intransitive verbs]]**: おきる (get up), ねる
(go to bed), はたらく (work), and verbs of motion like {行|い}く. You can't "get up
something", so おきる never takes を. You'll meet pairs of verbs that differ only in this way
later; for now, just notice whether a verb has a を in its example.

はじまる (begin) and おわる (end) are intransitive. What begins is marked with が, the subject
particle you used with あります:

しごとが {9時|くじ}に はじまります。 — Work starts at nine.

## に: at a time

に after a time says when the action happens:

{7時|しちじ}に おきます。 — I get up at seven.

{11時半|じゅういちじはん}に ねます。 — I go to bed at 11:30.

Use に after clock times, days and dates (Lesson 9). Don't use it after words that are
relative to now: {今|いま}, {今日|きょう}, あした, きのう, けさ, こんばん, {毎日|まいにち}, まいあさ.

きのう テレビを {見|み}ました。 — I watched TV yesterday. (Not きのうに.)

あした {6時|ろくじ}に おきます。 — Tomorrow I'll get up at six. (Here に goes with {6時|ろくじ},
not with あした.)

## で: where the action happens

で after a place says where something is done:

うちで ばんごはんを {食|た}べます。 — I eat dinner at home.

{会社|かいしゃ}で はたらきます。 — I work at a company. ({会社|かいしゃ} = company, Lesson 10)

Compare に from Lesson 5: に marks where something *is* (うちに います, I'm at home); で marks
where something *happens* (うちで {食|た}べます, I eat at home). If there's an action verb, use
で.

## Word order

A typical sentence runs: time, place, object, verb.

| Time | Place | Object | Verb |
|---|---|---|---|
| {毎日|まいにち} | {学校|がっこう}で | {日本語|にほんご}を | べんきょうします。 |
| きのう | うちで | えいがを | {見|み}ました。 |
| あした {7時|しちじ}に | — | — | おきます。 |

In English: "Every day I study Japanese at school." "Yesterday I watched a movie at
home." (えいが = movie) The order before the verb can move, because the particles show who
does what, but the verb stays last.

## Questions and answers

Ask with か; answer with the same verb:

コーヒーを {飲|の}みますか。 — Do you drink coffee?

はい、{飲|の}みます。 — Yes, I do.

いいえ、{飲|の}みません。 — No, I don't.

English answers with "do"; Japanese repeats the verb. To ask what, use {何|なに}を:

{何|なに}を {食|た}べましたか。 — What did you eat?

## なにも + negative: nothing

{何|なに}も with a negative verb means "nothing, not anything". It replaces を:

{何|なに}も {食|た}べませんでした。 — I didn't eat anything.

{何|なに}も しません。 — I don't do anything. / I won't do anything.

Japanese uses a double negative here, and it's correct: {何|なに}も must go with ません or
ませんでした, never with ます. 

## How often

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| いつも | always, usually |
| よく | often |
| {時々|ときどき} | sometimes |

These go before the verb or the object: よく えいがを {見|み}ます。 — I often watch movies.
{時々|ときどき} {新聞|しんぶん}を {読|よ}みます。 — I sometimes read the newspaper. 々 is a
repeat mark: {時々|ときどき} is {時|とき} twice, with the second one voiced (どき).

## Reading: Ken's day

> けんさんは {大学|だいがく}の {学生|がくせい}です。{毎日|まいにち} {7時|しちじ}に おきます。
> シャワーを あびます。それから、あさごはんを {食|た}べます。
>
> {9時|くじ}から {4時|よじ}まで {大学|だいがく}で べんきょうします。ひるごはんは {大学|だいがく}で
> {食|た}べます。
>
> よる、うちで しゅくだいを します。{時々|ときどき} テレビを {見|み}ます。{12時|じゅうにじ}ごろ ねます。
>
> でも、きのうは {日曜日|にちようび}でした。けんさんは {10時|じゅうじ}に おきました。
> {何|なに}も しませんでした。

Ken is a university student. Every day he gets up at seven. He takes a shower, then eats
breakfast. From nine to four he studies at the university. He eats lunch at the university.
At night he does his homework at home. Sometimes he watches TV. He goes to bed around twelve.
But yesterday was Sunday. Ken got up at ten. He didn't do anything.

({大学|だいがく} = university; でした is the past of です, "was".)

Notice ひるごはんは in the second paragraph: は has replaced を to make lunch the topic ("as
for lunch, he eats it at the university"). And きのうは puts weight on "yesterday", in
contrast to every other day.

## Dialogue: what did you do?

```dialogue
# Monday morning
さとう: リーさん、おはようございます。きのうは {何|なに}を しましたか。
= Good morning, Ms Li. What did you do yesterday?
リー: うちで えいがを {見|み}ました。さとうさんは？
= I watched a movie at home. And you?
さとう: わたしは {何|なに}も しませんでした。{午後|ごご} {3時|さんじ}まで ねました。
= I didn't do anything. I slept until 3 p.m.
リー: {3時|さんじ}まで！ばんごはんは つくりましたか。
= Until three! Did you make dinner?
さとう: いいえ、つくりませんでした。コンビニで パンを {買|か}いました。
= No, I didn't. I bought some bread at a convenience store.
リー: そうですか。わたしは まいばん つくりますよ。
= I see. I cook every evening.
```

{買|か}いました is the past of {買|か}う (buy), a verb you'll learn properly in Lesson 20.
まいばん is "every evening".

## Pronunciation

- In ます and です the final う is usually whispered: "mas", "des". {食|た}べます sounds
  like "tabemas". In ました and ませんでした you hear every vowel except in the し, which is
  often whispered too: "mash'ta".
- The ん in ません is a full beat: ma-se-n, three beats. ませんでした has six.
- Keep the stress flat. Japanese pitch rises and falls a little, but there's no strong
  English-style stress on ま.

```speak
{毎日|まいにち} {7時|しちじ}に おきます。
= I get up at seven every day.
コーヒーを {飲|の}みません。
= I don't drink coffee.
きのう えいがを {見|み}ました。
= I watched a movie yesterday.
{何|なに}も {食|た}べませんでした。
= I didn't eat anything.
うちで べんきょうします。
= I study at home.
```

## Common mistakes

- に with relative time words: きのうに, {毎日|まいにち}に. Leave it out.
- に instead of で for actions: うちに {食|た}べます is wrong; it's うちで.
- {何|なに}も with a positive verb: {何|なに}も {食|た}べます means nothing. Use ません/ませんでした.
- Treating かえる as group 2: かえます is wrong; it's かえります.
- {来|く}ます: the polite form of {来|く}る is {来|き}ます, with a different reading.
- Adding わたしは to every sentence. Once it's clear who you mean, leave it out.

## Key points

- Verbs come last. The ます form is polite: ます (do/will), ません (don't/won't), ました (did),
  ませんでした (didn't).
- Group 2 drop る ({食|た}べる → {食|た}べます); group 1 change the last kana to the い row
  ({飲|の}む → {飲|の}みます); group 3: する → します, {来|く}る → {来|き}ます.
- を marks the object; に the time (not after {今日|きょう}, きのう, {毎日|まいにち}…); で the place of
  an action.
- {何|なに}も + negative = nothing.
- New kanji: 食 飲 見 行 来.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Going places
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 7 gave you the ます form and actions at a time and in a place. This lesson is about
moving: going, coming and going home, how you get there and who you go with. You'll learn
three verbs of motion and four particles that go with them: へ or に for where you're going,
で for how, and と for who with. You'll also learn the words for getting around town and
four kanji you'll see at every station: 車, 電, 駅 and 道.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 車 | car, wheel | シャ | くるま | 7 | {車|くるま}, {電車|でんしゃ} |
| 電 | electricity | デン | — | 13 | {電車|でんしゃ}, {電話|でんわ} (telephone) |
| 駅 | station | エキ | — | 14 | {駅|えき} |
| 道 | road, way | ドウ | みち | 12 | {道|みち} |

Memory notes:

- 車: a cart seen from above, the long line in the middle is the axle and the box is the
  wheels and body.
- 電: rain 雨 on top and a bolt of lightning below. Lightning is electricity.
- 駅: the left half is "horse". Before trains, a station was where travelers changed horses.
- 道: the part on the left and bottom (⻌) means "moving along"; the part inside contains
  "head". A road is where you move along, head first.

{電車|でんしゃ} is "electric car": the word for a train in daily speech. {車|くるま} alone is a car.

## Going, coming and going home

| Dictionary form | ます form | Meaning | Group |
|---|---|---|---|
| {行|い}く | {行|い}きます | to go | 1 |
| {来|く}る | {来|き}ます | to come | 3 |
| かえる | かえります | to go home, to come home, to return | 1 |

{来|く}る is irregular, and its kanji is read differently in its forms: {来|き}ます, {来|き}ません,
{来|き}ました, {来|き}ませんでした. Always check the reading over 来.

かえる is "return to where you belong": home, your own country, your own office. You can't
かえる to a shop you're visiting for the first time.

### {行|い}く or {来|く}る?

In English, "I'll come to your party" is natural. In Japanese the choice depends on where
the *speaker* is now: {来|く}る is movement toward the speaker's place, {行|い}く is movement
away from it.

- On the phone, from home: あした パーティーに {行|い}きます。 — I'll come to the party tomorrow.
  (You're going away from where you are.)
- At the office, to a visitor: あした また {来|き}ますか。 — Will you come again tomorrow?
  (Toward where you are now.)

## Where to: へ and に

The destination takes へ (read "e") or に:

{駅|えき}へ {行|い}きます。 / {駅|えき}に {行|い}きます。 — I'm going to the station.

うちへ かえります。 / うちに かえります。 — I'm going home.

Both are correct and mean the same with these verbs. へ points a little more toward the
direction, に toward the arrival point, and に is more common in speech. Use either.

Ask with どこ: どこへ {行|い}きますか。 — Where are you going? To say "I'm not going
anywhere", use どこも + negative, just like {何|なに}も in Lesson 7: どこも {行|い}きません。

## How: で

で after a means of transport says how you travel:

{電車|でんしゃ}で {行|い}きます。 — I'll go by train.

バスで {来|き}ました。 — I came by bus.

{車|くるま}で かえります。 — I'll go home by car.

This is the same で as "at (a place)" in Lesson 7, with a second job: "by means of". The
context tells you which. "On foot" is different: say あるいて, with no で.

{駅|えき}まで あるいて {行|い}きます。 — I walk to the station. (Literally "I go to the station
walking.")

あるいて comes from あるく (to walk). You'll learn how it's made in Lesson 16; for now, use it as
a set word.

To ask how, say どうやって: どうやって {来|き}ましたか。 — How did you get here?

## Who with: と, {一人|ひとり}で

と after a person means "with":

{友|とも}だちと {行|い}きます。 — I'm going with a friend.

{先生|せんせい}と {来|き}ました。 — I came with my teacher.

To ask who with: だれと {行|い}きますか。 And to say "alone, by myself": {一人|ひとり}で.

{一人|ひとり}で {来|き}ました。 — I came alone.

## When: いつ

いつ asks "when". Like きのう and あした, it never takes に:

いつ {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きますか。 — When are you going to Japan?

らいねん {行|い}きます。 — I'm going next year. (らいねん = next year, Lesson 9)

## Putting it together

A full sentence of movement usually runs: time, who with, means, destination, verb. The order
can change, but the verb stays last.

| When | Who with | How | Where to | Verb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| あした | {友|とも}だちと | {電車|でんしゃ}で | デパートへ | {行|い}きます。 |
| きのう | {一人|ひとり}で | タクシーで | うちに | かえりました。 |

"Tomorrow I'm going to the department store with a friend by train." "Yesterday I went home
alone by taxi."

## Getting on and off

のる is "get on, ride" and おりる is "get off". The vehicle you get on takes に; the one you get
off takes を:

バスに のります。 — I get on the bus.

{電車|でんしゃ}を おります。 — I get off the train.

のる is group 1 (のります); おりる is group 2 (おります).

## Places in town

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {駅|えき} | station | こうえん | park |
| ぎんこう | bank | くうこう | airport |
| ゆうびんきょく | post office | まち | town, city |
| としょかん | library | {道|みち} | road, street, the way |
| デパート | department store | えいがかん | cinema |
| スーパー | supermarket | コンビニ | convenience store |

And ways to get there:

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {電車|でんしゃ} | train | ちかてつ | subway, underground |
| バス | bus | しんかんせん | the Shinkansen, bullet train |
| {車|くるま} | car | ひこうき | airplane |
| タクシー | taxi | じてんしゃ | bicycle |

じてんしゃ (bicycle) uses the kanji 車 at the end, but its first two kanji aren't in this
course, so it's in kana. ちかてつ is literally "underground iron (road)".

## Dialogue: weekend plans

```dialogue
# On Friday
まり: ジョンさん、あした どこかへ {行|い}きますか。
= John, are you going anywhere tomorrow?
ジョン: はい、かまくらへ {行|い}きます。
= Yes, I'm going to Kamakura.
まり: いいですね。だれと {行|い}きますか。
= Nice. Who are you going with?
ジョン: {会社|かいしゃ}の {友|とも}だちと {行|い}きます。
= With a friend from work.
まり: {車|くるま}で {行|い}きますか。
= Are you going by car?
ジョン: いいえ、{電車|でんしゃ}で {行|い}きます。{駅|えき}から おてらまで あるいて {行|い}きます。
= No, by train. From the station we'll walk to the temple.
まり: そうですか。{何時|なんじ}ごろ かえりますか。
= I see. What time will you get back?
ジョン: よる {8時|はちじ}ごろ かえります。まりさんは？
= Around eight in the evening. And you, Mari?
まり: わたしは どこも {行|い}きません。うちで ほんを {読|よ}みます。
= I'm not going anywhere. I'll read a book at home.
```

どこか is "somewhere, anywhere" in a question: どこかへ {行|い}きますか。 is "Are you going
anywhere?" おてら is a Buddhist temple; かまくら, an old city near Tokyo, has many. Notice
that まり answers with どこも + a negative verb.

## Reading: how I get to work

> わたしは {毎日|まいにち} {会社|かいしゃ}へ {行|い}きます。うちから {駅|えき}まで あるいて {行|い}きます。
> {10分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいです。{駅|えき}で {電車|でんしゃ}に のります。
>
> {会社|かいしゃ}は {大|おお}きい まちに あります。{駅|えき}で {電車|でんしゃ}を おります。それから、
> バスで {会社|かいしゃ}へ {行|い}きます。
>
> よるは {会社|かいしゃ}の {友|とも}だちと {電車|でんしゃ}で かえります。

I go to the office every day. I walk from home to the station. It's about ten minutes. At the
station I get on the train. The office is in a big city. I get off the train at the station. Then I go
to the office by bus. In the evening I go home by train with a friend from work.

(ぐらい is "about" for amounts, the partner of ごろ for times. {大|おお}きい is "big".)

## Pronunciation

- {来|き}ます is just き + ます: ki-ma-su. Don't say "kurimasu".
- {電車|でんしゃ} is three beats: で, ん, しゃ. The combination しゃ is a single beat, and ん
  is a full beat of its own.
- {駅|えき} has a short え: e-ki, two beats, not "eeki".
- ひこうき has a long お sound (こう): hi-ko-o-ki, four beats.

```speak
どこへ {行|い}きますか。
= Where are you going?
{電車|でんしゃ}で {行|い}きます。
= I'll go by train.
{友|とも}だちと {来|き}ました。
= I came with a friend.
{駅|えき}まで あるいて {行|い}きます。
= I walk to the station.
{一人|ひとり}で うちへ かえりました。
= I went home alone.
```

## Common mistakes

- あるいてで: あるいて already means "on foot"; no で.
- いつに: いつ never takes に.
- {来|く}ます: the polite form is {来|き}ます.
- Using {来|く}る for "I'll come to your place" when you're not there yet: use {行|い}く.
- バスを のります: the vehicle you get *on* takes に (バスに のります).

## Key points

- {行|い}く (go), {来|く}る (come, irregular: {来|き}ます), かえる (go home, group 1: かえります).
- Destination: へ or に. Means: で ({電車|でんしゃ}で), but あるいて alone. Company: と; alone:
  {一人|ひとり}で.
- いつ (when) takes no に. どこも / {何|なに}も + negative = nowhere / nothing.
- のる: に the vehicle; おりる: を the vehicle.
- New kanji: 車 電 駅 道.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Days, dates and weeks
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can say what time you do things. Now for which day: the days of the week, the months,
the date and the year, plus "last week", "this month", "next year" and "every week". You'll
also say when your birthday is. This lesson has the most kanji of the module, ten, but seven
of them come in one neat set: the days of the week.

Dates are where Japanese counting gets its most irregular readings, so expect to spend
time on the table of days of the month. They're used constantly, and once they're automatic
you'll hear them everywhere.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 年 | year | ネン | とし | 6 | {今年|ことし}, {来年|らいねん}, {毎年|まいとし} |
| 月 | moon, month | ゲツ, ガツ | つき | 4 | {月曜日|げつようび}, {4月|しがつ}, {毎月|まいつき} |
| 週 | week | シュウ | — | 11 | {今週|こんしゅう}, {毎週|まいしゅう} |
| 毎 | every | マイ | — | 6 | {毎日|まいにち}, {毎週|まいしゅう} |
| 曜 | day of the week | ヨウ | — | 18 | {曜日|ようび}, {何曜日|なんようび} |
| 火 | fire | カ | ひ | 4 | {火曜日|かようび} |
| 水 | water | スイ | みず | 4 | {水曜日|すいようび}, {水|みず} |
| 木 | tree, wood | モク | き | 4 | {木曜日|もくようび} |
| 金 | gold, metal, money | キン | かね | 8 | {金曜日|きんようび}, お{金|かね} (money) |
| 土 | earth, soil | ド | つち | 3 | {土曜日|どようび} |

日 (Lesson 1) has several readings in dates: ニチ in {日曜日|にちようび}, び in 〜{曜日|ようび},
か in {2日|ふつか}, and the old native word ひ (day).

Memory notes:

- The week is named after the sun, the moon and five elements: fire, water, wood, metal and
  earth. In order, Sunday to Saturday: 日 月 火 水 木 金 土. Say it as a chant: にち げつ
  か すい もく きん ど.
- 火: a person with sparks flying off both sides. Fire.
- 水: a stream in the middle with splashes either side. Water.
- 木: a tree, with its branches and roots.
- 金: a roof over the ground with nuggets buried in it. Gold.
- 土: a sprout coming up out of the ground. Earth.
- 曜 has 18 strokes, the most in this module. The sun 日 is on the left, as in many time
  kanji. You'll mostly read it, so it's fine if writing it takes a while.
- 週: the ⻌ part means moving along, as in 道. A week keeps moving.
- 毎: a mother figure who comes back "every" day. (The real history is different; it just
  helps.)

## Days of the week

| Day | Japanese | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Sunday | {日曜日|にちようび} | にちようび |
| Monday | {月曜日|げつようび} | げつようび |
| Tuesday | {火曜日|かようび} | かようび |
| Wednesday | {水曜日|すいようび} | すいようび |
| Thursday | {木曜日|もくようび} | もくようび |
| Friday | {金曜日|きんようび} | きんようび |
| Saturday | {土曜日|どようび} | どようび |

Each is [element] + {曜日|ようび}. In speech the び is often dropped: {月曜|げつよう}, {金曜|きんよう}.
On calendars and signs you'll see just the first kanji, often in brackets: ({月|げつ}), ({金|きん}). Ask
which day with {何曜日|なんようび}:

{今日|きょう}は {何曜日|なんようび}ですか。 — What day is it today?

{水曜日|すいようび}です。 — It's Wednesday.

Note どようび: 土 here is ド with a short vowel, not どう.

## Months

Months are simply number + {月|がつ}, with three irregular ones you know from the clock:

| Month | Reading | Month | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| {1月|いちがつ} | いちがつ | {7月|しちがつ} | しちがつ (irregular) |
| {2月|にがつ} | にがつ | {8月|はちがつ} | はちがつ |
| {3月|さんがつ} | さんがつ | {9月|くがつ} | くがつ (irregular) |
| {4月|しがつ} | しがつ (irregular) | {10月|じゅうがつ} | じゅうがつ |
| {5月|ごがつ} | ごがつ | {11月|じゅういちがつ} | じゅういちがつ |
| {6月|ろくがつ} | ろくがつ | {12月|じゅうにがつ} | じゅうにがつ |

Careful: for months, 4 is し (しがつ), but for hours it was よ (よじ). 7 and 9 behave the same
as with hours: しちがつ, くがつ. Ask with {何月|なんがつ}.

## Days of the month

Here is the hard part. The 1st to the 10th, the 14th, the 20th and the 24th use old native
Japanese numbers with 〜か. The rest are regular: number + {日|にち}.

| Date | Reading | Date | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| {1日|ついたち} | ついたち | {6日|むいか} | むいか |
| {2日|ふつか} | ふつか | {7日|なのか} | なのか |
| {3日|みっか} | みっか | {8日|ようか} | ようか |
| {4日|よっか} | よっか | {9日|ここのか} | ここのか |
| {5日|いつか} | いつか | {10日|とおか} | とおか |

| Date | Reading | Date | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| {11日|じゅういちにち} | じゅういちにち | {19日|じゅうくにち} | じゅうくにち |
| {12日|じゅうににち} | じゅうににち | {20日|はつか} | はつか |
| {14日|じゅうよっか} | じゅうよっか | {24日|にじゅうよっか} | にじゅうよっか |
| {17日|じゅうしちにち} | じゅうしちにち | {30日|さんじゅうにち} | さんじゅうにち |

Tips:

- ついたち (the 1st) is a word of its own, from an old phrase for the moon's return. It's
  completely different from the others.
- Most of them are three beats: ふ-つ-か, み-っ-か, よ-っ-か, い-つ-か, む-い-か, な-の-か,
  よ-う-か, と-お-か. Only ここのか (and ついたち) has four.
- よっか (the 4th) and ようか (the 8th) are easy to mix up. よっか has a pause (small っ); ようか
  has a long よう. Say both slowly.
- とおか (the 10th) is spelled with お, not う: とおか.
- はつか (the 20th) is irregular too; the 14th and 24th end in よっか.
- 17 and 19 use しち and く: じゅうしちにち, じゅうくにち.

These same words, {2日|ふつか}, {3日|みっか} and so on, also mean "two days", "three days" as a
length of time (except ついたち, which is only the 1st; "one day" is いちにち).

Ask with {何日|なんにち}: {今日|きょう}は {何日|なんにち}ですか。 — What's the date today?

## Years and the order of a date

Years are number + {年|ねん}: {2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}. 4 is よ: {4年|よねん}, and 9 is
きゅう: {9年|きゅうねん}.

A full date goes from the biggest unit to the smallest, the reverse of English:

{2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん} {11月|じゅういちがつ} {3日|みっか}（{火|か}） — Tuesday, 3 November 2026

The day of the week comes last, in brackets. Lesson 10h2 says more about writing dates and the
Japanese era years.

## Last, this, next, every

Japanese builds these from a few pieces: {先|せん} (previous), {今|こん} (this), {来|らい} (next),
{毎|まい} (every).

| | Week ({週|しゅう}) | Month ({月|つき}/げつ) | Year ({年|とし}/ねん) |
|---|---|---|---|
| last | {先週|せんしゅう} | {先月|せんげつ} | きょねん |
| this | {今週|こんしゅう} | {今月|こんげつ} | {今年|ことし} |
| next | {来週|らいしゅう} | {来月|らいげつ} | {来年|らいねん} |
| every | {毎週|まいしゅう} | {毎月|まいつき} | {毎年|まいとし} (also まいねん) |

Watch the exceptions in the last column. "Last year" is きょねん, a different word whose first
kanji isn't in this course. "This year" is {今年|ことし}, a special reading like {今日|きょう}.
And "every month" is まいつき, using the native reading つき, while "last/this/next month" use
げつ.

Days: きのう (yesterday), {今日|きょう} (today), あした (tomorrow), and {毎日|まいにち} (every
day). Two more: おととい (the day before yesterday) and あさって (the day after tomorrow).

All of these are relative to now, so, like いつ and きのう, they take no に:

{来週|らいしゅう} {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きます。 — I'm going to Japan next week.

But a day of the week or a date takes に: {土曜日|どようび}に {行|い}きます。 {5月|ごがつ}
{5日|いつか}に {行|い}きます。 With days of the week the に is sometimes dropped in speech;
with dates and clock times keep it.

## Birthdays

たんじょうび is "birthday". Ask with いつ or {何月何日|なんがつなんにち}:

たんじょうびは いつですか。 — When is your birthday?

{8月|はちがつ} {20日|はつか}です。 — It's the 20th of August.

おたんじょうび おめでとう ございます。 — Happy birthday.

## Dialogue: making a plan

```dialogue
# Two classmates
ゆい: アンナさん、たんじょうびは いつですか。
= Anna, when's your birthday?
アンナ: {7月|しちがつ} {4日|よっか}です。ゆいさんは？
= July 4th. And yours?
ゆい: わたしは {7月|しちがつ} {8日|ようか}です。
= Mine is July 8th.
アンナ: え、{来週|らいしゅう}ですね！{何曜日|なんようび}ですか。
= Oh, that's next week! What day is it?
ゆい: {水曜日|すいようび}です。
= It's a Wednesday.
アンナ: じゃあ、{水曜日|すいようび}に いっしょに ケーキを {食|た}べましょう。
= Then let's have cake together on Wednesday.
ゆい: ありがとう！
= Thank you!
```

ね after {来週|らいしゅう}ですね shows surprise and shared knowledge: "that's next week, isn't it!"
〜ましょう is "let's"; it's the topic of Lesson 10.

## Reading: a weekly schedule

> {月曜日|げつようび}と {水曜日|すいようび}は {日本語|にほんご}の クラスです。{7時|しちじ}から
> {9時|くじ}までです。
>
> {金曜日|きんようび}の よるは {友|とも}だちと ばんごはんを {食|た}べます。
>
> {土曜日|どようび}は アルバイトです。{午前|ごぜん} {10時|じゅうじ}から {午後|ごご} {4時|よじ}まで
> はたらきます。{日曜日|にちようび}は {何|なに}も しません。
>
> {来月|らいげつ}の {15日|じゅうごにち}に テストが あります。

Mondays and Wednesdays are Japanese class, from seven to nine. On Friday evenings I have
dinner with friends. Saturday is my part-time job: I work from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. On Sundays I
don't do anything. There's a test on the 15th of next month.

(アルバイト = part-time job. あります also says that an event takes place: テストが あります,
"there's a test". {来月|らいげつ}の {15日|じゅうごにち}: の joins "next month" to the date.)

## Pronunciation

- よっか (4th) has a pause; ようか (8th) a long vowel. Both three beats: よ-っ-か, よ-う-か.
- ここのか (9th) has four beats; don't swallow the の.
- {水曜日|すいようび}: the い in すい is short and the う in よう is long: su-i-yo-o-bi.
- はつか: three short beats, no long vowels.

```speak
{今日|きょう}は {何曜日|なんようび}ですか。
= What day is it today?
{今日|きょう}は {4月|しがつ} {1日|ついたち}です。
= Today is April 1st.
たんじょうびは {9月|くがつ} {20日|はつか}です。
= My birthday is September 20th.
{来週|らいしゅう}の {金曜日|きんようび}に {行|い}きます。
= I'm going next Friday.
{毎週|まいしゅう} {土曜日|どようび}に テニスを します。
= I play tennis every Saturday.
```

## Common mistakes

- よんがつ for April: it's しがつ. きゅうがつ for September: it's くがつ.
- いちにち for the 1st: it's ついたち. (いちにち is "one day" as a length.)
- Mixing よっか (4th) and ようか (8th).
- にじゅうにち for the 20th: it's はつか.
- English order: {3日|みっか} {11月|じゅういちがつ}. Japanese goes year, month, day.
- に after {来週|らいしゅう}, {今年|ことし}, {毎日|まいにち}: leave it out.
- こんねん for this year: it's ことし.

## Key points

- Days: {日|にち} {月|げつ} {火|か} {水|すい} {木|もく} {金|きん} {土|ど} + {曜日|ようび}; ask {何曜日|なんようび}.
- Months: number + {月|がつ}; {4月|しがつ}, {7月|しちがつ}, {9月|くがつ}; ask {何月|なんがつ}.
- Dates: ついたち, ふつか, みっか, よっか, いつか, むいか, なのか, ようか, ここのか, とおか, and
  {14日|じゅうよっか}, {20日|はつか}, {24日|にじゅうよっか}; the rest are number + にち. Ask {何日|なんにち}.
- Date order: year, month, day, (day of the week).
- {先週|せんしゅう}/{今週|こんしゅう}/{来週|らいしゅう}/{毎週|まいしゅう}; {先月|せんげつ}/{今月|こんげつ}/{来月|らいげつ}/{毎月|まいつき};
  きょねん/{今年|ことし}/{来年|らいねん}/{毎年|まいとし}. No に after these.
- New kanji: 年 月 週 毎 曜 火 水 木 金 土.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Inviting and suggesting
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say what you do, where you go and when. This lesson turns that into plans with
other people: inviting someone ("won't you come…?"), suggesting ("let's…"), offering ("shall
I…?"), accepting and, just as important, saying no politely. All three patterns are made from
the ます stem you learned in Lesson 7, so there's nothing new to conjugate. You'll also learn
two ways to say "but", words for weekends and free time, and four kanji: 休, 友, 会 and 社.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 休 | rest | キュウ | やす(む) | 6 | {休|やす}む, {休|やす}み |
| 友 | friend | ユウ | とも | 4 | {友|とも}だち |
| 会 | meet | カイ | あ(う) | 6 | {会|あ}う, {会社|かいしゃ} |
| 社 | company, shrine | シャ | やしろ | 7 | {会社|かいしゃ} |

Memory notes:

- 休: a person (the narrow shape on the left is a squeezed 人) leaning against a tree 木. Rest.
- 友: two hands reaching toward each other. Friends.
- 会: people gathering under one roof. Meet.
- 社: the narrow left part marks things to do with gods, as at a shrine; 土 on the right is the
  ground. The old meaning was a shrine to the local earth god, and from "people gathered
  together" came "company".

{友|とも}だち is normally written with one kanji and だち in kana. {会社|かいしゃ} is company:
literally "meeting + association". {休|やす}み is a day off, a holiday, a break: {今日|きょう}は {休|やす}みです。 —
I'm off today. (Or: It's closed today.)

## Inviting: 〜ませんか

Replace ます with ませんか: {行|い}きます → {行|い}きませんか. It's literally "won't you go?",
and it's the polite way to invite someone:

いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ませんか。 — Would you like to see a movie with me?

{土曜日|どようび}に テニスを しませんか。 — How about playing tennis on Saturday?

The negative form makes the invitation gentle: you leave room for a "no". In the same way,
English says "Wouldn't you like to…?" Use 〜ませんか when you're asking someone to join *you*.
いっしょに (together) often goes with it.

Don't confuse it with a real negative question. {行|い}きませんか can also mean "Aren't you
going?", but with いっしょに or in an invitation the meaning is clear.

## Suggesting: 〜ましょう

Replace ます with ましょう: "let's".

{行|い}きましょう。 — Let's go.

{駅|えき}で {会|あ}いましょう。 — Let's meet at the station.

〜ましょう is the usual way to *accept* an invitation, or to move a plan forward once
everyone agrees. As the first invitation it can sound a little pushy, because it doesn't ask;
start with 〜ませんか and answer with 〜ましょう.

## Offering and deciding together: 〜ましょうか

〜ましょうか, "shall we…? shall I…?", asks the other person to decide:

{何時|なんじ}に {会|あ}いましょうか。 — What time shall we meet?

どこで {食|た}べましょうか。 — Where shall we eat?

With a question word (what time, where, what), it plans the details together. Without one, it
can offer help: まどを あけましょうか。 — Shall I open the window? (まど = window, あける = to
open)

## Saying yes

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ええ、いいですね。 | Yes, that sounds good. |
| いいですね。{行|い}きましょう。 | Great, let's go. |
| ええ、ぜひ。 | Yes, I'd love to. (ぜひ = definitely, by all means) |

## Saying no without saying no

Japanese speakers rarely answer an invitation with a flat いいえ. Instead they start to give a
reason and let the sentence trail off:

すみません、{土曜日|どようび}は ちょっと…。 — Sorry, Saturday is a bit…

ちょっと means "a little", but here it's a polite way of saying "that doesn't work". The rest
(…"difficult", "inconvenient") is left unsaid, and the other person understands. Say it with a
slightly regretful tone and let the voice fade.

A fuller refusal adds ざんねんですが (it's a pity, but) and a reason:

ざんねんですが、{日曜日|にちようび}は アルバイトが あります。 — Unfortunately, I have work on Sunday.

And to keep the door open: また こんど。 — Another time.

## But: が and でも

が after a sentence that ends in です or ます joins it to another one: "…, but …".

{土曜日|どようび}は ひまですが、{日曜日|にちようび}は いそがしいです。 — I'm free on Saturday, but busy on Sunday.

テニスは しますが、サッカーは しません。 — I play tennis, but not football.

Note: this が comes at the *end* of a clause, after です or ます, and a comma usually follows it.
It's a different job from the が after a noun that marks the subject (いぬが います).

でも starts a new sentence: "But …".

えいがは あまり {見|み}ません。でも、テレビは よく {見|み}ます。 — I don't watch many movies.
But I often watch TV. (あまり + negative = not much; Lesson 11.)

## Free time

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| しゅうまつ | weekend | えいが | movie, film |
| {休|やす}み | day off, holiday, break | コンサート | concert |
| ひま (な) | free, not busy | パーティー | party |
| いそがしい | busy | カラオケ | karaoke |
| さんぽ | a walk, a stroll | スポーツ | sports |
| テニス | tennis | サッカー | soccer, football |
| うた | song | しゃしん | photo |

Verbs: あそぶ (to have fun, to hang out, to play), およぐ (to swim), うたう (to sing), とる (to
take: しゃしんを とる, take a photo), {休|やす}む (to rest, to take a day off), {会|あ}う (to
meet). All six are group 1: あそびます, およぎます, うたいます, とります, {休|やす}みます,
{会|あ}います.

Many activities use する: テニスを します, サッカーを します, さんぽを します (or さんぽします).

{会|あ}う takes に (or と) for the person, not を: {友|とも}だちに {会|あ}います。 — I meet a
friend. "Meeting" in Japanese is going *to* someone.

ひま is a な-adjective and いそがしい an い-adjective; Module 3 explains both kinds, and those
two words and うた join your vocabulary reviews there. For now use them before です, as here.

## Dialogue: an invitation

```dialogue
# Thursday, at work
やまだ: ケイトさん、しゅうまつは ひまですか。
= Kate, are you free this weekend?
ケイト: {土曜日|どようび}は ちょっと…。でも、{日曜日|にちようび}は ひまです。
= Saturday is a bit… But Sunday I'm free.
やまだ: じゃあ、{日曜日|にちようび}に いっしょに しんじゅくで えいがを {見|み}ませんか。
= Then would you like to see a movie in Shinjuku together on Sunday?
ケイト: いいですね。{見|み}ましょう。{何時|なんじ}に {会|あ}いましょうか。
= Sounds good. Let's. What time shall we meet?
やまだ: {1時|いちじ}は どうですか。
= How about one o'clock?
ケイト: いいですよ。どこで {会|あ}いましょうか。
= That's fine. Where shall we meet?
やまだ: しんじゅく{駅|えき}の {東口|ひがしぐち}で {会|あ}いましょう。
= Let's meet at the east exit of Shinjuku Station.
ケイト: わかりました。じゃあ、{日曜日|にちようび}に。
= OK. See you on Sunday, then.
```

〜は どうですか is "how about …?" {東口|ひがしぐち} is the east exit ({東|ひがし} east + {口|くち} mouth, opening); Lesson 10h1 has station exits.
じゃあ、{日曜日|にちようび}に is short for "then, (see you) on Sunday".

## Reading: a message

> まりさんへ
>
> {来週|らいしゅう}の {金曜日|きんようび}は {休|やす}みです。いっしょに さんぽしませんか。
> {午前|ごぜん} {10時|じゅうじ}に こうえんの {前|まえ}で {会|あ}いましょう。
> ひるごはんは こうえんの ちかくの カフェで {食|た}べましょう。
>
> ゆきより

To Mari: Next Friday is my day off. Would you like to go for a walk together? Let's meet in
front of the park at 10 a.m. Let's have lunch at the café near the park. From Yuki.

(〜へ at the top of a message is "To …", and 〜より at the end is "From …". こうえんの {前|まえ}
and こうえんの ちかく use the location words from Lesson 5.)

## Pronunciation

- 〜ませんか rises gently at the end, like a question. 〜ましょう falls: ma-SHO-o, with a long
  よう: "mashō".
- ちょっと has a small っ: cho-t-to, three beats. In a refusal, stretch the pause before the
  dots and let your voice drop.
- ざんねん: four beats, ざ-ん-ね-ん. Both ん are full beats.

```speak
いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ませんか。
= Would you like to see a movie together?
いいですね。{行|い}きましょう。
= Sounds good. Let's go.
{何時|なんじ}に {会|あ}いましょうか。
= What time shall we meet?
すみません、{土曜日|どようび}は ちょっと…。
= Sorry, Saturday's a bit…
ざんねんですが、また こんど。
= That's a pity, but maybe another time.
```

## Common mistakes

- Inviting with 〜ましょう before the other person has agreed. Start with 〜ませんか.
- Answering an invitation with いいえ. Use ちょっと… or ざんねんですが.
- {友|とも}だちを {会|あ}います. The person you meet takes に: {友|とも}だちに {会|あ}います.
- が for "but" in the middle of a single clause, English-style: が follows a full
  ます/です sentence.
- でも in the middle of a sentence. でも starts a new sentence; inside one, use が.

## Key points

- Invite: 〜ませんか (won't you…?). Suggest or accept: 〜ましょう (let's…). Plan or offer:
  〜ましょうか (shall we…? shall I…?). All three replace ます.
- Accept with いいですね / ええ、ぜひ; refuse with ちょっと… or ざんねんですが + reason.
- が joins two sentences: "…, but …"; でも starts a new one: "But …".
- {会|あ}う: the person takes に.
- New kanji: 休 友 会 社.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Getting around by train
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Trains are the backbone of daily life in Japanese cities. In Tokyo or Osaka most people get
to school and work by {電車|でんしゃ} and ちかてつ, and a visitor spends a surprising amount of
time in stations. This honors lesson takes the verbs and particles of Lessons 7 and 8 into a
real station: paying with an IC card, reading line names and signs, changing trains,
understanding a timetable and fitting in with train manners. Nothing here is new grammar;
it's practice reading the signs you'll actually see.

## Paying: tickets and IC cards

You can buy a paper ticket, きっぷ, from a machine. Above the machines is a route map with the
fare to every station: find where you're going, read the price in {円|えん}, and buy a ticket
for that amount. Children's fares are about half.

Most people don't bother. They use a rechargeable IC card, a contactless card you touch on the
reader at the gate. Each region's railways issue their own (in the Tokyo area the best known
are Suica and PASMO, in the Kansai area ICOCA), but the main cards are accepted on trains and
buses in each other's areas, and many shops take them too. You top them up at ticket
machines; the screen usually has an English button. A few things to know:

- Touch the card on the way in *and* on the way out. The fare is worked out when you leave.
- If the balance is too low, the gate closes. Use the fare adjustment machine (のりこし
  せいさんき) near the exit gates to pay the difference.
- Phones can carry IC cards too, and many people simply touch their phone.

The gate itself is the かいさつ. The station staff window by the gates is where to go when
something goes wrong with a ticket, or to ask the way: すみません、{東口|ひがしぐち}は どこですか。
(Excuse me, where is the east exit?)

## Lines and directions

Every line has a name ending in 〜せん (line) and a color. Station names on the signs are in
kanji, hiragana and the Latin alphabet, and in many cities each station also has a code: a
letter for the line and a number for the stop, so you can follow the numbers even if you
can't read the name.

Trains are labeled by where they're going, with 〜{行|ゆ}き ("bound for"): とうきょう{行|ゆ}き is
a train bound for Tokyo. 行き is read ゆき in railway use; in ordinary speech you'll also hear
いき. Both are correct.

The platform is ホーム, and platforms are numbered with 〜ばんせん: 3ばんせん (さんばんせん) is
platform (track) 3. To ask which one:

とうきょう{行|ゆ}きは {何|なん}ばんせんですか。 — Which platform is the train for Tokyo?

5ばんせんです。 — Platform 5.

## Train types

The same line can run several kinds of train. They differ in which stations they stop at:

| Name | Meaning | Stops |
|---|---|---|
| かくえきていしゃ (ふつう) | local | every station |
| かいそく | rapid | skips some stations |
| きゅうこう | express | skips more |
| とっきゅう | limited express | only major stations; on JR lines it usually needs an extra ticket |

The names and their order vary a little between railway companies, so the table is a rough guide.
かくえきていしゃ means "stops at every station"; its second kanji is our {駅|えき}, so you'll
see 駅 on the sign even when the rest is new. Before you get on a faster train, check that it
stops where you're going; station screens list the stops.

## Changing trains: のりかえ

のりかえる is "to change (trains)", a compound of のる (get on) and かえる (to change, a
different かえる from "go home"). It's group 2: のりかえます. The noun is のりかえ, "a
transfer". Signs that say のりかえ lead you to other lines.

しぶやで のりかえます。 — I change trains at Shibuya.

{駅|えき}で ちかてつに のりかえます。 — I change to the subway at the station.

Notice the particles: the station where you change takes で (the place where the action
happens, Lesson 7), and the train you change *to* takes に, like のる.

## Station signs

The kanji you know already open up most station signs.

| Sign | Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {出口|でぐち} | でぐち | exit |
| {入口|いりぐち} | いりぐち | entrance |
| {東口|ひがしぐち} | ひがしぐち | east exit |
| {西口|にしぐち} | にしぐち | west exit |
| {南口|みなみぐち} | みなみぐち | south exit |
| {北口|きたぐち} | きたぐち | north exit |

Big stations have many exits, and the right exit can save you ten minutes of walking. When
you arrange to meet someone at a station, always name the exit, as in the Lesson 10
dialogue: しんじゅく{駅|えき}の {東口|ひがしぐち}で {会|あ}いましょう。

On the platform, the station name board shows the current station in large type, with the
previous station and the next one on either side (つぎ means "next"). On the train, a screen
above the door shows the next stop, often in four languages, and an announcement gives the
next station and which side the doors will open.

## Timetables

Station timetables, じこくひょう, list departure times by hour. The hour runs down the middle
or the left side, and the minutes of each departure sit next to it.

Weekdays and weekends have different timetables: へいじつ (weekdays) and {土日|どにち}・しゅくじつ
({土|ど}, {日|にち}: Saturday, Sunday and national holidays). A small part of one might look
like this:

| Hour | へいじつ (weekdays) | {土日|どにち}・しゅくじつ |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 05 20 35 50 | 10 40 |
| 7 | 02 10 18 26 34 42 50 58 | 10 30 50 |
| 8 | 04 12 20 28 36 44 52 | 10 30 50 |

So on a weekday the trains after 7:00 leave at 7:02, 7:10, 7:18 and so on. Real timetables
also mark each departure's train type and destination with a color or a small symbol,
explained at the bottom. The first train of the day is しはつ and the last is しゅうでん.

It's {7時|しちじ}{20分|にじゅっぷん} on a {土曜日|どようび}. The next train? Look at the right-hand
column: {7時半|しちじはん}.

## Train manners

- Line up at the marks on the platform and let people get off before you get on.
- Don't talk on the phone on the train; set it to silent mode (マナーモード). Quiet
  conversation is fine; loud talk stands out.
- Priority seats (ゆうせんせき) near the doors are for older people, pregnant women, people
  with disabilities and people with small children.
- Take a large backpack off and hold it in front of you or put it on the rack.
- Eating on commuter trains is frowned on; on the Shinkansen and long-distance limited
  express trains it's normal, and station lunch boxes (えきべん) are part of the fun.
- Some lines have women-only cars at rush hour, marked in pink.
- The last train, しゅうでん, leaves around midnight in big cities. Miss it and it's a taxi
  or a long walk.

## Dialogue: asking at the station

```dialogue
# At the station window
ルカ: すみません。あさくさは どの せんですか。
= Excuse me. Which line is it for Asakusa?
えきいん: ぎんざせんです。2ばんせんですよ。
= The Ginza Line. It's platform 2.
ルカ: のりかえは ありますか。
= Do I have to change?
えきいん: いいえ、ありません。あさくさまで {20分|にじゅっぷん}ぐらいです。
= No, you don't. It's about twenty minutes to Asakusa.
ルカ: きっぷは いくらですか。
= How much is the ticket?
えきいん: 210{円|えん}です。ICカードでも いいですよ。
= It's 210 yen. An IC card is fine too.
ルカ: わかりました。ありがとうございます。
= I see. Thank you.
えきいん: いいえ。ぎんざせんは オレンジの せんです。
= Not at all. The Ginza Line is the orange line.
```

えきいん is a member of station staff. ICカードでも is で (by means of) + も (also): "with an IC card too". のりかえは ありますか, "is there a transfer?", uses
あります for an event, as テストが あります did in Lesson 9. (The fare is made up for the
dialogue.)

```speak
すみません、{出口|でぐち}は どこですか。
= Excuse me, where is the exit?
とうきょう{行|ゆ}きは {何|なん}ばんせんですか。
= Which platform is the train for Tokyo?
しぶやで のりかえます。
= I change trains at Shibuya.
この {電車|でんしゃ}は しんじゅくに とまりますか。
= Does this train stop at Shinjuku?
```

とまる (to stop) is group 1: とまります. The place where a train stops takes に.

## Key points

- きっぷ (ticket) or an IC card: touch in and out at the かいさつ (gate).
- Trains are named by line (〜せん) and destination (〜{行|ゆ}き); platforms by 〜ばんせん.
- かくえきていしゃ stops everywhere; かいそく, きゅうこう and とっきゅう skip stations.
- のりかえる: change trains; the station takes で, the new train に.
- {出口|でぐち}, {入口|いりぐち}, {東口|ひがしぐち}, {西口|にしぐち}, {南口|みなみぐち}, {北口|きたぐち}: always name the exit.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The Japanese calendar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 9 taught you to say any date. Japan uses the same calendar as most of the world, with
January to December and seven-day weeks, but it also counts years in a second way, by era,
and its year is shaped by a set of national holidays and a few big seasonal breaks. This
honors lesson shows you how to read era years on forms and documents, which holidays to
expect, what Golden Week and お{正月|しょうがつ} are, and how dates are written.

## Era years: れいわ and the others

Alongside the Western year (せいれき), Japan numbers years by era (ねんごう). A new era begins
when a new emperor comes to the throne, and years are counted from the start of the era:

| Era | Reading | Years |
|---|---|---|
| めいじ | Meiji | 1868–1912 |
| たいしょう | Taishō | 1912–1926 |
| しょうわ | Shōwa | 1926–1989 |
| へいせい | Heisei | 1989–2019 |
| れいわ | Reiwa | 2019– |

(These names are written with kanji outside this course, so they're in kana here.)

The current era, れいわ, began on 1 May 2019. That year is れいわ {元年|がんねん}, "the first
year of Reiwa": the first year of an era is called {元年|がんねん} rather than "year 1"
({元|がん} is the kanji from {元気|げんき}, in another reading). After that the years count up:
2020 was れいわ {2年|にねん}, and 2026 is れいわ {8年|はちねん}.

A quick way to convert: for Reiwa, subtract 2018 from the Western year (2026 − 2018 = 8). For
Heisei, subtract 1988 (2000 was へいせい {12年|じゅうにねん}). The year an era changes belongs to both: 2019
was へいせい {31年|さんじゅういちねん} until 30 April and れいわ {元年|がんねん} from 1 May.

Where will you meet era years? On official forms, bank and city-hall documents, driving
licenses, some receipts and coins. Japanese coins show the year they were minted in era
form: look for the kanji {年|ねん} after an era name and a number. Most everyday life (train tickets, websites,
business) uses Western years, and many forms let you circle which system you're using.
Writing your own date of birth on a Japanese form, you may be asked for it in era years;
it's fine to ask: せいれきで いいですか。 — Is the Western year OK?

## Writing dates

Dates go from big to small, and the day of the week follows in brackets:

{2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}{11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}（{火|か}）

You'll also see short forms:

| Form | Where |
|---|---|
| 2026/11/3 | forms, receipts, websites |
| 2026.11.3 | posters, shop signs |
| R8.11.3 | official forms (R = れいわ) |
| 11/3（{火|か}） | calendars, timetables, notices |

There is no day-first order as in Britain, so 3/11 is always the 11th of March, not the 3rd
of November.

Weeks on Japanese calendars usually start on Sunday, which is printed in red; Saturday is
often blue, and national holidays are red like Sundays. Many calendars also mark a traditional
six-day cycle of lucky and unlucky days; the luckiest is {大安|たいあん}, popular for weddings.

## National holidays

Japan has sixteen national holidays, しゅくじつ. When one falls on a Sunday, the next weekday
that is not already a holiday becomes a substitute day off. Several move to a Monday each year, to give a long weekend.

| Date | Holiday | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| {1月|いちがつ}{1日|ついたち} | {元日|がんじつ} | New Year's Day |
| second Monday of January | せいじんの{日|ひ} | Coming of Age Day, for people who turned adult |
| {2月|にがつ}{11日|じゅういちにち} | けんこくきねんの{日|ひ} | National Foundation Day |
| {2月|にがつ}{23日|にじゅうさんにち} | てんのうたんじょうび | the Emperor's Birthday |
| around {3月|さんがつ}{20日|はつか} | しゅんぶんの{日|ひ} | the spring equinox |
| {4月|しがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち} | しょうわの{日|ひ} | Shōwa Day |
| {5月|ごがつ}{3日|みっか} | けんぽうきねんび | Constitution Day |
| {5月|ごがつ}{4日|よっか} | みどりの{日|ひ} | Greenery Day |
| {5月|ごがつ}{5日|いつか} | {子|こ}どもの{日|ひ} | Children's Day |
| third Monday of July | うみの{日|ひ} | Marine Day (the sea) |
| {8月|はちがつ}{11日|じゅういちにち} | {山|やま}の{日|ひ} | Mountain Day |
| third Monday of September | けいろうの{日|ひ} | Respect for the Aged Day |
| around {9月|くがつ}{23日|にじゅうさんにち} | しゅうぶんの{日|ひ} | the autumn equinox |
| second Monday of October | スポーツの{日|ひ} | Sports Day |
| {11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか} | ぶんかの{日|ひ} | Culture Day |
| {11月|じゅういちがつ}{23日|にじゅうさんにち} | きんろうかんしゃの{日|ひ} | Labor Thanksgiving Day |

Notice that the holidays use 〜の{日|ひ}, "the day of …", with the native reading ひ. You'll
recognize {子|こ}どもの{日|ひ} (children's day) and {山|やま}の{日|ひ} (mountain day) from kanji
you know. The exact dates of the two equinox holidays are fixed each year by astronomers, so
they can move by a day.

## Golden Week

The holidays from {4月|しがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち} to {5月|ごがつ}{5日|いつか} come so close
together that, with a weekend or two, many people get a week or more off. This is
ゴールデンウィーク, Golden Week. Everyone travels at once, so trains, planes and hotels are
full and expensive, and popular places are crowded. If you visit Japan, it's a week to plan
around.

## The year's big breaks

Japan has two other times when the whole country seems to be on the move:

- おぼん, in mid-August, when many people go back to their family's home town to remember
  their ancestors. It isn't a national holiday, but many companies close for a few days.
- お{正月|しょうがつ}, the New Year. Most companies close from around {12月|じゅうにがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち}
  to {1月|いちがつ}{3日|みっか}. It's the most important family holiday of the year.

お{正月|しょうがつ} customs you'll hear about:

| Word | What it is |
|---|---|
| おおみそか | New Year's Eve, {12月|じゅうにがつ}{31日|さんじゅういちにち}; people eat long noodles (としこしそば) |
| はつもうで | the first visit of the year to a shrine or temple |
| ねんがじょう | New Year's postcards, delivered on {1月|いちがつ}{1日|ついたち} |
| おせち | special New Year food, prepared in advance in layered boxes |
| おとしだま | money given to children in small envelopes |

The New Year greeting is あけまして おめでとう ございます (Happy New Year), said from
{1月|いちがつ}{1日|ついたち}, not before. Before the New Year, people say よい おとしを (have a good
New Year) as a goodbye.

Schools also follow the calendar in their own way. The Japanese school and business year
starts in April: new pupils, new students and new employees all start in {4月|しがつ}, around the
time the cherry trees flower. Summer holidays, なつやすみ, run from late July to the end of
August for most schools.

## Reading: a notice

> {休|やす}みの おしらせ
>
> {12月|じゅうにがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち}（{月|げつ}）から {1月|いちがつ}{3日|みっか}（{土|ど}）まで {休|やす}みです。
>
> {1月|いちがつ}{4日|よっか}（{日|にち}）から {午前|ごぜん} {10時|じゅうじ}に あきます。
>
> {来年|らいねん}も よろしく おねがいします。

Holiday notice. We are closed from Monday 29 December to Saturday 3 January. We open at 10
a.m. from Sunday 4 January. We look forward to serving you next year too. (おしらせ =
notice, announcement; あく = to open, group 1. The dates fit the 2025–2026 New Year: 29
December 2025 was a Monday.)

## Key points

- Japan counts years by era as well as by the Western calendar: れいわ began in 2019, so 2026
  is れいわ {8年|はちねん}; the first year of an era is {元年|がんねん}.
- Dates go year, month, day, (day of the week): {2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}{11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}（{火|か}）.
- Sixteen national holidays (しゅくじつ), most called 〜の{日|ひ}; several are on Mondays.
- Golden Week: {4月|しがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち} to {5月|ごがつ}{5日|いつか}. おぼん: mid-August. お{正月|しょうがつ}: the New
  Year, the biggest family holiday.
- The school and business year starts in April.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: い-adjectives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In modules 1 and 2 you learned to say what things are (これは{本|ほん}です), where they are
(あります, います) and what people do (ます, ません, ました). This module is about describing:
big and small, new and old, cheap and expensive, quiet, pretty, famous, better and best. The
words that do this are **[[adjectives]]**, and Japanese has two kinds of them. This lesson teaches
the bigger group, the い-adjectives, in the present tense: affirmative ("it's expensive"),
negative ("it isn't expensive"), and in front of a noun ("an expensive book").

There's one more change, and you'll notice it straight away: from this lesson on, Japanese
sentences in this course are written without spaces, the way Japanese people write them.

## Reading without spaces

Until now this course put a space after each particle to help you find the words:
わたしは {学生|がくせい}です。 Real Japanese has no spaces at all. Books, signs, messages and web
pages run every word together, and readers find the word breaks without thinking about it.
From now on, sentences look like this:

| Modules 1–2 | From module 3 on |
|---|---|
| {毎日|まいにち} {電車|でんしゃ}で {会社|かいしゃ}へ {行|い}きます。 | {毎日|まいにち}{電車|でんしゃ}で{会社|かいしゃ}へ{行|い}きます。 |
| この {本|ほん}は {高|たか}いです。 | この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}いです。 |

It looks harder than it is, because the three scripts do the job that spaces did:

- **[[Kanji]]** usually start a content word: a noun, or the front of a verb or adjective
  ({電車|でんしゃ}, {行|い}きます, {高|たか}い).
- **Hiragana** after a kanji is usually an ending (きます, い) or a particle (で, へ, は, を).
- **Katakana** words stand out by their shape: アパート, コーヒー.

So read in chunks: find a kanji or katakana word, take the hiragana after it with it, and stop
at the particle. {毎日|まいにち} / {電車|でんしゃ}で / {会社|かいしゃ}へ / {行|い}きます. A
comma (、) also helps: Japanese writers put one where a reader needs a breath, often after the
topic or a time word.

Two more things make the change easy. When you type an answer, spaces never matter: the app
ignores them. And the furigana stays: every kanji still has its reading above it, and you can
turn the readings off whenever you feel ready.

## What an い-adjective is

An **[[い-adjective]]** is an adjective whose dictionary form ends in い: {高|たか}い (expensive;
tall, high), {安|やす}い (cheap), {新|あたら}しい (new), {古|ふる}い (old), {長|なが}い (long).
In the dictionary form it can end a casual sentence on its own; you'll meet that in module 5.
In polite speech you add です:

この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}いです。 — This book is expensive.
このかばんは{安|やす}いです。 — This bag is cheap. (かばん = bag)
{日本語|にほんご}はむずかしいです。 — Japanese is difficult.
この{店|みせ}のパンはおいしいです。 — The bread at this shop is delicious. (パン = bread)

Notice two things. First, there is no word for "is": the adjective itself means "is expensive",
and です only makes it polite. Second, い-adjectives change their ending (they conjugate,
like verbs), while です stays the same. That's the key to everything in this lesson.

The part before the last い is the stem: {高|たか} in {高|たか}い, むずかし in むずかしい. All
the forms are made by changing the final い.

## The negative: 〜くないです

To say an い-adjective is *not* so, drop the final い and add くないです:

| Dictionary form | Negative (polite) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}くないです | isn't expensive |
| {安|やす}い | {安|やす}くないです | isn't cheap |
| {新|あたら}しい | {新|あたら}しくないです | isn't new |
| おいしい | おいしくないです | isn't tasty |
| むずかしい | むずかしくないです | isn't difficult |

There's a second, slightly more formal negative: drop い and add くありません.
{高|たか}くありません means exactly the same as {高|たか}くないです. You'll hear くないです more
in conversation and see くありません in careful writing and polite speech. Both are correct.

この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}くないです。 — This book isn't expensive.
{日本語|にほんご}はむずかしくありません。 — Japanese isn't difficult.

A question is です + か, as always, and the answer repeats the adjective:

テストはむずかしいですか。 — Is the test difficult?
はい、むずかしいです。 — Yes, it is.
いいえ、むずかしくないです。 — No, it isn't.

## The odd one out: いい

いい (good) is the one irregular い-adjective. Its other forms are built on an older word, よい,
so the negative is よくないです, never いくないです:

| | Affirmative | Negative |
|---|---|---|
| good | いいです | よくないです / よくありません |

この{店|みせ}はいいです。 — This shop is good.
{天気|てんき}はよくないです。 — The weather isn't good. ({天気|てんき} = weather, Lesson 13)

Anything ending in いい does the same, for example かっこいい (cool, good-looking), whose
negative is かっこよくないです.

## Before a noun

An い-adjective goes straight in front of a noun, with nothing in between, just as in English:

{高|たか}い{本|ほん} — an expensive book
{新|あたら}しいアパート — a new apartment
いい{人|ひと} — a good person, a nice person
おもしろい{先生|せんせい} — an interesting (or funny) teacher

You can put the whole phrase anywhere a noun goes:

{古|ふる}い{車|くるま}があります。 — There's an old car.
おもしろい{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みました。 — I read an interesting book.
{安|やす}いコーヒーをください。 — A cheap coffee, please.

Don't put の between the adjective and the noun: {高|たか}い{本|ほん}, not {高|たか}いの{本|ほん}.
の joins two nouns ({日本語|にほんご}の{本|ほん}); an adjective doesn't need it.

## とても, あまり and ぜんぜん

Three adverbs say *how much*:

| Word | Goes with | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| とても | affirmative | very |
| あまり | negative | not very, not much |
| ぜんぜん | negative | not at all |

この{本|ほん}はとても{高|たか}いです。 — This book is very expensive.
この{本|ほん}はあまり{高|たか}くないです。 — This book isn't very expensive.
この{本|ほん}はぜんぜん{高|たか}くないです。 — This book isn't expensive at all.

あまり and ぜんぜん need a negative after them. あまり{高|たか}いです is a mistake, however
natural "not very" feels to an English speaker; think of あまり as half of a pair, あまり〜ない.
In casual speech you'll hear ぜんぜん with positive words too ("totally"), but in polite
Japanese keep it with negatives.

## Asking how something is: どう

どうですか asks "How is it?" or "What do you think of it?", and the answer is usually an
adjective:

{日本語|にほんご}のじゅぎょうはどうですか。 — How's your Japanese class? (じゅぎょう = class)
とてもおもしろいです。 — It's really interesting.

## Opposites

Adjectives are easiest to learn in pairs:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| {大|おお}きい big | {小|ちい}さい small | {高|たか}い expensive; tall, high | {安|やす}い cheap |
| {新|あたら}しい new | {古|ふる}い old (things) | {高|たか}い high, tall | ひくい low, short (height) |
| {長|なが}い long | みじかい short (length) | いい good | わるい bad |
| おいしい tasty | まずい tastes bad | むずかしい difficult | やさしい easy |
| おもしろい interesting, funny | つまらない boring | ひろい spacious, wide | せまい cramped, narrow |
| おもい heavy | かるい light (weight) | ちかい near | とおい far |
| あかるい bright | くらい dark | たのしい fun | いそがしい busy |

A few notes:

- {高|たか}い has two opposites: {安|やす}い (cheap) for prices, ひくい (low) for height.
- {古|ふる}い is for things: a {古|ふる}い{車|くるま}, a {古|ふる}い{店|みせ}. It is not used for a
  person's age; you'll learn the words for that in Lesson 15. ({古|ふる}い{友|とも}だち is fine:
  it means a friend you've known a long time.)
- みじかい is short in *length* (a short pencil, short hair); short in height is ひくい or
  せがひくい (Lesson 15).
- まずい is blunt. Use it about food you made yourself, not about someone's cooking; to be
  kind, say あまりおいしくないです.
- やさしい also means kind or gentle about a person: やさしい{人|ひと}, a kind person.
- ちかい and とおい take に and から: {駅|えき}にちかいです (it's near the station),
  {駅|えき}からとおいです (it's far from the station).
- たのしい is "fun" for things you do; おもしろい is "interesting" or "funny". A good party is
  たのしい; a good book is おもしろい.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | Readings | Strokes | Words in this lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 高 | high, tall; expensive | on: コウ · kun: たか(い) | 10 | {高|たか}い; later {高校|こうこう} (high school) |
| 安 | cheap; peaceful | on: アン · kun: やす(い) | 6 | {安|やす}い |
| 新 | new | on: シン · kun: あたら(しい) | 13 | {新|あたら}しい; later {新聞|しんぶん} (newspaper) |
| 古 | old | on: コ · kun: ふる(い) | 5 | {古|ふる}い |
| 長 | long; head (of a group) | on: チョウ · kun: なが(い) | 8 | {長|なが}い; later {社長|しゃちょう} (company president) |

The hiragana after the kanji in {高|たか}い, {新|あたら}しい and {長|なが}い is called okurigana:
it carries the ending that changes. That's why {高|たか}くない keeps the kanji and only the
hiragana changes.

Memory notes:

- 高 looks like a tall building: a roof, a window, a wide floor, a doorway: lots of storeys
  stacked up high.
- 安 is a roof over a woman ({女|おんな}, Lesson 15). Picture someone safe at home, at peace; the
  "cheap" meaning came later.
- 古 is {十|じゅう} (ten) over {口|くち} (mouth): a story passed through ten mouths is an old one.
- 長 has long lines streaming out to the right, like long hair blowing in the wind.
- 新 is the longest of the five. Split it: a standing shape over {木|き} (tree) on the left, and an axe
  on the right. Fresh-cut wood is new.

## Dialogue: a new apartment

```dialogue
# A new apartment
ゆい: エマさん、{新|あたら}しいアパートはどうですか。
= Emma, how's your new apartment?
エマ: いいですよ。{駅|えき}にとてもちかいです。
= It's good. It's really close to the station.
ゆい: へやはひろいですか。
= Is your room big?
エマ: いいえ、あまりひろくないです。でも、あかるいです。
= No, not very. But it's bright.
ゆい: アパートは{新|あたら}しいですか。
= Is the building new?
エマ: いいえ、ちょっと{古|ふる}いです。でも、やちんが{安|やす}いです。
= No, it's a bit old. But the rent is cheap.
ゆい: いいですね。
= Sounds great.
エマ: ゆいさんのアパートは？
= What about your apartment, Yui?
ゆい: わたしのアパートは{新|あたら}しいです。でも、{駅|えき}からとおいです。
= Mine is new. But it's far from the station.
```

アパート is an apartment building (or an apartment in one), へや is a room, and やちん is
rent. ちょっと, which you met as a polite way of saying no, here simply means "a little". In
やちんが{安|やす}いです, が marks what is cheap: "the rent is cheap". You'll see this pattern
again in Lesson 15. And notice ゆい's よ at the end of いいですよ: it adds "I'm telling you",
a friendly bit of emphasis.

## Reading: a bookshop

> {駅|えき}のちかくに{古|ふる}い{本|ほん}の{店|みせ}があります。{小|ちい}さい{店|みせ}です。でも、{本|ほん}がたくさんあります。{本|ほん}は{安|やす}いです。{新|あたら}しい{本|ほん}はあまりありません。{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}はとてもやさしいです。わたしは{毎週|まいしゅう}この{店|みせ}へ{行|い}きます。

Near the station there's a second-hand bookshop. It's a small shop, but it has lots of books.
The books are cheap. There aren't many new books. The person who runs the shop is very kind. I
go to this shop every week. (たくさん = a lot, many.)

Try reading it again in chunks: {駅|えき}の / ちかくに / {古|ふる}い / {本|ほん}の / {店|みせ}が /
あります. Notice あまりありません: あまり works with negative verbs too, "there aren't many".

## Say it

```speak
この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}いです。
= This book is expensive.
この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}くないです。
= This book isn't expensive.
{天気|てんき}はよくないです。
= The weather isn't good.
とてもおもしろい{本|ほん}です。
= It's a very interesting book.
あまりむずかしくないです。
= It isn't very difficult.
{駅|えき}にちかいです。
```
