```speak
= It's near the station.
```

## Common mistakes

- Using じゃないです with an い-adjective: {高|たか}いじゃないです. じゃない is for nouns
  (and な-adjectives, next lesson); い-adjectives change their own ending: {高|たか}くないです.
- Keeping the い: {高|たか}いくないです. The い goes; く takes its place.
- いくないです. いい is irregular: よくないです.
- あまり with an affirmative: あまり{高|たか}いです. Use a negative: あまり{高|たか}くないです.
- の between adjective and noun: {高|たか}いの{本|ほん}. Just {高|たか}い{本|ほん}.
- {古|ふる}い for an old person. It's for things (and long-standing friendships).
- Thinking です means "is" here. With an adjective it only adds politeness; the adjective
  already says "is big", "is cheap".

## Key points

- い-adjectives end in い in the dictionary form; polite: add です ({高|たか}いです).
- Negative: drop い, add くないです or くありません ({高|たか}くないです).
- いい is irregular: よくないです.
- Before a noun, nothing in between: {高|たか}い{本|ほん}.
- とても + affirmative; あまり and ぜんぜん + negative.
- どうですか asks how something is.
- From now on Japanese is written without spaces: read in chunks, using the kanji, katakana
  and particles as signposts.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: な-adjectives and likes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Last lesson's adjectives all ended in い and changed their ending: {高|たか}い, {高|たか}くない.
Japanese has a second kind of adjective that behaves much more like a noun. These are the
な-adjectives, named after the な they take in front of a noun: しずかなへや, a quiet room. Some
of the most useful words in the language are な-adjectives, including the words for liking and
disliking (すき, きらい) and for being good or bad at something ({上手|じょうず}, {下手|へた}). By the end of
this lesson you'll be able to say what you like, what you're good at, and what kind of place
your town is.

## What a な-adjective is

A **[[な-adjective]]** is an adjective that doesn't change its own ending. Instead it uses です and
its forms, exactly like a noun. Your word list gives them without な: しずか (quiet),
ゆうめい (famous), べんり (convenient), ひま (free, not busy), しんせつ (kind).

| | Noun | な-adjective | い-adjective (for comparison) |
|---|---|---|---|
| affirmative | {学生|がくせい}です | しずかです | {高|たか}いです |
| negative | {学生|がくせい}じゃないです | しずかじゃないです | {高|たか}くないです |
| negative (formal) | {学生|がくせい}ではありません | しずかではありません | {高|たか}くありません |
| before a noun | {学生|がくせい}の{本|ほん} | しずかなへや | {高|たか}い{本|ほん} |

The negative is the same as for nouns. In Lesson 1 you learned じゃありません and the more
formal ではありません ({学生|がくせい}じゃありません). In conversation you'll hear a third form
just as often: じゃないです. All three mean the same and work for nouns and な-adjectives
alike; this module mostly uses じゃないです, because it matches the い-adjective くないです.

このまちはしずかです。 — This town is quiet. (まち = town)
この{駅|えき}はべんりです。 — This station is convenient.
{今日|きょう}はひまじゃないです。 — I'm not free today.
この{店|みせ}はゆうめいではありません。 — This shop isn't famous.

## Before a noun: add な

In front of a noun, a な-adjective takes な. This is the one place where the two kinds of
adjective look different at a glance:

しずかなへや — a quiet room
ゆうめいな{人|ひと} — a famous person
べんりな{店|みせ} — a handy shop
しんせつな{先生|せんせい} — a kind teacher
にぎやかなまち — a lively town

ここはしずかなまちです。 — This is a quiet town.
{日本|にほん}のゆうめいな{山|やま}を{見|み}ました。 — I saw a famous Japanese mountain.

Without な the phrase is wrong (しずかへや), and with の it's wrong too (しずかのへや): の joins
nouns, な joins a な-adjective to a noun.

## The trap: きれい, きらい and ゆうめい

Most な-adjectives don't end in い, so they're easy to spot. A few do, and they fool everyone:

| Word | Kind | Negative | Before a noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| きれい (pretty, clean) | な | きれいじゃないです | きれいなへや |
| きらい (disliked) | な | きらいじゃないです | きらいなもの (a thing you dislike) |
| ゆうめい (famous) | な | ゆうめいじゃないです | ゆうめいな{店|みせ} |
| {大|おお}きい (big) | い | {大|おお}きくないです | {大|おお}きい{店|みせ} |

きれいくないです is one of the most common beginner mistakes in Japanese. The い at the end of
きれい is part of the word (it's "kirē", a long え), not an adjective ending. Learn these three as
な-adjectives and the problem disappears.

And げんき (well, healthy, lively), which you already know from おげんきですか, is a
な-adjective too. With kanji it's {元気|げんき}:

{元気|げんき}な{子|こ}どもです。 — It's a lively child.
{父|ちち}はあまり{元気|げんき}じゃないです。 — My father isn't very well. ({父|ちち} = my father, Lesson 15)

## Likes and dislikes: がすきです

To say you like something, use すき (liked) with が:

わたしはコーヒーがすきです。 — I like coffee.
ねこがすきです。 — I like cats. (ねこ = cat)
{何|なに}がすきですか。 — What do you like?

The thing you like takes **が**, not を. Literally the sentence says "As for me, coffee is
liked." The topic (わたしは) is the person who likes; が marks what is liked. Leave out
わたしは when it's clear.

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| すき | like | りょうりがすきです。 — I like cooking. |
| だいすき | love, like a lot | うたがだいすきです。 — I love singing (songs). |
| きらい | dislike | テストがきらいです。 — I hate tests. |
| だいきらい | hate | にがいコーヒーはだいきらいです。 — I can't stand bitter coffee (にがい = bitter). |

Some notes on using them:

- きらい is strong. Japanese people often soften it: あまりすきじゃないです (I don't really like
  it) sounds much more polite than きらいです.
- すき and きらい are な-adjectives, so before a noun: すきな{本|ほん} (a book I like), すきな
  {食|た}べもの (favourite food). すきな{食|た}べものは{何|なん}ですか。 — What's your favourite
  food? ({食|た}べもの = food)
- Saying すきです directly to a person means "I like you" in the romantic sense. To say you like
  a friend's company, talk about what you like doing together instead.
- In は-sentences that contrast, は replaces が: コーヒーはすきです。でも、おちゃはすきじゃない
  です。 — Coffee I like. But tea I don't.

## Skills: {上手|じょうず}, {下手|へた}, とくい, にがて

Four more な-adjectives describe skill, and they work the same way, with が:

| Word | Meaning | Who you say it about |
|---|---|---|
| {上手|じょうず} | good at, skilled | other people (praise) |
| {下手|へた} | bad at, poor at | yourself, or things |
| とくい | good at, strong in | yourself (also others) |
| にがて | weak at, not good with | yourself (also others) |

エマさんは{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}ですね。 — Emma, your Japanese is good!
わたしはりょうりが{下手|へた}です。 — I'm bad at cooking.
すうがくがとくいです。 — I'm good at math. (すうがく = math)
スポーツはにがてです。 — Sports aren't my thing.

The important point is about politeness. {上手|じょうず} is praise, and Japanese people don't praise
themselves: わたしはりょうりが{上手|じょうず}です sounds like bragging. When you want to say you're good
at something, use とくい, which means something like "my strong point". And when someone says
{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}ですね, the usual reply is a modest one:

いいえ、まだまだです。 — Oh no, I've still got a long way to go.

にがて is gentler than {下手|へた}: it can mean you're bad at something, or that you simply don't like
dealing with it (にがてな{食|た}べもの, a food you'd rather not eat).

## Asking what kind: どんな

どんな means "what kind of" and goes straight in front of a noun:

どんな{本|ほん}がすきですか。 — What kind of books do you like?
おもしろい{本|ほん}がすきです。 — I like interesting books.
たなかさんはどんな{人|ひと}ですか。 — What kind of person is Mr Tanaka?

The answer is usually an adjective + noun: しんせつな{人|ひと}です (he's a kind person),
にぎやかなまちです (it's a lively town). Compare どう from Lesson 11: どうですか asks for your
opinion of something ("How is it?"), どんな asks you to describe it ("What is it like?").

## More useful な-adjectives

- たいへん: hard, tough, a lot of trouble. しごとはたいへんです (work is tough; しごと = work).
  たいへんですね is a kind thing to say when someone tells you about a problem: "That sounds
  hard."
- だいじょうぶ: all right, OK, safe. だいじょうぶですか (Are you all right?) — はい、だいじょうぶ
  です.
- いろいろ: various. いろいろなりょうり, all sorts of dishes.
- じょうぶ: strong, sturdy (things), healthy (people). じょうぶなかばん, a sturdy bag.
- ふべん: inconvenient, the opposite of べんり.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | Readings | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 元 | origin, beginning | on: ゲン, ガン · kun: もと | 4 | {元気|げんき} |
| 気 | spirit, energy; air; mood | on: キ, ケ | 6 | {元気|げんき}, {天気|てんき} (weather, Lesson 13), {人気|にんき} (popularity) |

{元気|げんき} is "original energy": the strength you were born with. 気 is one of the most
common kanji in Japanese. It turns up in words about the weather, health and feelings, and
you'll meet it often.

{人気|にんき}があります means "is popular": この{店|みせ}は{人気|にんき}があります (this shop is
popular). The same two kanji can also be read {人気|ひとけ}, a different word (signs of people being
around), but at N5 you'll meet にんき.

Memory notes:

- 元 is {二|に} over a pair of legs: a person standing on their own two feet, where everything
  starts.
- The top of 気 looks like wisps of steam rising from a pot of rice: energy you can see in
  the air.

## Dialogue: what do you like?

```dialogue
# What do you like?
けん: リサさんは、どんな{食|た}べものがすきですか。
= Lisa, what kind of food do you like?
リサ: {日本|にほん}のりょうりがだいすきです。とくに、すしがすきです。
= I love Japanese food. Especially sushi.
けん: そうですか。なっとうはどうですか。
= Really? What about natto?
リサ: なっとうは…あまりすきじゃないです。
= Natto… I don't really like it.
けん: ははは。わたしもにがてです。リサさんはりょうりがとくいですか。
= Ha ha. I'm not keen on it either. Are you good at cooking?
リサ: いいえ、{下手|へた}です。でも、ケーキはときどきつくります。
= No, I'm bad at it. But I make cakes sometimes.
けん: すごいですね。ケーキはむずかしいですよ。
= That's impressive. Cakes are hard.
リサ: いいえ、かんたんなケーキです。こんど、いっしょに{食|た}べませんか。
= No, they're simple cakes. Shall we eat one together next time?
けん: いいですね。
= Sounds good.
```

とくに = especially; なっとう = natto (fermented soybeans, a food many visitors find hard to
like); ときどき = sometimes; つくります = make; すごい = amazing; かんたん = simple, easy (another
な-adjective); こんど = next time. Notice リサ's modest {下手|へた}です and her polite
あまりすきじゃないです instead of きらいです.

## Say it

```speak
コーヒーがすきです。
= I like coffee.
あまりすきじゃないです。
= I don't really like it.
しずかなまちです。
= It's a quiet town.
このへやはきれいじゃないです。
= This room isn't clean.
{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}ですね。
= Your Japanese is good!
いいえ、まだまだです。
= Oh no, I've got a long way to go.
```

## Common mistakes

- きれいくないです, ゆうめいくないです. These are な-adjectives: きれいじゃないです,
  ゆうめいじゃないです.
- Forgetting な before a noun: しずかへや. Say しずかなへや.
- Using な at the end of a sentence: しずかなです. な appears only before a noun; the sentence
  ends しずかです.
- Using を with すき: コーヒーをすきです. Use が: コーヒーがすきです.
- Calling yourself {上手|じょうず}. Say とくい, or be modest.
- Using きらいです when you mean "I'm not keen": あまりすきじゃないです is softer and more
  natural in polite talk.

## Key points

- な-adjectives work like nouns: しずかです, しずかじゃないです / ではありません.
- Before a noun they take な: しずかなへや.
- きれい, きらい, ゆうめい (and {元気|げんき}) are な-adjectives, even though some end in い.
- Likes and skills take が: Nがすきです, Nが{上手|じょうず}です, Nがとくいです.
- {上手|じょうず} is praise for others; for yourself use とくい, or {下手|へた} / にがて to be modest.
- どんな + noun asks "what kind of…?"

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The past of adjectives; weather and seasons
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can describe things as they are now: {高|たか}いです, しずかです. But a lot of describing
happens afterwards: how was the trip, the film, the test, yesterday's weather? This lesson
teaches the past tense of both kinds of adjective, the question どうでしたか (how was it?), and
the words for weather, the seasons and nature, which are what Japanese people talk about most
when they make small talk.

## The past of い-adjectives: 〜かったです

Drop the final い and add かったです:

| Dictionary form | Past | Past negative |
|---|---|---|
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}かったです (was expensive) | {高|たか}くなかったです (wasn't expensive) |
| さむい | さむかったです (was cold) | さむくなかったです (wasn't cold) |
| たのしい | たのしかったです (was fun) | たのしくなかったです (wasn't fun) |
| いい | よかったです (was good) | よくなかったです (wasn't good) |

The past negative is the negative くない with its い treated like any other い-adjective ending:
くない → くなかった. So once you know the past, the past negative comes free.

There's also a more formal past negative, built on くありません: {高|たか}くありませんでした.
It means the same as {高|たか}くなかったです.

Notice that the past is in the adjective, not in です. This is the single most important thing
in the lesson. English speakers want to say "was" with でした, but with an い-adjective that's
wrong:

- {高|たか}かったです — correct
- {高|たか}いでした — wrong

いい, as always, uses よ: よかったです, よくなかったです. よかったです is also what you say when
you hear good news: "I'm glad" or "That's great!"

きのうはさむかったです。 — It was cold yesterday. (きのう = yesterday)
テストはむずかしくなかったです。 — The test wasn't difficult.
パーティーはとてもたのしかったです。 — The party was a lot of fun.
{天気|てんき}はあまりよくなかったです。 — The weather wasn't very good.

## The past of な-adjectives and nouns: でした

な-adjectives and nouns don't change themselves. Their past is in です, which becomes でした:

| | Present | Past |
|---|---|---|
| affirmative | しずかです | しずかでした (was quiet) |
| negative | しずかじゃないです | しずかじゃなかったです (wasn't quiet) |
| negative (formal) | しずかではありません | しずかではありませんでした |

Nouns are exactly the same: {雨|あめ}でした (it was rainy), {雨|あめ}じゃなかったです (it
wasn't rainy).

ホテルはきれいでした。 — The hotel was clean. (ホテル = hotel)
{先週|せんしゅう}はひまじゃなかったです。 — I wasn't free last week.
きのうは{雨|あめ}でした。 — Yesterday it rained. (literally "Yesterday was rain.")
しけんはかんたんではありませんでした。 — The exam wasn't easy. (しけん = exam)

To keep the two kinds apart, ask: does the word end in an adjective い? Then the い changes
(かった). If not, or if it's one of the tricky な-adjectives such as きれい, the です changes
(でした).

## How was it? どうでしたか

どうですか from Lesson 11 becomes どうでしたか: "How was it?" It's the natural question after a
weekend, a trip or a meal, and the answer is a past adjective:

りょこうはどうでしたか。 — How was your trip? (りょこう = trip)
とてもたのしかったです。 — It was great fun.
{天気|てんき}はどうでしたか。 — How was the weather?
{毎日|まいにち}いい{天気|てんき}でした。 — The weather was good every day.

Notice that いい{天気|てんき}でした is a noun phrase (good weather) + でした, so the です changes
here, not the adjective.

## Talking about the weather

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {天気|てんき} | weather | {今日|きょう}はいい{天気|てんき}ですね。 — Lovely weather today. |
| はれ | sunny weather | あしたははれです。 — Tomorrow will be sunny. |
| くもり | cloudy weather | {今日|きょう}はくもりです。 — It's cloudy today. |
| {雨|あめ} | rain | きのうは{雨|あめ}でした。 — It rained yesterday. |
| ゆき | snow | ゆきがふりました。 — It snowed. |
| くも | cloud | くもが{多|おお}いです。 — There are lots of clouds. |

ふる (to fall, of rain or snow) is a group 1 verb: ふります, ふりました. {雨|あめ}がふります is "it
rains", and to say "it's raining right now" you'll use a form from module 4; until then,
{雨|あめ}です does the job. はれ and くもり are nouns, so they take です and でした:
きのうははれでした (it was sunny yesterday).

Temperature has its own pairs, and English speakers mix up two of them:

| Word | Meaning | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| あつい | hot | the weather, and things you touch or drink |
| さむい | cold | the weather, the air in a room: how *you* feel |
| つめたい | cold | things you touch or drink: water, a drink, a hand |
| あたたかい | warm | the weather, and food and drinks |
| すずしい | cool, pleasantly cool | the weather, a breeze |

So the weather is さむい, but a drink is つめたい: {今日|きょう}はさむいです (it's cold today),
つめたいコーヒー (iced coffee). Saying さむいコーヒー would sound like the coffee is shivering.
(Written with kanji, the two あつい are different: one for weather, one for things. Both are
outside this course, so they're written in kana.)

Japanese weather talk usually ends in ね, which invites the other person to agree:

あついですね。 — Hot, isn't it?
ええ、ほんとうにあついですね。 — Yes, it's really hot. (ええ = yes, a softer はい)

## Seasons

| Season | Word | Typical weather |
|---|---|---|
| spring | はる | あたたかい; the cherry blossoms |
| summer | なつ | あつい; the rainy season comes first |
| autumn | あき | すずしい; red leaves |
| winter | ふゆ | さむい; snow in the north and the mountains |

The word for season is きせつ. どのきせつがすきですか asks "Which season do you like?" (You'll
learn the best way to ask which one you like *most* in the next lesson.)

## Nature

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {山|やま} | mountain |
| {川|かわ} | river |
| うみ | sea, ocean |
| いけ | pond |
| {木|き} | tree |
| {花|はな} | flower |
| そら | sky |

なつはうみへ{行|い}きました。 — In the summer I went to the sea.
{山|やま}はとてもきれいでした。 — The mountains were really beautiful.
この{木|き}は{高|たか}いですね。 — This tree is tall, isn't it?

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | Readings | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 天 | heaven, sky | on: テン | 4 | {天気|てんき} |
| 雨 | rain | on: ウ · kun: あめ, あま- | 8 | {雨|あめ}, {大雨|おおあめ} (heavy rain) |
| 花 | flower | on: カ · kun: はな | 7 | {花|はな}, {花見|はなみ} (cherry-blossom viewing, Lesson 15h1) |
| 山 | mountain | on: サン · kun: やま | 3 | {山|やま}; サン in mountain names (ふじさん, Mount Fuji) |
| 川 | river | on: セン · kun: かわ | 3 | {川|かわ}; -がわ in river names |

In names, 川 often becomes がわ after another word: a river called "Sumida" is すみだがわ. In
the same way, mountain names use the reading サン: ふじさん (Mount Fuji, whose first two
kanji aren't in this course).

Memory notes:

- 天 is {大|だい} (a person with arms spread) with a line above the head: what's above
  everyone is the sky.
- 雨 is a window with four raindrops behind it, and a line of sky on top.
- 花 has grass on top (the little cross-shapes, a sign for plants) over a person changing shape:
  a plant changing into a flower.
- 山 is a picture: three peaks, the middle one highest.
- 川 is a picture too: three lines of flowing water.

## Dialogue: after a trip

```dialogue
# After a trip
さとう: エマさん、ひさしぶりですね。りょこうはどうでしたか。
= Emma, long time no see. How was your trip?
エマ: とてもたのしかったです。ほっかいどうへ{行|い}きました。
= It was great fun. I went to Hokkaido.
さとう: いいですね。さむかったですか。
= Lovely. Was it cold?
エマ: はい、とてもさむかったです。{毎日|まいにち}ゆきでした。
= Yes, very cold. It snowed every day.
さとう: {山|やま}はどうでしたか。
= What were the mountains like?
エマ: きれいでした。でも、ホテルはあまりよくなかったです。
= Beautiful. But the hotel wasn't very good.
さとう: そうですか。{高|たか}かったですか。
= Oh no. Was it expensive?
エマ: いいえ、{高|たか}くなかったです。でも、へやがせまかったです。
= No, it wasn't. But the room was cramped.
さとう: {食|た}べものは？
= And the food?
エマ: おいしかったです！ラーメンがとくによかったです。
= Delicious! The ramen was especially good.
```

ひさしぶりですね = it's been a while; ほっかいどう is Hokkaido, Japan's northern island; {食|た}べもの = food; とくに = especially. Look at how every
answer changes form: さむかった, よくなかった, {高|たか}くなかった, せまかった, おいしかった for
い-adjectives, but きれいでした and ゆきでした for a な-adjective and a noun.

## Reading: a postcard from the mountains

> ゆいさん、お{元気|げんき}ですか。わたしは{今|いま}、{山|やま}のちかくの{小|ちい}さいホテルにいます。きのうは{雨|あめ}でした。とてもさむかったです。でも、{今日|きょう}はいい{天気|てんき}です。そらがとてもきれいです。けさ、{川|かわ}のちかくをあるきました。{花|はな}がたくさんありました。{川|かわ}の{水|みず}はとてもつめたかったです。あしたうちへかえります。

Yui, how are you? I'm at a small hotel near the mountains right now. Yesterday it rained. It
was very cold. But today the weather is lovely. The sky is so beautiful. This morning I walked
near the river. There were lots of flowers. The river water was really cold. Tomorrow I'm
going home.

(けさ = this morning; あるきました = walked; the を in {川|かわ}のちかくをあるきました marks the area you walk
through, which you'll practise in Lesson 27.)

## Say it

```speak
きのうはさむかったです。
= It was cold yesterday.
とてもたのしかったです。
= It was great fun.
あまりよくなかったです。
= It wasn't very good.
きれいでした。
= It was beautiful.
{天気|てんき}はどうでしたか。
= How was the weather?
いい{天気|てんき}ですね。
= Lovely weather, isn't it?
```

## Common mistakes

- {高|たか}いでした. The past goes into an い-adjective: {高|たか}かったです.
- {高|たか}かったでした. Only one past: {高|たか}かったです. The です here is just for
  politeness.
- いかったです. いい is irregular: よかったです.
- きれいかったです. きれい is a な-adjective: きれいでした.
- さむいコーヒー, さむい{水|みず}. Things you touch are つめたい; さむい is the air and how you
  feel.
- いい{天気|てんき}かったです. The adjective いい is inside a noun phrase here; the past goes on
  です: いい{天気|てんき}でした.

## Key points

- い-adjectives: 〜かったです (past), 〜くなかったです or 〜くありませんでした (past negative).
- いい → よかったです, よくなかったです.
- な-adjectives and nouns: 〜でした, 〜じゃなかったです or 〜ではありませんでした.
- Never {高|たか}いでした: for い-adjectives the past is in the adjective.
- どうでしたか asks "How was it?"
- The weather is さむい when it's cold; things you touch are つめたい.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Comparing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now describe one thing: この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}いです. Often, though, you want to put
two or more things side by side: this one is cheaper, the train is faster than the bus, winter
is my favourite season. English does this by changing the adjective (cheap, cheaper,
cheapest). Japanese never changes the adjective at all. Instead, a few small words do the
comparing: より, ほう, どちら and いちばん. This lesson teaches them, along with
{多|おお}い and {少|すく}ない (there are many, there are few), and more colours.

## "Than": AはBより〜です

より means "than". It comes straight after the thing you compare *against*, and the adjective
stays in its ordinary form:

{電車|でんしゃ}はバスよりはやいです。 — The train is faster than the bus.
この{本|ほん}はあの{本|ほん}より{安|やす}いです。 — This book is cheaper than that one.
{日本語|にほんご}はえいごよりむずかしいです。 — Japanese is harder than English. (えいご = English)
なつはふゆよりすきです。 — I like summer more than winter.

Read it as "A, compared with B, is fast". The adjective はやい on its own means "fast"; より
turns it into "faster than". This is the **[[comparative]]**, and in Japanese it is made with
words, never with endings.

Two words make a comparison stronger:

- もっと (more, even more): こちらのほうがもっと{安|やす}いです — this one is even cheaper (こちら = this one, a polite これ).
- ずっと (much, by far): {電車|でんしゃ}はバスよりずっとはやいです — the train is much faster than
  the bus.

## Which of the two? AとBと、どちらが〜ですか

To ask which of two things is more so, name them with と, add a comma, and ask with どちら
(which one, of two) + が:

{電車|でんしゃ}とバスと、どちらがはやいですか。 — Which is faster, the train or the bus?
コーヒーとおちゃと、どちらがすきですか。 — Which do you like better, coffee or tea?

The answer uses ほう ("side", "the one that is"): Aのほうが〜です.

{電車|でんしゃ}のほうがはやいです。 — The train is faster.
コーヒーのほうがすきです。 — I like coffee better.

You can combine ほう and より to say the whole thing: バスより{電車|でんしゃ}のほうがはやいです
(the train is faster than the bus). And if there's no difference, use どちらも (both):

どちらもすきです。 — I like them both.
どちらもおいしいです。 — They're both delicious.

In conversation you'll often hear どっち, a casual どちら. With an adjective, ほう can follow it
directly: {高|たか}いほう (the more expensive one), {小|ちい}さいほうをください (I'll take the
smaller one, please).

## The most: 〜の{中|なか}で、〜がいちばん〜です

いちばん means "number one", and in front of an adjective it means "most": the
**[[superlative]]**. To say what you're choosing from, use の{中|なか}で ("among", literally
"inside"):

きせつの{中|なか}で、はるがいちばんすきです。 — Of all the seasons, I like spring best.
この{店|みせ}の{中|なか}で、これがいちばん{安|やす}いです。 — This is the cheapest thing in the
shop.
{日本|にほん}の{山|やま}の{中|なか}で、ふじさんがいちばん{高|たか}いです。 — Of Japan's mountains,
Mount Fuji is the highest.

To ask, put a question word + が in front of いちばん. Choose the question word by what the
answer will be:

| Asking about | Question word | Example |
|---|---|---|
| one of the things in front of you | どれ | この{中|なか}で、どれがいちばんいいですか。 — Which of these is best? |
| a kind of thing (food, sport…) | {何|なに} | くだものの{中|なか}で、{何|なに}がいちばんすきですか。 — What's your favourite fruit? |
| a person | だれ | クラスの{中|なか}で、だれがいちばんせが{高|たか}いですか。 — Who's tallest in the class? |
| a place | どこ | {日本|にほん}の{中|なか}で、どこがいちばんすきですか。 — Where in Japan do you like best? |
| a time | いつ | {一年|いちねん}の{中|なか}で、いつがいちばんさむいですか。 — When is it coldest in the year? |

(くだもの = fruit; クラス = class; せが{高|たか}い = tall, of a person, Lesson 15.)

Two rules matter here. First, a question word is never followed by は: {何|なに}がいちばんすきですか,
not {何|なに}はいちばん…. Second, for exactly two things use どちら; for three or more use どれ,
{何|なに}, だれ, どこ or いつ.

The answer names the winner with が: はるがいちばんすきです, or simply はるです.

## Many and few: {多|おお}い and {少|すく}ない

{多|おお}い (many, a lot) and {少|すく}ない (few, little) are い-adjectives with one quirk: they
are used at the end of a sentence, with が marking what there is a lot (or little) of:

このまちは{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。 — This town has a lot of people.
この{川|かわ}は{水|みず}が{少|すく}ないです。 — This river has little water in it.
ふゆは{雨|あめ}が{少|すく}ないです。 — There isn't much rain in winter.

Unlike most adjectives, they are not normally put in front of a noun. "Many people" is not
{多|おお}い{人|ひと}; say たくさんの{人|ひと} instead, or turn the sentence round with
{多|おお}いです at the end:

たくさんの{人|ひと}が{来|き}ました。 — Lots of people came.
{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。 — There are lots of people.

Don't mix up {少|すく}ない (few) with {少|すこ}し (a little, a bit). {少|すこ}し is an adverb or a
noun, used like ちょっと but more polite: {少|すこ}しさむいです (it's a bit cold), コーヒーを
{少|すこ}しください (a little coffee, please). The two words share a kanji, with different
readings.

## Colours

You met colours in Lesson 4. Some colour words are い-adjectives, and they also have a noun
form without the い:

| Colour | Adjective | Noun |
|---|---|---|
| white | {白|しろ}い | {白|しろ} |
| black | くろい | くろ |
| red | あかい | あか |
| blue | あおい | あお |

Others are nouns only, and take の in front of a noun:

| Colour | Noun | Before a noun |
|---|---|---|
| green | みどり | みどりのかばん |
| brown | ちゃいろ | ちゃいろのくつ (brown shoes) |

{白|しろ}いシャツ — a white shirt (シャツ = shirt)
みどりのかさ — a green umbrella (かさ = umbrella)
{何|なに}いろがすきですか。 — What colour do you like? (いろ = colour)

ちゃいろ also has an adjective form, ちゃいろい, which you'll hear in speech. Note that あおい
covers more than English blue: a green traffic light and fresh green leaves are often called
あお in Japanese.

## More adjectives for comparing

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| はやい fast; early | おそい slow; late | つよい strong | よわい weak |
| ふとい thick, fat (of a line, a tree) | ほそい thin, slender | あまい sweet | からい spicy, hot |

おなじ means "the same" and goes straight before a noun, with no な or の: おなじいろ (the same colour), おなじ{店|みせ}
(the same shop). Its opposite is the verb ちがう (to be different), polite ちがいます. ちがいます
is also the polite way to say "No, that's not right": これはエマさんの{本|ほん}ですか。 —
いいえ、ちがいます。

ぜんぶ means "all, everything": ぜんぶでいくらですか (how much is it all together?), and
ぜんぶの{中|なか}で (out of all of them).

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | Readings | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 多 | many, much | on: タ · kun: おお(い) | 6 | {多|おお}い |
| 少 | few, a little | on: ショウ · kun: すく(ない), すこ(し) | 4 | {少|すく}ない, {少|すこ}し |
| 白 | white | on: ハク · kun: しろ, しろ(い) | 5 | {白|しろ}い, {白|しろ} |

Memory notes:

- 多 is the same shape written twice, one stacked on the other. More than one of something:
  many.
- 少 is the kanji of {小|ちい}さい with an extra slanting stroke underneath: small, and then a
  little less.
- 白 is the sun ({日|ひ}) with a short ray shining from its top: bright, white light.

## Dialogue: which bag?

```dialogue
# Which bag?
てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome.
マリア: すみません。この{白|しろ}いかばんと、あのくろいかばんと、どちらが{安|やす}いですか。
= Excuse me. Which is cheaper, this white bag or that black one?
てんいん: {白|しろ}いほうが{安|やす}いです。{三千円|さんぜんえん}です。
= The white one is cheaper. It's 3,000 yen.
マリア: くろいのはいくらですか。
= How much is the black one?
てんいん: {五千円|ごせんえん}です。でも、くろいほうが{大|おお}きいですよ。
= 5,000 yen. But the black one is bigger.
マリア: そうですか。{白|しろ}いのはちょっと{小|ちい}さいですね。
= I see. The white one is a bit small, isn't it?
てんいん: こちらのみどりのかばんはどうですか。くろいのより{大|おお}きいです。{四千円|よんせんえん}です。
= How about this green bag? It's bigger than the black one. It's 4,000 yen.
マリア: いいですね。この{中|なか}で、どれがいちばんじょうぶですか。
= Nice. Of these, which is the sturdiest?
てんいん: みどりのがいちばんじょうぶです。
= The green one is the sturdiest.
マリア: じゃあ、みどりのをください。
= Then I'll take the green one, please.
```

てんいん is a shop assistant. Look at くろいの and みどりの: after an adjective, or a noun with
の, the word の can stand for a thing you've already mentioned, "the black one", "the green
one". So {白|しろ}いの = {白|しろ}いかばん here. マリア uses どちら while there are two bags, and
switches to どれ once there are three.

## Reading: my favourite season

> わたしは{日本|にほん}のきせつの{中|なか}で、あきがいちばんすきです。なつはあついです。ふゆはさむいです。あきはなつよりずっとすずしいです。そして、{山|やま}の{木|き}がとてもきれいです。はるもきれいです。でも、はるはどこも{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。あきのほうが{人|ひと}が{少|すく}ないです。

Of Japan's seasons, I like autumn best. Summer is hot. Winter is cold. Autumn is much cooler
than summer. And the trees on the mountains are really beautiful. Spring is beautiful too. But
in spring there are crowds everywhere. In autumn there are fewer people. (そして = and, and
also; どこも = everywhere.)

## Say it

```speak
{電車|でんしゃ}はバスよりはやいです。
= The train is faster than the bus.
コーヒーとおちゃと、どちらがすきですか。
= Which do you like better, coffee or tea?
コーヒーのほうがすきです。
= I like coffee better.
どちらもすきです。
= I like both.
きせつの{中|なか}で、はるがいちばんすきです。
= Of the seasons, I like spring best.
このまちは{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。
= This town has lots of people.
```

## Common mistakes

- Looking for an ending like English "-er" or "-est". The adjective never changes:
  はやい, より〜はやい, いちばんはやい.
- Mixing up the order: in AはBよりはやい, A is the faster one. より follows the *loser*.
- Forgetting の before ほう after a noun: {電車|でんしゃ}ほうが. Say {電車|でんしゃ}のほうが.
  After an adjective there's no の: {高|たか}いほう.
- どちら for three or more things, or どれ for two. Two: どちら; three or more: どれ.
- {何|なに}はいちばん…. Question words take が: {何|なに}がいちばん….
- {多|おお}い{人|ひと} for "many people". Say たくさんの{人|ひと}, or {人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです.
- Mixing up {少|すく}ない (few) and {少|すこ}し (a little).

## Key points

- AはBより〜です: A is more ~ than B. The adjective doesn't change.
- AとBと、どちらが〜ですか asks which of two; answer Aのほうが〜です, or どちらも〜.
- 〜の{中|なか}で、Nがいちばん〜です: N is the most ~ of the group. Ask with どれ, {何|なに}, だれ,
  どこ or いつ + がいちばん.
- {多|おお}い and {少|すく}ない usually end the sentence: {人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです.
- Some colours are い-adjectives ({白|しろ}い, くろい, あかい, あおい); みどり and ちゃいろ are
  nouns and take の.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Family
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Family is one of the first things people ask about when they get to know you, and Japanese
treats it in a way English doesn't: most family words come in two sets, one for your own family
and one for other people's. This lesson teaches both sets, how to count people (ひとり,
ふたり, さんにん…), how to say someone is married, and how to describe what people look like,
using the adjectives from this module: せが{高|たか}い (tall), かみが{長|なが}い (long-haired),
わかい (young).

## Two sets of family words

When you talk to someone outside your family about your own family, you use plain, modest
words: {父|ちち} (my father), {母|はは} (my mother). When you talk about someone else's family,
you use polite words with お〜さん: お{父|とう}さん (your father, his father). The idea behind
this is **[[uchi and soto]]**, "inside" and "outside" groups: in Japanese you are modest about
your own side and polite about the other person's, in the same way you never put さん after
your own name.

| | My own (modest) | Someone else's (polite) |
|---|---|---|
| family | かぞく | ごかぞく |
| father | {父|ちち} | お{父|とう}さん |
| mother | {母|はは} | お{母|かあ}さん |
| parents | りょうしん | ごりょうしん |
| older brother | あに | おにいさん |
| older sister | あね | おねえさん |
| younger brother | おとうと | おとうとさん |
| younger sister | いもうと | いもうとさん |
| brothers and sisters | きょうだい | ごきょうだい |
| grandfather | そふ | おじいさん |
| grandmother | そぼ | おばあさん |
| child, children | {子|こ}ども | お{子|こ}さん |

Notice what the polite set does. Most words get お〜 in front and さん behind; a few take ご
instead (ごかぞく, ごりょうしん, ごきょうだい). お{父|とう}さん and お{母|かあ}さん also change the
reading of the kanji: 父 is ちち on its own but とう inside お{父|とう}さん, and 母 is はは but かあ
inside お{母|かあ}さん.

Japanese also keeps older and younger siblings apart. There's no everyday word for just
"brother" or "sister": you say which. きょうだい covers all your brothers and sisters together,
like "siblings".

{父|ちち}は{会社|かいしゃ}いんです。 — My father works for a company.
たなかさんのお{父|とう}さんは{先生|せんせい}です。 — Mr Tanaka's father is a teacher.
あには{大学生|だいがくせい}です。 — My older brother is a university student.
おにいさんは{大学生|だいがくせい}ですか。 — Is your older brother a university student?

## Inside the family

There's one twist. *Inside* the family, when you speak to an older relative, you use the
polite words as names: a child calls out お{母|かあ}さん！ (Mum!), and says おにいさん or the
more affectionate おにいちゃん to an older brother. Younger brothers and sisters are just called by
their names. So the same person is お{母|かあ}さん when you speak *to* her, and {母|はは} when
you tell your teacher about her.

Many young people say お{母|かあ}さん about their own mother when chatting with friends, too.
That's fine among friends, but in polite situations (with a teacher, at work, in a job
interview) use {母|はは}. Getting this right sounds grown-up.

## Counting people

People are counted with the **[[counter]]** 〜{人|にん}, but the first two numbers are special:

| Number | Reading | | Number | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| {一人|ひとり} | ひとり | | {六人|ろくにん} | ろくにん |
| {二人|ふたり} | ふたり | | {七人|しちにん} | しちにん, ななにん |
| {三人|さんにん} | さんにん | | {八人|はちにん} | はちにん |
| {四人|よにん} | よにん | | {九人|きゅうにん} | きゅうにん |
| {五人|ごにん} | ごにん | | {十人|じゅうにん} | じゅうにん |

How many people? {何人|なんにん}ですか。

Watch {四人|よにん}: not よんにん and not しにん. (しにん is a different, unlucky word.)
{一人|ひとり} and {二人|ふたり} are old Japanese numbers, the same ones as ひとつ and ふたつ, and
you met ひとり already in ひとりで (alone).

To say how many brothers, sisters or children someone has, put the number after the particle,
right before います:

あにが{一人|ひとり}います。 — I have one older brother.
いもうとが{二人|ふたり}います。 — I have two younger sisters.
ごきょうだいがいますか。 — Do you have any brothers or sisters?
いいえ、いません。 — No, I don't.
お{子|こ}さんは{何人|なんにん}ですか。 — How many children do you have?

The number works like an adverb: no particle after it. And people take います, not あります,
as you learned in Lesson 5.

The size of your family is asked like this:

{何人|なんにん}かぞくですか。 — How many people are in your family?
{四人|よにん}かぞくです。{父|ちち}と{母|はは}とあにとわたしです。 — There are four of us: my father,
my mother, my older brother and me.

Japanese people count themselves in: {四人|よにん}かぞく includes you.

## Ages

You learned 〜さい in Lesson 3. With family it often comes with the polite question
おいくつですか (how old is…?):

いもうとさんはおいくつですか。 — How old is your younger sister?
{十二|じゅうに}さいです。 — She's twelve.
あには{二十五|にじゅうご}さいです。 — My older brother is twenty-five.

## Married: けっこんしています

To say someone is married, use けっこんしています as a set phrase for now (you'll learn how the
form works in Lesson 17):

あねはけっこんしています。 — My older sister is married.
けっこんしていますか。 — Are you married?
いいえ、けっこんしていません。 — No, I'm not married.

Careful: けっこんします means "will get married", not "is married". "I'm married" is always
けっこんしています.

## Describing people: AはBがCです

To describe someone's appearance, Japanese uses a pattern you've seen with やちんが{安|やす}い
in Lesson 11: the person is the topic (は), the feature is marked by が, and an adjective
follows.

あにはせが{高|たか}いです。 — My older brother is tall. (literally "As for my brother, his
height is high.")
いもうとはかみが{長|なが}いです。 — My younger sister has long hair.
{母|はは}は{目|め}が{大|おお}きいです。 — My mother has big eyes. ({目|め} = eye)
{父|ちち}はせがあまり{高|たか}くないです。 — My father isn't very tall.

| Feature | Words |
|---|---|
| height (せ) | せが{高|たか}い (tall), せがひくい (short) |
| hair (かみ) | かみが{長|なが}い (long), かみがみじかい (short) |
| age | わかい (young) |
| looks | かわいい (cute), きれい (pretty, beautiful) |
| personality | やさしい (kind), しんせつ (kind, helpful), おもしろい (funny), {元気|げんき} (lively) |

Before a noun, the whole phrase can describe a person: せが{高|たか}い{人|ひと} (a tall person),
かみが{長|なが}い{女|おんな}の{人|ひと} (a woman with long hair). Don't say {高|たか}い{人|ひと} on its own
for "a tall person": with people, height needs せが.

わかい is for people and animals, not things: a new car is {新|あたら}しい{車|くるま}, never
わかい{車|くるま}. And remember from Lesson 11 that {古|ふる}い is never for people.

## Men, women, boys and girls

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {男|おとこ}の{人|ひと} | man |
| {女|おんな}の{人|ひと} | woman |
| {男|おとこ}の{子|こ} | boy |
| {女|おんな}の{子|こ} | girl |

{男|おとこ} and {女|おんな} on their own exist, but they sound blunt, even rude, about a person.
Use {男|おとこ}の{人|ひと} and {女|おんな}の{人|ひと}: あの{女|おんな}の{人|ひと}はだれですか (who's that
woman?).

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | Readings | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 父 | father | on: フ · kun: ちち; とう in お{父|とう}さん | 4 | {父|ちち}, お{父|とう}さん |
| 母 | mother | on: ボ · kun: はは; かあ in お{母|かあ}さん | 5 | {母|はは}, お{母|かあ}さん |
| 子 | child | on: シ · kun: こ | 3 | {子|こ}ども, お{子|こ}さん, {女|おんな}の{子|こ} |
| 女 | woman | on: ジョ, ニョ · kun: おんな | 3 | {女|おんな}の{人|ひと}, {女|おんな}の{子|こ} |
| 男 | man | on: ダン, ナン · kun: おとこ | 7 | {男|おとこ}の{人|ひと}, {男|おとこ}の{子|こ} |

Memory notes:

- 父 is two short strokes over a big cross: a father's strong arms crossed, two worry lines on
  his forehead.
- 母 is a mother holding a baby; the two dots inside are the baby she carries.
- 子 is a baby wrapped up tight, with only its arms free: the line across.
- 女 is a woman sitting gracefully with her legs folded under her.
- 男 is a rice field on top and a sign for strength below: in old farming villages, the man
  was the one who put his strength into the field. Count the strokes: the field is 5, the
  strength 2.

## Dialogue: a family photo

```dialogue
# A family photo
たなか: それはごかぞくのしゃしんですか。
= Is that a photo of your family?
エマ: はい、そうです。{父|ちち}と{母|はは}とあにといもうとです。
= Yes, it is. My father, my mother, my older brother and my younger sister.
たなか: {五人|ごにん}かぞくですね。おにいさんはせが{高|たか}いですね。
= So there are five of you. Your brother is tall, isn't he?
エマ: ええ。あにはわたしより{十|じゅっ}センチ{高|たか}いです。
= Yes. He's ten centimetres taller than me.
たなか: おにいさんはけっこんしていますか。
= Is your brother married?
エマ: はい、けっこんしています。{子|こ}どもが{二人|ふたり}います。
= Yes, he is. He has two children.
たなか: いもうとさんはかわいいですね。おいくつですか。
= Your sister is cute. How old is she?
エマ: {十五|じゅうご}さいです。とても{元気|げんき}ですよ。たなかさんは、ごきょうだいがいますか。
= She's fifteen. She's very lively. Do you have any brothers or sisters, Mr Tanaka?
たなか: いいえ、いません。{一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ}です。
= No, I don't. I'm an only child.
```

しゃしん = photo; センチ = centimetre ({十|じゅっ}センチ, 10 cm: じゅう shortens to じゅっ before
some sounds, as you saw with numbers in Lesson 3); {一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ} = an only child. Look at
the two sets at work: エマ says {父|ちち}, あに, いもうと about her own family, and たなか says
ごかぞく, おにいさん, いもうとさん about hers. Notice also あにはわたしより{十|じゅっ}センチ
{高|たか}いです: より from Lesson 14, with the amount before the adjective.

## Reading: my family

> わたしのかぞくは{四人|よにん}です。{父|ちち}と{母|はは}とおとうととわたしです。{父|ちち}は{五十|ごじゅう}さいです。せがとても{高|たか}いです。{母|はは}は{父|ちち}より{二|に}さいわかいです。かみが{長|なが}いです。とてもやさしいです。おとうとは{高校生|こうこうせい}です。サッカーが{上手|じょうず}です。でも、べんきょうはあまりすきじゃないです。そふとそぼはいなかにいます。

There are four people in my family: my father, my mother, my younger brother and me. My father
is fifty. He's very tall. My mother is two years younger than my father. She has long hair.
She's very kind. My younger brother is a high-school student. He's good at football. But he
doesn't much like studying. My grandparents live in the countryside. (いなか = the countryside;
{高校生|こうこうせい} = high-school student; サッカー = football, soccer.)

より{二|に}さいわかい puts the difference (two years) before the adjective, just like
{十|じゅっ}センチ{高|たか}い in the dialogue. And look: the writer uses {上手|じょうず} about a younger brother, which is fine. It's only about
yourself that {上手|じょうず} sounds like bragging.

## Say it

```speak
{何人|なんにん}かぞくですか。
= How many people are in your family?
{四人|よにん}かぞくです。
= There are four of us.
あにが{一人|ひとり}います。
= I have one older brother.
ごきょうだいがいますか。
= Do you have any brothers or sisters?
あねはけっこんしています。
= My older sister is married.
{父|ちち}はせが{高|たか}いです。
= My father is tall.
```

## Common mistakes

- Using the polite words for your own family to outsiders: うちのお{父|とう}さんは… in a polite
  conversation. Say {父|ちち}は….
- Using the modest words for someone else's family: たなかさんの{母|はは}. Say たなかさんの
  お{母|かあ}さん.
- よんにん or しにん for four people. It's よにん.
- いちにん, ににん. One and two people are ひとり and ふたり.
- A particle after the number: あにが{一人|ひとり}がいます. The number takes no particle:
  あにが{一人|ひとり}います.
- あります for people: きょうだいがあります. People and animals take います.
- けっこんします for "I'm married". That's "I'll get married"; "I'm married" is
  けっこんしています.
- {高|たか}い{人|ひと} for a tall person. Say せが{高|たか}い{人|ひと}.

## Key points

- Own family (modest): {父|ちち}, {母|はは}, あに, あね, おとうと, いもうと, かぞく.
- Someone else's (polite): お{父|とう}さん, お{母|かあ}さん, おにいさん, おねえさん, おとうとさん,
  いもうとさん, ごかぞく. Inside the family, the polite words are also used to address older
  relatives.
- People: {一人|ひとり}, {二人|ふたり}, then 〜{人|にん} ({三人|さんにん}, {四人|よにん}…); ask
  {何人|なんにん}.
- N が [number] います: あにが{一人|ひとり}います.
- けっこんしています = is married.
- Describing people: AはBが〜です: せが{高|たか}い, かみが{長|なが}い.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Seasons and nature in Japan
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 13 you learned はる, なつ, あき, ふゆ and the words for weather. This honors lesson
looks at what the seasons actually mean in Japan: the rainy season, cherry-blossom picnics,
summer fireworks, autumn leaves, and the way people use the weather to start a conversation or
a letter. At the end you'll read a short weather forecast of the kind you hear on Japanese TV
every evening.

Japan stretches a long way from north to south, from snowy ほっかいどう to subtropical
おきなわ, so the dates below are for the middle of the country, around Tokyo and Osaka; the
north is later, the south earlier.

## Spring: さくら and {花見|はなみ}

さくら is the cherry tree and its blossom, the symbol of spring. Around Tokyo the blossoms open
in late March or early April and last only a week or so before the petals fall. Because the
blooming moves slowly up the country from south to north, TV news follows it on a map, and
forecasters announce when each city's trees are expected to open.

{花見|はなみ} (literally "flower viewing") means going out to look at the blossoms, usually as a
picnic with friends, family or colleagues under the trees, with food and drink on a blue
plastic sheet. In popular parks, people arrive early in the morning to save a good spot for
their group, and on a sunny weekend the parks are full.

さくらがとてもきれいですね。 — The cherry blossoms are beautiful, aren't they?
{日曜日|にちようび}に、{友|とも}だちと{花見|はなみ}をしました。 — On Sunday I had a
blossom-viewing picnic with friends.

The Japanese school and business year starts in April, so さくら also goes with new beginnings:
the first day at school or at a new job.

## The rainy season: つゆ

In June, most of Japan enters つゆ, the rainy season. It lasts about six weeks, until mid or
late July. It doesn't rain all day every day, but the sky is often grey, it drizzles a lot, and
the air is warm and damp. Laundry won't dry, and people carry an umbrella everywhere. Hokkaido
has almost no rainy season, and in Okinawa it comes earlier, in May.

The flower of つゆ is the hydrangea (あじさい), which blooms blue and purple in the rain.

{今日|きょう}も{雨|あめ}ですね。 — Rain again today, isn't it?
つゆはあまりすきじゃないです。 — I don't much like the rainy season.

## Summer: むしあつい, {花火|はなび} and たいふう

After つゆ ends, summer is hot and very humid. The word for this sticky heat is むしあつい
(hot and humid): むしあついですね is the summer small-talk line. Summer is also the season of
festivals (まつり) and of {花火|はなび}, fireworks: big fireworks displays over rivers and
bays draw huge crowds, many people in light cotton kimono called ゆかた.

Late summer and early autumn bring たいふう, typhoons, which cross or pass near Japan most
years, with strong wind and heavy rain ({大雨|おおあめ}). The forecast follows each one closely.

{花火|はなび}はとてもきれいでした。 — The fireworks were really beautiful.

## Autumn: もみじ

あき is cool and often clear: many people say it's the best season. In late autumn the leaves
turn red and yellow. もみじ is the Japanese maple and its red autumn leaves; going to see them is
as popular as {花見|はなみ} in spring. Around Tokyo the colours peak in late November or early
December, earlier in the mountains and the north.

{山|やま}のもみじがとてもきれいでした。 — The autumn leaves in the mountains were beautiful.

## Winter: snow on one side, sun on the other

Winter is very different depending on where you are. On the side of Japan that faces the Sea
of Japan, and in the mountains, it snows heavily, sometimes several metres in a winter. On the
Pacific side, where Tokyo is, winter is cold but mostly dry and sunny, and snow is rare enough
to make the news.

とうきょうはふゆもはれの{日|ひ}が{多|おお}いです。 — Even in winter Tokyo has a lot of sunny days.

## The weather as a greeting

In English, talking about the weather can sound like you have nothing to say. In Japanese it's
a normal, friendly way to greet a neighbour or start a chat, and the other person is expected to
agree. The ね at the end invites them to:

| Season | Line | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| any | いい{天気|てんき}ですね。 | Lovely weather, isn't it? |
| spring | あたたかくなりましたね。 | It's got warmer, hasn't it? |
| つゆ | よくふりますね。 | It really keeps raining, doesn't it? |
| summer | むしあついですね。 | Hot and sticky, isn't it? |
| autumn | すずしくなりましたね。 | It's got cooler, hasn't it? |
| winter | さむいですね。 | Cold, isn't it? |

なりました means "has become"; you'll learn how adjectives join なる in Lesson 26. For now,
use these as set phrases. The usual answer is ええ, ほんとうに (Yes, really), or a repeat of the
line: ええ、さむいですね.

Letters and formal emails in Japanese traditionally open with a line about the season before
getting to the point, something like "The cherry blossoms are out at last" or "The heat goes on
day after day". You'll write short messages in Lesson 30h2.

## A weather forecast

A TV or radio forecast uses words you know, plus a few set expressions:

| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {天気|てんき}よほう | weather forecast |
| はれのちくもり | sunny, cloudy later ("sunny, later cloudy") |
| くもりときどき{雨|あめ} | cloudy with occasional rain |
| さいこうきおん | the high (highest temperature) |
| さいていきおん | the low (lowest temperature) |
| 〜ど | degrees (Celsius) |
| 〜でしょう | will probably be (Lesson 24) |

のち means "later, then", and ときどき means "sometimes". Japan uses degrees Celsius:
{三十|さんじゅう}ど is a hot summer day, and {五|ご}ど a cold winter one.

> あしたの{天気|てんき}です。{東|ひがし}{日本|にほん}は{午前|ごぜん}ははれですが、{午後|ごご}はくもりときどき{雨|あめ}でしょう。さいこうきおんは{二十八|にじゅうはち}ど、さいていきおんは{二十|にじゅう}どです。かさをわすれないでください。

Here's tomorrow's weather. In eastern Japan it will be sunny in the morning, but in the
afternoon it will probably be cloudy with occasional rain. The high will be 28 degrees and the
low 20. Don't forget your umbrella. (わすれないでください = please don't forget, a form you'll
learn in Lesson 22.)

## Dialogue: small talk with a neighbour

```dialogue
# Small talk with a neighbour
すずき: おはようございます。むしあついですね。
= Good morning. Hot and sticky, isn't it?
エマ: おはようございます。ほんとうにあついですね。つゆはもうおわりですか。
= Good morning. It really is. Is the rainy season over now?
すずき: ええ、きのうおわりました。これから{毎日|まいにち}あついですよ。
= Yes, it ended yesterday. From now on it's hot every day.
エマ: そうですか。わたしはなつより、あきのほうがすきです。
= Oh dear. I like autumn better than summer.
すずき: わたしもです。でも、なつは{花火|はなび}がありますよ。{土曜日|どようび}に{川|かわ}で{花火|はなび}があります。
= Me too. But summer has fireworks. There's a fireworks display at the river on Saturday.
エマ: いいですね！
= Oh, lovely!
```

もう = already, now; おわり = the end, おわりました = ended; これから = from now on. Notice
すずき's opening line: the weather first, then the conversation.

## Key points

- さくら blooms around late March and early April; {花見|はなみ} is a picnic under the blossoms.
- つゆ, the rainy season, runs from June to mid or late July in most of Japan.
- Summer is むしあつい, with {花火|はなび}, festivals and, later, たいふう.
- もみじ, the red autumn leaves, peak around late November near Tokyo.
- Winter is snowy on the Sea of Japan side and dry and sunny on the Pacific side.
- Weather lines ending in ね are everyday greetings; agree with ええ、ほんとうに.
- Forecasts: はれのちくもり (sunny, then cloudy), くもりときどき{雨|あめ} (cloudy, occasional
  rain), temperatures in 〜ど.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Talking about people
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 15 gave you the two sets of family words and the pattern for describing someone:
あにはせが{高|たか}いです. This honors lesson goes further: more words for looks and
personality, the rest of the family (grandparents, uncles and aunts, husbands and wives), and
how ちゃん and くん work inside a Japanese family, where people are often called by their role
rather than their name.

## Looks

You already have せが{高|たか}い, かみが{長|なが}い, {目|め}が{大|おお}きい, わかい, かわいい and
きれい. Some more:

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| かっこいい | cool, good-looking (mostly of men) | negative かっこよくない, like いい |
| ハンサム | handsome | a な-adjective; sounds a little old-fashioned |
| きれい | beautiful, pretty | な-adjective; for women, places, things |
| かわいい | cute | for children, animals, things, and often young women |

かわいい is one of the most used words in Japanese: people say it about clothes, shops, food,
pets and little drawings. かっこいい is the everyday word for an attractive man, a cool car or a
stylish jacket.

A few descriptions use a verb form from Lesson 17. Learn them as set phrases for now:

- めがねをかけています — wears glasses
- ふとっています — is heavy, is plump (careful: about other people this is rude)
- やせています — is slim, is thin

あの{人|ひと}はめがねをかけています。 — That person wears glasses.

Japanese people rarely comment on someone's body or weight to their face, and the same goes
for age. Compliments on clothes (かわいいですね, すてきですね) are safer.

## Personality

| Word | Meaning | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| あかるい | cheerful, outgoing (literally "bright") | い-adjective |
| くらい | gloomy, withdrawn (literally "dark") | い-adjective |
| やさしい | kind, gentle | い-adjective |
| おもしろい | funny, fun to be with | い-adjective |
| しんせつ | kind, helpful (to others) | な-adjective |
| まじめ | serious, hard-working, earnest | な-adjective |
| しずか | quiet | な-adjective |
| にぎやか | lively, chatty | な-adjective |
| {元気|げんき} | energetic, full of life | な-adjective |

あかるい{人|ひと} is high praise: someone who lifts the mood. くらい about a person is harsh, so
don't use it to someone's face. まじめ is usually a compliment in Japan (reliable, takes work
seriously), though まじめすぎる (too serious) is not.

やさしい and しんせつ both translate as "kind". やさしい is about a person's nature (gentle,
warm, easy-going with others); しんせつ is about what they do for you (helpful, going out of
their way). A stranger who shows you the way to the station is しんせつ; a grandmother is
やさしい.

The question, as in Lesson 12, is どんな:

おねえさんはどんな{人|ひと}ですか。 — What's your older sister like?
あかるい{人|ひと}です。それに、とてもまじめです。 — She's cheerful. And she's very
hard-working. (それに = and also, what's more)

## The rest of the family

| | My own (modest) | Someone else's (polite) |
|---|---|---|
| grandfather | そふ | おじいさん |
| grandmother | そぼ | おばあさん |
| uncle | おじ | おじさん |
| aunt | おば | おばさん |
| husband | おっと (or しゅじん) | ごしゅじん |
| wife | つま | おくさん |

Listen carefully to the long vowels. おじいさん (grandfather) and おじさん (uncle), おばあさん
(grandmother) and おばさん (aunt) differ only in the length of one vowel, as you saw in the kana
course. Say おじいさん with a clear "jii".

For husband and wife, the old words しゅじん ("master") and かない ("inside the house") are
still heard, but many people now prefer the neutral おっと and つま. For someone else's
spouse, ごしゅじん and おくさん are the standard polite words:

おくさんはお{元気|げんき}ですか。 — How is your wife?
つまは{会社|かいしゃ}いんです。 — My wife works for a company.

Cousins are いとこ, and an only child is {一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ}, which you met in the Lesson 15
dialogue.

## ちゃん and くん in the family

You learned in Lesson 5h1 that ちゃん is a friendly title for children and close friends, and
くん for boys and young men. Inside families they're everywhere:

- Older siblings are called by their role, usually with ちゃん: おにいちゃん, おねえちゃん. Small
  children and teenagers alike use these.
- Grandparents become おじいちゃん and おばあちゃん: warmer and more childlike than
  おじいさん and おばあさん.
- Younger siblings and children are called by their names, often with ちゃん (ゆきちゃん,
  たろうちゃん), and boys at school with くん (けんくん).
- Small children often call their parents パパ and ママ; later most switch to お{父|とう}さん and
  お{母|かあ}さん.

There's an interesting rule underneath: a family often names people from the point of view of
its youngest member. Once a couple has children, the parents may call each other
お{父|とう}さん and お{母|かあ}さん (or パパ and ママ), the way the children do, and grandparents
may call their own son "お{父|とう}さん" when the grandchildren are there. A mother may even
call her older child おにいちゃん, because that's what he is to the little one.

## Family words for strangers

Family words are also used for people you don't know at all:

| Word | Used for |
|---|---|
| おにいさん | a young man (a waiter, a shop assistant) |
| おねえさん | a young woman |
| おじさん | a middle-aged man |
| おばさん | a middle-aged woman |
| おじいさん, おばあさん | an elderly man or woman |

A child might say あのおじさん for "that man". Be careful as an adult: being called おばさん or
おじさん can feel like being told you look old. Shop staff tend to use おきゃくさま (honoured
customer) and avoid them altogether.

## Dialogue: the new teacher

```dialogue
# The new teacher
ゆい: {新|あたら}しい{先生|せんせい}はどんな{人|ひと}ですか。
= What's the new teacher like?
けん: やさしい{人|ひと}ですよ。それに、とてもおもしろいです。
= He's nice. And he's really funny.
ゆい: わかいですか。
= Is he young?
けん: ええ、わかいです。せが{高|たか}いです。めがねをかけています。
= Yes, he's young. He's tall. He wears glasses.
ゆい: かっこいいですか。
= Is he good-looking?
けん: うーん、ふつうです。でも、とてもまじめな{先生|せんせい}です。
= Hmm, he's ordinary. But he's a very hard-working teacher.
ゆい: けっこんしていますか。
= Is he married?
けん: はい。おくさんも{先生|せんせい}ですよ。
= Yes. His wife is a teacher too.
```

ふつう = ordinary, average (a な-adjective); うーん = hmm.
Native speakers do this kind of thing all the time.

## Key points

- Looks: かっこいい, ハンサム, きれい, かわいい; set phrases めがねをかけています, やせています.
- Personality: あかるい, まじめ, やさしい (by nature), しんせつ (helpful), しずか, にぎやか.
- Grandparents: そふ / そぼ (mine), おじいさん / おばあさん (yours). Uncles and aunts: おじ / おば,
  おじさん / おばさん. Watch the long vowels.
- Spouses: おっと, つま (mine); ごしゅじん, おくさん (yours).
- In families, older relatives are called by role (おにいちゃん, おばあちゃん), younger ones by
  name + ちゃん; people are often named from the youngest child's point of view.
- おにいさん, おねえさん, おじさん, おばさん also mean "that young man", "that middle-aged
  woman" and so on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The て form and requests
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far every verb you've used has ended in ます: {食|た}べます, {行|い}きます, {見|み}ました. That's
enough to say what you do. It isn't enough to ask someone to do something, to say what's
happening right now, or to join two actions in one sentence. For all of that Japanese uses one
form of the verb, the **[[て form]]**: {書|か}いて, {読|よ}んで, {食|た}べて, して.

The て form is the most useful form you'll learn this year. This whole module is built on it:
this lesson shows how to make it and uses it for requests (please do…); lesson 17 adds います
for "is doing"; lesson 18 uses it to put actions in order; lesson 19 builds permission and
rules on it. Learn to make it quickly now and the next four lessons are easy.

## Verb groups, again

In lesson 7 you sorted verbs into three groups by how they make the ます form. The same groups
decide the て form, so it pays to be sure of them.

| Group | What it looks like | ます form | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ends in an u-sound: う つ る む ぶ ぬ く ぐ す | u → i + ます | {書|か}く → {書|か}きます, {話|はな}す → {話|はな}します |
| 2 | ends in -iる or -eる | drop る + ます | {食|た}べる → {食|た}べます, {見|み}る → {見|み}ます |
| 3 | only two verbs | irregular | する → します, {来|く}る → {来|き}ます |

The trap is group 1 verbs that end in -iる or -eる and look like group 2. There aren't many,
but they're common: かえる (to go home), {入|はい}る (to enter), しる (to know), はしる (to run),
きる (to cut), いる (to need). You can't see the group in the dictionary form; you have to
learn it with the word. The ます form gives it away: group 1 keeps an り (かえります,
{入|はい}ります, はしります), group 2 has none ({食|た}べます, {見|み}ます). Verbs ending in -aる,
-uる or -oる (わかる, うる, とる, つくる, すわる) are always group 1, apart from the two group 3 verbs
する and {来|く}る.

From now on your word list gives each verb's group and its ます and て forms in the note.

## Making the て form

### Group 2: just add て

Drop the る and add て. That's all.

| Dictionary form | ます form | て form |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べます | {食|た}べて |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}ます | {見|み}て |
| おしえる | おしえます | おしえて |
| あける | あけます | あけて |
| {見|み}せる | {見|み}せます | {見|み}せて |

### Group 3: して and きて

する → して, {来|く}る → {来|き}て. Every する verb follows: べんきょうする → べんきょうして,
{電話|でんわ}する → {電話|でんわ}して. Notice {来|く}る changes its vowel: the て form is {来|き}て, read "kite",
like the ます form {来|き}ます.

### Group 1: the sound changes

Group 1 verbs don't just add て. The end of the verb changes to make the word easier to say.
This is the **[[sound change]]**, and it follows the last kana of the dictionary form:

| Last kana | becomes | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| う つ る | って | かう → かって, まつ → まって, かえる → かえって |
| む ぶ ぬ | んで | {読|よ}む → {読|よ}んで, よぶ → よんで, しぬ → しんで |
| く | いて | {書|か}く → {書|か}いて, {聞|き}く → {聞|き}いて |
| ぐ | いで | いそぐ → いそいで |
| す | して | {話|はな}す → {話|はな}して, かす → かして |

Three things to notice:

- The んで row has で, not て. So does the ぐ row: いそいで. The voiced ending comes from a
  voiced sound (む, ぶ, ぬ, ぐ).
- う, つ and る all end the same way, with a small っ. So かう (to buy) and かつ (to win) both
  give かって: context tells you which.
- ぬ has only one everyday verb, しぬ (to die). You'll rarely need it, but it completes the
  pattern.

### The one exception: {行|い}く

{行|い}く ends in く, so it "should" become {行|い}いて. It doesn't: it's {行|い}って. This is the
only group 1 verb that breaks the rule, and it's one of the most common verbs in the
language, so it's worth saying aloud a few times: {行|い}って、{行|い}って、{行|い}って.

### A way to remember

Group the endings into three sounds you can chant: "u-tsu-ru, tte; mu-bu-nu, nde; ku-ite,
gu-ide, su-shite". Say it every day this week and you'll stop needing the table.

Another route, if you know the ます form better than the dictionary form: drop ます and look
at the last kana. い, ち, り → って (かいます → かって); み, び, に → んで; き → いて; ぎ → いで;
し → して. If the verb is group 2, the stem plus て is the answer ({食|た}べ → {食|た}べて).

## Please do: 〜てください

The て form + ください is a polite request: "please do …". You know ください from shopping
(これをください, "this, please"); here it follows a verb.

{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてください。 — Please write your name.
ちょっとまってください。 — Please wait a moment.
もういちど{言|い}ってください。 — Please say it once more.
ゆっくり{話|はな}してください。 — Please speak slowly. (ゆっくり = slowly)
どうぞ、すわってください。 — Please, have a seat.

Particles stay the same as in a ます sentence: the object keeps を, a place keeps に or で. Only
the verb changes.

〜てください sounds polite, but it is still a request the listener is expected to follow.
Teachers, doctors, shop staff and signs use it constantly: こちらに{来|き}てください (please
come this way). It's also what you say when you offer something: どうぞ、{食|た}べてください
(please, eat).

## Would you please…? 〜てくださいませんか

When you're asking a favour, especially of a stranger or someone above you, make it a
question: 〜てくださいませんか, literally "won't you please …?". It's softer and more polite.

すみません、しゃしんをとってくださいませんか。 — Excuse me, would you mind taking our photo?
ペンをかしてくださいませんか。 — Could you lend me a pen?
ちょっとてつだってくださいませんか。 — Could you give me a hand?

You'll often hear すみません at the start. If someone asks you, agree with いいですよ or はい、
どうぞ; to decline politely, use the ちょっと… you learned in lesson 10.

| Pattern | Feels like | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| 〜てください | please do | instructions, offers, simple requests |
| 〜てくださいませんか | would you please | favours, strangers, people above you |

## Kanji

Five kanji for the things people do with words. You've seen three of the verbs in kana since
the kana course (かく, よむ, いう); now they get their kanji.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 書 | write | ショ | か(く) | 10 | {書|か}く, {書|か}いてください |
| 読 | read | ドク | よ(む) | 14 | {読|よ}む, {読書|どくしょ} (reading for pleasure) |
| 聞 | hear, listen, ask | ブン, モン | き(く) | 14 | {聞|き}く, {新聞|しんぶん} (newspaper) |
| 話 | talk, story | ワ | はな(す), はなし | 13 | {話|はな}す, {話|はなし}, {電話|でんわ} |
| 言 | say, word | ゲン, ゴン | い(う), こと | 7 | {言|い}う |

Memory notes:

- 言 looks like words coming out of a mouth (口) with lines of speech stacked above it. It
  appears on the left of 読, 話 and 語 (lesson 18): every one is about language.
- 聞 is an ear (耳, lesson 19) inside the two doors of a gate: listening at the gate.
- 書 has a brush held in a hand at the top and a shape like 日 at the bottom: writing in daylight.
- 話 is words (言) plus, on the right, a shape that pictures a tongue: talking.

{聞|き}く covers listen, hear and ask: ラジオを{聞|き}く (listen to the radio), {先生|せんせい}に{聞|き}く (ask the teacher). The person you ask takes に.

The noun {話|はなし} (talk, story) is written with the kanji alone, no okurigana; the verb is
{話|はな}す.

## Dialogue: in class

```dialogue
# In class
{先生|せんせい}: では、{二十|にじゅう}ページを{見|み}てください。
= Right then, please look at page twenty.
エマ: すみません、{先生|せんせい}。もういちど{言|い}ってくださいませんか。
= Excuse me, could you say that again, please?
{先生|せんせい}: はい。{二十|にじゅう}ページです。
= Of course. Page twenty.
エマ: わかりました。
= OK.
{先生|せんせい}: このぶんを{読|よ}んでください。{大|おお}きいこえで。
= Please read this sentence. In a loud voice.
エマ: 「わたしは{毎日|まいにち}{新聞|しんぶん}を{読|よ}みます。」
= "I read the newspaper every day."
{先生|せんせい}: いいですね。じゃあ、ノートに{書|か}いてください。
= Good. Now please write it in your notebook.
エマ: すみません、ペンをわすれました。かしてくださいませんか。
= Sorry, I forgot my pen. Could you lend me one?
{先生|せんせい}: はい、どうぞ。このペンをつかってください。
= Sure, here. Use this pen.
```

ぶん = sentence; ページ = page; ノート = notebook.

## Say it

```speak
ちょっとまってください。
= Please wait a moment.
もういちど{言|い}ってください。
= Please say it once more.
ゆっくり{話|はな}してください。
= Please speak slowly.
{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてください。
= Please write your name.
しゃしんをとってくださいませんか。
= Would you mind taking a photo?
いそいでください。
= Please hurry.
```

## Common mistakes

- {行|い}いて for {行|い}って. {行|い}く is the one exception; every other く verb takes いて.
- Treating かえる, {入|はい}る or しる as group 2: かえて, {入|はい}て, して. They're group 1:
  かえって, {入|はい}って, しって.
- て where the rule needs で: {読|よ}んて, いそいて. After ん and after the ぐ change, it's で.
- Mixing up かす (lend) and かりる (borrow). If you want the other person to give you their pen
  for a while, they lend: ペンをかしてください.
- Using 〜てください for a favour from a stranger. It isn't rude, but 〜てくださいませんか (with
  すみません first) is kinder.
- Forgetting {来|く}る changes its vowel: {来|く}て is wrong; it's {来|き}て.

## Key points

- The て form joins actions and is the base of many patterns.
- Group 2: drop る, add て. Group 3: して, {来|き}て.
- Group 1 sound changes: う つ る → って; む ぶ ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して.
  The exception: {行|い}く → {行|い}って.
- Some -iる/-eる verbs are group 1 (かえる, {入|はい}る, しる, はしる, きる "cut"); their ます form
  has り.
- 〜てください: please do. 〜てくださいませんか: would you please (more polite).
- New kanji: 書 読 聞 話 言.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: 〜ています
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 16 you learned to make the て form. Put います after it and you get the
**[[ている form]]**: {読|よ}んでいます, {食|た}べています, けっこんしています. It's one of the most
common shapes in Japanese, and it answers questions like "what are you doing?", "where do you
live?", "do you know…?" and "what is she wearing?".

The surprise for English speakers is that it doesn't always mean "-ing". This lesson sorts out
its three meanings, then uses it to describe what people are wearing.

The います is the same いる you know from lesson 5 (people and animals "are" somewhere). It's
group 2, so it changes like any ます verb: います, いません, いました, いませんでした.

## Meaning 1: doing it right now

With verbs for activities that take a while ({食|た}べる, {読|よ}む, {話|はな}す, まつ, {聞|き}く),
〜ています is an **[[action in progress]]**, like English "is doing":

{今|いま}、{何|なに}をしていますか。 — What are you doing now?
{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいます。 — I'm reading a book.
エマさんは{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}しています。 — Emma is talking on the phone.
{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}で{友|とも}だちをまっています。 — I'm waiting for a friend in front of the station.

Compare the ます form, which is for habits and the future: {本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます is "I read
books" or "I'll read a book", not "I'm reading one now".

## Meaning 2: doing it regularly

The same form describes something you do repeatedly over a period, a bit like "I've been
doing" or "these days I do":

{毎日|まいにち}{日本語|にほんご}をべんきょうしています。 — I study Japanese every day.
{父|ちち}は{毎日|まいにち}{新聞|しんぶん}を{読|よ}んでいます。 — My father reads the paper every day.

Jobs and long-term activities work this way too. つとめる (to work for) is almost always used
like this: あにはぎんこうにつとめています (my brother works for a bank; ぎんこう = bank).

## Meaning 3: a state that results from a change

Some verbs describe a change that happens in a moment: you get married, you move somewhere to
live, you get to know something, you go in, you go out, you put on clothes. With these verbs,
〜ています is a **[[resulting state]]**: the change happened earlier, and its result is still
true now.

| Verb | 〜ています | Means | Not |
|---|---|---|---|
| けっこんする (marry) | けっこんしています | is married | is getting married |
| すむ (come to live) | すんでいます | lives (somewhere) | — |
| しる (get to know) | しっています | knows | is learning |
| {出|で}かける (go out) | {出|で}かけています | is out | — |
| {来|く}る (come) | {来|き}ています | has come, is here | is coming |
| {行|い}く (go) | {行|い}っています | has gone, is there | is going |
| きる (put on) | きています | is wearing | — |

あねはけっこんしています。 — My sister is married.
おおさかにすんでいます。 — I live in Osaka.
{母|はは}は{今|いま}{出|で}かけています。 — My mother is out right now.
{父|ちち}は{今|いま}{外国|がいこく}へ{行|い}っています。 — My father is abroad at the moment (he's gone and
is there).

The last two rows trip up everyone. {行|い}っています never means "I'm on my way"; for that, say
{今|いま}{行|い}きます ("I'm coming / I'm going now").

### すむ and the place

すむ takes に for the place, and it's nearly always in the ている form:

どこにすんでいますか。 — Where do you live?
とうきょうにすんでいます。 — I live in Tokyo.

### しっています and しりません

しる is a group 1 verb (しります, しって) even though it ends in -iる. "I know" is
しっています. But "I don't know" is not しっていません: it's しりません.

あの{人|ひと}をしっていますか。 — Do you know that person?
はい、しっています。 — Yes, I do.
いいえ、しりません。 — No, I don't.

Don't confuse しりません (I don't know that fact, I've never met that person) with わかりません
(I don't understand). If someone asks you a question you can't answer, わかりません is softer
and more common in everyday talk; しりません can sound blunt, "no idea". For a fact you have
never heard of, しりません is right.

### Which meaning?

Context and the verb decide. A useful test: can you do it for an hour? {読|よ}む, {食|た}べる,
まつ: yes, so 〜ています is usually "is doing". けっこんする, しる, {入|はい}る, {来|く}る: no, they
happen in a moment, so 〜ています is the resulting state.

In speech the い often drops: {読|よ}んでます, しってます. That's casual; write the full form.

## Getting dressed: clothing verbs

English says "wear" or "put on" for everything. Japanese chooses the verb by where the
clothing goes on your body. Using the wrong one sounds as odd as "I'm wearing my glasses on
my feet".

| Verb | For | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| きる (group 2) | the top half or the whole body | シャツ, セーター, コート, ふく |
| はく (group 1) | the legs and feet | ズボン, スカート, くつ, くつした |
| かぶる (group 1) | the head | ぼうし |
| かける (group 2) | glasses | めがね |
| する (group 3) | accessories | ネクタイ, とけい |

All of these describe the moment of putting something on. So "is wearing" is the resulting
state: シャツをきています ("has put on a shirt" = is wearing a shirt). The opposite for almost
everything is ぬぐ (to take off): くつをぬいでください. Glasses are taken off with とる.

{白|しろ}いシャツをきています。 — He's wearing a white shirt.
くろいズボンをはいています。 — He's wearing black trousers.
{子|こ}どもはぼうしをかぶっています。 — The child is wearing a hat.
たなかさんはめがねをかけています。 — Ms Tanaka wears glasses.

### Two verbs called きる

きる (to wear) is group 2: きます, きて. きる (to cut) is group 1: きります, きって. They sound
the same in the dictionary form and split in every other form:

セーターをきています。 — I'm wearing a sweater.
パンをきっています。 — I'm cutting the bread.

The kanji are different too, but neither is in this course.

## Kanji

Three kanji for moving and standing.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 立 | stand | リツ | た(つ) | 5 | {立|た}つ |
| 入 | enter, put in | ニュウ | はい(る), い(れる) | 2 | {入|はい}る, {入|い}れる, {入口|いりぐち} |
| 出 | go out, put out | シュツ | で(る), だ(す) | 5 | {出|で}る, {出|だ}す, {出|で}かける, {出口|でぐち} |

Memory notes:

- 立 is a person standing on the ground with arms out: the line at the bottom is the floor.
- 入 is two legs stepping in through a doorway. Don't confuse it with 人 (person): in 入 the
  right-hand stroke rises to the top point and the short left stroke leans against it; in 人 it's
  the left-hand stroke that reaches the top.
- 出 is two mountain shapes (山) stacked: something rising up and out.

入 and 出 each give a pair of verbs: one for moving yourself, one for moving something else
(which takes を). Watch the groups, because they cross over: {入|はい}る is group 1 but
{入|い}れる is group 2; {出|で}る is group 2 but {出|だ}す is group 1.

| Something moves by itself | You move something |
|---|---|
| {入|はい}る (group 1): へやに{入|はい}る — go into the room | {入|い}れる (group 2): コーヒーにさとうを{入|い}れる — put sugar in coffee |
| {出|で}る (group 2): うちを{出|で}る — leave home | {出|だ}す (group 1): しゅくだいを{出|だ}す — hand in homework |

{出|で}る takes を for the place you leave: {駅|えき}を{出|で}ます. {入|はい}る takes に for the place
you enter: {駅|えき}に{入|はい}ります. The signs you'll see everywhere: {入口|いりぐち} (entrance) and
{出口|でぐち} (exit). 口 means mouth; in these words it means an opening, and it's read ぐち.

## Dialogue: at the station

```dialogue
# Waiting at the station
ゆうき: もしもし、エマさん？{今|いま}どこにいますか。
= Hello, Emma? Where are you now?
エマ: {駅|えき}の{中|なか}です。{北口|きたぐち}の{前|まえ}で{立|た}っています。
= Inside the station. I'm standing in front of the north exit.
ゆうき: え、ぼくも{北口|きたぐち}にいますよ。どんなふくをきていますか。
= Huh, I'm at the north exit too. What are you wearing?
エマ: {白|しろ}いコートをきています。ぼうしもかぶっています。
= I'm wearing a white coat. And a hat.
ゆうき: ああ、わかりました。めがねをかけていますか。
= OK, got it. Are you wearing glasses?
エマ: いいえ、かけていません。ゆうきさんは？
= No, I'm not. What about you?
ゆうき: くろいセーターをきて、{手|て}をあげています。
= I'm in a black sweater, with my hand up.
エマ: あ、いました！
= Oh, there you are!
```

もしもし = hello (on the phone); {北口|きたぐち} = north exit (北, north, is lesson 21's kanji);
ぼく = I (used by men and boys); {手|て}をあげる = raise your hand. あ、いました！ is literally
"oh, (you) were (there)!", the natural thing to say when you spot someone.

## Reading: a family photo

> これはわたしのかぞくのしゃしんです。{父|ちち}はめがねをかけて、ネクタイをしています。{父|ちち}は
> {車|くるま}の{会社|かいしゃ}につとめています。{母|はは}は{白|しろ}いセーターをきています。{母|はは}は
> {高校|こうこう}の{先生|せんせい}です。あには{今|いま}カナダにすんでいます。あねはけっこんしています。
> しゃしんの{子|こ}どもは、あねの{子|こ}どもです。くろいぼうしをかぶっています。

This is a photo of my family. My father wears glasses and a tie. He works for a car company.
My mother is wearing a white sweater. She's a high school teacher. My older brother lives in
Canada now. My older sister is married. The child in the photo is my sister's child. He's
wearing a black hat.

## Say it

```speak
{今|いま}、{何|なに}をしていますか。
= What are you doing now?
どこにすんでいますか。
= Where do you live?
しっています。
= I know.
しりません。
= I don't know.
めがねをかけています。
= I wear glasses.
くつをぬいでください。
= Please take off your shoes.
```

## Common mistakes

- しっていません for "I don't know". It's しりません.
- Reading けっこんしています as "is getting married". It's "is married". "I'm getting married
  next month" is {来月|らいげつ}けっこんします.
- {行|い}っています for "I'm on my way". It means "has gone (and is there)".
- One verb for all clothing: くつをきます. Shoes, socks, trousers and skirts take はく.
- Treating しる and {入|はい}る as group 2: して, {入|はい}て. They're group 1: しって, {入|はい}って.
- すむ with で: とうきょうですんでいます. The place you live takes に.

## Key points

- 〜ています: an action in progress, a regular activity, or a state resulting from a change.
- Verbs that happen in a moment (けっこんする, すむ, しる, {来|く}る, {行|い}く, きる…) give a
  resulting state: けっこんしています, is married.
- しっています (I know), しりません (I don't know).
- Clothing: きる for the top or whole body, はく for legs and feet, かぶる for hats, かける for
  glasses, する for ties and watches; ぬぐ to take off.
- New kanji: 立 入 出, and the signs {入口|いりぐち} and {出口|でぐち}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Doing things in order
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Up to now each of your sentences has held one action. Real life comes in chains: I got up,
had breakfast and went to school; after class I asked the teacher a question; before the
test I memorized the words. This lesson gives you four ways to say what happens in what
order: a chain of て forms, 〜てから, 〜まえに and 〜のあとで. The setting is school and
language learning, and the new kanji are 校, 国 and 語.

## Chains of actions: 〜て、〜て、〜ます

To join actions that happen one after another, put every verb but the last in the て form.
The last verb decides the tense and the politeness for the whole sentence.

あさ{七時|しちじ}におきて、シャワーをあびて、{学校|がっこう}へ{行|い}きます。
— At seven I get up, take a shower and go to school. (シャワーをあびる = to take a shower)

きのうはうちにかえって、ばんごはんを{食|た}べて、ねました。
— Yesterday I went home, had dinner and went to bed.

The first sentence is about every day, because it ends in {行|い}きます; the second is about
the past, because it ends in ねました. The て forms in the middle have no tense of their own.
You never say おきました、シャワーをあびました… inside one sentence: that's three sentences
stuck together.

The order of the verbs is the order of the actions: swap the verbs and you swap what happened
first.

Two or three verbs in a chain is natural. After that, start a new sentence with それから
(and then):

{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んで、しゅくだいをしました。それから、{友|とも}だちと{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}しました。
— I read a book and did my homework. After that, I talked with a friend on the phone.

The て form can also join two actions that belong together as one, where English uses a
preposition: めがねをかけて{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます (I put on my glasses and read = I read with my
glasses on).

## After doing: 〜てから

〜て + から makes the order explicit: "after doing A, B" or "do A first, then B". Use it when
the order matters or is the point of the sentence:

{手|て}をあらってから、{食|た}べてください。 — Wash your hands before you eat. (literally:
after washing your hands, please eat)
しゅくだいをしてから、テレビを{見|み}ます。 — I watch TV after I've done my homework.
{日本|にほん}へ{来|き}てから、{日本語|にほんご}をべんきょうしています。 — I've been studying
Japanese since I came to Japan.

The last example shows a second use: 〜てから + 〜ています is "since doing".

This から is the same word as the から of "from" (lesson 6: {九時|くじ}から): "from doing A on".
In this pattern it always follows a て form.

## Before: 〜まえに

You know まえ as "in front of" (lesson 5) and as "before" with times (lesson 6:
{九時|くじ}{五分|ごふん}まえ). Add に and it's "before" for events.

With a noun, use の: N のまえに.

じゅぎょうのまえに、{先生|せんせい}にしつもんしました。 — Before class, I asked the teacher a
question.
ごはんのまえに、{手|て}をあらいます。 — I wash my hands before meals.
テストのまえに、ことばをおぼえます。 — Before the test, I memorize the words.

With a verb, use the plain form you find in the dictionary, without ます and without の. This
is the dictionary form: ねる, {食|た}べる, {行|い}く. Module 5 teaches it properly; for now,
every verb in your word list is already given in it, so you can use it here:

ねるまえに、はをみがきます。 — I brush my teeth before I go to bed. (はをみがく = brush teeth)
{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}くまえに、ひらがなをおぼえました。 — Before going to Japan, I learned hiragana.

The verb before まえに never changes for tense, even in the past: {行|い}くまえに, not
{行|い}きましたまえに. The final verb carries the tense.

## After: 〜のあとで

N + のあとで is "after N":

じゅぎょうのあとで、としょかんへ{行|い}きます。 — After class I'm going to the library.
(としょかん = library)
しごとのあとで、{友|とも}だちと{会|あ}いました。 — I met a friend after work. (しごと = work)

On its own, {後|あと}で means "later": じゃあ、{後|あと}で{電話|でんわ}します (I'll call you later). After a
verb, あとで needs another form you'll meet in module 5; with verbs, use 〜てから for now.

| Pattern | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A て、B | A, then B | おきて、ごはんを{食|た}べます |
| A てから、B | after A, B (order matters) | しゅくだいをしてから、あそびます |
| N のまえに、B | before N, B | テストのまえに |
| dictionary form + まえに、B | before doing A, B | ねるまえに |
| N のあとで、B | after N, B | じゅぎょうのあとで |

## School and languages

Japanese schools run in three stages before university: {小学校|しょうがっこう} (elementary school,
six years), {中学校|ちゅうがっこう} (junior high, three years) and {高校|こうこう} (senior high, three
years). A {高校生|こうこうせい} is a high-school student; {大学|だいがく} is university. The school
year starts in April.

{国|くに} is country, and {外国|がいこく} (outside country) is abroad. Japanese makes language
names by adding {語|ご} to a country name, as you saw in lesson 1: {日本語|にほんご}, スペイン{語|ご},
{中国語|ちゅうごくご} (Chinese, from {中国|ちゅうごく}, China). English is えいご (its first kanji isn't
in this course). To ask which language: {何語|なにご}ですか (what language is it?).

Asking where someone is from, the polite way is おくにはどちらですか, using おくに for the other
person's country. You answer with your own {国|くに} and no お: わたしの{国|くに}はカナダです.

{外国人|がいこくじん} (foreigner) is the neutral, polite word; the shortened がいじん can sound
rude, so avoid it. A りゅうがくせい is an international student studying in Japan.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 校 | school | コウ | — | 10 | {学校|がっこう}, {高校|こうこう}, {高校生|こうこうせい} |
| 国 | country | コク (ゴク) | くに | 8 | {国|くに}, {外国|がいこく}, {外国人|がいこくじん}, {中国|ちゅうごく} |
| 語 | language, word | ゴ | — | 14 | {日本語|にほんご}, {外国語|がいこくご}, {何語|なにご} |

Memory notes:

- 校 has a tree (木) on the left. Picture the school built of wood with a tree in the
  playground.
- 国 is a jewel (three lines joined by a vertical stroke, plus a dot) inside a border (the
  box): a country guards its treasure inside its borders.
- 語 is 言 (say, lesson 16) on the left plus 五 over 口 on the right: five mouths talking, a
  language.

Notice how the reading changes in {中国|ちゅうごく}: コク becomes ゴク after ちゅう. Readings often
soften like this in compounds; learn the word, not just the kanji.

## Dialogue: after class

```dialogue
# After class
けんた: マリアさん、じゅぎょうのあとで、{何|なに}をしますか。
= Maria, what are you doing after class?
マリア: としょかんへ{行|い}って、しゅくだいをします。それから、うちにかえります。
= I'm going to the library to do my homework. After that I'm going home.
けんた: いつも{日本語|にほんご}で{書|か}いていますか。
= Do you always write in Japanese?
マリア: はい。でも、ときどきじしょをつかいます。
= Yes. But sometimes I use a dictionary.
けんた: ぼくはスペイン{語|ご}をならっています。ブラジルのことばですね。
= I'm learning Spanish. That's the language of Brazil, isn't it?
マリア: いいえ、ブラジルはポルトガル{語|ご}ですよ。
= No, in Brazil it's Portuguese.
けんた: あ、そうでした。じゃあ、ポルトガル{語|ご}をおしえてください！
= Oh, right. Then please teach me Portuguese!
マリア: いいですよ。しゅくだいをしてから、カフェで{話|はな}しましょう。
= Sure. Let's talk at a café after I've done my homework.
```

## Reading: Maria's day

> わたしはブラジルからのりゅうがくせいです。{毎日|まいにち}、{七時|しちじ}におきて、あさごはんを
> {食|た}べて、{学校|がっこう}へ{行|い}きます。じゅぎょうは{九時|くじ}にはじまって、{三時|さんじ}に
> おわります。じゅぎょうのあとで、としょかんでしゅくだいをします。ねるまえに、{新|あたら}しい
> ことばを{十|とお}おぼえます。{日本|にほん}へ{来|き}てから、{毎日|まいにち}そうしています。

I'm an international student from Brazil. Every day I get up at seven, have breakfast and go
to school. Classes begin at nine and finish at three. After class I do my homework in the
library. Before I go to bed I memorize ten new words. I've done that every day since I came to
Japan. (そうする = to do so)

## Say it

```speak
{手|て}をあらってから、{食|た}べます。
= I wash my hands before I eat.
じゅぎょうのまえに、しつもんしました。
= I asked a question before class.
ねるまえに、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます。
= I read before going to bed.
おくにはどちらですか。
= Where are you from?
これは{何語|なにご}ですか。
= What language is this?
じゃあ、{後|あと}で。
= See you later, then.
```

## Common mistakes

- Putting tense on every verb in a chain: おきました、{食|た}べました、{行|い}きました. Use て
  forms and let the last verb carry the tense.
- Using the ます form before まえに: {食|た}べますまえに. It's {食|た}べるまえに.
- Leaving out の with a noun: じゅぎょうまえに. Say じゅぎょうのまえに.
- Confusing はじまる and はじめる. じゅぎょうがはじまります (class begins, by itself);
  {先生|せんせい}がじゅぎょうをはじめます (the teacher begins the class). Likewise おわる (to end).
- Saying おくに for your own country. The お is for other people's.

## Key points

- A て、B て、C ます: actions in order; the last verb sets the tense and politeness.
- 〜てから: after doing; 〜てから〜ています: since doing.
- N のまえに / dictionary form + まえに: before. N のあとで: after. {後|あと}で: later.
- それから joins sentences: and then.
- {語|ご} makes language names; {国|くに} country, {外国|がいこく} abroad, {高校|こうこう} high school.
- New kanji: 校 国 語.
