The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Permission, rules and the body
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Two more patterns grow out of the て form: one for asking whether something is all right
(May I sit here? Can I take photos?) and one for rules (You must not smoke here). You'll need
both the moment you step into a Japanese school, office, temple or doctor's surgery, so the
second half of the lesson is about the body and health: saying what hurts, catching a cold,
taking medicine. The new kanji are five body parts: 手, 足, 目, 口 and 耳.

## May I…? 〜てもいいですか

The て form + もいいですか asks for **[[permission]]**: "is it all right if I…?" The も is "even" or
"also", and いい is "good", so the literal sense is "even if I do it, is it good?"

ここにすわってもいいですか。 — May I sit here?
しゃしんをとってもいいですか。 — Can I take photos?
まどをあけてもいいですか。 — Do you mind if I open the window?
このペンをつかってもいいですか。 — May I use this pen?

### Saying yes and no

| Answer | Feels like |
|---|---|
| はい、どうぞ。 | Yes, go ahead. (the most common, and kindest) |
| ええ、いいですよ。 | Sure, that's fine. |
| すみません、ちょっと…。 | Sorry, I'd rather you didn't. (soft no) |
| いいえ、〜てはいけません。 | No, you mustn't. (strict: see below) |

The soft no should look familiar: it's the ちょっと… from lesson 10. Japanese speakers rarely
answer a polite request with a flat いいえ; they apologize and let the sentence trail off, and
the listener understands.

### Saying something is allowed

Drop the か and it's a statement: "you may".

{日本語|にほんご}で{話|はな}してもいいです。 — You can speak Japanese.
えんぴつで{書|か}いてもいいですか。はい、えんぴつで{書|か}いてもいいです。 — May I write in pencil?
Yes, you may write in pencil. (えんぴつ = pencil)

## Must not: 〜てはいけません

The て form + はいけません is **[[prohibition]]**: "you must not". いけない means "no good, not
allowed", so the literal sense is "if you do it, it won't do".

ここでたばこをすってはいけません。 — You must not smoke here.
びじゅつかんでしゃしんをとってはいけません。 — You may not take photos in the museum.
(びじゅつかん = art museum)
ろうかではしってはいけません。 — No running in the corridor. (ろうか = corridor)
テストのとき、じしょをつかってはいけません。 — You must not use dictionaries during the test.
(とき = time, when)

〜てはいけません is strong. It's what rules, signs, teachers and parents say. Don't use it to
refuse someone politely, and never to someone above you. If a classmate asks to borrow your pen
and you need it, いいえ、つかってはいけません sounds like a teacher scolding a child; say
すみません、ちょっと… instead.

In speech you'll hear the short forms 〜ちゃだめ and 〜てはだめ. They're casual; module 5 deals
with casual speech.

### も or は?

Notice the two particles in the patterns: も in 〜てもいい, は in 〜てはいけません. Mixing them up
(〜てはいい, 〜てもいけません) is the most common mistake with these patterns. A memory hook: "も
is more" (more is allowed), "は halts" (stop).

| Ask | Yes | No (rule) |
|---|---|---|
| 〜てもいいですか | はい、〜てもいいです / どうぞ | いいえ、〜てはいけません |

## The body

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| あたま | head |
| かお | face |
| {目|め} | eye |
| {耳|みみ} | ear |
| はな | nose |
| {口|くち} | mouth |
| は | tooth, teeth |
| のど | throat |
| {手|て} | hand, arm |
| おなか | stomach, belly |
| {足|あし} | foot, leg |
| からだ | body |

Japanese doesn't split "hand" and "arm" or "foot" and "leg" as sharply as English: {手|て} can
cover the whole arm, and {足|あし} the whole leg. Context tells you which.

Two homophones to watch: はな (nose) sounds like {花|はな} (flower), and は (tooth) is written
like the particle は but read "ha".

Body words also appear in common expressions: {目|め}がいい (good eyesight), {目|め}がわるい
(poor eyesight), あたまがいい (clever), {耳|みみ}がいたい (my ear hurts). The part of the body is
the subject, marked with が.

## Health: saying what's wrong

The key adjective is いたい (painful, sore). Put the part that hurts before が:

あたまがいたいです。 — I have a headache.
おなかがいたいです。 — I have a stomachache.
のどがいたいです。 — I have a sore throat.
{足|あし}がいたいです。 — My feet hurt.

On its own, いたい！ is "ouch!"

Other things you can say:

| Japanese | English |
|---|---|
| かぜをひきました。 | I've caught a cold. |
| かぜをひいています。 | I have a cold. |
| ねつがあります。 | I have a fever. |
| {気分|きぶん}がわるいです。 | I feel sick. |
| つかれました。 | I'm tired. |
| くすりを{飲|の}みます。 | I'll take medicine. |
| びょういんへ{行|い}きます。 | I'm going to the doctor. |

Three things English speakers find surprising:

- Medicine is "drunk": くすりを{飲|の}む, even pills.
- かぜ (a cold) sounds exactly like かぜ (wind); the kanji differ, and context decides.
- びょういん covers everything from a small clinic to a large hospital. Most people see a
  doctor at a local clinic, also called びょういん in everyday talk. Don't mix it up with
  びよういん (hair salon), which has a full-size よ and one more beat (bi-yo-u-i-n).

When someone tells you they're ill, say おだいじに (take care, get well soon). To ask how
someone is: だいじょうぶですか (are you all right?).

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 手 | hand | シュ | て | 4 | {手|て}, {上手|じょうず}, {下手|へた} |
| 足 | foot, leg; be enough | ソク | あし, た(りる) | 7 | {足|あし} |
| 目 | eye | モク | め | 5 | {目|め} |
| 口 | mouth | コウ | くち | 3 | {口|くち}, {入口|いりぐち}, {出口|でぐち} |
| 耳 | ear | ジ | みみ | 6 | {耳|みみ} |

Memory notes:

- 手 is a hand: the vertical stroke is the arm, the three crossing lines are fingers spread
  out.
- 目 is an eye turned on its side: the frame is the eye, the two inside lines the pupil.
- 口 is an open mouth. It's also the small box at the bottom right of 語.
- 耳 is an ear: the outer curve and the folds inside.
- 足 has a 口 on top (the knee) and a leg below that steps forward.

{上手|じょうず} and {下手|へた} (good at, bad at; lesson 12) use 手 with special readings that belong to the
whole word. 口 becomes ぐち in {入口|いりぐち} and {出口|でぐち} (lesson 17).

## Dialogue: at the clinic

```dialogue
# At the clinic
いしゃ: どうしましたか。
= What seems to be the problem?
エマ: きのうからあたまがいたいです。のどもいたいです。
= I've had a headache since yesterday. My throat hurts too.
いしゃ: ねつはありますか。
= Do you have a fever?
エマ: はい、{少|すこ}しあります。
= Yes, a slight one.
いしゃ: {口|くち}をあけてください。…かぜですね。このくすりを{飲|の}んでください。ごはんの{後|あと}で{飲|の}んでください。
= Please open your mouth. … It's a cold. Take this medicine. Take it after meals.
エマ: わかりました。あの、おふろに{入|はい}ってもいいですか。
= All right. Um, can I take a bath?
いしゃ: きょうは{入|はい}ってはいけません。シャワーはいいですよ。
= Not today. A shower is fine.
エマ: あしたは{学校|がっこう}へ{行|い}ってもいいですか。
= Can I go to school tomorrow?
いしゃ: あしたも{休|やす}んでください。うちでねてください。
= Please stay off tomorrow too. Rest in bed at home.
エマ: はい。ありがとうございました。
= OK. Thank you very much.
いしゃ: おだいじに。
= Take care.
```

いしゃ = doctor. Notice the doctor's 〜てはいけません: a doctor giving instructions is exactly
the kind of person who uses it. Asking about a bath with a cold is a very Japanese question;
many people skip the bath when they have a fever.

## Reading: rules at a swimming pool

> プールのきまり
>
> ・プールに{入|はい}るまえに、シャワーをあびてください。
>
> ・プールのまわりではしってはいけません。
>
> ・{子|こ}どもは{大人|おとな}と{入|はい}ってください。
>
> ・{食|た}べものや{飲|の}みものをもって{入|はい}ってはいけません。
>
> ・{水|みず}の{中|なか}で、ぼうしをかぶってください。

Pool rules: Shower before you go into the pool. No running around the pool. Children must go
in with an adult. Do not bring food or drink in. Wear a cap in the water. (きまり = rule;
まわり = around; {大人|おとな} = adult; {食|た}べもの / {飲|の}みもの = food / drink)

## Say it

```speak
ここにすわってもいいですか。
= May I sit here?
はい、どうぞ。
= Yes, go ahead.
しゃしんをとってはいけません。
= You may not take photos.
あたまがいたいです。
= I have a headache.
かぜをひきました。
= I've caught a cold.
おだいじに。
= Get well soon.
```

## Common mistakes

- The wrong particle: 〜てはいいですか or 〜てもいけません. Permission takes も, prohibition
  takes は.
- Answering a polite request with いいえ、〜てはいけません. It sounds like a rule being read out;
  すみません、ちょっと… is the polite no.
- わたしはあたまがいたいです is fine, but あたまはいたいです sounds like you're contrasting your
  head with other parts. The usual form is あたまがいたいです.
- くすりをたべます. Medicine is {飲|の}む.
- Saying びよういん (hair salon) for びょういん (hospital).

## Key points

- 〜てもいいですか: may I…? Answers: はい、どうぞ / ええ、いいですよ / すみません、ちょっと….
- 〜てもいいです: you may. 〜てはいけません: you must not (rules, signs, people in charge).
- も for permission, は for prohibition.
- Body part + がいたいです: …hurts. かぜをひく, ねつがある, くすりを{飲|の}む, おだいじに.
- New kanji: 手 足 目 口 耳.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Wanting and going to do
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about wishes and plans: I want to go to Japan, I want a new bag, I'm going to
the shop to buy bread. You'll learn three patterns. 〜たいです (want to do) and ほしいです (want
a thing) both behave like い-adjectives, which you learned in lesson 11, so their negatives
and pasts are already familiar. 〜に{行|い}きます (go to do) gives a reason for going
somewhere. All three meet in shops and restaurants, so the lesson ends with shopping and
ordering. One new kanji: 買 (buy).

This lesson doesn't use the て form. It uses the ます stem: the part before ます
({食|た}べ-ます, {行|い}き-ます, {買|か}い-ます), which you met in module 2.

## Want to do: 〜たいです

Take the ます stem and add たい. The result is the **[[たい form]]**: "want to do". Add です to make
it polite.

| Dictionary form | ます form | たい form |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べます | {食|た}べたい(です) |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}きます | {行|い}きたい(です) |
| {買|か}う | {買|か}います | {買|か}いたい(です) |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}みます | {読|よ}みたい(です) |
| する | します | したい(です) |
| {来|く}る | {来|き}ます | {来|き}たい(です) |

There are no sound changes and no exceptions: every verb works the same way.

{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}きたいです。 — I want to go to Japan.
{何|なに}が{食|た}べたいですか。 — What do you want to eat?
しゃしんをとりたいです。 — I want to take a photo.

### It changes like an い-adjective

たい ends in い, and it conjugates exactly like {高|たか}い or おいしい:

| | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| want to | 〜たいです | {見|み}たいです |
| don't want to | 〜たくないです | {見|み}たくないです |
| wanted to | 〜たかったです | {見|み}たかったです |
| didn't want to | 〜たくなかったです | {見|み}たくなかったです |

きょうは{何|なに}もしたくないです。 — I don't want to do anything today.
そのえいがを{見|み}たかったです。 — I wanted to see that film.

### を or が

With たい, the object can take を or が: {水|みず}を{飲|の}みたいです and {水|みず}が{飲|の}みたいです are
both correct. が puts a little more weight on the thing itself ("water is what I want to
drink"). If you're unsure, を is always safe. Other particles (に, へ, で) don't change.

### Whose wish?

〜たいです states your own wish, or asks the listener about theirs. Japanese doesn't state
another person's feelings directly, because you can't be inside their head. So
エマさんは{行|い}きたいです sounds wrong; you'll learn ways to report someone else's wishes later.
For now, ask them: エマさんも{行|い}きたいですか.

Asking 〜たいですか is fine with friends. With a teacher, a customer or anyone above you, it
can sound nosy; offer instead with 〜ませんか (lesson 10): コーヒーを{飲|の}みませんか.

## Want a thing: ほしいです

To want a thing (a noun), use ほしい, an い-adjective. The thing wanted takes が:

{新|あたら}しいくつがほしいです。 — I want new shoes.
{今|いま}、{何|なに}がいちばんほしいですか。 — What do you want most right now?
{車|くるま}はほしくないです。 — I don't want a car.
{子|こ}どものとき、いぬがほしかったです。 — When I was a child, I wanted a dog. (とき = when)

The same rule applies as for たい: it's your own wish, or a question to the listener.

| You want… | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| a thing | N がほしいです | カメラがほしいです |
| to do something | ます stem + たいです | カメラを{買|か}いたいです |

A common mix-up is ほしい with a verb: {買|か}いほしいです is wrong. ほしい follows nouns; たい
follows verbs.

## Going to do: 〜に{行|い}きます

To say why you're going somewhere, use the ます stem + に + {行|い}く, {来|く}る or かえる. This に
marks **[[purpose]]**.

{本|ほん}を{買|か}いに{行|い}きます。 — I'm going to buy a book.
{友|とも}だちとえいがを{見|み}に{行|い}きました。 — I went to see a film with a friend.
{日本|にほん}へ{日本語|にほんご}をべんきょうしに{来|き}ました。 — I came to Japan to study Japanese.
ひるごはんを{食|た}べにうちへかえります。 — I'm going home to have lunch.

With a する verb you can also use just the noun: {買|か}いものに{行|い}きます (I'm going
shopping), さんぽに{行|い}きます (I'm going for a walk), べんきょうに{来|き}ました.

The place you go is still marked with へ or に. When both are in a sentence, the usual order
is place, then purpose, then verb, and へ for the place keeps the two に apart:

デパートへくつを{買|か}いに{行|い}きます。 — I'm going to the department store to buy shoes.

## Shopping and ordering

Most of what you need in a shop you already have: これをください (lesson 4), いくらですか
(lesson 3), ぜんぶでいくらですか (how much altogether?). Add these:

| Japanese | English |
|---|---|
| くろいかばんをさがしています。 | I'm looking for a black bag. |
| ほかのいろはありますか。 | Do you have it in another colour? |
| もう{少|すこ}し{大|おお}きいサイズはありますか。 | Do you have a slightly bigger size? |
| きてもいいですか。 | May I try it on? |
| じゃあ、これにします。 | Right, I'll take this one. |
| ちょっと{見|み}ているだけです。 | I'm just looking. |

〜にします ("I'll go with ~") is how you decide, in a shop or a restaurant:
コーヒーにします (I'll have coffee). In restaurants you can also order with 〜をおねがいします or
〜をください. The staff may ask ごちゅうもんは？ (what would you like?), from ちゅうもん (an
order).

The sentence ちょっと{見|み}ているだけです uses だけ (only) and ている from lesson 17: "I'm only
looking."

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 買 | buy | バイ | か(う) | 12 | {買|か}う, {買|か}いもの |

Memory note: the top of 買 is a net (it looks like 目 lying on its side), and the bottom is a
shell, which people in ancient China once used as money. Buying is catching something in
your net with a handful of shells.

{買|か}いもの (shopping) is usually written with a second kanji that isn't in this course, so
it's written {買|か}いもの here.

## Dialogue: at a department store

```dialogue
# At a department store
てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome.
エマ: すみません、セーターをさがしています。
= Excuse me, I'm looking for a sweater.
てんいん: こちらはいかがですか。{新|あたら}しいセーターです。
= How about this one? It's new in.
エマ: いいですね。でも、{白|しろ}いのがほしいです。ほかのいろはありますか。
= Nice. But I want a white one. Do you have other colours?
てんいん: はい、{白|しろ}もあります。どうぞ。
= Yes, we have white too. Here you are.
エマ: きてもいいですか。
= May I try it on?
てんいん: はい、どうぞ。
= Of course.
エマ: …ちょっと{小|ちい}さいです。もう{少|すこ}し{大|おお}きいサイズはありますか。
= …It's a bit small. Do you have a slightly bigger size?
てんいん: はい。こちらです。
= Yes. Here.
エマ: ちょうどいいです。じゃあ、これにします。
= It's just right. OK, I'll take it.
```

てんいん = shop assistant; いかがですか = how about…? (polite); {白|しろ}いの = a white one;
ちょうどいい = just right.

## Reading: Ken's Saturday

> {土曜日|どようび}、{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}のデパートへ{買|か}いものに{行|い}きました。{母|はは}のたんじょうびの
> プレゼントを{買|か}いたかったです。{母|はは}は「{新|あたら}しいかばんがほしいです」と{言|い}っていました。
> でも、かばんは{高|たか}かったです。それで、{白|しろ}いセーターを{買|か}いました。それから、
> おなかがすきました。デパートのレストランへひるごはんを{食|た}べに{行|い}きました。

On Saturday I went shopping at the department store in front of the station. I wanted to buy a
birthday present for my mother. She had said she wants a new bag. But the bags were
expensive, so I bought a white sweater. After that I got hungry, so I went to the restaurant in
the department store for lunch.

(「…」と{言|い}っていました = (she) was saying "…": this is how Japanese reports someone else's
wish; it's here only to read. それで = so, and so.)

## Say it

```speak
{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}きたいです。
= I want to go to Japan.
{何|なに}が{食|た}べたいですか。
= What do you want to eat?
{新|あたら}しいカメラがほしいです。
= I want a new camera.
{買|か}いものに{行|い}きます。
= I'm going shopping.
{本|ほん}を{買|か}いに{行|い}きます。
= I'm going to buy a book.
これにします。
= I'll take this one.
```

## Common mistakes

- ほしい with a verb ({買|か}いほしい) or たい with a noun (カメラたい). Things are ほしい; actions
  are たい.
- Telling someone else's wishes: たなかさんはすしが{食|た}べたいです. Ask them instead, or wait
  for the forms in a later module.
- The dictionary form before たい or に: {食|た}べるたい, {買|か}うに{行|い}きます. Both use the ます
  stem: {食|た}べたい, {買|か}いに{行|い}きます.
- Negative like a verb: {行|い}きたいません. たい is an adjective: {行|い}きたくないです.
- ほしい with を: カメラをほしいです. The usual particle is が.

## Key points

- ます stem + たいです: want to do. Negative たくないです, past たかったです.
- N がほしいです: want a thing. Negative ほしくないです.
- Both are for your own wishes (or questions to the listener).
- ます stem + に + {行|い}く / {来|く}る / かえる: go (come, go home) to do. With する nouns:
  {買|か}いものに{行|い}く.
- 〜をさがしています, 〜はありますか, 〜にします: shopping and ordering.
- New kanji: 買.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Eating out
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Eating out is one of the great pleasures of a trip to Japan, and one of the first places
you'll use your Japanese for real. This honors lesson walks through a restaurant visit from
the door to the register: being greeted and seated, the towel and the free water, menus and
set meals, calling the staff, ordering, table manners, and paying. Along the way you'll use
everything from this module: 〜てください, 〜てもいいですか, 〜たいです and 〜にします.

## At the door

As you walk in, the staff call out いらっしゃいませ (welcome). You don't need to answer it; a
nod or a smile is enough. It isn't a question, and saying it back would sound odd, like a
customer welcoming the waiter.

The first question is how many you are:

{何名|なんめい}さまですか。 — How many in your party?

The staff use the polite counter 〜{名|めい} with さま (the very polite form of さん). Customers
don't use 〜{名|めい} about themselves; answer with the ordinary people counter from lesson 15,
often while holding up the number on your fingers:

| Number | Staff say | You say |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {一名|いちめい}さま | {一人|ひとり}です |
| 2 | {二名|にめい}さま | {二人|ふたり}です |
| 3 | {三名|さんめい}さま | {三人|さんにん}です |
| 4 | {四名|よんめい}さま | {四人|よにん}です |

For one person, staff often say おひとりさまですか instead. If you're alone, {一人|ひとり}です is fine; many restaurants have counter seats meant for people
eating alone, and eating alone is completely normal in Japan.

You may be asked about your booking (ごよやくは？) or where you'd like to sit. Then:

こちらへどうぞ。 — This way, please.

## The towel and the water

Once you sit down, you're usually given an おしぼり, a small wet towel, hot in winter and cold
in summer. It's for your hands. Many people also wipe their face with it in casual places, but
it's better not to in a smart restaurant.

Water or green tea usually comes free, without asking, and is refilled. In some places it's
self-service from a jug or a machine. Water served this way is often called おひや ("the cold
one").

## Menus and set meals

Japanese menus often have photos, and many restaurants display realistic plastic models of
their dishes in the window. If you can't read the menu, you can point at the picture or take
the staff outside to the window: これをください.

The best value, especially at lunch, is usually a ていしょく (set meal): one main dish
(grilled fish, fried chicken, pork cutlet…) with rice, miso soup and small side dishes such as
pickles. At lunch you'll also see ランチ or ランチセット. In some places, a second bowl of rice
(おかわり) is free: ごはんのおかわりをください.

In many ramen, curry and beef-bowl shops you don't order from a person at all. There's a
ticket machine at the entrance: you put in money, press the button for your dish and hand the
ticket to the staff. If you're not sure what to do, ask:

すみません、どうしますか。 — Excuse me, what do I do?

To ask what's good:

おすすめは{何|なん}ですか。 — What do you recommend?

## Calling the staff

Waiters in Japan don't usually come to check on you. When you're ready, catch someone's eye
and call すみません！ (excuse me!), with a hand slightly raised. It isn't rude; it's how
everyone does it. Many chain restaurants have a call button on the table instead: press it
and someone comes.

Never snap your fingers or whistle; just すみません.

## Ordering

You know three ways to order. All are polite enough for any restaurant:

| Pattern | Example | Feels like |
|---|---|---|
| N をください | ビールをください | X, please |
| N をおねがいします | ビールをおねがいします | X, please (a little softer) |
| N にします | ビールにします | I'll go with X (choosing) |

When there are several of you, quantities use the 〜つ counter (lesson 4) for dishes:

カレーを{二|ふた}つと、コーヒーを{一|ひと}つおねがいします。 — Two curries and one coffee, please.

Use what you've learned this module to ask questions and make requests:

| Japanese | English |
|---|---|
| メニューを{見|み}せてください。 | Could I see the menu? |
| これは{何|なん}ですか。 | What's this? |
| わたしはさかなが{食|た}べたいです。 | I'd like fish. |
| {少|すこ}しまってください。 | Just a moment, please (I haven't decided). |
| しゃしんをとってもいいですか。 | May I take a photo (of the food)? |
| わりばしをもう{一|ひと}つください。 | Another pair of chopsticks, please. |

Many restaurants now use tablets on the table for ordering, often with an English button. It's
still worth trying your Japanese with the staff; they'll usually be pleased.

## Table manners

Before you start, say いただきます (from the kana course), quietly, hands together if you
like. After the meal, say ごちそうさまでした, and say it again to the staff as you leave.

With chopsticks:

- Don't stand chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. It's done at funerals.
- Don't pass food from your chopsticks to someone else's. That too is a funeral custom.
- When you put them down, rest them on the chopstick rest (or the paper wrapper),
  not stuck in the food, laid across the top of a bowl, or pointing at someone.
- わりばし, the disposable wooden ones, come joined: split them apart, and don't rub them
  together in front of others (it suggests the restaurant's chopsticks are cheap).

Other customs:

- Lift small bowls, such as rice and miso soup, to your mouth. Drinking miso soup straight
  from the bowl is normal; there's usually no spoon.
- Slurping noodles is fine, even expected: it cools them and shows you're enjoying them.
- With drinks, people pour for each other rather than for themselves.

## Paying

When you're done, you usually pay at the register (レジ) by the door, not at the table. Often
the bill has been left on your table: take it to the register.

おかいけいをおねがいします。 — The bill, please.
ぜんぶでいくらですか。 — How much is it altogether?
べつべつでおねがいします。 — Separately, please.

There's no tipping in Japan. If you leave money on the table, the staff may run after you to
give it back. Good service is included in the price. Cash is still widely used, though cards
and IC cards are accepted in more and more places: カードでもいいですか (can I pay by card?).

On your way out, ごちそうさまでした is the perfect goodbye, and the staff will answer ありがとう
ございました.

## Dialogue: lunch for two

```dialogue
# Lunch for two
てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。{何名|なんめい}さまですか。
= Welcome. How many in your party?
けん: {二人|ふたり}です。
= Two.
てんいん: こちらへどうぞ。メニューです。
= This way, please. Here's the menu.
エマ: ありがとうございます。けんさん、{何|なに}が{食|た}べたいですか。
= Thank you. Ken, what do you feel like eating?
けん: ぼくはさかなのていしょくにします。エマさんは？
= I'll have the fish set meal. What about you?
エマ: うーん…すみません！おすすめは{何|なん}ですか。
= Hmm… Excuse me! What do you recommend?
てんいん: きょうのおすすめは、とりのからあげていしょくです。
= Today's recommendation is the fried chicken set meal.
エマ: じゃあ、それをおねがいします。
= Then I'll have that, please.
てんいん: さかなのていしょくと、からあげていしょくですね。しょうしょうおまちください。
= One fish set and one fried chicken set. Just a moment, please.
けん: ごはんのおかわりは{何円|なんえん}ですか。
= How much is a second helping of rice?
てんいん: おかわりはただです。
= Seconds are free.
```

うーん = hmm; とりのからあげ = fried chicken; しょうしょうおまちください = please wait a moment (the
very polite form staff use; to recognize, not to say yourself); ただ = free (of charge).

## Reading: a sign at a ramen shop

> しょっけんを{買|か}ってから、すわってください。
>
> お{水|みず}はセルフサービスです。
>
> ごはんのおかわりはいっかいだけ、ただです。
>
> おかいけいは{先|さき}におねがいします。

Please buy a meal ticket before you sit down. Water is self-service. One refill of rice is
free. Please pay first. (しょっけん = meal ticket; いっかいだけ = only once;
{先|さき}に = first, in advance)

## Key points

- いらっしゃいませ needs no answer. To {何名|なんめい}さまですか, answer {一人|ひとり}です,
  {二人|ふたり}です…
- おしぼり is for your hands; water and tea are usually free.
- ていしょく is a set meal; おすすめは{何|なん}ですか asks for a recommendation.
- Call staff with すみません！; order with 〜をください, 〜をおねがいします, 〜にします.
- No chopsticks upright in rice, no chopstick-to-chopstick passing; slurping noodles is fine.
- Pay at the レジ: おかいけいをおねがいします. No tipping.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Japanese homes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

If you visit a Japanese friend, stay with a host family or rent a flat in Japan, a few
customs will matter from the moment you open the door: where to take your shoes off, which
slippers to wear where, how to use the bath, and how flats are described in an estate agent's
window. This honors lesson covers them, with the phrases you'll need, built on this module's
て-form patterns: 〜てください, 〜ています and 〜てもいいですか.

## The げんかん

Every Japanese home, from a tiny studio to a large house, starts with a げんかん: an entryway
just inside the front door. The floor there is lower, often tiled or concrete, and level with
the outside. The rest of the home is a step up.

That step is the line between outside and inside. You take your shoes off in the lower part
and step up in socks or slippers; outdoor shoes never go past the step. Even delivery people
and repair workers who come inside will take off their shoes or wear covers over them.

A few details:

- Step out of your shoes and onto the raised floor without putting your socked foot down on
  the lower part.
- Turn your shoes so the toes point to the door, or set them neatly to one side. Your host
  may do it for you if you forget.
- There's often a shoe cupboard in the げんかん; in your own home, that's where shoes live.

The phrases go with the step. When you enter someone's home, say おじゃまします (literally "I'm
going to disturb you", the standard polite greeting on entering). The host will say どうぞ、
あがってください (please come up = please come in). When you leave: おじゃましました.

Hosts often put out slippers for guests: このスリッパをはいてください.

## Slippers, socks and the toilet

Slippers are worn in corridors, the kitchen and most rooms with wooden or vinyl floors. Two
places have their own rules:

- The toilet. There's usually a separate pair of toilet slippers inside the toilet room.
  Change into them at the door and change back when you leave. Walking back into the living
  room in the toilet slippers is the classic visitor's mistake, and everyone will notice.
- Tatami rooms. Take your slippers off before stepping onto たたみ. Socks or bare feet only.

In most Japanese homes the toilet and the bath are in separate rooms, so "where's the
bathroom?" needs care: the toilet is トイレ (or おてあらい), and the bath is おふろ.

## たたみ and the わしつ

たたみ are thick mats of woven rush straw over a firm core, edged with cloth. A room floored
with them is a わしつ (Japanese-style room). Most new flats have Western-style rooms with
wooden floors, but many homes still have one わしつ, used as a living room, a guest room or a
bedroom.

A わしつ often has:

- ふすま: sliding doors covered with thick paper, between rooms and on closets;
- しょうじ: sliding screens of thin paper on a wooden lattice, which let light through;
- an おしいれ: a deep built-in closet with a shelf, designed to hold ふとん.

A ふとん is a mattress and quilt that you lay on the tatami at night and fold away in the
おしいれ in the morning, so the same room can be a living room by day and a bedroom by night.
On sunny days people hang ふとん over the balcony rail to air them.

Tatami also measure rooms. Room sizes are given in じょう, the number of mats the room would
hold: a 6じょう room is a typical bedroom. Mats differ a little by region, so in rental ads one
じょう is counted as at least about 1.6 square metres; a 6じょう room is about 10 square metres.

## The bath

A Japanese bath is for soaking, not washing. The bathroom has two parts: a deep tub, and an
open area with a drain in the floor, a stool, a bowl and a shower. The routine:

1. Wash and rinse thoroughly with the shower, sitting on the stool, outside the tub.
2. Then get into the tub, clean, and soak in the hot water.
3. Don't pull the plug when you get out. The same water is used by the whole family, one after
   another, and is often kept warm with a lid (ふた) and a reheating button.

That's why soap must never go in the tub. Guests are often offered the first bath, which is an
honour. Many families bathe in the evening, often before dinner or before bed.

おふろに{入|はい}ってもいいですか。 — May I take a bath?
どうぞ、お{先|さき}に。 — Please, go first. (literally "please, ahead of me")

Japanese uses {入|はい}る for baths: おふろに{入|はい}る, "go into the bath".

## Flats and room layouts

Most people in cities live in flats. Two words are used, and neither is quite like English:

| Word | What it usually is |
|---|---|
| アパート | a small, low-rise building (two or three floors), often wood or light steel; cheaper, thinner walls |
| マンション | a larger, solid building of reinforced concrete, often with a lift; not a "mansion" |

Estate agents' windows describe flats with a code such as 1K, 1LDK or 2LDK. The letters are
L (living room), D (dining area) and K (kitchen); the number is how many other rooms there are.

| Code | Means | Typical for |
|---|---|---|
| 1R | one room, with a small kitchen in the same room | students |
| 1K | one room plus a separate small kitchen | one person |
| 1DK | one room plus a kitchen big enough to eat in | one or two people |
| 1LDK | one room plus a living-dining-kitchen area | a couple |
| 2LDK | two rooms plus a living-dining-kitchen area | a small family |
| 3LDK | three rooms plus a living-dining-kitchen area | a family |

An ad might say: 2LDK、{駅|えき}まで{五分|ごふん}、{南|みなみ}むき. That's two rooms plus an LDK, five
minutes to the station, facing south (for sunlight; {南|みなみ} = south, lesson 21's kanji).

Renting also brings two costs that surprise many newcomers: しききん, a deposit, and in many
places れいきん ("key money"), a non-refundable payment to the landlord. Each is often one or
two months' rent, though more and more flats ask for neither.

Rubbish is sorted carefully, with different days for burnable rubbish, plastics, cans and
bottles. Your building will have a calendar; follow it.

## Dialogue: visiting a friend

```dialogue
# Visiting a friend
ゆき: いらっしゃい！どうぞ、あがってください。
= Welcome! Come on in.
エマ: おじゃまします。
= Thank you for having me.
ゆき: このスリッパをはいてください。
= Put on these slippers.
エマ: ありがとう。わあ、きれいなうちですね。
= Thanks. Wow, what a lovely home.
ゆき: ありがとう。このへやはわしつです。スリッパをぬいでください。
= Thanks. This room is a tatami room. Take your slippers off, please.
エマ: はい。たたみ、いいですね。ここでねていますか。
= OK. I like the tatami. Do you sleep in here?
ゆき: はい。ふとんはおしいれに{入|はい}っています。
= Yes. The futon is in the closet.
エマ: すみません、トイレをかりてもいいですか。
= Excuse me, may I use the toilet?
ゆき: どうぞ。あ、トイレのスリッパをはいてください。
= Sure. Oh, please wear the toilet slippers.
エマ: はい。…{出|で}てから、スリッパをかえますね。
= OK. …I'll change slippers again after I come out.
```

いらっしゃい = welcome (casual, at home); トイレをかりる = "borrow the toilet", the polite way to
ask to use someone's; かえる (group 2) = to change. Notice ふとんはおしいれに{入|はい}っています:
〜ています for a resulting state (the futon has been put in, and it's there).

## Key points

- Shoes come off in the げんかん; step up in socks or slippers. Say おじゃまします going in.
- Toilet slippers stay in the toilet; no slippers on たたみ.
- ふとん are laid on the tatami at night and stored in the おしいれ.
- Wash before getting into the bath; leave the water in for the next person.
- アパート is small and low-rise; マンション is a solid block of flats. 2LDK = two rooms plus
  a living-dining-kitchen. Rooms are measured in じょう.
