lessons.title: The dictionary form
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since Module 2 you've said almost every verb with ます: {食|た}べます, {行|い}きます, {読|よ}みます.
In Module 4 you added the て form. But every verb in your word list has been listed in a third
shape: {食|た}べる, {行|い}く, {読|よ}む. That's the form a dictionary uses, and this module is
about it and its relatives, the **[[plain forms]]**.

This lesson does three things. You'll learn to make the **[[dictionary form]]** from the ます form
you already know, and to use it inside polite sentences: {本|ほん}を{読|よ}むのがすきです (I like
reading books), ねるまえに (before going to bed), しゅみは〜ことです (my hobby is …). You'll
also learn the four directions and their kanji 東, 西, 南 and 北, which you'll see at every
station exit in Japan.

## Two kinds of verb form

Each Japanese verb comes in two sets of forms. The ます forms are polite: you use them with
people you don't know well, at work, with teachers. The plain forms are the same meanings
without the politeness. Here are the four basic ones for {食|た}べる:

| Meaning | Plain form | ます form |
|---|---|---|
| eat, will eat | {食|た}べる | {食|た}べます |
| don't eat | {食|た}べない | {食|た}べません |
| ate | {食|た}べた | {食|た}べました |
| didn't eat | {食|た}べなかった | {食|た}べませんでした |

The plain non-past form, {食|た}べる, is the dictionary form. Lesson 22 teaches the ない form,
Lesson 23 the た form, and Lesson 24 shows when to talk in plain forms with friends and family.

Plain forms aren't only for casual talk, though. Many patterns need a plain form in the
middle of the sentence even when the sentence ends politely with です or ます. The patterns in
this lesson are like that: {本|ほん}を{読|よ}むのがすきです is perfectly polite, because the
ending です is polite. Only the end of a sentence decides how polite it sounds.

## Making the dictionary form

Start from the ます form, take off ます, and look at what's left (the ます stem). What you do
next depends on the verb group from Module 2.

### Group 2 (る verbs): add る

Take off ます and put る in its place.

| ます form | Dictionary form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べます | {食|た}べる | to eat |
| {見|み}ます | {見|み}る | to see, to watch |
| ねます | ねる | to sleep, to go to bed |
| あつめます | あつめる | to collect |
| おきます | おきる | to get up |

### Group 3: two irregular verbs

| ます form | Dictionary form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| します | する | to do |
| {来|き}ます | {来|く}る | to come |

Watch the kanji: {来|き}ます has the reading き, but the dictionary form is {来|く}る, read くる.
Verbs made with する work the same way: べんきょうします → べんきょうする.

### Group 1 (う verbs): the い sound becomes an う sound

The stem of a group 1 verb ends in an い-row sound (き, ぎ, し, ち, に, び, み, り, or い).
Move that kana one step down its column in the kana chart, to the う row:

| ます form | Change | Dictionary form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {買|か}います | い → う | {買|か}う | to buy |
| {書|か}きます | き → く | {書|か}く | to write |
| およぎます | ぎ → ぐ | およぐ | to swim |
| {話|はな}します | し → す | {話|はな}す | to speak |
| {立|た}ちます | ち → つ | {立|た}つ | to stand |
| しにます | に → ぬ | しぬ | to die |
| あそびます | び → ぶ | あそぶ | to play |
| {飲|の}みます | み → む | {飲|の}む | to drink |
| とります | り → る | とる | to take (a photo) |

Say the pairs aloud and you'll hear it: ki-masu → ku, mi-masu → mu. Only one change is
irregular in spelling: い becomes う, so {買|か}います is {買|か}う (not かゆ or かる). しぬ is the
only verb that ends in ぬ; you'll rarely need it, but it completes the table.

### The catch: you need to know the group

Look at おきます (get up) and {書|か}きます (write). Both stems end in き. One is group 2, so it
becomes おきる; the other is group 1, so it becomes {書|か}く. Nothing in the ます form tells you
which. The same goes for {見|み}ます (group 2, {見|み}る) and {飲|の}みます (group 1, {飲|の}む).

The rule of thumb:

- A stem ending in an え-row sound ({食|た}べ, ね, あつめ) is always group 2: add る.
- A stem ending in an い-row sound could be either. Most are group 1, but some common verbs
  ({見|み}る, おきる, いる, きる (to wear)) are group 2.

That's why every verb in your word list has a note with its group. When you learn a new
verb, learn its group along with it, the way you learn the gender of a noun in German or
French.

## Likes and skills: 〜のがすきです

In Module 3 you said what you like with a noun: おんがくがすきです (I like music). To like an
*activity*, put a verb phrase in the dictionary form, add の, and use it like a noun:

{本|ほん}を{読|よ}むのがすきです。 — I like reading books.

うたをうたうのがすきです。 — I like singing (songs).

およぐのはあまりすきじゃないです。 — I don't really like swimming.

The の turns "read books" into "reading books", something that can take が. Inside the phrase
everything stays as usual: the book is still marked with を, because it's the object of
{読|よ}む. Only the whole phrase gets が.

The same works with the other words that take が from Lesson 12: じょうず (good at), へた (bad
at), とくい (good at, strong in) and きらい (dislike).

けんさんはえをかくのがじょうずですね。 — Ken, you're good at drawing, aren't you?

わたしはうたをうたうのがへたです。 — I'm bad at singing.

かく means "to write", and also "to draw" when the object is a picture: えをかく.

## Hobbies: しゅみは〜ことです

The usual question about hobbies is しゅみは{何|なん}ですか (What are your hobbies?). Answer with a
noun, or with a verb phrase + こと:

しゅみはしゃしんです。 — My hobby is photography.

しゅみはしゃしんをとることです。 — My hobby is taking photos.

わたしのしゅみはピアノをひくことです。 — My hobby is playing the piano.

こと is a noun meaning "thing" or "matter", for things you can't touch: facts, actions,
experiences. Here it plays the role の played above: it turns a verb phrase into a noun. The
two aren't always interchangeable. After しゅみは, use こと (しゅみは〜のです sounds wrong). Before
すき, じょうず and へた, both の and こと are possible, but の is far more common in speech.
You'll meet こと again in Lesson 23.

Some hobbies, as nouns and as verb phrases:

| Noun | Verb phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {読書|どくしょ} | {本|ほん}を{読|よ}む | reading |
| りょうり | りょうりをつくる | cooking |
| {山|やま}のぼり | {山|やま}にのぼる | hiking, mountain climbing |
| つり | つりをする | fishing |
| ダンス | おどる | dancing |
| ジョギング | ジョギングをする | jogging |
| まんが, アニメ, ドラマ | まんがを{読|よ}む, アニメを{見|み}る | manga, anime, TV dramas |
| — | ピアノ/ギターをひく | playing the piano/guitar |
| — | えをかく | drawing, painting |
| — | {古|ふる}いカメラをあつめる | collecting old cameras |

{読書|どくしょ} uses the on'yomi of {読|よ}む and {書|か}く: "reading books". のぼる (to climb) takes
に for the mountain: {山|やま}にのぼる. あつめる (to collect) is group 2.

ひく is "to play" for instruments you play with your fingers: ピアノをひく, ギターをひく. For
sports and games you use する (テニスをする).

## Before doing: 〜まえに

In Lesson 18 you met まえに after a noun (ごはんのまえに, before the meal). After a verb, use the
dictionary form, with no の:

ねるまえに、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}みます。 — Before I go to bed, I read.

{食|た}べるまえに、{手|て}をあらいます。 — I wash my hands before eating. (あらう = to wash)

{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}くまえに、{日本語|にほんご}をべんきょうしました。 — Before going to Japan, I studied Japanese.

Look at the last one: it's about the past, but the verb before まえに is still the dictionary
form, {行|い}く. The verb before まえに is always in the dictionary form; the verb at the end shows
the tense. "Before I went" is never ×{行|い}ったまえに.

## Directions: 東, 西, 南, 北

| Direction | Kanji | Reading | Station exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| east | 東 | ひがし | {東口|ひがしぐち} |
| west | 西 | にし | {西口|にしぐち} |
| south | 南 | みなみ | {南口|みなみぐち} |
| north | 北 | きた | {北口|きたぐち} |

{口|くち} means "mouth" (Lesson 19), and also "opening, way in or out". Large stations have
exits named by direction, and they are the usual place to meet: {北口|きたぐち}で{会|あ}いましょう
(Let's meet at the north exit). In compounds くち becomes ぐち, a sound change you've seen in
words like {出口|でぐち} (exit).

To say where something is, use the pattern from Lesson 5:

ほっかいどうは{日本|にほん}の{北|きた}にあります。 — Hokkaido is in the north of Japan.

コンビニは{駅|えき}の{西口|にしぐち}のまえにあります。 — The convenience store is in front of the station's west exit.

Japanese lists the four directions in its own order: {東西南北|とうざいなんぼく} (east, west,
south, north), where English says "north, south, east and west". For the in-between
directions, north or south comes first, as in English: {北東|ほくとう} (northeast),
{南西|なんせい} (southwest). In these compounds the kanji take their on'yomi: トウ, ザイ/セイ,
ナン, ホク.

## Kanji

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 東 | east | トウ | ひがし | 8 | {東|ひがし}, {東口|ひがしぐち}, {東西南北|とうざいなんぼく} |
| 西 | west | セイ, サイ (ザイ) | にし | 6 | {西|にし}, {西口|にしぐち}, {南西|なんせい} |
| 南 | south | ナン | みなみ | 9 | {南|みなみ}, {南口|みなみぐち}, {南西|なんせい} |
| 北 | north | ホク | きた | 5 | {北|きた}, {北口|きたぐち}, {北東|ほくとう} |

Memory notes:

- 東: the sun 日 caught in the branches of a tree 木. Where do you see the sun low behind the
  trees in the morning? In the east.
- 西: a lid on top of a box with two legs tucked inside. Picture a bird's nest box: birds go
  back to the nest when the sun sets in the west.
- 南: a 十 on top, like a signpost pointing to the warm south, over a tall box with a little
  pattern inside. It has the most strokes of the four (9).
- 北: two figures sitting back to back, turning away from the cold north wind.

The capital, とうきょう, is written with 東 and a second kanji that this course leaves for
later (so it's in kana here). The name means "eastern capital": the old capital, きょうと, lies to
its west.


## Dialogue: at the north exit

Emma is meeting Mr Tanaka, a friend of a friend, for a day out. They don't know each other
well, so they speak politely, with です and ます at the end of every sentence. The plain forms
appear only in the middle of sentences.

```dialogue
# At the north exit
エマ: すみません、たなかさんですか。
= Excuse me, are you Mr Tanaka?
たなか: はい、たなかです。エマさんですね。{北口|きたぐち}はすぐわかりましたか。
= Yes, I'm Tanaka. You must be Emma. Did you find the north exit easily?
エマ: はい。でも、この{駅|えき}は{大|おお}きいですね。{東口|ひがしぐち}も{西口|にしぐち}もありますね。
= Yes. But this station is big, isn't it? There's an east exit and a west exit too.
たなか: ええ、{南口|みなみぐち}もありますよ。エマさん、しゅみは{何|なん}ですか。
= Yes, and a south exit as well. Emma, what are your hobbies?
エマ: しゃしんをとることです。{山|やま}や{川|かわ}のしゃしんをとるのがすきです。
= Taking photos. I like taking pictures of mountains and rivers.
たなか: いいですね。わたしは{山|やま}にのぼるのがすきです。
= Nice. I like climbing mountains.
エマ: そうですか。たなかさんはギターもひきますね。
= Really? And you play the guitar too, don't you?
たなか: はい。でも、うたをうたうのはへたです。
= Yes. But I'm bad at singing.
エマ: わたしもです。じゃあ、{山|やま}へ{行|い}くまえに、{駅|えき}でおべんとうを{買|か}いましょう。
= Me too. Well then, before we go to the mountains, let's buy boxed lunches at the station.
```

Notes: すぐ is "right away, easily". エマさんですね and ギターもひきますね use ね to check
something the speaker is fairly sure of ("You must be Emma"; "You play the guitar too, don't
you?"). おべんとう is a boxed lunch. In うたをうたうのはへたです, は replaces が to contrast: guitar
yes, singing no.

## Say it

```speak
{本|ほん}を{読|よ}むのがすきです。
= I like reading books.
しゅみはしゃしんをとることです。
= My hobby is taking photos.
ねるまえに、おんがくを{聞|き}きます。
= I listen to music before I go to bed.
{北口|きたぐち}で{会|あ}いましょう。
= Let's meet at the north exit.
ギターをひくのがじょうずですね。
= You're good at playing the guitar.
```

## Common mistakes

- Putting すき right after the verb: ×およぐがすきです. A verb needs の first: およぐのがすきです.
- Marking the object with が instead of を inside the phrase: ×{本|ほん}が{読|よ}むのがすき. The
  book is the object of {読|よ}む, so it stays {本|ほん}を.
- Using the past before まえに: ×{行|い}ったまえに. Always the dictionary form: {行|い}くまえに.
- Guessing the group from the ます form: ×おきます → おく (that's "to put"). おきる (get up) is
  group 2. Check the note in your word list.
- Reading {来|き}ます's kanji the same way in the dictionary form: it's {来|く}る, not きる.
- Saying the directions in English order: Japanese says {東西南北|とうざいなんぼく}.

## Key points

- Every verb has plain forms and ます forms. The dictionary form is the plain non-past:
  {食|た}べる, {行|い}く, する.
- Group 2: ます → る. Group 3: します → する, {来|き}ます → {来|く}る. Group 1: the い-row sound
  before ます becomes the う-row sound ({飲|の}みます → {飲|の}む, {買|か}います → {買|か}う).
- An い-row stem can be group 1 or group 2, so learn each verb's group.
- Verb + のがすき / じょうず / へた / きらい です: liking or being good at an activity.
- しゅみは + verb + ことです: my hobby is (doing) ….
- Dictionary form + まえに: before doing, whatever the tense of the sentence.
- {東|ひがし}, {西|にし}, {南|みなみ}, {北|きた}; station exits {東口|ひがしぐち}, {西口|にしぐち},
  {南口|みなみぐち}, {北口|きたぐち}.
- A sentence is polite when its last verb is polite, even with plain forms inside it.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The ない form
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can already say "I don't eat" politely: {食|た}べません. This lesson teaches its plain
partner, {食|た}べない, the **[[ない form]]**. It's the second of the four plain forms from Lesson 21,
and you'll use it in two everyday patterns that stay polite:

- 〜ないでください — please don't …: ここでしゃしんをとらないでください。
- 〜なくてもいいです — you don't have to …: くつをぬがなくてもいいです。

Both are everywhere in notices, rules and instructions, so this lesson's theme is rules and
signs: what you may not do in a park, a temple or someone's home.

## Making the ない form

The ない form is the plain negative non-past: "don't …", "won't …". You can make it from the
dictionary form or from the ます form, whichever you find easier.

### Group 2 (る verbs): る → ない

| Dictionary form | ない form | ます form |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べない | {食|た}べません |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}ない | {見|み}ません |
| わすれる | わすれない | わすれません |
| すてる | すてない | すてません |

As always, group 2 is the easy one: the stem never changes.

### Group 1 (う verbs): the う sound becomes an あ sound

Move the last kana of the dictionary form from the う row to the あ row and add ない. (From the
ます form: move the い-row kana to the あ row.)

| Dictionary form | ない form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {書|か}く | {書|か}かない | not write |
| いそぐ | いそがない | not hurry |
| {話|はな}す | {話|はな}さない | not speak |
| {立|た}つ | {立|た}たない | not stand |
| しぬ | しなない | not die |
| あそぶ | あそばない | not play |
| {飲|の}む | {飲|の}まない | not drink |
| とる | とらない | not take |
| {買|か}う | {買|か}わない | not buy |

One kana is the exception: a verb ending in う takes わ, not あ. {買|か}う becomes {買|か}わない,
{言|い}う becomes {言|い}わない, {会|あ}う becomes {会|あ}わない, すう (to smoke) becomes すわない.
(×{買|か}あない doesn't exist. In older Japanese these verbs had a consonant before the final
vowel; today it survives only as the w of わ.)

Group 1 includes some verbs that end in いる or える and look like group 2. Their ない form
shows which group they're in:

| Verb | Group | ない form |
|---|---|---|
| かえる (go home) | 1 | かえらない |
| {入|はい}る (enter) | 1 | {入|はい}らない |
| はしる (run) | 1 | はしらない |
| しる (know) | 1 | しらない |
| おきる (get up) | 2 | おきない |

### Group 3 and ある

| Dictionary form | ない form | ます form |
|---|---|---|
| する | しない | しません |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}ない | {来|き}ません |
| ある | ない | ありません |

{来|く}る changes its vowel three ways: {来|く}る, {来|き}ます, {来|こ}ない. The kanji stays the
same, so read it from the ending.

ある (there is, to have) is the one verb whose ない form is just ない: ×あらない doesn't exist.
You've known this ない for a long time without the label: お{金|かね}がない (I have no money)
is the plain version of お{金|かね}がありません.

### ない behaves like an い-adjective

ない ends in い, and it conjugates like one: {高|たか}い → {高|たか}かった, so {食|た}べない →
{食|た}べなかった (didn't eat). You'll use that in Lesson 23. Add です to make it polite:
{食|た}べないです means the same as {食|た}べません, and both are correct; ません is a little
more formal, ないです is very common in conversation.

## Please don't: 〜ないでください

Add でください to the ない form:

ここでしゃしんをとらないでください。 — Please don't take photos here.

{花|はな}にさわらないでください。 — Please don't touch the flowers.

しんぱいしないでください。 — Please don't worry.

わすれないでください。 — Please don't forget.

You know 〜てください (please do) from Lesson 16. This is its negative, and it's built from the
ない form + で, *not* from the て form. Compare:

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| すててください (please throw it away) | すてないでください (please don't throw it away) |
| {来|き}てください (please come) | {来|こ}ないでください (please don't come) |

〜ないでください is a request: polite, but direct. With people you know, soften it with ね:
いそがないでくださいね (No need to rush, OK?). For a firm rule, you also know 〜てはいけません
(you must not) from Lesson 19. Signs and rule sheets use both; ないでください sounds like asking,
てはいけません like forbidding.

## You don't have to: 〜なくてもいいです

Take the ない form, change the final い to くて, and add もいいです:

{食|た}べない → {食|た}べなくて → {食|た}べなくてもいいです。 — You don't have to eat it.

あした{来|こ}なくてもいいです。 — You don't have to come tomorrow.

くつをぬがなくてもいいです。 — You don't need to take off your shoes. (ぬぐ = to take off)

The pattern means "it's all right even if you don't …". It answers questions like these:

> A: {名前|なまえ}をかたかなで{書|か}きますか。
>
> B: いいえ、かたかなで{書|か}かなくてもいいですよ。ひらがなでいいです。

A: Do I write my name in katakana? B: No, you don't have to write it in katakana. Hiragana is
fine.

You can also ask: {今日|きょう}、しゅくだいをしなくてもいいですか。 (Is it OK if I don't do the
homework today? しゅくだい = homework.) The answer is はい、しなくてもいいです or いいえ、してください.

## Rules and signs

Notices in Japan use several styles, and you'll want to recognize them all:

| Style | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a noun on its own | きんえん | No smoking |
| a short warning | ちゅうい / あぶない！ | Caution / Danger! |
| ないでください | さわらないでください | Please don't touch |
| てはいけません | ここで{食|た}べてはいけません | You may not eat here |
| ましょう | ごみはもちかえりましょう | Let's take our rubbish home |

The last style is common in parks and on posters: it's friendly, "let's all do this". Signs
also use kanji compounds that this course writes in kana, such as きんえん. One you can read
already: {立|た}ち{入|い}りきんし, "No entry" (from {立|た}ち{入|い}る, "to step into, enter").

In conversation, people often say だめ (no good, not allowed) instead of a full rule:
ここでたばこはだめですよ (You can't smoke here). On paper, the stronger warning word is きけん
(danger), as in きけん！{入|はい}らないでください。

Two adverbs make a rule stronger: かならず (always, without fail: かならずきそくをまもってください)
and ぜったい(に) (absolutely: ぜったいにさわらないでください, never touch it). In a car park
(ちゅうしゃじょう) you'll see the opposite request: ここにとめてください.

Some useful verbs for rules: まもる (to keep, obey: きそくをまもる, やくそくをまもる "keep a
promise"), すう (to smoke:
たばこをすう), すてる (to throw away), とめる (to park, to stop something), おす (to push),
さわる (to touch: さわる takes に, {花|はな}にさわる).

### Reading: rules at a park

> ひがしこうえんのルール
>
> ・ごみはここにすてないでください。もちかえりましょう。
>
> ・{花|はな}や{木|き}にさわらないでください。
>
> ・{入口|いりぐち}のまえにじてんしゃをとめないでください。
>
> ・ペットといっしょに{入|はい}ってもいいです。でも、ペットのごみはかならずもちかえってください。
>
> ・こうえんの{中|なか}はきんえんです。

East Park rules. Please don't throw rubbish away here; let's take it home. Please don't
touch the flowers or trees. Please don't park bicycles in front of the entrance. You may come
in with your pets, but always take your pet's mess home. No smoking in the park. (こうえん =
park, じてんしゃ = bicycle, もちかえる = to take home, かならず = without fail, always.)

## Dialogue: house rules

Maria has just arrived at her host family's house. Mrs Sato explains a few rules. They speak
politely: Maria is a guest, and they've only just met.

```dialogue
# House rules
さとう: マリアさん、うちのルールを{少|すこ}し{話|はな}しますね。
= Maria, let me tell you a few of our house rules.
マリア: はい、おねがいします。
= Yes, please.
さとう: げんかんでくつをぬいでください。でも、スリッパははいてもいいですよ。
= Please take your shoes off in the entrance. But you can wear slippers.
マリア: たたみのへやでもスリッパをはきますか。
= Do I wear slippers in the tatami room too?
さとう: いいえ、たたみのへやではスリッパをはかないでくださいね。
= No, please don't wear slippers in the tatami room.
マリア: わかりました。あさごはんは{何時|なんじ}ですか。
= I see. What time is breakfast?
さとう: {七時|しちじ}です。でも、{土曜日|どようび}と{日曜日|にちようび}は、はやくおきなくてもいいですよ。
= Seven o'clock. But on Saturdays and Sundays you don't have to get up early.
マリア: よかった！ ごみはどこにすてますか。
= Great! Where do I throw away rubbish?
さとう: このはこにすててください。びんやかんは{入|い}れないでください。
= Please put it in this box. Please don't put in bottles or cans.
さとう: びんとかんは{木曜日|もくようび}です。まちがえないでくださいね。
= Bottles and cans go out on Thursdays. Please don't mix them up.
マリア: はい、わすれません。
= OK, I won't forget.
```

げんかん is the entrance hall, where shoes come off; たたみ is the straw mat floor (more on
both in Lesson 20h2). はこ is a box, びん a bottle, かん a can, まちがえる "to make a mistake, get wrong" (group 2), {入|い}れる "to put in" (a group 2
verb related to {入|はい}る: {入|い}れない). Japanese towns sort their rubbish carefully, and
the rules differ from town to town.

## Say it

```speak
しゃしんをとらないでください。
= Please don't take photos.
しんぱいしないでください。
= Please don't worry.
くつをぬがなくてもいいです。
= You don't have to take off your shoes.
あした{来|こ}なくてもいいですよ。
= You don't need to come tomorrow.
きそくをまもってください。
= Please follow the rules.
```

## Common mistakes

- Using あ for verbs that end in う: ×{買|か}あない, ×{言|い}あない. It's {買|か}わない, {言|い}わない.
- Treating ある like other verbs: ×あらない. The ない form of ある is ない.
- ×{来|き}ない or ×くない for {来|く}る. It's {来|こ}ない.
- Treating かえる, {入|はい}る, はしる as group 2: ×かえない. They're group 1: かえらない.
- Making "please don't" from the て form: ×{食|た}べてないでください. It's ない form + で:
  {食|た}べないでください.
- Mixing up "don't have to" and "must not". {食|た}べなくてもいいです is "you don't have to
  eat"; {食|た}べてはいけません is "you must not eat".

## Key points

- The ない form is the plain negative: {食|た}べない (don't eat), {行|い}かない (don't go).
- Group 2: る → ない. Group 1: う-row → あ-row + ない, but う → わ ({買|か}わない).
  Group 3: しない, {来|こ}ない. ある → ない.
- ない works like an い-adjective: {食|た}べなかった (didn't eat); {食|た}べないです = {食|た}べません.
- ない form + でください: please don't …
- ない form − い + くてもいいです: you don't have to …
- Signs: nouns (きんえん), ないでください, てはいけません, and friendly ましょう.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The た form: past and experiences
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The **[[た form]]** is the plain past: {食|た}べた (ate), {行|い}った (went), した (did). It's the
third plain form, after the dictionary form and the ない form, and there's good news: you
already know how to make it. If you can make the て form (Module 4), you can make the た form.

With it come two patterns that are perfect for talking about travel:

- 〜たことがあります — I have (ever) done …: おんせんに{入|はい}ったことがあります。
- 〜たり〜たりします — I do things like … and …: {山|やま}にのぼったり、しゃしんをとったりしました。

## Making the た form: the て form with a

Take the て form and change its final vowel: て becomes た, で becomes だ. Every rule you
learned for the て form, including the exception {行|い}く → {行|い}って, carries over.

| Dictionary form ends in | て form | た form | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| う, つ, る (group 1) | って | った | {買|か}う → {買|か}った, {立|た}つ → {立|た}った, とる → とった |
| む, ぶ, ぬ | んで | んだ | {飲|の}む → {飲|の}んだ, あそぶ → あそんだ, しぬ → しんだ |
| く | いて | いた | {書|か}く → {書|か}いた, {聞|き}く → {聞|き}いた |
| ぐ | いで | いだ | およぐ → およいだ, いそぐ → いそいだ |
| す | して | した | {話|はな}す → {話|はな}した |
| {行|い}く (exception) | {行|い}って | {行|い}った | — |
| る (group 2) | て | た | {食|た}べる → {食|た}べた, {見|み}る → {見|み}た |
| する, {来|く}る | して, {来|き}て | した, {来|き}た | — |

A few to say aloud, so the shapes sink in: {飲|の}んだ, {書|か}いた, {行|い}った, {来|き}た, とまった
(stayed), つかれた (got tired).

The verb ある has the た form あった (there was). The negative past is the ない form with
なかった, just as for an い-adjective: {行|い}かない → {行|い}かなかった (didn't go), ない →
なかった (there wasn't).

So the four plain forms of {行|い}く are:

| | Affirmative | Negative |
|---|---|---|
| Non-past | {行|い}く | {行|い}かない |
| Past | {行|い}った | {行|い}かなかった |

Lesson 24 uses these as the verbs of casual conversation. In this lesson, the た form
appears inside polite sentences again.

## Experiences: 〜たことがあります

た form + ことがあります says that something has happened at least once in your life: "I have
(ever) done …".

ほっかいどうへ{行|い}ったことがあります。 — I've been to Hokkaido.

おんせんに{入|はい}ったことがありますか。 — Have you ever been in a hot spring?

りょかんにとまったことはありません。 — I've never stayed at a Japanese inn.

Literally it's "there is the experience (こと) of having gone". That's why the verb at the end is
ある: you have, or haven't, such a こと. In the negative, が usually becomes は, as with other
negatives.

Answers are short, because the verb carries the meaning:

> A: すしを{食|た}べたことがありますか。
>
> B: はい、あります。 / いいえ、ありません。

To stress "never, not even once", add いちども (once + even): いちども{行|い}ったことがありません
(I've never been there, not once). はじめて means "for the first time": はじめておんせんに
{入|はい}りました (I went in a hot spring for the first time).

More words for experiences:

せかいのいろいろな{国|くに}へ{行|い}きたいです。いつか、アフリカへ{行|い}きたいです。 — I want to go to lots of
countries around the world. Someday I want to go to Africa.

むかし、いなかにすんだことがあります。 — Long ago, I lived in the countryside for a while.

キャンプをしたことがありますか。 — Have you ever been camping?

おんせんにはなんど{行|い}きましたか。 — How many times have you been to hot springs?

りょかんにとまったのは、いいけいけんでした。 — Staying at a ryokan was a good experience.

(せかい = world, いつか = someday, むかし = long ago, いなか = the countryside, なんど = how many
times, けいけん = experience. In the last one, の turns a phrase into a noun, as in Lesson 21.)

### When not to use it

〜たことがあります is about life experience, not about one recent event. If you add a time like
"yesterday", use the ordinary past (〜ました) instead:

きのう、すしを{食|た}べました。 — I had sushi yesterday. (×きのう、すしを{食|た}べたことがあります。)

It also sounds strange for everyday things everyone has done: ×ごはんを{食|た}べたことがあります
is like saying "I have, at some point in my life, eaten a meal". Use it for something a little
special: a place, a food, an activity.

## Doing things like … and …: 〜たり〜たりします

To give a few examples of what you do (or did), out of a longer list, put each verb in the
た form + り, and finish with する:

{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んだり、えいがを{見|み}たりします。
— On my days off I read books, watch films and so on.

りょこうで、{山|やま}にのぼったり、おんせんに{入|はい}ったりしました。
— On the trip we climbed mountains, went in hot springs and things like that.

The tense and the politeness are on the last する only: します for what you usually do, しました
for the past. The たり verbs never change.

Compare it with the て form from Lesson 18. A て-form sequence tells what you did *in order*,
and usually all of it. たり picks *examples*, in no particular order:

| | Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| て | おきて、ごはんを{食|た}べて、{出|で}かけました。 | I got up, ate, then went out. |
| たり | {話|はな}したり、うたったりしました。 | We talked, sang and so on. |

With a single verb, 〜たりします means "do things like …": {日曜日|にちようび}はテニスをしたりします
(On Sundays I play tennis, among other things). It makes a sentence sound less blunt.

## Travel words

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| りょこう / りょこうする | a trip, travel / to travel |
| りょかん | a Japanese-style inn |
| とまる | to stay (overnight): りょかんにとまる (it sounds like とまる, "to stop", from Lesson 10h1, but it's written with a different kanji) |
| おんせん | a hot spring (and the bathhouse or town around it) |
| おてら / じんじゃ | a Buddhist temple / a Shinto shrine |
| おみやげ | a souvenir (usually a gift you bring back for others) |
| けしき | scenery, a view |
| くうこう | an airport |
| パスポート / にもつ | passport / luggage |
| しま | an island |
| みずうみ | a lake |
| つかれる | to get tired: つかれました (I'm tired) |

おみやげ are an important custom: after a trip, people bring small boxes of local sweets for
their colleagues, classmates or neighbours. つかれる is a group 2 verb that describes a change
("get tired"), so "I'm tired" is つかれました, the past: you got tired, and you still are.

## Reading: a message from Emma

Emma writes to her Japanese teacher after a trip. It's a polite message, so it ends in です and
ます, with plain forms inside the sentences.

> きむら{先生|せんせい}
>
> こんにちは。エマです。{先週|せんしゅう}、{友|とも}だちとほっかいどうへりょこうに{行|い}きました。ほっかいどうは{日本|にほん}の{北|きた}にあります。{東|ひがし}のほうの{小|ちい}さいまちで、りょかんにとまりました。りょかんにとまったことはありませんでしたから、とてもたのしかったです。
>
> {毎日|まいにち}、{山|やま}をあるいたり、みずうみのしゃしんをとったりしました。けしきがとてもきれいでした。よるは、はじめておんせんに{入|はい}りました。{先生|せんせい}は、ほっかいどうへ{行|い}ったことがありますか。
>
> おみやげを{買|か}いました。{来週|らいしゅう}、{学校|がっこう}でわたしますね。
>
> エマ

Ms Kimura, hello, it's Emma. Last week I went on a trip to Hokkaido with a friend. Hokkaido is
in the north of Japan. We stayed at a ryokan in a small town in the east. I'd never stayed at
a ryokan, so it was a lot of fun. Every day we did things like walking in the mountains and
taking photos of the lakes. The scenery was really beautiful. In the evening I went in a hot
spring for the first time. Have you ever been to Hokkaido? I bought you a souvenir. I'll give
it to you at school next week. Emma

Notes: ほう is "direction, side" ({東|ひがし}のほう, the eastern part); まち is a town; から after
a sentence means "so, because" (more in Lesson 26); わたす is "to hand over". Notice that the
experience pattern is past here: とまったことはありませんでした, "I had never stayed".

## Dialogue: after the trip

```dialogue
# After the trip
けん: エマさん、ほっかいどうはどうでしたか。
= Emma, how was Hokkaido?
エマ: とてもよかったです。{山|やま}にのぼったり、おんせんに{入|はい}ったりしました。
= It was great. We climbed mountains, went in hot springs and so on.
けん: いいですね。わたしはまだ{行|い}ったことがありません。
= Sounds great. I haven't been there yet.
エマ: けんさんは{外国|がいこく}へ{行|い}ったことがありますか。
= Ken, have you ever been abroad?
けん: はい、にかいあります。かんこくと、タイへ{行|い}きました。
= Yes, twice. I went to Korea and Thailand.
エマ: タイで{何|なに}をしましたか。
= What did you do in Thailand?
けん: うみでおよいだり、おてらを{見|み}たりしました。でも、とてもあつかったです。
= Things like swimming in the sea and seeing temples. But it was really hot.
エマ: そうですか。じゃあ、つぎはいっしょにほっかいどうへ{行|い}きませんか。
= I see. Then shall we go to Hokkaido together next time?
けん: いいですね。{行|い}きましょう！
= Sounds good. Let's go!
```

にかい is "twice" (2 + the counter for times), まだ is "(not) yet" (Lesson 26), うみ is the sea,
あつい is "hot" and つぎ is "next". Notice the short answer はい、にかいあります: ある carries the
whole meaning "I have been".

## Say it

```speak
おんせんに{入|はい}ったことがありますか。
= Have you ever been in a hot spring?
いいえ、いちどもありません。
= No, never.
りょかんにとまったことがあります。
= I've stayed at a Japanese inn.
{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は、{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んだり、えいがを{見|み}たりします。
= On my days off I do things like reading and watching films.
つかれました。
= I'm tired.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{行|い}いた. {行|い}く is the exception: {行|い}った, like {行|い}って.
- ×{書|か}きた, ×{飲|の}みた. Group 1 verbs follow the sound rules: {書|か}いた, {飲|の}んだ.
- Using 〜たことがあります with a specific time: ×きのう{行|い}ったことがあります. Say
  きのう{行|い}きました.
- Forgetting the final する: ×{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んだり、えいがを{見|み}たり。 In a full sentence, end
  with します or しました.
- Putting the tense on the たり verbs: ×{見|み}ましたり. たり is always the plain た form + り.
- Saying ×つかれます for "I'm tired" now. It's つかれました (or つかれています).

## Key points

- The た form is the plain past. Make it from the て form: て → た, で → だ.
  {飲|の}んで → {飲|の}んだ, {行|い}って → {行|い}った, {来|き}て → {来|き}た.
- Negative past: ない → なかった ({行|い}かなかった).
- た form + ことがあります: I have (ever) done …; ことはありません: I've never …
  Not with a specific past time.
- た form + り, た form + り + します: doing things like … and …; the tense goes on する.
- Travel: りょこう, りょかんにとまる, おんせん, おみやげ, けしき.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Casual speech
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've used plain forms only in the middle of sentences, with です or ます at the end.
This lesson lets them stand at the end. That's **[[casual speech]]**: the way Japanese people talk
to family and close friends. {行|い}きますか becomes {行|い}く？, {高|たか}いです becomes {高|たか}い,
{雨|あめ}です becomes {雨|あめ}だ or just {雨|あめ}.

You'll learn who speaks casually to whom, the plain forms of adjectives and nouns (with the
plain copula だ), how casual questions work, the sentence-final particles ね and よ, and
でしょう (probably; right?). If you watch Japanese dramas or anime, or have Japanese friends,
this is the Japanese you hear most.

## Who speaks how

Japanese speakers choose a speech style for each person they talk to. As a learner, keep to
two styles:

| Style | Sounds like | Use it with |
|---|---|---|
| polite (です/ます) | {行|い}きますか。 | people you don't know, people older than you, teachers, colleagues, shop staff, anyone when in doubt |
| casual (plain forms) | {行|い}く？ | family, close friends, classmates once you're friends, children, pets |

Some guidelines that Japanese speakers follow without thinking:

- Start polite. Even people of the same age use です/ます when they first meet, and move to
  casual speech as they become friends. A friend may tell you so: ためぐちでいいよ ("You can
  talk casually with me", ためぐち = casual speech between equals).
- It doesn't have to be equal. An older person, a boss or a teacher may speak casually to
  you while you stay polite. That's normal, not rude.
- Writing has its own rules. Diaries, newspapers, essays and many websites use plain
  forms without being "casual": the reader isn't a person being spoken to. Messages to friends
  are casual, like speech.

Speaking casually to a stranger or a teacher sounds rude or childish; speaking very politely
to a close friend sounds cold, as if you're angry. A learner who stays polite is always
forgiven, so when you aren't sure, use です and ます.

## The plain forms of everything

Here is the full set: four forms each for verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives and nouns. Only
the right-hand words of each row differ from what you know with です.

| | Non-past | Negative | Past | Negative past |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| verb | {行|い}く | {行|い}かない | {行|い}った | {行|い}かなかった |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}い | {高|たか}くない | {高|たか}かった | {高|たか}くなかった |
| いい | いい | よくない | よかった | よくなかった |
| な-adjective | ひまだ | ひまじゃない | ひまだった | ひまじゃなかった |
| noun | {雨|あめ}だ | {雨|あめ}じゃない | {雨|あめ}だった | {雨|あめ}じゃなかった |

Look at what happened:

- Verbs: the forms from Lessons 21–23.
- い-adjectives: take off です. {高|たか}いです → {高|たか}い, {高|たか}かったです → {高|たか}かった. The
  です was only there for politeness; the adjective already changes for tense by itself.
- な-adjectives and nouns: です becomes だ, the plain copula, and でした becomes だった.
  The negatives are じゃない and じゃなかった, the same forms you've used with です
  (じゃないです) without the です.

Never put だ after an い-adjective: ×{高|たか}いだ, ×おいしいだ. い-adjectives don't need a copula.
(You'll hear {高|たか}いです, but that です is only politeness.)

In writing and in careful speech, じゃない is ではない; you'll see both.

## だ in conversation

だ is the plain form of です, but in real conversation it behaves a little differently:

- A sentence ending in a bare だ can sound blunt or forceful: あしたは{休|やす}みだ。 sounds like a
  statement in a story or someone stating a hard fact.
- With よ or ね it sounds natural and friendly: あしたは{休|やす}みだよ。 (Tomorrow's a day off, you
  know.) きれいだね。 (It's pretty, isn't it?)
- Often it's simply left out: あした、{休|やす}み。 これ、ぼくの。 (This is mine.)
- In a question, だ is always left out: {休|やす}み？ (Is it a day off?), ひま？ (Are you free?), not
  ×{休|やす}みだ？

## Casual questions

In casual speech, a question doesn't need か. Say the plain form with a rising voice and
write ？:

| Polite | Casual | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {行|い}きますか。 | {行|い}く？ | Are you going? |
| おいしいですか。 | おいしい？ | Is it good? |
| {元気|げんき}ですか。 | {元気|げんき}？ | How are you? |
| {何|なに}を{食|た}べましたか。 | {何|なに}{食|た}べた？ | What did you eat? |

か at the end of a casual question sounds rough, so it's mostly avoided. Notice also that
casual speech drops particles that are clear from context, especially は, を and へ: ごはん、
{食|た}べた？ (Did you eat?), どこ{行|い}く？ (Where are you going?).

Casual "why?" is なんで？ (polite: どうしてですか). Reactions are short too: すごい！ (Wow!),
ほんとう？ (Really?), やった！ (Yay! I did it!).

You'll often hear の (or ん) added to casual questions: どこ{行|い}くの？ It asks for an
explanation and sounds softer and more interested. You can recognize it for now.

A negative question is a casual invitation, the plain version of 〜ませんか (Lesson 10):
いっしょに{行|い}かない？ (Want to come along?). Answer:

- うん: yes, yeah (casual はい)
- ううん: no, nope (casual いいえ). The two sound different: うん is one short, falling "un";
  ううん is "u-un", with a small dip and rise.
- いいよ: sure, OK. わかった: got it, OK (casual わかりました).

### Casual requests and "don't"

Casual requests simply drop ください: ちょっとまって (wait a second), これ{見|み}て (look at this),
わすれないで (don't forget). For "you mustn't", the casual form of 〜てはいけない is 〜ちゃだめ
(or 〜ちゃいけない), from 〜ては + だめ; after a で form it's 〜じゃだめ:

さわっちゃだめ！ — Don't touch! (さわってはだめ)

それ、{飲|の}んじゃだめだよ。 — You mustn't drink that. ({飲|の}んではだめ)

Parents say this to children all the time. Between adults, わすれないでね (don't forget, OK?) is
gentler.

## ね and よ

These two **[[sentence-final particles]]** come at the very end, after the verb, adjective or だ.
You've already used them politely (そうですね, いいですよ); in casual speech they're
everywhere.

ね asks the listener to share what you feel or to confirm something you both know:
"…, isn't it?", "…, right?"

さむいね。 — It's cold, isn't it?

このケーキ、おいしいね。 — This cake is good, isn't it?

よ gives the listener something new: "…, you know", "I'm telling you".

あの{店|みせ}、{安|やす}いよ。 — That shop is cheap, you know.

あしたはテストだよ。 — There's a test tomorrow, you know. (Did you forget?)

よね checks something you think is true: あしたは{休|やす}みだよね？ (Tomorrow's a day off,
right?)

Use よ with care when speaking to people above you: telling a teacher いいですよ can sound as if
you're giving permission. ね is almost always safe.

## でしょう: probably, and "right?"

でしょう after a plain form says something is probable. It's what you hear in every weather
forecast:

あしたは{雨|あめ}でしょう。 — It will probably rain tomorrow.

たなかさんも{来|く}るでしょう。 — Mr Tanaka will probably come too.

たぶん (probably, maybe) often goes with it: たぶん{高|たか}いでしょう (It's probably expensive).
Before でしょう, verbs and い-adjectives are plain ({来|く}るでしょう, {高|たか}いでしょう), and nouns
and な-adjectives drop だ ({雨|あめ}でしょう, ひまでしょう).

With a rising voice, でしょう？ asks for agreement: "…, right?". In casual speech it's shortened
to でしょ？: これ、おいしいでしょ？ (This is good, right?). The casual "probably" is だろう, used
more by men; you'll hear it, but たぶん + plain form (たぶん{来|く}る) is an easy casual choice.

## Words for people in casual speech

- I: わたし is fine for everyone. Many men and boys say ぼく; おれ is a rough, casual "I"
  used by men among friends. Some women say あたし in casual speech.
- you: Japanese avoids "you" and uses names instead: はると、{行|い}く？ (Haruto, are you
  going?). きみ (you) is used by some men to friends or juniors, and in songs.
- he / she: かれ and かのじょ, which also mean "boyfriend" and "girlfriend". Using the name is
  more common.

Between close friends, given names without さん are normal. Don't drop さん yourself until the
other person does.

## Dialogue: two friends

Haruto and Sakura are university friends, so they speak casually.

```dialogue
# Monday morning
さくら: はると、おはよう。きのうのパーティー、{来|こ}なかったね。
= Morning, Haruto. You didn't come to the party yesterday.
はると: うん、ごめん。アルバイトだった。パーティー、どうだった？
= Yeah, sorry. I had work. How was the party?
さくら: たのしかったよ。ケーキもおいしかった。
= It was fun. The cake was good too.
はると: いいなあ。だれが{来|き}た？
= Lucky you. Who came?
さくら: けんとマリア。マリアがうたをうたったよ。すごくじょうずだった。
= Ken and Maria. Maria sang. She was really good.
はると: ほんとう？ {聞|き}きたかったなあ。
= Really? I wish I'd heard it.
さくら: ねえ、こんどの{土曜日|どようび}、ひま？ みんなで{山|やま}に{行|い}くの。はるとも{行|い}かない？
= Hey, are you free this Saturday? We're all going to the mountains. Want to come?
はると: {行|い}く！ でも、{土曜日|どようび}は{雨|あめ}だよね？
= I'm in! But it's going to rain on Saturday, right?
さくら: ううん、たぶんはれだよ。
= No, it'll probably be sunny.
はると: やった！ じゃあ、またね。
= Yay! See you, then.
```

Notes: アルバイト is a part-time job; いいなあ is "lucky you!" (なあ is a softer, more personal
ね); すごく is "really, very" (casual); {聞|き}きたかった is the past of {聞|き}きたい (I wanted to hear);
こんどの is "this coming, next"; みんなで is "all together"; はれ is sunny weather.

The same conversation between two people who don't know each other well would sound like
this:

| Casual | Polite |
|---|---|
| パーティー、どうだった？ | パーティーはどうでしたか。 |
| たのしかったよ。 | たのしかったですよ。 |
| だれが{来|き}た？ | だれが{来|き}ましたか。 |
| {土曜日|どようび}、ひま？ | {土曜日|どようび}はひまですか。 |
| はるとも{行|い}かない？ | はるとさんも{行|い}きませんか。 |
| うん / ううん | はい / いいえ |

## Say it

```speak
{元気|げんき}？
= How are you?
うん、{元気|げんき}だよ。
= Yeah, I'm good.
きのう、{何|なに}した？
= What did you do yesterday?
いっしょに{行|い}かない？
= Want to come along?
あしたは{雨|あめ}でしょう。
= It will probably rain tomorrow.
これ、おいしいね。
= This is good, isn't it?
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{高|たか}いだ. い-adjectives never take だ: {高|たか}い, {高|たか}いよ, {高|たか}いね.
- ×ひまだ？ as a question. Drop だ: ひま？
- Forgetting that いい changes to よ-: ×いくない, ×いかった. It's よくない, よかった.
- Speaking casually to a teacher, a host parent you've just met or shop staff. Stay polite
  until you're invited to change.
- Overusing よ. It can sound pushy; ね is the friendlier default.
- Mixing styles in one sentence by accident: ×{行|い}くですか. Either {行|い}きますか or {行|い}く？

## Key points

- Casual speech uses plain forms at the end of sentences. Use it with family, close friends and
  children; use です/ます with everyone else, and when in doubt.
- い-adjectives: drop です ({高|たか}い, {高|たか}かった). な-adjectives and nouns: だ, じゃない, だった,
  じゃなかった. Never ×{高|たか}いだ.
- In conversation だ is often dropped, and always dropped in questions.
- Casual questions: rising voice, no か: {行|い}く？ Particles like は and を are often dropped.
- うん (yes), ううん (no), いいよ (sure), わかった (got it).
- ね: shared feeling, "isn't it?"; よ: new information, "you know"; よね: "right?"
- Plain form + でしょう: probably (nouns and な-adjectives without だ). でしょ？: right?

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Describing nouns with verbs; とき
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English describes a noun with a whole sentence after it: "the book *that I bought
yesterday*", "the person *who is taking photos*". Japanese does it too, but the description
goes *before* the noun, and it's made of plain forms:

きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん} — the book (I) bought yesterday

しゃしんをとっている{人|ひと} — the person taking photos

This lesson teaches these **[[relative clauses]]**, then とき (when …), which works the same way.
It ends with a review of the particle の, which has turned up in many patterns. With this
lesson, the plain forms of Module 5 come together: you'll use all four of them every time you
describe something.

## What you already know

You've been putting words before nouns since Module 1:

| Before the noun | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a noun + の | わたしの{本|ほん} | my book |
| an い-adjective | {新|あたら}しい{本|ほん} | a new book |
| a な-adjective + な | きれいな{花|はな} | a pretty flower |

The rule is always the same: the describing part comes first, the noun last. A relative clause
just makes the describing part longer.

## Verbs before nouns

Put a verb phrase in a plain form directly in front of a noun:

| Clause | Noun | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| いつも{行|い}く | {店|みせ} | the shop I always go to |
| あまり{行|い}かない | {店|みせ} | a shop I don't go to much |
| きのう{行|い}った | {店|みせ} | the shop I went to yesterday |
| まだ{行|い}ったことがない | {店|みせ} | a shop I haven't been to yet |

There's no word for "that", "which" or "who": the plain form touching the noun does the job.
The tense works as in English: {行|い}った{店|みせ} is a shop already visited, {行|い}く{店|みせ} one you go
to (or will go to).

Use the whole thing anywhere a noun can go:

これはきのう{買|か}った{本|ほん}です。 — This is the book I bought yesterday.

きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん}をもう{読|よ}みました。 — I've already read the book I bought yesterday.

きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん}はおもしろいです。 — The book I bought yesterday is interesting.

The clause uses plain forms even in the most polite sentence. Politeness is shown only at the
end: ×きのう{買|か}いました{本|ほん} is wrong.

More examples:

わたしが{生|う}まれたところは、{小|ちい}さいまちです。 — The place where I was born is a small town.
(ところ = place)

{駅|えき}でひろったさいふを、うけつけにもって{行|い}きました。 — I took the wallet I picked up at
the station to the reception desk. (ひろう = to pick up, もって{行|い}く = to take along)

なくしたかぎがみつかりました。 — The key I lost has been found. (なくす = to lose)

これはおとなも{子|こ}どももすきなところです。 — This is a place adults and children both like.

### Building one, step by step

Start with a sentence and turn it into a description:

1. {友|とも}だちがケーキをつくりました。 — My friend made a cake.
2. Make the verb plain: {友|とも}だちがケーキをつくった
3. Take out the noun you want to describe (ケーキ) and put it at the end:
   {友|とも}だちがつくったケーキ — the cake my friend made
4. Use it: {友|とも}だちがつくったケーキはとてもおいしかったです。

(つくる = to make.)

### が, not は, inside the clause

The person doing the action in a relative clause is marked with が, never は:

{父|ちち}が{書|か}いた{本|ほん} — the book my father wrote (×{父|ちち}は{書|か}いた{本|ほん})

は marks the topic of the whole sentence, and a clause inside a noun can't have its own topic.
In speech and writing you'll also see の in place of が: {父|ちち}の{書|か}いた{本|ほん}. Both mean the same;
が is the safer one to use yourself.

## The person who …

{人|ひと} (person) is the noun you'll describe most:

あそこでしゃしんをとっている{人|ひと}はだれですか。 — Who's the person taking photos over there?

めがねをかけている{人|ひと}がたなかさんです。 — The person wearing glasses is Mr Tanaka.

{日本|にほん}で{生|う}まれた{人|ひと} — a person born in Japan ({生|う}まれる = to be born)

For "the person who is doing …", use the ている form from Lesson 17 in its plain shape, 〜ている
(plain of 〜ています). It's also the way to point someone out in a crowd:

> A: エマさんはどの{人|ひと}ですか。
>
> B: あのあかいぼうしをかぶっている{人|ひと}です。

A: Which one is Emma? B: The one wearing the red hat.

Adjectives and nouns can join in too, in their plain forms: かみが{長|なが}い{人|ひと} (a person with long
hair, Lesson 15), {先生|せんせい}だった{人|ひと} (a person who was a teacher), {車|くるま}がない{人|ひと} (people
without a car).

## とき: when …

とき is a noun meaning "time", and you describe it like any other noun. The result means "when
…":

| Before とき | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb (plain) | こまったとき | when you're in trouble |
| い-adjective | さむいとき | when it's cold |
| な-adjective + な | ひまなとき | when I'm free |
| noun + の | {子|こ}どものとき | when I was a child |

ひまなとき、ギターをひきます。 — When I'm free, I play the guitar.

{子|こ}どものとき、ほっかいどうにすんでいました。 — When I was a child, I lived in Hokkaido.

こまったとき、{先生|せんせい}に{聞|き}いてください。 — When you're stuck, please ask the teacher.
(こまる = to be in trouble, not know what to do)

あかちゃんがねているとき、しずかにしてください。 — Please be quiet while the baby is sleeping.

{子|こ}どものとき、ゆめはパイロットでした。 — When I was a child, my dream was to be a pilot. (ゆめ =
dream)

Put a comma after the とき part when it starts a long sentence. You'll also see とき written with
its kanji, {時|とき}; in grammar like this, many writers prefer kana.

### Before or after? {行|い}くとき and {行|い}ったとき

With a verb, the tense *inside* the とき clause shows whether the action has happened at the
time of the main event:

{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}くとき、くうこうでおみやげを{買|か}いました。
— When I was going to Japan, I bought souvenirs at the airport. (at home, before leaving)

{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}ったとき、おんせんに{入|はい}りました。
— When I went to Japan, I went in a hot spring. (after arriving, in Japan)

The dictionary form says "not yet done", the た form says "already done". The tense of the
whole sentence comes at the end, as usual.

## The many jobs of の: a review

You've now met の in many patterns. Here they all are:

| Use | Example | Meaning | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| owner | わたしの{本|ほん} | my book | 1 |
| type or topic | {日本語|にほんご}の{先生|せんせい} | a Japanese teacher | 1 |
| position | つくえの{上|うえ} | on the desk | 5 |
| "the one" (noun left out) | このかさはわたしのです。 | This umbrella is mine. | 2 |
| same person | {友|とも}だちのけんさん | my friend Ken | — |
| noun + とき, まえに | {子|こ}どものとき, ごはんのまえに | when (I was) a child, before the meal | 18, 25 |
| verb → noun | {読|よ}むのがすきです | I like reading | 21 |
| doer in a clause | {父|ちち}の{書|か}いた{本|ほん} | the book my father wrote | 25 |

In every case, the の links something to what follows it, or stands in for a noun.

## Reading: a family photo

> これはきょねんのなつ、うみへ{行|い}ったときのしゃしんです。まんなかでわらっている{人|ひと}が{母|はは}です。{左|ひだり}でギターをひいている{人|ひと}は{父|ちち}です。{父|ちち}がいつもひくギターは、とても{古|ふる}いです。{右|みぎ}にいるめがねをかけている{女|おんな}の{人|ひと}は、{母|はは}の{友|とも}だちです。{日本|にほん}で{生|う}まれた{人|ひと}で、{母|はは}にりょうりをおしえています。しゃしんをとった{人|ひと}はわたしです。

This is a photo from when we went to the seaside last summer. The person laughing in the middle
is my mother. The person playing the guitar on the left is my father. The guitar my father
always plays is really old. The woman wearing glasses on the right is my mother's friend.
She's someone who was born in Japan, and she teaches my mother cooking. The person who took
the photo is me.

(きょねん = last year, なつ = summer, まんなか = the middle, わらう = to laugh, smile, りょうり =
cooking, おしえる = to teach. 〜{人|ひと}で、… joins two sentences: "she's someone born in Japan,
and …".)

Count the relative clauses: うみへ{行|い}ったとき, わらっている{人|ひと}, ギターをひいている{人|ひと},
{父|ちち}がいつもひくギター, {右|みぎ}にいる…{女|おんな}の{人|ひと}, {日本|にほん}で{生|う}まれた{人|ひと},
しゃしんをとった{人|ひと}. Notice {右|みぎ}にいるめがねをかけている{女|おんな}の{人|ひと}: a noun can have two
clauses in front of it.

## Dialogue: lost and found

Emma left her bag on a train. She goes to the station office. A station worker (えきいん)
helps her; they speak politely.

```dialogue
# At the station office
エマ: すみません、わすれものをしました。きのう、{電車|でんしゃ}にかばんをわすれました。
= Excuse me, I've lost something. I left my bag on a train yesterday.
えきいん: どの{電車|でんしゃ}ですか。
= Which train?
エマ: {午後|ごご}{三時|さんじ}ごろこの{駅|えき}に{来|き}た{電車|でんしゃ}です。{東口|ひがしぐち}のほうからのりました。
= The train that came into this station at about three in the afternoon. I got on from the east exit side.
えきいん: どんなかばんですか。
= What kind of bag is it?
エマ: くろくて{小|ちい}さいかばんです。
= It's a small black bag.
えきいん: {中|なか}に{何|なに}がありますか。
= What's in it?
エマ: さいふと、かぎと、{友|とも}だちに{買|か}ったおみやげと、{学校|がっこう}でつかう{日本語|にほんご}の{本|ほん}です。
= My wallet, my keys, a souvenir I bought for a friend, and the Japanese book I use at school.
えきいん: ちょっとまってください。……このかばんですか。
= Just a moment, please. ... Is this the bag?
エマ: いいえ、ちがいます。わたしのはもっと{小|ちい}さいです。
= No, that's not it. Mine is smaller.
えきいん: じゃあ、これはどうですか。{北口|きたぐち}のちかくでみつかったかばんです。
= Then how about this one? It's a bag that was found near the north exit.
エマ: あっ、それです！ よかった。
= Oh, that's it! What a relief.
えきいん: では、ここに{名前|なまえ}と{電話|でんわ}ばんごうを{書|か}いてください。
= Then please write your name and phone number here.
エマ: はい。ほんとうにありがとうございました。
= OK. Thank you so much.
```

Notes: わすれもの is something left behind (わすれる + もの, thing); something you dropped is an おとしもの; のる is "to get on (a train)", ちがいます is "that's not right, it's a different one",
もっと is "more", and みつかる is "to be found" (みつける is "to find"). くろくて{小|ちい}さい joins two
い-adjectives: change the final い to くて (black and small), the same change you made in
〜なくてもいいです (Lesson 22). よかった, the past of いい, is what you say when
something turns out well.

## Say it

```speak
きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん}です。
= It's the book I bought yesterday.
めがねをかけている{人|ひと}はだれですか。
= Who's the person wearing glasses?
ひまなとき、{何|なに}をしますか。
= What do you do when you're free?
{子|こ}どものとき、よくおよぎました。
= I swam a lot when I was a child.
こまったとき、{先生|せんせい}に{聞|き}きます。
= When I don't know what to do, I ask the teacher.
```

## Common mistakes

- Putting the clause after the noun, English-style: ×{本|ほん}きのう{買|か}った. The clause always
  comes first: きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん}.
- Using ます or です in the clause: ×{買|か}いました{本|ほん}. Plain forms only.
- Using は in the clause: ×{父|ちち}は{書|か}いた{本|ほん}. Use が (or の).
- Forgetting な or の before とき: ×ひまとき, ×{子|こ}どもとき. It's ひまなとき, {子|こ}どものとき.
- Adding の after a verb before a noun: ×{買|か}ったの{本|ほん}. A verb touches the noun directly.
- Using the wrong tense with {行|い}くとき / {行|い}ったとき. Ask yourself: had it happened yet?

## Key points

- A relative clause is a plain-form phrase put right before a noun: きのう{買|か}った{本|ほん},
  {行|い}かない{店|みせ}, しゃしんをとっている{人|ひと}. There's no word for "that/who/which".
- Politeness goes only on the last verb of the sentence; the clause is always plain.
- The doer in a clause takes が (or の), never は.
- Plain form + とき: when … ; な-adjective + なとき; noun + のとき.
- {行|い}くとき: before it has happened; {行|い}ったとき: after it has happened.
- の links nouns, stands for a noun, and turns verbs into nouns.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Polite, casual and respectful
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now know two speech styles: polite (です/ます) and casual (plain forms). Step into a shop,
a train or an office in Japan, though, and you'll hear a third kind of Japanese that sounds
quite different: いらっしゃいませ, しょうしょうおまちください, かしこまりました. That's
**[[keigo]]**, respectful language.

This lesson is about recognizing keigo, not producing it. Learners at N5 aren't expected to
speak it, and Japanese people don't expect foreigners to. But you'll hear it every day as a
customer, a passenger and a visitor, and it's much less mysterious once you know its patterns.
You'll also see why Japanese speakers switch styles the way they do.

## One meaning, several styles

Here is "to eat" in the styles you'll meet:

| Style | Verb | Example | Who it's for |
|---|---|---|---|
| casual | {食|た}べる | {何|なに}{食|た}べる？ | friends, family |
| polite | {食|た}べます | {何|なに}を{食|た}べますか。 | people you don't know well |
| respectful | めしあがる | {何|なに}をめしあがりますか。 | raising the person you speak to or about |
| humble | いただく | いただきます。 | lowering yourself, the speaker |

The last two are both keigo, but they work in opposite directions. Respectful verbs are
used for the *other* person's actions: a waiter asks what *you* will eat with めしあがる. Humble
verbs are used for *your own* actions: you say いただきます before *you* eat. Both show
respect. You never use a respectful verb about yourself.

## Three kinds of keigo

Japanese grammar books divide keigo into three kinds:

- **[[teineigo]]** (polite language): です, ます and the very polite ございます. This is what you've
  used all course. It's polite to the listener without raising or lowering anyone.
- **[[sonkeigo]]** (respectful language): special verbs and forms that raise the person who does
  the action: いらっしゃる, めしあがる, おっしゃる.
- **[[kenjougo]]** (humble language): special verbs and forms that lower the speaker and the
  speaker's side: まいる, いただく, もうす.

A shop assistant may use all three in a single sentence. A company employee uses sonkeigo for
customers and kenjougo for themselves and their own company.

## Who speaks how: inside and outside

Why does the same person speak casually one minute and in keigo the next? Because Japanese
speakers sort people into **[[uchi and soto]]**: their own group (uchi, inside: family, close
friends, one's own company) and others (soto, outside: customers, strangers, other
companies). Age and position matter too.

| Situation | Usual style |
|---|---|
| friends, family, younger siblings | casual |
| classmates you've just met, neighbours, a doctor | polite |
| a junior student speaking to a senior student (せんぱい) | polite |
| a teacher speaking to students | often casual or plain polite |
| shop and hotel staff to customers | keigo |
| an employee to customers or another company | keigo, humble about their own company |
| train, airport and lift announcements | keigo |

One surprise: when speaking to an outsider, an employee talks about *their own boss* with
humble forms and without さん, because the boss is part of their uchi. Inside the company,
the same boss gets respectful forms. You don't need to do this, but it explains phone calls
that might otherwise sound odd: たなかはいま、せきをはずしております (Tanaka is away from his desk
at the moment), with no さん on the speaker's own colleague.

## Keigo you'll hear every day

| You hear | Meaning | Where |
|---|---|---|
| いらっしゃいませ。 | Welcome! | entering a shop or restaurant |
| しょうしょうおまちください。 | Please wait a moment. | anywhere you wait |
| かしこまりました。 | Certainly. (I understand and will do it.) | after you order or ask |
| もうしわけありません。 | I'm very sorry. | an apology from staff |
| こちらでおめしあがりですか。 | Will you be eating here? | a café or fast-food counter |
| ポイントカードはおもちですか。 | Do you have a points card? | a shop till |
| おはしはおつけしますか。 | Shall I put in chopsticks? | a convenience store |
| どうぞおかけください。 | Please have a seat. | an office, a clinic |
| どうぞお{入|はい}りください。 | Please come in. | someone's home, an office |
| まもなく、{電車|でんしゃ}がまいります。 | The train will be arriving shortly. | a station platform |
| ドアがしまります。ごちゅういください。 | The doors are closing. Please be careful. | inside a train |
| トイレはあちらでございます。 | The toilets are over there. | a shop, a hotel |
| こちらのかたはきむらさまです。 | This is Mr Kimura. | introducing a guest |
| おつかれさまです。 | Thanks for your hard work. / Hello. | between colleagues at work |

You'll recognize parts of many of them. いらっしゃいませ comes from いらっしゃる, the respectful
"come". おまちください is まつ (wait) in a respectful request pattern. まいります is the humble
"come", used by train companies about their own trains. かた is the polite word for
"person": このかた instead of この{人|ひと}. おつかれさまです is something you can use yourself: it's
how colleagues and classmates greet each other at work or after a club practice. ございます is the very polite
version of ある or です: トイレはあちらです becomes トイレはあちらでございます.

## Patterns that make keigo

Most keigo is made with a few patterns:

### お + ます stem + ください

A respectful request, more polite than 〜てください:

| 〜てください | Keigo | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| まってください | おまちください | please wait |
| {入|はい}ってください | お{入|はい}りください | please come in |
| かけてください (sit down) | おかけください | please have a seat |

Words of Chinese origin take ご instead: ごちゅういください (please be careful), ごりようください
(please use).

### Special verbs

The most common verbs have their own respectful and humble partners:

| Plain verb | Respectful (others) | Humble (yourself) |
|---|---|---|
| いる, {行|い}く, {来|く}る | いらっしゃる | まいる ({行|い}く, {来|く}る), おる (いる) |
| する | なさる | いたす |
| {言|い}う | おっしゃる | もうす |
| {食|た}べる, {飲|の}む | めしあがる | いただく |
| {見|み}る | ごらんになる | はいけんする |

Two of these you've used for a long time without knowing they were keigo: いただきます is the
humble "I receive", and おねがいします contains ねがう (to ask, request) in a humble pattern.

Humble ending in self-introductions: in a job interview or a formal speech you'll hear
エマ・ブラウンともうします (My name is Emma Brown) instead of エマ・ブラウンです, and よろしく
おねがいいたします instead of よろしくおねがいします. いたします is the humble する.

## What you say back

As a customer, you don't answer keigo with keigo. Ordinary です/ます is right:

> てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。こちらでおめしあがりですか。
>
> エマ: はい、ここで{食|た}べます。
>
> てんいん: かしこまりました。ポイントカードはおもちですか。
>
> エマ: いいえ、ないです。
>
> てんいん: しょうしょうおまちください。

Shop assistant: Welcome. Will you be eating here? Emma: Yes, I'll eat here. Assistant:
Certainly. Do you have a points card? Emma: No, I don't. Assistant: Please wait a moment.

Nobody answers いらっしゃいませ: customers usually just nod, or say nothing. A useful phrase for
saying no politely to an offer (a bag, chopsticks, a receipt) is けっこうです (No, thank
you), or だいじょうぶです, which many younger people use the same way.

## Dialogue: at the office

Emma visits a company for a meeting. The receptionist and Mr Kimura speak keigo; Emma speaks
ordinary polite Japanese, which is exactly right.

```dialogue
# At reception
うけつけ: いらっしゃいませ。
= Welcome.
エマ: すみません、エマ・ブラウンです。きむらさんと{十時|じゅうじ}にやくそくがあります。
= Excuse me, I'm Emma Brown. I have an appointment with Mr Kimura at ten.
うけつけ: ブラウンさまですね。しょうしょうおまちください。
= Ms Brown. Please wait a moment.
うけつけ: おまたせしました。きむらはすぐまいります。どうぞおかけください。
= Thank you for waiting. Kimura will be with you shortly. Please have a seat.
エマ: ありがとうございます。
= Thank you.
きむら: ブラウンさん、おまたせしました。きむらです。
= Ms Brown, sorry to keep you waiting. I'm Kimura.
エマ: はじめまして。きょうはよろしくおねがいします。
= Nice to meet you. Thank you for meeting me today.
きむら: こちらこそ、よろしくおねがいいたします。どうぞ、こちらへ。
= The pleasure is mine. This way, please.
```

Notes: やくそく is an appointment; さま is the very polite さん (honors Lesson 5h1); おまたせしました is
"sorry to keep you waiting" (a humble form of まつ); こちらこそ is "likewise, it's me who should
say so". The receptionist says きむらはすぐまいります: her own colleague, no さん, humble まいる.
Emma calls him きむらさん: he's not in her group.

## Common mistakes

- Using a respectful verb about yourself: ×わたしはめしあがります. Respectful forms are for other
  people; for yourself, use ordinary ます (or humble いただきます).
- Answering いらっしゃいませ with いらっしゃいませ. It's said only by the staff.
- Thinking keigo is required from you. です and ます are polite enough for a learner in almost
  every situation.
- Putting さん on your own name: ×エマさんです. The rule from Module 1 still holds, in every style.

## Key points

- Casual, polite (です/ます) and keigo are three levels of formality. Learners use the first
  two and recognize the third.
- Keigo has three kinds: teineigo (です, ます, ございます), sonkeigo (raises others: めしあがる,
  いらっしゃる) and kenjougo (lowers yourself: いただく, まいる, もうす).
- Styles follow uchi and soto (inside and outside groups), age and position.
- お + ます stem + ください is a keigo request: おまちください, おかけください.
- Answer keigo with ordinary です/ます. けっこうです: no, thank you.

lessons.title: Sound and feeling words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A dog in English says "woof"; in Japanese it says ワンワン. That much every language has. But
Japanese goes much further. It has words for the sound of heavy rain (ザーザー), for a pounding
heart (ドキドキ), for a person smiling (にこにこ), for speaking a language fluently (ペラペラ)
and for doing something slowly (ゆっくり). Some of these imitate real sounds; many describe
things that make no sound at all, such as a feeling or a way of moving.

These words are called **[[onomatopoeia]]** in English, and they are very common in Japanese:
in conversation, manga, adverts, children's books and even weather forecasts. This lesson
introduces some of the most useful ones and, just as important, the grammar that goes with
them: と, する and だ.

## Two kinds: sounds and states

Japanese grammar books separate these words into two groups:

| Kind | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| giongo (sound words) | imitate a real sound, including animal and human voices | ワンワン (dog), ニャー (cat), ザーザー (pouring rain), ドンドン (banging) |
| gitaigo (manner and state words) | describe how something looks, moves or feels | にこにこ (smiling), キラキラ (sparkling), ゆっくり (slowly), ドキドキ (heart racing) |

Many have the shape of a two-mora part said twice: ドキ + ドキ, にこ + にこ, ペラ + ペラ.
Others have a small っ and り: ゆっくり, ぐっすり. A sound word with a long vowel (ザー) is
often doubled too: ザーザー.

### Hiragana or katakana?

Both are possible, and writers choose by feeling. Katakana makes a word look like a sound
effect (it's the usual choice in manga), and hiragana looks softer: ドキドキ and どきどき are the
same word. In this lesson each word is written the way you'll see it most often, but expect
the other spelling too.

## Grammar: how to use them

The word itself never changes. What changes is the little word after it.

With と + a verb, the word describes how an action is done (like an English adverb). The と is often
left out, especially in speech:

{雨|あめ}がザーザー(と)ふっています。 — It's pouring with rain. (ふる = to fall, of rain)

あかちゃんがにこにこ(と)わらっています。 — The baby is smiling happily.

With する, many words become verbs with する and describe a feeling or state:

しけんのまえは、ドキドキします。 — Before an exam my heart races. / I get nervous. (しけん = exam)

あしたはりょこうです。ワクワクしています。 — Tomorrow's the trip. I'm so excited.

With だ or です, some describe a condition, like a な-adjective:

おなかがぺこぺこです。 — I'm starving. (おなか = stomach)

マリアさんは{日本語|にほんご}がペラペラです。 — Maria speaks fluent Japanese.

On its own, as an adverb: some words, like ゆっくり and ぐっすり, are used directly before a verb:

ゆっくり{話|はな}してください。 — Please speak slowly.

きのうはぐっすりねました。 — I slept really well last night.

Each word has its favourite pattern, so learn it with its example: ペラペラ goes with です or
{話|はな}す, ドキドキ with する, ザーザー with ふる.

## Words to know

| Word | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| ワンワン | woof (a dog barking) | いぬがワンワンないています。 (なく = to bark, to cry) |
| ザーザー | pouring (heavy rain) | {雨|あめ}がザーザーふっています。 |
| ドキドキ | (heart) pounding: nervous, thrilled | ドキドキしました。 |
| ワクワク | excited, looking forward to something | ワクワクしています。 |
| にこにこ | smiling, beaming | にこにこしている{人|ひと} |
| キラキラ | sparkling, glittering | ほしがキラキラひかっています。 (ほし = star, ひかる = to shine) |
| ペラペラ | fluent (in a language) | えいごがペラペラです。 |
| ぺこぺこ | starving (also: bowing again and again) | おなかがぺこぺこです。 |
| ぐっすり | (sleep) soundly | ぐっすりねました。 |
| ゆっくり | slowly; taking your time | ゆっくりしてください。 |

ゆっくりしてください deserves a note. It means "make yourself at home, relax, take your time",
and hosts say it to guests. ゆっくり{話|はな}してください (Please speak slowly) is one of the most
useful phrases a learner can have.

ペラペラ and ぺこぺこ look almost alike in kana but sound different: the first is ぺ + ら, the
second ぺ + こ. Read carefully!

## Weather and animals

Weather forecasts and everyday talk about the weather are full of these words:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ザーザー | heavy rain |
| しとしと | gentle, steady rain |
| ぽつぽつ | a few drops: rain starting |
| ゴロゴロ | rumbling (thunder); also lazing about at home |

And animals, as Japanese ears hear them:

| Animal | Japanese | English |
|---|---|---|
| いぬ (dog) | ワンワン | woof |
| ねこ (cat) | ニャー, ニャンニャン | meow |
| とり (bird) | ピヨピヨ (chick), チュンチュン (sparrow) | cheep, tweet |
| うし (cow) | モー | moo |

Children call a dog ワンワン and a cat ニャンニャン, as English-speaking children say "doggy".

## Dialogue: before the interview

```dialogue
# Before the interview
けん: マリアさん、あしたのめんせつ、だいじょうぶ？
= Maria, are you OK about tomorrow's interview?
マリア: うーん、ドキドキしている。{日本語|にほんご}ではじめてのめんせつだから。
= Hmm, I'm nervous. It's my first interview in Japanese.
けん: だいじょうぶだよ。マリアさん、{日本語|にほんご}ペラペラでしょう？
= You'll be fine. Your Japanese is fluent, right?
マリア: ペラペラじゃないよ！ でも、ゆっくり{話|はな}すのはできる。
= It's not fluent! But I can speak slowly.
けん: それでいいよ。きょうはぐっすりねてね。
= That's fine. Get a good night's sleep tonight.
マリア: うん。あ、おなかがぺこぺこ。ごはん{食|た}べに{行|い}かない？
= Yeah. Oh, I'm starving. Want to go and eat?
けん: いいね、{行|い}こう！
= Good idea. Let's go!
```

Notes: they're friends, so they speak casually (Lesson 24). めんせつ is an interview; だから at the
end is "because …" (casual, Lesson 26); できる is "can do"; ねてね is a casual request (〜て +
ね, "do …, OK?"); {行|い}こう is the casual "let's go", the plain form of {行|い}きましょう.

## Common mistakes

- Using する with every word: ×ペラペラします. ペラペラ goes with です or {話|はな}す: ペラペラです,
  ペラペラ{話|はな}します.
- Mixing up ペラペラ (fluent) and ぺこぺこ (starving).
- Translating word for word. ドキドキします is "I'm nervous" or "I'm thrilled", not "My heart
  goes doki-doki".
- Overusing them in formal writing. They're lively and a bit casual; reports and essays use
  them much less.

## Key points

- Japanese has many sound words (giongo) and manner/state words (gitaigo); together, they're
  onomatopoeia.
- Typical shapes: a doubled part (ドキドキ, にこにこ) or 〜っ〜り (ゆっくり, ぐっすり).
- Grammar: word + (と) + verb, word + する, word + だ/です, or the word alone as an adverb.
- Katakana makes them look like sound effects; hiragana is softer. Both are correct.
- Learn each word with an example: ドキドキする, ペラペラだ, ザーザーふる, ゆっくり{話|はな}す.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reasons and changes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the first lesson of the last module. You already have most of the pieces of N5
Japanese: polite and plain forms, adjectives, the て form, the ない and た forms, and clauses
that describe nouns. This module puts them together into longer, more natural speech and
reading.

Real conversation is full of two things you can't say neatly yet: *why* something happens and
how something *changes*. "I'm not going out, because it's raining." "It's got cold." "I want to
become a teacher." "Have you eaten yet? No, not yet." This lesson gives you the tools for all
of them:

- から, "because", after a reason;
- けど, a casual "but", next to the polite が you met in Lesson 10;
- なる, "to become", with adjectives and nouns;
- もう (already) and まだ (still, not yet);
- つもり, for what you plan to do.

## 〜から: because

To give a reason, say the reason first and put から after it. Then say what follows from it.
The part that gives the reason is a **[[reason clause]]**:

| Reason | から | Result |
|---|---|---|
| {雨|あめ}がふっています | から、 | {出|で}かけません。 |
| あしたしけんがあります | から、 | {今日|きょう}はべんきょうします。 |
| このくつは{安|やす}かったです | から、 | {二|に}そく{買|か}いました。 |

{雨|あめ}がふっていますから、{出|で}かけません。 — It's raining, so I'm not going out.

あしたしけんがありますから、{今日|きょう}はべんきょうします。 — I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll study today.

このくつは{安|やす}かったですから、{二|に}そく{買|か}いました。 — These shoes were cheap, so I bought two pairs. (〜そく counts pairs of shoes and socks.)

Notice the order. English can put the reason last: "I'm not going out because it's raining."
Japanese almost always puts the reason first, and から stays attached to the end of it. Think
of から as "…, so": "It's raining, so I'm not going out." A particle like this, which joins
two clauses into one sentence, is a **[[conjunctive particle]]**.

You already know から as "from" (Lesson 6: {九時|くじ}から). It's the same word, and the idea is
related: the result comes *from* the reason. What tells them apart is what stands in front.
After a time or a place, から means "from"; after a whole clause ending in a verb, an adjective
or です, it means "because".

### What comes before から

In polite speech the reason clause usually ends in です or ます, like the rest of the sentence.
In casual speech it ends in the plain form from Module 5, and the plain form is also common
inside polite sentences:

| Before から | Polite | Plain |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | {行|い}きますから | {行|い}くから |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}いですから | {高|たか}いから |
| な-adjective | しずかですから | しずかだから |
| Noun | {日曜日|にちようび}ですから | {日曜日|にちようび}だから |

Careful with な-adjectives and nouns: in the plain form they need だ before から. Without it,
{日曜日|にちようび}から means "from Sunday", not "because it's Sunday".

{今日|きょう}は{日曜日|にちようび}だから、{店|みせ}は{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いよ。 — It's Sunday, so the shop's crowded. (casual)

この{本|ほん}はおもしろいから、{読|よ}んでください。 — This book is interesting, so do read it.

### Asking and answering "why?"

The question words are どうして and なぜ. Both mean "why". どうして is the everyday one; なぜ
sounds more formal and is common in writing. Answer with the reason plus からです:

「どうしてきのう{来|き}ませんでしたか。」「あたまがいたかったからです。」 — "Why didn't you come yesterday?" "Because I had a headache."

「なぜ{日本語|にほんご}をべんきょうしていますか。」「{日本|にほん}のアニメがすきだからです。」 — "Why are you studying Japanese?" "Because I like Japanese anime."

In these answers the plain form goes before からです: いたかったからです, すきだからです.

### だから: "so" at the start of a sentence

だから begins a new sentence with "so" or "that's why". It points back to what was just said:

{雨|あめ}がふっています。だから、{出|で}かけません。 — It's raining. So I'm not going out.

だから is a little casual. In polite speech people often use ですから in the same place.

## が and けど: but

In Lesson 10 you joined two clauses with が, "but": {日本語|にほんご}はむずかしいですが、おもしろいです。 けど does the same job and is more casual. It's extremely common in
speech. けれど and けれども are longer, slightly more careful versions of けど.

{日本語|にほんご}はむずかしいけど、おもしろい。 — Japanese is hard, but it's fun. (casual)

このレストランは{高|たか}いですけど、おいしいですよ。 — This restaurant is expensive, but the food is good.

Like から, が and けど come at the end of the first clause, and that clause can be polite or
plain. Both also have a softening use: a sentence can stop on が or けど and leave the rest
unsaid. The listener understands. This is how people decline politely:

「あした、{山|やま}へ{行|い}きませんか。」「あしたはちょっと……。ようじがありますから。」 — "Shall we go to the mountains tomorrow?" "Tomorrow's a bit… I have something I need to do."

The reply never says "no". It stops on ちょっと……, then gives a reason with から, and the other
person understands. In the same way, a request can stop on けど or が:
すみません、この{店|みせ}をさがしていますけど…… (Excuse me, I'm looking for this shop…) asks
for help without asking outright. さがす is "to look for".

## なる: to become

なる means "to become", "to get" or "to turn into". It's a group 1 verb: なります, なって,
なった, ならない. It describes a **[[change of state]]**: something was one way and is now
another. How you join it depends on the word before it.

### い-adjectives: 〜くなる

Change the final い to く, then add なる:

| Adjective | + なる | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| さむい | さむくなる | to get cold |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}くなる | to get expensive; to get tall |
| {大|おお}きい | {大|おお}きくなる | to get big, to grow up |
| いい | よくなる | to get better |

{十一月|じゅういちがつ}になって、さむくなりました。 — It's November now, and it's got cold.

このパンは{高|たか}くなりましたね。 — This bread has got expensive, hasn't it?

かぜはよくなりましたか。 — Is your cold better?

いい uses the stem よ, just as it does in よくない (Lesson 11), so it's よくなる, never
\*いくなる.

### な-adjectives and nouns: 〜になる

な-adjectives and nouns take に before なる:

| Word | + になる | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {元気|げんき} | {元気|げんき}になる | to get well; to cheer up |
| しずか | しずかになる | to become quiet |
| {上手|じょうず} | {上手|じょうず}になる | to get good at |
| {先生|せんせい} | {先生|せんせい}になる | to become a teacher |
| はる | はるになる | to become spring |
| はたち | はたちになる | to turn twenty |

{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}になりましたね。 — Your Japanese has got really good.

{子|こ}どもたちがねて、うちがしずかになりました。 — The children went to sleep, and the house went quiet.

わたしは{先生|せんせい}になりたいです。 — I want to become a teacher.

The last example combines なる with たい from Lesson 20: なりたい, "want to become".

### です or なる?

です describes how things are; なる describes a change. Compare:

| です: a state | なる: a change |
|---|---|
| さむいです。 It's cold. | さむくなりました。 It's got cold. |
| {先生|せんせい}です。 She's a teacher. | {先生|せんせい}になりました。 She became a teacher. |
| {元気|げんき}です。 I'm well. | {元気|げんき}になりました。 I've got better. |

Japanese uses なりました far more than English uses "became". Whenever something is different
from before, a Japanese speaker reaches for なる: the weather, prices, a child's height, a
skill, the season, someone's age.

## もう and まだ

もう and まだ are a pair. もう says the change has already happened; まだ says it hasn't happened
yet, or that the old state still goes on.

| | With an affirmative | With a negative |
|---|---|---|
| もう | already: もう{食|た}べました | not any more: もう{食|た}べません |
| まだ | still: まだねています | not yet: まだ{来|き}ていません |

もう{十時|じゅうじ}ですよ。 — It's already ten o'clock!

たなかさんはもうかえりました。 — Tanaka has already gone home.

いもうとはまだねています。 — My little sister is still asleep.

この{車|くるま}はもう{古|ふる}いですから、もうのりません。 — This car is old now, so I don't drive it any more.

That last line has both meanings of もう: "already" ({古|ふる}い now) and "not any more".

### "Have you … yet?" "No, not yet."

A question with もう asks whether something has happened yet:

「もうひるごはんを{食|た}べましたか。」 — "Have you had lunch yet?"

- Yes: 「はい、もう{食|た}べました。」 — "Yes, I've already eaten."
- No: 「いいえ、まだです。」 — "No, not yet."

The short まだです is the natural answer. The full form is まだ{食|た}べていません, with the
ています form from Lesson 17: "I'm still in the state of not having eaten". Don't answer
\*いいえ、{食|た}べませんでした: that means "No, I didn't eat (then)", as if the chance were over,
and it isn't what you mean.

### もう with an amount: "more"

Before a number or an amount, もう means "more": もう{一|ひと}つ (one more), もう{少|すこ}し (a bit
more), もういちど (once more), which you know from the kana course.

コーヒーをもう{一|いっ}ぱいください。 — One more coffee, please.

### もうすぐ and すぐ

もうすぐ is "soon", "any moment now": もうすぐはるです。 (Spring is almost here.) Don't confuse
it with すぐ, "right away": すぐ{行|い}きます。 (I'll go right away.)

## つもり: what you plan to do

Put つもりです after a verb in the dictionary form to say what you intend to do:

{来年|らいねん}、{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}くつもりです。 — I'm planning to go to Japan next year.

なつやすみは{山|やま}にのぼるつもりです。 — In the summer holidays I'm planning to climb a mountain.

For a plan *not* to do something, use the ない form:

{今日|きょう}はおさけを{飲|の}まないつもりです。 — I'm not planning to drink alcohol today.

Ask about someone's plans with つもりですか:

「なつやすみはどうするつもりですか。」「{国|くに}へかえるつもりです。」 — "What are you planning to do in the summer holidays?" "I'm planning to go back to my country."

つもり is an **[[intention]]**: a plan you have already made up your mind about. It is firmer than
〜たいです (just wanting) and less fixed than a plain ます sentence, which can sound like a
scheduled fact. Two cautions:

- Use the dictionary form, never the ます form: {行|い}くつもり, not \*{行|い}きますつもり.
- Asking a teacher or a boss directly about their つもり can sound blunt. With friends and
  classmates it's fine.

## More words for changes

A few more words come up again and again when people talk about change and time:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| これから | from now on, after this | これから{毎日|まいにち}べんきょうします。 (From now on I'll study every day.) |
| さいきん | recently, lately | さいきん、さむくなりましたね。 (It's got cold lately, hasn't it?) |
| だんだん | gradually, little by little | だんだん{上手|じょうず}になりました。 (I gradually got better.) |
| また | again | また{来|き}てください。 (Please come again.) |
| {生|う}まれる | to be born | {子|こ}どもが{生|う}まれました。 (A baby was born.) |
| {大人|おとな} | adult, grown-up | {大人|おとな}になりました。 (I've become an adult.) |
| ようじ | something to do, an errand | ようじがありますから、かえります。 (I have something to do, so I'm going home.) |

{生|う}まれる is a group 2 verb ({生|う}まれます, {生|う}まれて) and is almost always used in the past:
わたしは{十二月|じゅうにがつ}に{生|う}まれました。 (I was born in December.) {大人|おとな} has a special
reading: the word is read おとな as a whole, and the reading doesn't split over the two kanji.



```dialogue
# Lunch
けん: エマさん、もうひるごはんを{食|た}べましたか。
= Emma, have you had lunch yet?
エマ: いいえ、まだです。{今日|きょう}はいそがしかったですから。
= No, not yet. I've been busy today.
けん: じゃあ、いっしょに{食|た}べませんか。{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}の{店|みせ}は{安|やす}いですよ。
= Then shall we eat together? The place in front of the station is cheap.
エマ: いいですね。でも、{一時|いちじ}からじゅぎょうがありますから、はやく{食|た}べましょう。
= Sounds good. But I have class from one, so let's eat quickly.
けん: エマさん、{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}になりましたね。
= Emma, your Japanese has got really good.
エマ: ありがとうございます。でも、かんじはまだむずかしいです。
= Thank you. But kanji are still hard.
けん: {来年|らいねん}も{日本|にほん}でべんきょうするつもりですか。
= Are you planning to study in Japan next year too?
エマ: はい。{日本|にほん}の{大学|だいがく}に{入|はい}るつもりです。だから、{毎日|まいにち}べんきょうしています。
= Yes. I'm planning to go to a Japanese university. That's why I study every day.
けん: そうですか。がんばってください。
= I see. Good luck!
```

Look at how much of this lesson is in it: もう…ましたか and まだです, two reasons with から,
{上手|じょうず}になりました, a つもり question and answer, and だから. はやく is "quickly" or
"early", the adverb from はやい. がんばってください ("do your best", "good luck") is a phrase
you'll use constantly; Lesson 30 has the verb がんばる.

## Reading: my town

> わたしのまちは、{十年前|じゅうねんまえ}はとてもしずかでした。{店|みせ}も{少|すく}なかったです。
>
> でも、{新|あたら}しい{駅|えき}ができてから、{人|ひと}が{多|おお}くなりました。{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}に{店|みせ}や{高|たか}いビルがたくさんできました。
>
> まちはべんりになりましたけど、{前|まえ}よりうるさくなりました。わたしは{前|まえ}のしずかなまちがすきでした。でも、{今|いま}のまちもきらいじゃありません。
>
> {来年|らいねん}、わたしは{大学生|だいがくせい}になります。{大学|だいがく}はとおいですから、まちを{出|で}るつもりです。

My town was very quiet ten years ago. There weren't many shops, either. But since the new
station was built, there have been more people. Lots of shops and tall buildings went up in
front of the station. The town has become convenient, but it's got noisier than before. I
liked the old, quiet town. But I don't dislike the town as it is now. Next year I'll be a
university student. The university is far away, so I'm planning to leave town.

できる here means "to be built" or "to open" (a meaning you'll meet properly at N4); ビル is a
building, usually a tall one; うるさい is "noisy". Count the changes: {多|おお}くなりました,
べんりになりました, うるさくなりました, {大学生|だいがくせい}になります.

## Say it

```speak
{雨|あめ}がふっていますから、{出|で}かけません。
= It's raining, so I'm not going out.
どうして{来|き}ませんでしたか。
= Why didn't you come?
さむくなりましたね。
= It's got cold, hasn't it?
{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}になりたいです。
= I want to get good at Japanese.
もう{食|た}べましたか。
= Have you eaten yet?
いいえ、まだです。
= No, not yet.
{来年|らいねん}、{日本|にほん}へ{行|い}くつもりです。
= I'm planning to go to Japan next year.
```

## Common mistakes

- Putting the reason second, English-style: \*{出|で}かけません、{雨|あめ}がふっていますから.
  You'll hear this as an afterthought in speech, but the standard order is reason first.
- Forgetting だ before plain から with nouns and な-adjectives: \*しずかから → しずかだから.
- Using く with な-adjectives: \*しずかくなる → しずかになる; and \*きれいくなる → きれいになる
  (きれい is a な-adjective, even though it ends in い).
- \*いいくなる → よくなる.
- Answering a もう question with \*いいえ、{食|た}べませんでした. Say いいえ、まだです.
- \*{行|い}きますつもり → {行|い}くつもり: つもり takes the dictionary form.
- Mixing up もうすぐ (soon) and もう (already): もうすぐ{来|き}ます is "will come soon";
  もう{来|き}ました is "has already come".

## Key points

- Reason + から, result: {雨|あめ}ですから、{出|で}かけません。 The reason comes first. Plain
  nouns and な-adjectives need だ: {雨|あめ}だから.
- どうして / なぜ ask why; answer with 〜からです. だから starts a sentence with "so".
- が (polite) and けど (casual) mean "but"; both can end a sentence softly to decline or ask.
- なる describes a change: い-adjective 〜くなる (いい → よくなる), な-adjective or noun 〜になる.
- もう: already / not any more / (with an amount) more. まだ: still / not yet. "Not yet" is
  まだです.
- Dictionary form + つもりです: I intend to…; ない form + つもりです: I intend not to….

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.body:
