## What this lesson is for

Sooner or later every visitor to Japan stands on a street corner with a phone that has lost its
signal. This lesson is for that moment. You'll learn to stop someone politely, ask where a place
is and how to get there, and, just as important, understand the answer: "Go straight, turn
right at the second corner, cross at the lights, and it's on the left."

Almost everything here is grammar you already have. Directions are strings of て forms
(Lesson 18) ending in 〜てください (Lesson 16), with location words from Lesson 5. The new parts
are a handful of verbs and nouns, を for the route you move along, and the ordinals "first",
"second", "third".

## Stopping a stranger

Start with すみません. It works as "excuse me" for getting attention, and nobody minds being
asked the way: in Japan it's a normal, friendly request. Then ask your question:

すみません、{駅|えき}はどこですか。 — Excuse me, where's the station?

すみません、このちかくにコンビニはありますか。 — Excuse me, is there a convenience store near here?

すみません、{駅|えき}までどうやって{行|い}きますか。 — Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

どうやって means "how", "by what way". It asks about the route or the means, so it's the right
question for directions and transport: どうやって{行|い}きますか (how do I get there?),
どうやって{食|た}べますか (how do you eat this?).

For an even politer question, use こちら, そちら, あちら and どちら, the polite partners of ここ,
そこ, あそこ and どこ. They also mean "this way", "that way":

すみません、{出口|でぐち}はどちらですか。 — Excuse me, which way is the exit?

{出口|でぐち}はあちらです。 — The exit is over that way.

こちらへどうぞ。 — This way, please.

Station staff and shop assistants use these all the time, so learn to recognize them even if
you mostly say ここ and どこ yourself. You may also hear a very polite opener such as
すみません、ちょっとうかがいますが… (Excuse me, may I ask…?). うかがう is a humble verb you
don't need to produce yet.

## The words of the street

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| かど | corner (of a street or a block) |
| しんごう | traffic lights |
| こうさてん | crossroads, intersection |
| {右|みぎ}がわ / {左|ひだり}がわ | the right side / the left side |
| むこう | the other side, over there, beyond |
| まん{中|なか} | the middle |
| つぎ | next |
| ちず | map |
| こうばん | police box |
| おまわりさん | police officer (a friendly, everyday word) |

むこう is "the far side" of something: しんごうのむこう (past the lights), {川|かわ}のむこう
(across the river). がわ means "side", so {駅|えき}の{右|みぎ}がわ is "on the right side of the
station". まん{中|なか} is the exact middle: まちのまん{中|なか} (the middle of town),
{道|みち}のまん{中|なか} (the middle of the road).

## The verbs: まっすぐ, まがる, わたる

Three verbs and one adverb do most of the work:

| Word | Type | ます form | て form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| まっすぐ | adverb | | | straight (ahead) |
| {行|い}く | group 1 | {行|い}きます | {行|い}って | to go |
| まがる | group 1 | まがります | まがって | to turn |
| わたる | group 1 | わたります | わたって | to cross |

まっすぐ{行|い}ってください。 — Please go straight on.

かどを{右|みぎ}にまがってください。 — Please turn right at the corner.

しんごうをわたってください。 — Please cross at the lights.

まがる and わたる end in る, but they are group 1 verbs (like かえる and {入|はい}る), so their て
forms are まがって and わたって, not \*まがて or \*わたて. Pronounce まっすぐ with the small っ as a
full beat: ma-s-su-gu.

## を for the route

In Lesson 7 を marked the object of a verb: {水|みず}を{飲|の}みます. With verbs of moving, を
marks the space you move through, along, across or out of: the route.

| Sentence | を marks |
|---|---|
| この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}ってください。 | the road you go along |
| {道|みち}をわたります。 | the road you cross |
| こうえんをあるきます。 | the park you walk through |
| かどを{右|みぎ}にまがります。 | the corner you turn at |
| {駅|えき}を{出|で}ます。 | the place you leave |

Compare the particles you know for places:

- に / へ: where you're heading. {駅|えき}に{行|い}きます。 (I go to the station.)
- で: where an action happens. {駅|えき}で{友|とも}だちに{会|あ}います。 (I meet a friend at the station.)
- を: the route. {駅|えき}の{前|まえ}をあるきます。 (I walk past the front of the station.)

In かどを{右|みぎ}にまがります there are two particles: を for the corner (the place you turn)
and に for the direction you turn to. Either can be left out when it's obvious:
{右|みぎ}にまがってください is a complete instruction.

## First, second, third: 〜め

Add {目|め} to a number with a counter to make an **[[ordinal suffix]]**, "-th":

| Ordinal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {一|ひと}つ{目|め} | the first (one) |
| {二|ふた}つ{目|め} | the second |
| {三|みっ}つ{目|め} | the third |
| {四|よっ}つ{目|め} | the fourth |

{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{左|ひだり}にまがってください。 — Turn left at the second corner.

{三|みっ}つ{目|め}のしんごうをわたってください。 — Cross at the third set of lights.

{一|ひと}つ{目|め}の{駅|えき}でおります。 — I get off at the first station.

{目|め} works with other counters too: {一|いち}ばん{目|め} (number one, the first in order),
{三|さん}ばん{目|め}, {二|に}かい{目|め} (the second time). For streets and stations, 〜つ{目|め} is
the usual choice. You know {目|め} as "eye" from Lesson 19; as a suffix it's the same kanji with the
same reading.

## How far is it? 〜ぐらい

ぐらい (also くらい) after an amount means "about":

あるいて{五分|ごふん}ぐらいです。 — It's about five minutes on foot.

{車|くるま}で{二十分|にじゅっぷん}ぐらいかかります。 — It takes about twenty minutes by car.

{駅|えき}から{三百|さんびゃく}メートルぐらいです。 — It's about 300 metres from the station.

かかる is "to take (time or money)". For an approximate point in time ("at about three
o'clock") Japanese uses a different word, ごろ: {三時|さんじ}ごろ. ぐらい is for amounts and lengths
of time: さんじかんぐらい (for about three hours).

If it's very close, people say すぐです or すぐそこです: "it's right there".

## Putting directions together

A full set of directions is a chain of て forms, with the last verb in 〜てください or a plain
statement of where the place is:

{北口|きたぐち}を{出|で}て、まっすぐ{行|い}って、{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}にまがってください。ゆうびんきょくは{左|ひだり}がわにあります。 — Leave by the north exit, go straight on, and turn right at the second corner. The post office is on the left.

When you're the one listening, do what Japanese speakers do: repeat the key points back.

「{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}ですね。」「はい、そうです。」 — "Right at the second corner, yes?" "Yes, that's right."

Repeating back is polite, and it catches mistakes. Notice the short form: {右|みぎ}ですね, with
no verb. If you don't understand, say so: すみません、もういちどおねがいします。 And if
someone asks *you* the way and you don't know, the polite answer is
すみません、ちょっとわかりません。

## Asking the police

Most neighbourhoods in Japanese towns and cities have a こうばん, a small police box, often near a station. The
officers there, the おまわりさん, give directions every day. They have detailed local maps and
will often point to your destination on one. A こうばん is also where lost property is handed
in. おまわりさん is the friendly everyday word; you say it about someone, and you can say
すみません to start talking to one.

## Dialogue: the post office

```dialogue
# The post office
アンナ: すみません、このちかくにゆうびんきょくはありますか。
= Excuse me, is there a post office near here?
おんなのひと: ゆうびんきょくですか。ええと、この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}って、{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のしんごうを{右|みぎ}にまがってください。
= The post office? Let me see. Go straight along this road and turn right at the second set of lights.
アンナ: {二|ふた}つ{目|め}のしんごうを{右|みぎ}ですね。
= Right at the second set of lights, yes?
おんなのひと: はい。それから、はしをわたって、すぐ{左|ひだり}がわにあります。{大|おお}きいビルのとなりです。
= Yes. Then you cross the bridge, and it's right there on the left. Next to a big building.
アンナ: あるいてどのぐらいですか。
= About how long is it on foot?
おんなのひと: そうですね、{十分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいですね。
= Let's see, about ten minutes.
アンナ: わかりました。どうもありがとうございました。
= I see. Thank you very much.
おんなのひと: いいえ。
= Not at all.
```

はし here is "bridge". どのぐらい asks "about how much / how long". The final いいえ is a modest
"not at all", a common reply to thanks. ありがとうございました, in the past, thanks someone for
something they have just finished doing for you.


## Reading: a message from Yui

Your friend ゆい has invited you to her flat and sends you the way from the station:

> {南口|みなみぐち}を{出|で}て、{右|みぎ}へ{行|い}ってください。
>
> {一|ひと}つ{目|め}のしんごうをわたって、こうえんの{前|まえ}をまっすぐ{行|い}ってください。
>
> {二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{左|ひだり}にまがってください。わたしのアパートは{右|みぎ}がわの{三|みっ}つ{目|め}のたてものです。{白|しろ}いアパートです。へやは{二|に}かいです。
>
> {駅|えき}からあるいて{七分|ななふん}ぐらいです。わからないときは、{電話|でんわ}してください。

Leave by the south exit and go right. Cross at the first set of lights and go straight on past
the front of the park. Turn left at the second corner. My flat is the third building on the
right. It's a white block of flats. My room is on the first floor (the second floor, counting
the way Japan does). It's about seven minutes on foot from the station. If you can't find it,
give me a call.

たてもの is "building". Japanese counts floors from the ground: {一|いっ}かい is the ground floor,
{二|に}かい the one above it. Try tracing the route with your finger on an imaginary map: south
exit, right, lights, park, second corner, left, third building on the right.

## Say it

```speak
すみません、{駅|えき}はどこですか。
= Excuse me, where is the station?
{駅|えき}までどうやって{行|い}きますか。
= How do I get to the station?
まっすぐ{行|い}ってください。
= Please go straight on.
{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}にまがってください。
= Turn right at the second corner.
しんごうをわたってください。
= Cross at the lights.
{左|ひだり}がわにあります。
= It's on the left.
あるいて{五分|ごふん}ぐらいです。
= It's about five minutes on foot.
{二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかどを{右|みぎ}ですね。
= Right at the second corner, yes?
```

## Common mistakes

- \*まがてください, \*わたてください: まがる and わたる are group 1 verbs, so the て forms are
  まがって and わたって.
- Using に for the road you cross: \*{道|みち}にわたります → {道|みち}をわたります. The route takes
  を; the direction you turn to takes に ({右|みぎ}に).
- Using で for the road you walk along: \*この{道|みち}でまっすぐ{行|い}く → この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}く.
- Forgetting the counter in ordinals: \*{二|に}{目|め}のかど → {二|ふた}つ{目|め}のかど.
- Using ぐらい for a clock time: \*{三時|さんじ}ぐらいに{会|あ}いましょう is heard in speech, but the
  standard word for "at about three" is ごろ: {三時|さんじ}ごろ. ぐらい is for amounts: {五分|ごふん}ぐらい.
- Walking off after "OK". Repeat the key step back ({二|ふた}つ{目|め}ですね) and thank the person
  with ありがとうございました.

## Key points

- Start with すみません, then 〜はどこですか, このちかくに〜はありますか or
  〜までどうやって{行|い}きますか. こちら, そちら, あちら, どちら are the polite "this way, that
  way, which way".
- まっすぐ{行|い}く (go straight), まがる (turn), わたる (cross); both verbs are group 1:
  まがって, わたって.
- を marks the route: {道|みち}をわたる, この{道|みち}をまっすぐ{行|い}く, かどを{右|みぎ}にまがる.
- Ordinals: number + counter + {目|め}: {一|ひと}つ{目|め}, {二|ふた}つ{目|め}, {三|みっ}つ{目|め}.
- ぐらい (くらい) is "about" for amounts and durations; ごろ is "about" for clock times.
- Directions are chains of て forms ending in 〜てください. Repeat them back to check.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Up to now you've mostly read sentences written to show one piece of grammar. Real reading is
different: a notice on a door, a note on the fridge, an email from a colleague, a timetable, a
menu. Each mixes everything you've learned, with dates, times and prices, and none of them is
spaced or simplified for you.

This lesson gives you five short texts of exactly that kind, written for N5, and the
strategies that make them manageable. The same kinds of text appear in the reading part of the
JLPT N5 (Lesson 30), so this is also exam practice. Read each text before you look at the
translation. Then read it again with furigana turned off, using the switch at the top of the
lesson, and see how many kanji you can read by yourself. The kanji list in the Study tools box
lists every kanji in this course with its readings.

## How Japanese texts show dates, times and prices

Everyday texts use a few conventions you haven't seen in sentences:

| You see | It means | Read |
|---|---|---|
| {11月3日|じゅういちがつみっか}（{月|げつ}） | 3 November (Monday) | じゅういちがつみっか、げつようび |
| 10:00〜17:00 | from 10:00 to 17:00 | じゅうじからごごごじまで |
| 18:30 | 6:30 p.m. | ごごろくじはん (or じゅうはちじはん) |
| 500{円|えん} | 500 yen | ごひゃくえん |
| ※ | a note (like an asterisk) | こめじるし |

Numbers in notices, messages and menus are usually written in Arabic numerals, not kanji.
The day of the week is often shortened to one kanji in brackets: （{月|げつ}） for {月曜日|げつようび},
（{土|ど}） for {土曜日|どようび}. Times on signs and timetables use the 24-hour clock, but people
read them aloud as ごご plus the 12-hour time just as often as with the 24-hour number. The wave
dash 〜 means "from … to".

## Strategies

These work for every text in this lesson, and for the exam.

1. *Look at the shape first.* Before you read a word, ask what kind of text it is. A heading
   and a date: a notice. A name at the top and another at the bottom: a message or an email.
   A table with prices: a menu. The type tells you what information to expect.
2. *Read the question before the text.* If the question asks "what time", you're hunting for
   {時|じ}, {分|ふん} and numbers. Moving your eyes over a text to find one piece of information like this
   is **[[scanning]]**. Reading the whole text quickly to get the general idea, without stopping on
   every word, is **[[skimming]]**. Use skimming first, then scanning for the answer.
3. *Let the kanji guide you.* Even with furigana off, the kanji you know stand out:
   {曜日|ようび}, {時|じ}, {円|えん}, {休|やす}み, {入口|いりぐち}, {出口|でぐち}. They are usually the
   key facts.
4. *Read to the end of the sentence.* The verb comes last, and the last few kana decide the
   meaning: {行|い}きます (will go), {行|い}きません (won't go), {行|い}ってください (please go),
   {行|い}かないでください (please don't go), {行|い}きましょう (let's go). Never decide what a
   sentence means before you reach its end.
5. *Watch for changes.* Notices and emails often correct earlier plans: 〜でしたが、〜になりました
   (it was …, but it has become …). The new information is the one that counts.
6. *Don't stop at unknown words.* Skip them and keep going; the sentence around them, or a
   kanji you know inside them, often tells you enough. Katakana words are often English words
   in disguise: say them aloud.
7. *Use the particles.* から and まで mark ranges, に marks a time or a destination, で a place
   or a means, を an object. Even in a sentence full of new words, the particles show its shape.

## Text 1: a notice

> としょかんのおしらせ
>
> {11月3日|じゅういちがつみっか}（{月|げつ}）から{5日|いつか}（{水|すい}）まで、としょかんは{休|やす}みです。
>
> {6日|むいか}（{木|もく}）から、またあいています。じかんは10:00〜19:00です。
>
> ※{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}に{本|ほん}をかえすときは、{入口|いりぐち}の{右|みぎ}がわのポストに{入|い}れてください。


The library's notice. From Monday 3 November to Wednesday 5 November, the library is closed.
From Thursday 6 November it is open again. Opening hours are 10:00 to 19:00. ※ If you return
books on a closing day, please put them in the box on the right-hand side of the entrance.

としょかん is a library; おしらせ is a notice or announcement, the word at the top of countless
signs and letters. あいています is "is open" (あく, to open, in the ています form for a state);
かえす is "to return (something)"; ポスト here is a return box. Notice how the ※ line adds an
extra rule at the end, just as an asterisk would in English.

Check yourself: you want to borrow a book on 4 November. Can you? (No: the library is closed
from the 3rd to the 5th. Come back on the 6th.)

## Text 2: a note on the fridge

> ゆいへ
>
> {母|はは}は{今日|きょう}、しごとでおそくなります。{8時|はちじ}ごろかえります。
>
> れいぞうこにカレーがありますから、{先|さき}に{食|た}べてください。{食|た}べたあとで、おさらをあらってくださいね。
>
> {母|はは}より

To Yui. I'll be late today because of work. I'll be home at about eight. There's curry in the
fridge, so eat first, without me. After you've eaten, wash the dishes, OK?
Love, Mum.

A message opens with the reader's name and へ ("to …") and ends with the writer's name and より
("from …"). しごとで uses で for a cause: "because of work". おそくなります is なる from Lesson 26:
"I'll become late". {先|さき}に means "first, ahead (of someone)". れいぞうこ is a fridge, おさら
plates or dishes, あらう "to wash". The ね on the last request makes it friendly.

Check yourself: what must Yui do after dinner? (Wash the dishes.)

## Text 3: an email

> けんさん
>
> こんにちは。やまだです。
>
> あしたのミーティングは{午後|ごご}{2時|にじ}からでしたが、{3時|さんじ}からになりました。ばしょはおなじです。3がいのへやです。
>
> すみませんが、よろしくおねがいします。
>
> やまだ

Ken, hello. This is Yamada. Tomorrow's meeting was going to be from 2 p.m., but it's now from 3.
The place is the same: the room on the third floor. Sorry about this, and thank you.
Yamada.

This is strategy 5 in action: 〜でしたが、〜になりました. The time that counts is {3時|さんじ}, not
{2時|にじ}. ミーティング is a meeting, ばしょ is the place where something happens, and おなじ means
"the same". Emails between colleagues often start with the reader's name and こんにちは, then the
writer says who they are. よろしくおねがいします at the end is hard to translate: it asks the
reader for their understanding and help. Lesson 30h2 has more on writing emails.

Check yourself: what changed, and what didn't? (The start time changed; the room didn't.)

## Text 4: a class timetable

{日本語|にほんご}クラス　{12月|じゅうにがつ}のよてい

| {日|ひ} | じかん | クラス |
|---|---|---|
| {1日|ついたち}（{火|か}） | 18:00〜19:30 | {会話|かいわ} |
| {3日|みっか}（{木|もく}） | 18:00〜19:30 | かんじ |
| {8日|ようか}（{火|か}） | 18:00〜19:30 | {聞|き}くれんしゅう |
| {10日|とおか}（{木|もく}） | {休|やす}み | |
| {15日|じゅうごにち}（{火|か}） | 18:00〜20:00 | テスト |

※{15日|じゅうごにち}のテストは、いつもより{30分|さんじゅっぷん}{長|なが}いです。

Japanese class: the December schedule. Tuesday 1st, 18:00–19:30, conversation. Thursday 3rd,
kanji. Tuesday 8th, listening practice. Thursday 10th, no class. Tuesday 15th, 18:00–20:00,
test. ※ The test on the 15th is thirty minutes longer than usual.

よてい is a schedule or plan. {会話|かいわ} is "conversation", and {聞|き}くれんしゅう is
"listening practice" (practice of listening). Look at the dates: {1日|ついたち}, {3日|みっか},
{8日|ようか} and {10日|とおか} use the special readings from Lesson 9, but {15日|じゅうごにち} is regular.
The ※ note explains why the last row ends at 20:00: it agrees with いつもより{30分|さんじゅっぷん}{長|なが}い.

Check yourself: on which day is there no class? (Thursday the 10th.)

## Text 5: a menu

カフェ・みどり　メニュー

| のみもの | |
|---|---|
| コーヒー | 400{円|えん} |
| こうちゃ | 400{円|えん} |
| オレンジジュース | 350{円|えん} |
| たべもの | |
| サンドイッチ | 550{円|えん} |
| カレーライス | 800{円|えん} |
| ケーキ | 450{円|えん} |

※ランチセット（11:00〜14:00）：カレーライスとのみもの　1,000{円|えん}

※{日曜日|にちようび}は{休|やす}みです。

Café Midori, menu. Drinks: coffee 400 yen, tea 400 yen, orange juice 350 yen. Food: sandwich
550 yen, curry and rice 800 yen, cake 450 yen. ※ Lunch set (11:00–14:00): curry and a drink,
1,000 yen. ※ Closed on Sundays.

Menus are pure scanning: find the item, read the number. The ※ lines are where the real
information hides. Curry and a coffee cost 800 + 400 = 1,200 yen separately, so at lunchtime
the set saves 200 yen, but only between 11:00 and 14:00, and never on a Sunday.

Check yourself: you arrive at 15:00 and order curry and an orange juice. How much do you pay?
(1,150 yen: it's after 14:00, so there's no lunch set.)

## Words for reading

These words turn up again and again in the kinds of text above:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| おしらせ | notice, announcement | としょかんのおしらせ (the library's notice) |
| メール | email; a message on a phone | メールを{読|よ}みました。 (I read the email.) |
| よてい | schedule, plan | {来週|らいしゅう}のよてい (next week's schedule) |
| ばしょ | place (where something happens) | ばしょは{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}です。 (It's in front of the station.) |
| うけつけ | reception (desk) | うけつけは{一|いっ}かいです。 (Reception is on the ground floor.) |
| ページ | page | {十|じゅう}ページ{読|よ}みました。 (I read ten pages.) |
| ことば | word; language | このことばはわかりません。 (I don't know this word.) |
| ニュース | news | {毎日|まいにち}ニュースを{見|み}ます。 (I watch the news every day.) |

ばしょ and ところ both mean "place"; ばしょ is the one on notices and forms, for where an event
happens. ことば is a single word or a language in general; the word for "language" in names of
languages is {語|ご}, as in {日本語|にほんご}.

## Reading on your own

Reading a little every day matters more than reading a lot once a week. Good next steps:

- *Graded readers.* Short books written for learners, sorted into levels by how many words
  and how much grammar they use. The lowest levels are written for learners at about your
  level, many with audio. Several free ones are listed in this course's reading list (the
  Reading tab).
- *Easy news.* Some news sites rewrite the day's news in simple Japanese with furigana. They
  are above N5, but with this lesson's strategies you can get the gist of a headline and the
  first sentence, and that is real progress.
- *The world around you.* Packaging, signs, timetables and menus are exactly the texts of this
  lesson. If you can't go to Japan, look up photos of Japanese station signs and shop fronts and
  read what you can.

Don't look up every word. If you understand most of a page and enjoy it, it's the right level;
if you're stopping on every line, choose something easier. The aim is many pages, not perfect
ones.

## Common mistakes

- Reading word by word from the start and translating as you go. Skim first, read the question,
  then scan.
- Deciding the meaning before the end of the sentence: {出|で}かけます and {出|で}かけません differ
  only in the last two kana.
- Missing the ※ lines, which usually hold the exceptions.
- Using the old time after 〜でしたが、〜になりました. The new one counts.
- Reading {1日|ついたち} as いちにち. いちにち means "one day (long)"; the first of the month is
  ついたち.

## Key points

- Notices, messages, emails, timetables and menus each have a typical shape; recognize it first.
- Dates are written like {11月3日|じゅういちがつみっか}（{月|げつ}）; times on the 24-hour clock;
  〜 means "from … to"; ※ marks a note.
- Skim for the gist, then scan for the answer. Let the kanji you know point to the key facts.
- The end of the sentence decides its meaning. 〜でしたが、〜になりました signals a change.
- Messages start with name + へ and end with name + より; emails often start with name + さん
  and end with よろしくおねがいします.
- Read something easy every day, and don't look up every word.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Listening and conversation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Knowing the grammar is one thing; following a real person who is speaking to you is another.
Speech is fast, words run together, and you can't go back and read it again. The good news is
that conversation has its own habits, and once you know them you can keep a conversation going
with very little Japanese.

This lesson covers three of those habits and one skill:

- the small "I'm listening" words Japanese speakers use constantly;
- what to say when you don't understand, so that the other person helps you;
- the basics of a telephone call;
- strategies for listening, in conversation and in the JLPT.

The quiz at the end has many listening questions. Turn your sound on.

## Aizuchi: showing you're listening

When an English speaker listens, they mostly stay quiet and nod. A Japanese listener is much
more active. Every few seconds they give a short spoken signal that means "I'm with you, go
on". These signals are called **[[aizuchi]]**. Without them, a Japanese speaker soon wonders whether
you're still listening, or whether something is wrong. On the telephone, where nobody can see
you nod, they matter even more.

| Aizuchi | Meaning | When |
|---|---|---|
| はい / ええ | yes, uh-huh | all the time; ええ is a little softer |
| そうですか | I see; is that so? | taking in new information |
| そうですね | that's right; yes, indeed | agreeing with something the speaker said |
| へえ | wow, really? | surprise and interest |
| ほんとうですか | really? | stronger surprise |
| なるほど | I see (now I understand) | when an explanation makes sense |
| たいへんですね | that must be hard | sympathy for a problem |
| よかったですね | that's great; I'm glad | sharing good news |
| すごいですね | that's amazing | admiration |

Here is a short stretch of conversation with aizuchi in it. Notice how often the listener
speaks without taking over:

「きのう、{駅|えき}でさいふをおとしました。」「えっ、たいへんですね。」「でも、{駅|えき}の{人|ひと}がひろって、こうばんにとどけました。」「へえ、よかったですね。」 — "Yesterday I dropped my wallet at the station." "Oh no, that's awful." "But someone at the station picked it up and took it to the police box." "Oh, I'm so glad."

おとす is "to drop", ひろう "to pick up", とどける "to deliver, hand in".

### はい doesn't always mean "yes"

As aizuchi, はい and ええ mean "I'm listening", not "I agree". A Japanese business partner who
says はい、はい while you explain your offer is following you, not accepting it. In the same
way, when you say はい while someone talks, they will hear "go on", which is what you want.

### そうですか and そうですね

These two are easy to mix up. そうですか, said with a falling voice, takes in something you
didn't know: "Oh, I see." そうですね agrees with something both of you can see: "Yes, it is."

「この{店|みせ}、{先月|せんげつ}{新|あたら}しくなりましたよ。」「そうですか。」 — "This shop was renovated last month, you know." "Oh, really?"

「{今日|きょう}はさむいですね。」「そうですね。」 — "It's cold today, isn't it?" "It is, isn't it."

そうですね has a second job: with a long ね, そうですねえ…, it means "let me think" while you look
for an answer. ええと and あのう do this too: ええと while you search your memory, あのう when
you're about to ask or say something a bit awkward.

「{何|なに}が{食|た}べたいですか。」「そうですねえ……ええと、すしがいいです。」 — "What would you like to eat?" "Let me see… um, sushi would be good."

あのう、すみません、このせきはあいていますか。 — Um, excuse me, is this seat free?

(せき is "seat"; あいています is "is free, is empty".)

### How much is enough?

You don't need to fill every pause. Give an aizuchi when the speaker pauses at the end of a
phrase, often after ね or よ, and nod in between. Keep your voice short and light: an aizuchi is
not a turn of its own. A few cautions:

- なるほど can sound as if you are judging the explanation, so many people avoid it with a boss
  or a teacher. はい、わかりました is safer there.
- へえ is casual; with someone senior, そうですか or ほんとうですか sounds better.
- Repeating the same aizuchi every time sounds mechanical. Mix them.

## When you don't understand

The most useful sentences for a learner are the ones that make the other person slow down,
repeat or explain. Use them early and without embarrassment. Japanese people are used to
helping learners and will usually switch to simpler words.

| Japanese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| すみません、もういちどおねがいします。 | Sorry, once more, please. |
| もう{少|すこ}しゆっくりおねがいします。 | A little more slowly, please. |
| 「〜」はどういういみですか。 | What does "…" mean? |
| すみません、よくきこえません。 | Sorry, I can't hear you very well. |
| すみません、ちょっとわかりません。 | Sorry, I don't quite understand. |
| 〜ですか。 | (repeating a word with a rising voice to check it) |

ゆっくり is "slowly". いみ is "meaning", so どういういみですか is "what sort of meaning is it?". きこえる
means "to be audible": きこえません is "I can't hear (it)", which is what you say on a bad phone line
or in a noisy station. こえ is "voice": こえが{小|ちい}さいです (the voice is quiet).

The checking question is the quickest of all. Repeat the word you heard with a rising voice, and
the speaker will confirm it or correct you:

「パーティーは{四日|よっか}ですね。」「{八日|ようか}ですか？」「いいえ、{四日|よっか}です。」 — "So the party's on the fourth." "The eighth?" "No, the fourth."

{四日|よっか} and {八日|ようか} are a classic pair to mix up by ear, as are {一時|いちじ} and
{七時|しちじ}, which is why many people say ななじ for seven o'clock when it matters.

### Correcting and being corrected

ちがう means "to be different" or "to be wrong". ちがいます is the normal polite way to say "No,
that's not right" when someone has a fact wrong:

「エマさんはアメリカ{人|じん}ですか。」「いいえ、ちがいます。カナダ{人|じん}です。」 — "Are you American, Emma?" "No, I'm not. I'm Canadian."

In listening, ちがいます and いいえ are signals: the correct information comes right after them.

## On the telephone

A phone call has a few fixed pieces. もしもし is "hello" on the phone; you can also use it to
check that the other person is still there. Saying your name first, with です, is the usual
start.

| Situation | You say |
|---|---|
| Starting | もしもし、エマです。 |
| Asking for someone | ゆいさんをおねがいします。 |
| Asking who is calling | どなたですか。 (polite: who is it?) |
| Someone is out | ゆいは{今|いま}るすです。 / {出|で}かけています。 |
| Saying you'll call again | また{後|あと}で{電話|でんわ}します。 |
| Ending | しつれいします。 / じゃあ、また。 |

るす means "being out, not at home": るすです is "(they're) out". どなた is the polite word for
だれ. しつれいします (literally "I'm being rude") is how a polite call ends, as well as how you
excuse yourself when you leave a room. じゃあ means "well then" and closes many casual
conversations: じゃあ、また (see you).

You'll also hear the very polite ゆいさんはいらっしゃいますか (Is Yui there?), which uses
respectful language (the honors Lesson 25h1 introduces it). You don't need to produce it; おねがいします is
polite and correct.

### Phone numbers

You learned phone numbers in Lesson 3. On the phone, each digit is read separately, and the
dashes are read as の: 090-1234-5678 is ゼロきゅうゼロの、いちにいさんよんの、ごおろくななはち.
Short digits are stretched to two beats (にい, ごお) to make them clearer, and 4, 7 and 9 are
よん, なな and きゅう, never し, しち or く. Zero is ゼロ or まる (and れい in formal readings).

## Dialogue: a phone call

```dialogue
# A phone call
おかあさん: はい、やまだです。
= Hello, Yamada speaking.
エマ: もしもし、エマです。ゆいさんをおねがいします。
= Hello, it's Emma. May I speak to Yui, please?
おかあさん: あ、エマさん。すみません、ゆいは{今|いま}るすです。{友|とも}だちと{出|で}かけています。
= Oh, Emma. I'm sorry, Yui's out at the moment. She's gone out with friends.
エマ: そうですか。{何時|なんじ}ごろかえりますか。
= I see. About what time will she be back?
おかあさん: たぶん{六時|ろくじ}ごろです。
= Probably around six.
エマ: {六時|ろくじ}ごろですね。じゃあ、{七時|しちじ}ごろまた{電話|でんわ}します。
= Around six, then. In that case I'll call again at about seven.
おかあさん: はい。ゆいに{言|い}います。
= All right. I'll tell Yui.
エマ: ありがとうございます。しつれいします。
= Thank you. Goodbye.
おかあさん: しつれいします。
= Goodbye.
```

The mother answers with the family name, はい、やまだです, as many people do on a home phone.
Emma checks the time by repeating it, {六時|ろくじ}ごろですね, and both sides close with
しつれいします.

## Dialogue: Monday morning

```dialogue
# Monday morning
たなか: エマさん、しゅうまつは{何|なに}をしましたか。
= Emma, what did you do at the weekend?
エマ: {友|とも}だちと{山|やま}に{行|い}きました。さんじかんぐらいあるきました。
= I went to the mountains with friends. We walked for about three hours.
たなか: へえ、すごいですね。つかれたでしょう。
= Wow, that's amazing. You must have been tired.
エマ: ええ、ちょっと。でも、{天気|てんき}がよかったですから、たのしかったです。
= Yes, a bit. But the weather was good, so it was fun.
たなか: よかったですね。{山|やま}まで{電車|でんしゃ}でどのぐらいですか。
= I'm glad. How long is it to the mountains by train?
エマ: いちじかんぐらいです。
= About an hour.
たなか: なるほど、ちかいですね。わたしも{行|い}きたいです。
= I see, that's close. I'd like to go too.
エマ: じゃあ、こんどいっしょに{行|い}きませんか。
= Then why don't we go together next time?
たなか: ほんとうですか。ぜひ！
= Really? I'd love to!
```

Count the aizuchi: へえ, すごいですね, よかったですね, なるほど, ほんとうですか. Each one keeps the
conversation moving. こんど is "next time" and ぜひ "by all means, definitely".

## Listening strategies

### In conversation

- *Expect the topic.* In a shop you'll hear prices and いかがですか (would you like…?); at a
  station, times, platforms and destinations. Guessing what's coming makes it far easier to
  catch.
- *Catch the key words, not every word.* Who, when, where, how much. Numbers, days and times
  are the most useful things to catch exactly; ask again if you miss one.
- *Wait for the end.* As in reading, the end of the sentence decides the meaning: ます or
  ません, ください or ないでください. Don't stop listening halfway through.
- *Say what you understood.* Repeat the key fact with ですね. It's polite, and it gets you a
  correction if you were wrong.

### In the JLPT

The listening section of the JLPT N5 plays each recording once only, so these habits matter even
more. Lesson 30 describes the parts. In general:

- Read the question and look at the pictures or choices before the audio starts, and decide what
  kind of information you need.
- Listen for changes of plan. A speaker who says ちがいます, いいえ or でも is usually about to
  give the real answer. The first thing mentioned is often a trap.
- Many questions ask what someone will do *next* or *first*. Listen for {先|さき}に, まず (first),
  それから and てから.
- If you miss one item, let it go and get ready for the next. There's no second chance to hear it,
  and worrying costs you the following question.

## Say it

```speak
そうですか。
= I see.
へえ、すごいですね。
= Wow, that's amazing.
たいへんですね。
= That must be hard.
すみません、もういちどおねがいします。
= Sorry, once more, please.
もう{少|すこ}しゆっくりおねがいします。
= A little more slowly, please.
「こうばん」はどういういみですか。
= What does "kōban" mean?
もしもし、エマです。
= Hello, it's Emma.
また{後|あと}で{電話|でんわ}します。
= I'll call again later.
```

## Common mistakes

- Listening in silence. To a Japanese speaker it can sound as if you've stopped following. Use
  はい, ええ and そうですか.
- Taking a listener's はい as agreement. It usually means "I'm following".
- Answering "It's cold today, isn't it?" with そうですか, as if this were news. Agree with
  そうですね.
- Pretending to understand. もういちどおねがいします or a checking 〜ですか is always better
  than a wrong guess.
- Saying しち and し for 7 and 4 in phone numbers. Use なな and よん.
- Ending a phone call with さようなら. Use しつれいします (polite) or じゃあ、また (casual).

## Key points

- Aizuchi (はい, ええ, そうですか, そうですね, へえ, ほんとうですか, なるほど, たいへんですね, よかったですね,
  すごいですね) show you're listening; はい often means "go on", not "I agree".
- そうですか takes in new information; そうですね agrees, or with a long ね means "let me
  think". ええと and あのう fill a pause.
- Ask for help: もういちどおねがいします, もう{少|すこ}しゆっくりおねがいします, 「〜」はどういういみですか,
  よくきこえません; check a fact by repeating it with ですか or ですね.
- ちがいます is a polite "no, that's wrong"; after it comes the correct information.
- Phone calls: もしもし、〜です; 〜さんをおねがいします; るすです; また{後|あと}で{電話|でんわ}します;
  しつれいします.
- When listening, predict the topic, catch key words, wait for the end of the sentence, and
  repeat back what you understood.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The JLPT N5 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for This is the last core lesson of the course. It does three things. It explains the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test at level N5: what the level means, how the test is built and how it's scored. It gives you strategies for each part. And it reviews the grammar of the whole course, so you can see what you know and where to go back. The quiz at the end mixes questions from every module, so treat it as a final check. You don't have to take the exam. But the level it describes is exactly what this course has taught, and the free official sample questions are a good way to find out whether you've reached it. ## The JLPT and the level N5 The **[[JLPT]]** (Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, in Japanese {日本語|にほんご}のうりょくしけん) is the most widely taken test of Japanese for non-native speakers. It is run by the Japan Foundation and Japan Educational Exchanges and Services, and held in Japan and in many other countries. There are five levels. N5 is the first and easiest; N1 is the hardest. Put simply, someone who has reached N5 can understand some basic Japanese: - they can read typical everyday phrases and short sentences written in hiragana, katakana and basic kanji; - they can follow short conversations about everyday topics and the classroom, as long as people speak slowly, and pick out the information they need. That is a fair description of where you are now. N5 doesn't expect you to follow fast conversation between native speakers or to read a newspaper. It expects you to manage simple, concrete situations, slowly and with support. The JLPT tests only reading and listening. There is no speaking test and no writing (apart from filling in the answer sheet). Every question is multiple choice. ## How the N5 test is built The test is taken in one sitting, in three timed parts: ```mermaid flowchart LR accTitle: The three parts of the JLPT N5 accDescr: The N5 test has three timed parts taken in order. First, language knowledge (vocabulary), 20 minutes. Second, language knowledge (grammar) and reading, 40 minutes. Third, listening, 30 minutes. The first two parts are scored together out of 120 points, and listening out of 60, for a total of 180. A["1. Vocabulary
20 min"] --> B["2. Grammar and reading
40 min"] B --> C["3. Listening
30 min"] A -.-> S1["Scored together: 0 to 120"] B -.-> S1 C -.-> S2["Scored: 0 to 60"] ``` | Part | Time | What it tests | |---|---|---| | Language knowledge: vocabulary | 20 minutes | reading kanji words in kana; choosing the right kanji or katakana spelling; choosing the word that fits a sentence; choosing a sentence with the same meaning | | Language knowledge: grammar, and reading | 40 minutes | choosing the right particle or form; putting words in the right order; filling gaps in a short text; reading short texts, a longer text, and a notice or timetable to find information | | Listening | 30 minutes | short conversations where you decide what someone will do or which detail is true; choosing what to say in a situation shown in a picture; choosing the right quick reply to something said to you | These are the current times. Until the December 2020 test the first two parts were a little longer, so older books may give different figures. Here is each part in more detail, described in this course's own words. ### Vocabulary (20 minutes) - *Kanji readings.* A sentence with one word in kanji; you choose its reading in hiragana. This is why the course asked you to read kanji without furigana. - *Writing.* The reverse: a word in hiragana; you choose how it's written in kanji or katakana. Expect lookalike kanji ({木|き} and {本|ほん}, {人|ひと} and {入|い}る, {日|ひ} and {目|め}) and wrong katakana spellings. - *Words in context.* A sentence with a gap and four words; only one fits the meaning. - *Paraphrase.* A sentence and four others; you choose the one that means the same. ### Grammar and reading (40 minutes) - *Choosing the form.* A sentence with a gap: which particle, verb form or expression fits? Typical traps are は and が, に and で, を and に, and the wrong form before a pattern (\*{行|い}きますつもり). - *Word order.* A sentence with four gaps and four pieces; you put them in order and report the piece in one particular position. Build the whole sentence first, then answer. - *Text grammar.* A short passage, such as a student's composition, with gaps; you choose what fits each gap, often a connecting word (でも, それから, だから) or a sentence ending. - *Reading.* Short texts of a few lines (a note, a message, a short description) with one question each; a slightly longer text with two questions; and an information text such as a notice, a timetable or a list of prices, where you find the answer to a practical question. These are the text types of Lesson 28. ### Listening (30 minutes) - *What to do.* A short conversation, often between a teacher and a student or two colleagues; you decide what someone will do, or do first. Pictures or written choices are in the booklet. - *Key detail.* You hear a question first, then a conversation, and choose the detail that answers it: a time, a place, a reason. - *What do you say?* A picture shows a situation (an arrow points at one person) and you choose what that person would say: thanking, asking, apologizing. - *Quick reply.* Someone says one short sentence; you choose the natural reply from the ones you hear. Nothing is printed, so you rely on your ears alone. Each recording is played once. The answer sheet is a mark sheet: you fill in one circle per question. ## Scoring Your results come in two scoring sections, not three: the vocabulary part and the grammar and reading part are scored together. | Scoring section | Score range | Minimum to pass | |---|---|---| | Language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) and reading | 0–120 | 38 | | Listening | 0–60 | 19 | | Total | 0–180 | 80 | To pass you need *both*: a total of at least 80, *and* at least the minimum in each section. This minimum is the **[[sectional pass mark]]**. A candidate with 100 points overall but only 15 in listening fails. So you can't make up for weak listening with strong reading. The scores are **[[scaled scores]]**, not simply the number of questions you got right: they are adjusted so that a score means the same level of ability from one test date to the next. Don't try to calculate a "percentage needed"; aim to be comfortable in every part. The test is usually held twice a year, in July and December, in Japan and in many other countries; some places hold it only once a year. Registration closes months before the test. Dates, fees, rules and even the format can change, so always check the official website and your local test centre: - [The official JLPT website](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/) - [Official sample questions for learners](https://www.jlpt.jp/e/samples/forlearners.html) The official samples show the real layout of every question type, with audio. Use them near the end of your preparation, under timed conditions. ## Strategies ### Before the test - *Vocabulary first.* Most points at N5 depend on knowing words: their meaning, their kana spelling and their kanji. Keep up your daily vocabulary reviews in this app until the test. - *Read without furigana.* The test doesn't print readings over basic kanji like the ones in this course. Turn furigana off when you review lessons and texts. - *Listen every day.* Replay the dialogues in this course with the words hidden, then with them shown. Do the listening questions in this lesson's quiz and Lesson 29's. - *Practise the timing.* Do at least one full set of sample questions with a timer. ### During the test - *Vocabulary part:* it's short, so work steadily, and don't spend more than half a minute on a question. A wrong reading is often a near miss: a long vowel missing (しょうがつ / しょがつ), a small っ missing, a voicing mark added or dropped. Check those. - *Grammar and reading part:* do the grammar questions quickly to leave time for reading. For the reading texts, read the question first, then scan (Lesson 28). For word-order questions, write the numbers of the pieces in the margin in order before you mark the answer. - *Listening:* read the choices or look at the pictures before the audio starts; listen for changes of plan (でも, いいえ, ちがいます); for "what will they do first?", listen for まず, {先|さき}に, てから and まえに. If you miss one item, mark your best guess and move on. - *Always answer.* There's no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a question blank. ## The whole course in one table Use this to find what to review. If a pattern in the middle column doesn't feel familiar, go back to its lesson. | Module | Patterns | Lessons | |---|---|---| | 1. First sentences | N は N です / じゃありません; か questions; の; これ・この・ここ; numbers and prices; 〜をください; 〜つ; あります / います; location words | 1–5 | | 2. Daily life and time | times; ます / ません / ました / ませんでした; に (time), で (place of action), へ / に (destination), と (with); dates; 〜ませんか / 〜ましょう; が (but) | 6–10 | | 3. Describing things | い- and な-adjectives, present and past; すき / {上手|じょうず} が; より, のほうが, いちばん; family words; counting people | 11–15 | | 4. The て form | making the て form; 〜てください; 〜ています; 〜てから, 〜まえに, 〜のあとで; 〜てもいいです / 〜てはいけません; 〜たい, ほしい, 〜に{行|い}く | 16–20 | | 5. Plain forms | dictionary form; ない form and 〜ないでください; た form, 〜たことがあります, 〜たり〜たりします; casual speech, ね / よ, でしょう; describing nouns with verbs; とき | 21–25 | | 6. Putting it together | から (because), けど; 〜くなる / 〜になる; もう / まだ; つもり; directions and を for the route; reading and listening strategies | 26–29 | ### Five things to check These are the points that cost learners the most marks at N5: 1. *は and が.* は marks the topic, what you're talking about: わたしは{学生|がくせい}です。 が marks the subject when it is the new or important information, as in the answer to a question with だれ or {何|なに}: 「だれが{来|き}ましたか。」「たなかさんが{来|き}ました。」 が is also used with すき, {上手|じょうず}, ある and いる: ねこがすきです。 {車|くるま}があります。 2. *Particles for places.* に for where something is and where you go ({駅|えき}にいます、{駅|えき}に{行|い}きます), で for where an action happens ({駅|えき}で{会|あ}います), を for the route ({道|みち}をわたります). 3. *Verb groups and the て form.* かえる, {入|はい}る and しる end in -eru or -iru and look like group 2, but they are group 1: かえって, {入|はい}って, しって. まがる and わたる are group 1 too. {行|い}く is the one exception among く verbs: {行|い}って. 4. *Adjective forms.* いい becomes よ- in every other form: よくない, よかった, よくなる. きれい is a な-adjective: きれいじゃない, きれいになる. The past of a な-adjective is でした or だった, never \*きれかった. 5. *The form before a pattern.* Dictionary form before つもり and まえに; た form before ことがあります and あとで; て form before ください, います and から ("after"); ない form before ないでください. Many grammar questions are about exactly this. ## Words for studying | Word | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | しけん | exam, test | {来月|らいげつ}しけんがあります。 (I have an exam next month.) | | もんだい | question (on a test); problem | このもんだいはむずかしいです。 (This question is hard.) | | しつもん | question (that you ask) | しつもんがあります。 (I have a question.) | | こたえ | answer | こたえを{書|か}いてください。 (Write the answer.) | | こたえる | to answer | しつもんにこたえます。 (I answer the question.) | | えらぶ | to choose | {一|ひと}つえらんでください。 (Choose one.) | | まちがい | mistake | まちがいが{三|みっ}つありました。 (There were three mistakes.) | | れんしゅう | practice | {毎日|まいにち}れんしゅうします。 (I practise every day.) | | ふくしゅう | review (of what you've learned) | しけんのまえにふくしゅうします。 (I review before the exam.) | | がんばる | to do your best | しけん、がんばってください。 (Good luck in the exam.) | もんだい is a question set for you to answer, on a test or in a textbook, and also a problem in life: もんだいありません (no problem). しつもん is a question you ask someone. こたえる takes に for what you answer: しつもんにこたえる. えらぶ (group 1: えらびます, えらんで) is the verb in the instructions of many test questions, which ask you to choose the best answer. れんしゅう and ふくしゅう both combine with する: れんしゅうする, ふくしゅうする. がんばる (group 1: がんばって) is "to try hard, to keep going"; がんばってください is "good luck", and がんばります is "I'll do my best". ## A study plan for the last month | Week | What to do | |---|---| | 1 | Modules 1 and 2: reread each lesson's Key points and redo the module quizzes. Every day: your vocabulary reviews and one dialogue with the words hidden. | | 2 | Modules 3 and 4, the same way. Reread the texts of Lesson 28 with furigana off. | | 3 | Modules 5 and 6. Every day: ten minutes of listening, from this course's dialogues, Lesson 29's questions, or a podcast or video for learners. | | 4 | The official sample questions, timed. Go back to the lesson behind each mistake. Rest the day before the test. | The kanji notecards and the kanji list (in the Study tools box) cover every kanji in the course. Go through the list with the readings covered and say each word aloud. ## Dialogue: before the test ```dialogue # Before the test エマ: けんさん、{十二月|じゅうにがつ}のしけんをうけますか。 = Ken, are you taking the exam in December? けん: はい、N5をうけるつもりです。エマさんは？ = Yes, I'm planning to take N5. What about you, Emma? エマ: わたしもです。でも、{聞|き}くもんだいがむずかしいですね。 = Me too. But the listening questions are hard, aren't they? けん: そうですね。だから、わたしは{毎日|まいにち}{日本語|にほんご}のポッドキャストを{聞|き}いています。 = They are. That's why I listen to a Japanese podcast every day. エマ: へえ、いいですね。わたしはかんじがまだよくわかりませんから、{毎日|まいにち}れんしゅうしています。 = Oh, good idea. I still don't know kanji very well, so I practise every day. けん: しけんの{日|ひ}は、はやく{出|で}かけましょう。{駅|えき}からちょっととおいですから。 = On the day of the test, let's leave early. It's a bit far from the station. エマ: そうですね。いっしょにがんばりましょう！ = Good idea. Let's both do our best! ``` うける is "to take (an exam)"; ポッドキャスト is a podcast. The dialogue reuses this module's patterns: つもり, から and だから for reasons, まだ, and aizuchi (そうですね, へえ). ## Can you do this? By the end of this course you should be able to do everything below. If one feels shaky, the lesson number shows where to go back. - Introduce yourself and others, with your job, country and languages (1, 15). - Ask for things in a shop, count them and understand prices (3, 4). - Say where things are and ask the way (5, 27). - Tell the time, give dates and talk about your daily routine (6, 7, 9). - Invite someone, accept, and decline politely (10, 26). - Describe things and people, compare them, and talk about the weather (11–15). - Ask for things, ask permission, and say what is and isn't allowed (16, 19, 22). - Say what you want, what you've done before, and what you plan to do (20, 23, 26). - Talk casually with friends and politely with strangers (24). - Give reasons and describe changes (26). - Read short notices, messages, timetables and menus (28). - Keep a conversation going, and ask for help when you don't understand (29). ## Common mistakes - Studying only reading. Listening has its own pass mark, and missing it means failing the test, whatever your total. - Spending too long on the first vocabulary questions and running out of time for reading. - Translating every listening sentence into English in your head. Listen for the key facts. - Leaving questions blank. A guess can score; a blank can't. - Arriving late. Check the test centre and the route the day before; latecomers may not be let in. ## Key points - The JLPT has five levels; N5 is the first. It tests reading and listening only, all multiple choice. - N5 has three timed parts: vocabulary (20 minutes), grammar and reading (40 minutes) and listening (30 minutes). - Two scoring sections: language knowledge and reading (0–120, at least 38) and listening (0–60, at least 19). You pass with 80 of 180 *and* both section minimums. - Scores are scaled, every recording is played once, and there's no penalty for guessing. - Check the official website for dates, rules and sample questions. - Review with the table above; the five points (は / が, place particles, verb groups, adjective forms, the form before a pattern) cost the most marks. The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: A longer story
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Everything you've read so far has been a few lines long. This lesson is one complete story of
about 850 characters, written for this course at N5 level. It has no new grammar. What's new is
the length: keeping track of who is doing what, across many sentences, without losing the
thread.

Reading a lot of easy text, quickly and for pleasure, is called **[[extensive reading]]**. It's the
fastest way to make the grammar you know automatic. The rules of extensive reading are simple:
don't look things up unless you must, skip what you don't understand, and keep going. This
lesson bends the rules a little, with notes after each part, but try reading each part through
once before you look at the notes.

## Before you read

The story is about ミア, a university student from Australia who has been in Japan for three
months. One Saturday she takes a train on her own. Five words will help:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| わすれもの | something left behind, a lost item |
| こまる | to be in trouble, to not know what to do |
| {見|み}つける | to find |
| {気|き}をつける | to be careful, to take care |
| {学生|がくせい}しょう | student ID card |

こまる is a group 1 verb, and it's usually used in the past or the ています form: こまりました,
こまっています (I'm in a fix). {見|み}つける is group 2: {見|み}つけます, {見|み}つけて. {気|き}をつけて
is how Japanese says "take care" or "be careful", and {気|き}をつけてください is a common warning.

## The story: わすれもの

### Part 1

> ミアはオーストラリアから{来|き}た{大学生|だいがくせい}です。{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、もう{三|さん}か{月|げつ}になりました。{日本語|にほんご}はまだ{上手|じょうず}じゃありませんが、{毎日|まいにち}べんきょうしています。
>
> ある{土曜日|どようび}、ミアは{一人|ひとり}で{電車|でんしゃ}にのって、{山|やま}のちかくの{小|ちい}さいまちへ{行|い}きました。{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}で、ミアは{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいました。とてもおもしろい{本|ほん}でしたから、ずっと{読|よ}んでいました。
>
> 「つぎは、みどりやま、みどりやまです。」
>
> ミアはびっくりしました。みどりやまでおりるつもりでした。ミアは{本|ほん}をかばんに{入|い}れて、いそいで{電車|でんしゃ}をおりました。

{来|き}た{大学生|だいがくせい} is a noun described by a verb (Lesson 25): "a university student who
came from Australia". もう{三|さん}か{月|げつ}になりました uses もう and なる from Lesson 26: "it has
already become three months". ある{土曜日|どようび} is "one Saturday". びっくりする is "to be
startled". おりるつもりでした is the past of つもり: "she had meant to get off".

### Part 2

> {駅|えき}を{出|で}て、ミアは{店|みせ}で{水|みず}を{買|か}いたかったです。でも、さいふがありません。かばんの{中|なか}を{見|み}ましたが、ありませんでした。ポケットの{中|なか}にもありませんでした。
>
> 「あ、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}だ……。」
>
> さいふの{中|なか}には、お{金|かね}と{学生|がくせい}しょうと{電車|でんしゃ}のカードがありました。ミアはとてもこまりました。

{買|か}いたかったです is the past of 〜たい: "she wanted to buy". The short line 「あ、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}だ……。」
is what Mia says to herself, in casual speech (Lesson 24): "Oh, it's on the train…".

### Part 3

> ミアは{駅|えき}にもどって、まどぐちの{人|ひと}に{話|はな}しました。
>
> 「すみません、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}にさいふをわすれました。」
>
> 「どの{電車|でんしゃ}ですか。」
>
> 「{十時|じゅうじ}ごろの{電車|でんしゃ}です。{前|まえ}から{二|に}ばん{目|め}のところにすわっていました。」
>
> 「さいふはどんなさいふですか。」
>
> 「あかくて、{小|ちい}さいさいふです。」
>
> {駅|えき}の{人|ひと}はどこかに{電話|でんわ}をかけました。ミアは{十五分|じゅうごふん}ぐらいまちました。
>
> 「ありましたよ。おばあさんがさいふを{見|み}つけて、{二|ふた}つ{先|さき}の{駅|えき}の{人|ひと}にわたしました。」

もどる is "to go back"; まどぐち is a ticket or service window. {前|まえ}から{二|に}ばん{目|め} is
"second from the front", an ordinal from Lesson 27. あかくて、{小|ちい}さい joins two adjectives
with the て form of an い-adjective (あかい → あかくて): "red and small". どこかに is "somewhere";
わたす is "to hand over". {二|ふた}つ{先|さき}の{駅|えき} is "the station two stops further on".

### Part 4

> ミアはつぎの{電車|でんしゃ}にのって、その{駅|えき}へ{行|い}きました。{駅|えき}の{人|ひと}がさいふを{出|だ}しました。{中|なか}のお{金|かね}もカードも、ぜんぶありました。
>
> {駅|えき}には、{白|しろ}いぼうしのおばあさんもいました。このおばあさんがさいふを{見|み}つけました。
>
> 「ほんとうにありがとうございました。」
>
> 「いいえ。よかったですね。{日本|にほん}の{電車|でんしゃ}は{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いから、{気|き}をつけてね。」
>
> おばあさんはにこにこして、{電車|でんしゃ}にのりました。

{出|だ}す is "to take out". ぜんぶ is "all, everything". {白|しろ}いぼうしのおばあさん is "the old
woman in the white hat": の links the hat to her. The old woman speaks casually and warmly, as an
older person may to a young one: {多|おお}いから (plain form + から, Lesson 26) and {気|き}をつけてね.
にこにこする is "to smile" (one of the sound words of Lesson 25h2).

### Part 5

> そのばん、ミアはオーストラリアの{母|はは}にメールを{書|か}きました。
>
> 「{今日|きょう}、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}にさいふをわすれました。でも、{駅|えき}の{人|ひと}もおばあさんも、とてもしんせつでした。わたしは{日本|にほん}がもっとすきになりました。これからは、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}で{本|ほん}を{読|よ}むときは、{気|き}をつけます。」

そのばん is "that evening". しんせつ is "kind". もっとすきになりました is なる with a な-adjective:
"I've come to like (Japan) even more". 〜ときは is "when …" from Lesson 25, and これからは is
"from now on".

## The whole story in English

Mia is a university student from Australia. It has already been three months since she came to
Japan. Her Japanese isn't good yet, but she studies every day.

One Saturday, Mia took a train on her own to a small town near the mountains. On the train she
was reading a book. It was a very interesting book, so she kept on reading.

"The next stop is Midoriyama. Midoriyama."

Mia was startled. She had meant to get off at Midoriyama. She put the book in her bag and got
off the train in a hurry.

After she left the station, Mia wanted to buy some water in a shop. But she had no wallet. She
looked inside her bag, but it wasn't there. It wasn't in her pocket either. "Oh no, it's on the
train…" In the wallet were her money, her student ID and her train card. Mia didn't know what to
do.

Mia went back into the station and spoke to the person at the window. "Excuse me, I left my
wallet on the train." "Which train?" "The one at about ten o'clock. I was sitting second from
the front." "What is the wallet like?" "It's small and red." The station worker
phoned somewhere. Mia waited for about fifteen minutes. "It's been found. An old woman found the
wallet and handed it to the staff at the station two stops on."

Mia took the next train to that station. A station worker brought out the wallet. The money and
the cards inside were all there. At the station there was also an old woman in a white hat. She
was the one who had found the wallet. "Thank you so much." "Not at all. I'm glad. Japanese
trains are crowded, so do be careful." The old woman smiled and got on a train.

That evening, Mia wrote an email to her mother in Australia. "Today I left my wallet on a
train. But the station staff and an old woman were very kind. I like Japan even more now. From
now on, I'll be careful when I read on the train."

## Reading it again

Read the story a second time with furigana turned off. Then try reading it aloud, at a steady
speed, without stopping to translate. Notice how much of the module is in it: もう〜になりました,
から for reasons, つもり, an ordinal with {目|め}, もっとすきになりました. If you can follow the whole
story, you can read the easiest levels of the graded readers in the reading list, which are
written in just this way.

Some questions to think about, in English or in Japanese:

- Where did Mia notice the wallet was missing, and why did she want it at that moment?
- How did the station staff find the wallet so quickly?
- Why do you think the old woman speaks casually to Mia, while Mia speaks politely?
- What does Mia decide at the end?

## Key points

- Long texts are easier if you keep track of who is speaking and where the story is: names,
  places and time words (ある{土曜日|どようび}, そのばん) are your landmarks.
- Quoted speech in 「」 often appears on its own line, without "she said".
- Read for the story first; return to the details afterwards.
- Extensive reading, a lot of easy text, is the best next step after this course.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This course has mostly asked you to read and listen. But the first thing many learners actually
write in Japanese is a message to a real person: a postcard to a host family, an email to a
teacher, a quick chat message to a friend, an address on an envelope. Each of these has a shape
that Japanese readers expect. With the right shape, even very simple sentences look correct and
polite.

## Postcards: はがき

A postcard is a はがき. In Japan you can buy them at post offices and convenience stores with the
stamp already printed on; for an ordinary postcard you stick on a stamp, a きって. A postcard has
an address side and a message side, and the message usually follows this order:

1. The reader's name, with さん (or さま for someone you should be formal with).
2. An opening question or remark, often about health or the season: お{元気|げんき}ですか。
   さむくなりましたね。
3. Your news, in the past tense or the ています form.
4. A friendly closing: また{会|あ}いましょう (let's meet again), からだに{気|き}をつけてください (take
   care of yourself), お{元気|げんき}で (keep well).
5. The date, and your name.

> けんさん
>
> お{元気|げんき}ですか。わたしは{今|いま}、{北|きた}の{山|やま}のまちに{来|き}ています。{毎日|まいにち}さむいですけど、{山|やま}も{川|かわ}もとてもきれいです。きのうは{友|とも}だちと{山|やま}にのぼりました。
>
> {来週|らいしゅう}かえります。また{会|あ}いましょう。
>
> {二月|にがつ}{十日|とおか}
>
> エマ

Ken, how are you? I'm in a mountain town in the north at the moment. It's cold every day, but
the mountains and the rivers are beautiful. Yesterday I climbed a mountain with friends. I'll be
back next week. Let's meet up then. 10 February. Emma.

{来|き}ています is "I have come (and am here)", the resulting-state use of ています from Lesson 17. The
けど sentence is from Lesson 26.

### Cards for the seasons

Two kinds of card are a Japanese custom:

- *New Year cards*, ねんがじょう. They are posted in late December and delivered on 1 January,
  and they start with あけましておめでとうございます (Happy New Year) or a written equivalent.
  Fewer people send them than in the past, but some still send dozens, to friends, relatives
  and colleagues.
- *Summer greeting cards*, しょちゅうみまい, sent in the hottest part of the summer to ask how
  the other person is coping with the heat.

You don't need to write either yet, but if you receive one, a short card back is a kind reply.

## Email

An email to a teacher, a colleague or a host family is polite and short. The shape:

| Part | Example |
|---|---|
| Subject | あしたのクラス (tomorrow's class) |
| Name | やまだ{先生|せんせい} / やまださん |
| Greeting and who you are | こんにちは。{日本語|にほんご}クラスのエマです。 |
| Your message | the reason, then what you'd like |
| Closing | よろしくおねがいします。 |
| Your name | エマ |

> Subject: あしたのクラス
>
> やまだ{先生|せんせい}
>
> こんにちは。{日本語|にほんご}クラスのエマです。
>
> すみませんが、かぜをひきましたから、あしたのクラスを{休|やす}みます。しゅくだいは、つぎのクラスで{出|だ}してもいいですか。
>
> よろしくおねがいします。
>
> エマ

Ms Yamada, hello. This is Emma from the Japanese class. I'm sorry, but I've caught a cold, so I'll
miss tomorrow's class. May I hand in the homework at the next class? Thank you. Emma.

Notice the order of the message: apology (すみませんが), reason (から), then the request
(〜てもいいですか). Saying who you are at the start matters, because the teacher may not recognize
your email address. A teacher is addressed as name + {先生|せんせい}, never {先生|せんせい}さん.

In business emails you'll see a fixed opening, おせわになっております ("thank you for your
continued support"), before anything else. Recognize it; you don't need to write it yet.

A reply is a へんじ: へんじをください (please reply), へんじがおそくなってすみません (sorry for the
late reply), which is also a good use of なる.

## Chat messages

Most people in Japan chat on their phones with a messaging app, LINE being by far the most
common. Chat between friends is casual: plain forms (Lesson 24), short lines, few greetings, and
lots of ね and よ.

```dialogue
# Planning Saturday
ゆい: あした{何時|なんじ}に{会|あ}う？
= What time shall we meet tomorrow?
エマ: {11時|じゅういちじ}はどう？
= How about 11?
ゆい: いいよ！{駅|えき}の{北口|きたぐち}でいい？
= Sounds good! Is the north exit of the station OK?
エマ: うん、いいよ。
= Yeah, fine.
ゆい: じゃあ、またあしたね〜
= OK then, see you tomorrow~
```

Some habits of chat writing:

- Questions end in ？ instead of か: {会|あ}う？ (casual questions, Lesson 24).
- 〜 or ー stretch a sound and make the tone friendly: ね〜, はーい.
- Stickers, called スタンプ, often replace a whole sentence: a cartoon bowing for "thank you",
  for example. Emoji and kaomoji, faces made of characters such as (^_^), are common too.
- Laughter is written with a kanji meaning "laugh" in brackets, or simply with the letter w,
  sometimes repeated.

Keep chat casual with friends only. To a teacher or a colleague, even on a chat app, use です and
ます.

## Addresses and envelopes

An envelope is a ふうとう, and the postbox, which is red in Japan, is a ポスト. A Japanese address,
a じゅうしょ, runs from the largest unit to the smallest, the opposite of English:

1. 〒 and the postal code: seven digits, written 123-4567.
2. The prefecture (〜けん, 〜と, 〜ふ, or ほっかいどう).
3. The city or ward (〜し, 〜く), then the district.
4. The block numbers, written with dashes: 3-5-2.
5. The building name and room number.
6. The person's name, with さま after it.

Here is a made-up address, written horizontally:

> 〒123-4567
>
> みどりけん　あおばし　なかまち　3-5-2
>
> さくらアパート　201
>
> やまだ　ゆい　さま

The name is written larger than the address and followed by さま, the polite title used on all
mail, even to friends. Don't use さん on an envelope. For a company with no particular person,
write the company name followed by おんちゅう, the form for organizations.

On a traditional envelope the address is written vertically, in columns from right to left: the
postal code in the boxes at the top, the address in a column on the right, and the name large in
the middle. Numbers are then usually written in kanji ({三|さん}の{五|ご}の{二|に} or similar). Your own
address and name go on the back, on the left, in the same order. Horizontal envelopes are also
fine, with the address at the top left and the name in the middle.

## Writing on squared paper

At school in Japan, compositions are written on **[[genkō yōshi]]**, squared paper with one square for
each character. A few rules are worth knowing if you ever use it: each kana, kanji or punctuation
mark gets its own square, including small kana like っ and ょ; a new paragraph starts one square in;
and in vertical writing the columns run from right to left, like a vertical envelope.

## Common mistakes

- Starting with the news. Begin with the reader's name and a greeting, and end with a closing
  and your name.
- Writing an English-order address. In Japanese, start with the postal code and prefecture, and
  end with the name.
- Using さん on an envelope; use さま.
- Writing {先生|せんせい}さん. {先生|せんせい} is already a title.
- Sending a casual chat message to a teacher: \*あした{休|やす}む. Write あした{休|やす}みます。
- Forgetting to say who you are at the start of an email.

## Key points

- Postcards: name, greeting (お{元気|げんき}ですか), news, closing (また{会|あ}いましょう), date, your name.
- Emails: subject, name + {先生|せんせい} or さん, こんにちは and who you are, message (apology, reason,
  request), よろしくおねがいします, your name. A reply is a へんじ.
- Chat with friends is casual: plain forms, ？, ね and よ, stickers. Stay polite with teachers.
- Addresses go from large to small: 〒 code, prefecture, city, block numbers, building, name +
  さま.
- はがき, きって, ふうとう, ポスト and じゅうしょ are the words you need at the post office.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: わたし ___ エマです。 (I'm Emma.)
questions.explanation: は (read "wa") marks the topic, what the sentence is about: "As for me, I'm Emma". を marks an object, か ends a question, and の links two nouns ("my …"), so none of them fits here.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm not a teacher."?
choices: {先生|せんせい}じゃ ありません。
{先生|せんせい}の ありません。
questions.explanation: The negative of です is じゃ ありません (or the more formal では ありません). {先生|せんせい}です is "I'm a teacher", {先生|せんせい}ですか is a question, and の can't replace じゃ.

questions.stem: How do you say "a Japanese teacher" (a teacher of Japanese)?
choices: {日本人|にほんじん}の {日本語|にほんご}
{先生|せんせい}の {日本語|にほんご}
{日本語|にほんご}は {先生|せんせい}
{日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい}
questions.explanation: In A の B, A describes B, and the main word comes last: {日本語|にほんご}の {先生|せんせい} is a teacher of Japanese. The English order, {先生|せんせい}の {日本語|にほんご}, means "the teacher's Japanese". は would make a whole sentence, not a phrase.

questions.stem: Emma introduces herself. Which sentence is correct?
choices: わたしは エマさんです。
わたしは エマです。
あなたは エマです。
questions.explanation: さん shows respect, so it goes after other people's names, never your own: わたしは エマです. Both versions with エマさん put さん on yourself, and あなたは エマです means "You are Emma".

questions.stem: How is 学生 read in "わたしは 学生です。"?
questions.explanation: 学生 is がくせい: 学 with its on'yomi ガク, 生 with セイ. The long "e" is written せい. There is no small っ (がっせい), and ショウ and まな(ぶ) are readings these kanji have in other words.

questions.stem: How is 日本人 read in "{山本|やまもと}さんは 日本人です。"?
questions.explanation: 日本人 is にほんじん: {日本|にほん} (Japan) + 人 read じん, the reading used after a country for nationality. ひと is the reading when 人 stands alone ("a person"), not after a country name.

questions.stem: What does "いいえ、ちがいます。" mean?
questions.explanation: ちがいます ("it's different") politely corrects a wrong guess: "No, that's not right." "Yes, that's right" is はい、そうです, "I see" is そうですか, and "Pleased to meet you too" is こちらこそ.

questions.stem: A says: "はじめまして。{木下|きのした}です。よろしく おねがいします。" What is the best reply?
choices: はじめまして。エマです。よろしく おねがいします。
{木下|きのした}さんは エマです。
questions.explanation: The natural reply mirrors the introduction: はじめまして, your name with です, and よろしく おねがいします. そうですか (I see) and いいえ、ちがいます (no, that's wrong) don't answer an introduction, and the last choice says "Kinoshita is Emma".

questions.stem: Which word means "English" (the language)?
questions.explanation: English is えいご, wherever it's spoken. Most languages are country + ご, but not English: アメリカご and イギリスご aren't used. アメリカ{人|じん} is an American person.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Emma is American."?
choices: エマさんの アメリカ{人|じん}です。
エマさんは アメリカ{語|ご}です。
エマさんは アメリカ{人|じん}です。
エマさんは アメリカの です。
questions.explanation: Country + {人|じん} gives the nationality: アメリカ{人|じん}. アメリカ{語|ご} would be a language (and English is えいご anyway). The topic needs は, not の, and アメリカの です leaves the noun out.

questions.stem: How do you turn "{学生|がくせい}です。" (I'm a student.) into a polite question?
choices: {学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません。
questions.explanation: か goes at the very end, after です, and the word order stays the same: {学生|がくせい}ですか。 It can't go before です or at the start, and じゃ ありません makes a negative, not a question.

questions.stem: Type the word for "university" (kana or kanji): ___
questions.explanation: University is {大学|だいがく}, "big learning". A university student is {大学生|だいがくせい}.

questions.stem: Type the missing particle: エマさんは {日本語|にほんご}___ {学生|がくせい}です。 (Emma is a student of Japanese.)
questions.explanation: の joins two nouns, the describing one first: {日本語|にほんご}の {学生|がくせい}, a student of Japanese. は is already used for the topic エマさん.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the sentence mean?

audio.text: 山本さんは先生です。

questions.explanation: You heard {山本|やまもと}さんは {先生|せんせい}です: "Ms Yamamoto is a teacher." There was no か at the end (a question) and no じゃ ありません (a negative), and {学生|がくせい} would start with "ga".

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: いいえ、学生じゃありません。

choices: はい、{学生|がくせい}です。
いいえ、{学生|がくせい}です。
いいえ、{学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません。
いいえ、{先生|せんせい}じゃ ありません。
questions.explanation: "No, I'm not a student": いいえ、{学生|がくせい}じゃ ありません. The sentence ended in ありません, not です, and the word was がくせい (student), not せんせい (teacher).

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear (kana or kanji): ___

audio.text: 日本語

questions.explanation: You heard にほんご, the Japanese language: {日本|にほん} + ご (language). にほんじん would be a Japanese person.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: {人|じん} after a country is a person, ご a language. かいしゃいん is a company employee, いしゃ a doctor, {大学生|だいがくせい} a university student. A teacher would be {先生|せんせい}.

questions.stem: Read: "はじめまして。リサ・ブラウンです。カナダ{人|じん}です。{大学|だいがく}の {先生|せんせい}じゃ ありません。{大学生|だいがくせい}です。よろしく おねがいします。" What is true about Lisa?
questions.explanation: リサ is カナダ{人|じん} (Canadian) and says she is not a university teacher ({先生|せんせい}じゃ ありません) but a university student ({大学生|だいがくせい}です). Watch for じゃ ありません: it reverses the sentence.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "person"?
questions.explanation: 人 (ひと, ジン) is person: two legs walking. 入 (enter) is its mirror image, 大 (big) is a person with arms spread wide, and 八 is eight.

questions.stem: You want to ask Mr Kinoshita whether he is a student. What do you say?
choices: あなたは {学生|がくせい}ですか。
{木下|きのした}さんは {学生|がくせい}ですか。
{木下|きのした}さんは {学生|がくせい}です。
わたしは {学生|がくせい}ですか。
questions.explanation: When you know someone's name, use it instead of "you": {木下|きのした}さんは … ですか. あなた is grammatical but sounds distant or blunt to someone you know. Without か it isn't a question, and わたしは asks about yourself.

questions.stem: Your friend is holding a pen you don't recognize. You ask: "___は {何|なん}ですか。"
questions.explanation: The pen is near the listener, so it's それ (that, by you). これ is for something near you, あれ for something away from both of you, and どれ means "which one?".

questions.stem: Which is correct for "this umbrella"?
questions.explanation: Before a noun you need the の-form: この かさ. これ stands alone ("this one"), これの かさ would mean "this one's umbrella", and ここ is a place ("here").

questions.stem: Which sentence asks "Where is the toilet?"
choices: トイレは どこですか。
トイレは どれですか。
トイレは だれですか。
どこは トイレですか。
questions.explanation: どこ is "where": トイレは どこですか. どれ is "which one", だれ "who", and a question word can't take は, so どこは is wrong.

questions.stem: A: "これは だれの かさですか。" B (it's B's umbrella): ___
choices: わたしは かさです。
questions.explanation: わたしの stands for わたしの かさ: "It's mine." わたしです would be "It's me", わたしは かさです "I am an umbrella", and だれのです repeats the question word.

questions.stem: Ken is a student. Which sentence means "I'm a student too."?
choices: わたしは {学生|がくせい}もです。
わたしはも {学生|がくせい}です。
わたしもは {学生|がくせい}です。
わたしも {学生|がくせい}です。
questions.explanation: も ("too") replaces は and goes right after the word that is "also": わたしも. It never sits next to は (はも, もは), and putting it after {学生|がくせい} changes the meaning.

questions.stem: How is 何 read in "これは 何ですか。"?
questions.explanation: Before です, 何 is read なん: なんですか. なに is used before most particles (なにが) and in {何語|なにご}; カ is its on'yomi, rarely used alone; なにか means "something".

questions.stem: How is 何語 (what language?) read?
questions.explanation: "What language" is なにご. The rule "なん before です and の" doesn't cover it; it's one of the words to learn as it is. なんご isn't standard, and かご is a basket.

questions.stem: What does "{先生|せんせい}は あそこです。" mean?
choices: The teacher is there, by you.
questions.explanation: あそこ is "over there", away from both speakers. Here is ここ, there by you is そこ, and the question would need どこ and か.

questions.stem: Match each place word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: こ near me, そ near you, あ away from both, ど the question. The place words are ここ, そこ, あそこ (not "あこ") and どこ. "Which one" is どれ, "who" is だれ.

questions.stem: There are several bags. How do you ask Emma which one is hers?
choices: どれは エマさんの かばんですか。
エマさんの かばんは どのですか。
エマさんの かばんは どれですか。
エマさんの かばんは どこですか。
questions.explanation: どれ ("which one") stands alone before です. どの needs a noun after it, a question word can't take は (どれは), and どこ asks where the bag is, not which one it is.

questions.stem: A, holding a book, asks: "これは {何|なん}の {本|ほん}ですか。" What does B answer?
choices: それは {日本語|にほんご}の {本|ほん}です。
これは {日本語|にほんご}の {本|ほん}です。
あれは {日本語|にほんご}の {本|ほん}です。
どれは {日本語|にほんご}の {本|ほん}です。
questions.explanation: The book is in A's hand, near the listener from B's side, so B says それ. これ would mean the book is near B, あれ that it's far from both, and どれ is a question word.

questions.stem: What does "ジョンさんも {日本人|にほんじん}じゃ ありません。" mean?
choices: John isn't Japanese, but Emma is.
questions.explanation: も with a negative means "not … either": John isn't Japanese either. "Is Japanese too" would end in です, a question in か, and nothing in the sentence mentions Emma.

questions.stem: Type the word for "who" in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: "Who" is だれ; "whose" is だれの. Don't confuse it with どれ (which one).

questions.stem: Complete the question: この かさは ___ですか。 (Whose umbrella is this?)
questions.explanation: "Whose" is だれ + の: この かさは だれのですか. だれですか alone would ask "who is this umbrella?".

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: それは何ですか。

choices: それは だれですか。
questions.explanation: You heard "sore wa nan desu ka": それは {何|なん}ですか, "What's that (by you)?" これ starts with "ko", あれ with "a", and だれ would ask "who".

questions.stem: Listen. What does the question mean?

audio.text: あの人はだれですか。

choices: Who is that person over there?
questions.explanation: あの {人|ひと}は だれですか: "Who is that person over there?" この would be "this", {何|なん} would ask "what", and どこ "where".

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?

audio.text: えんぴつ

questions.explanation: えんぴつ (pencil), with ぴ: the ん sounds like "m" before it. The other choices change one sound and aren't words.

questions.stem: How is 名前 read in "わたしの 名前は エマです。"?
questions.explanation: 名前 is なまえ (name), with the kun'yomi な for 名 and まえ for 前. メイ and ミョウ are on'yomi of 名, used in other words.

questions.stem: Read: "A: すみません、これは {先生|せんせい}の かさですか。 B: いいえ、ちがいます。わたしのです。 A: そうですか。じゃあ、あの かさは？ B: あれは {先生|せんせい}のです。" Whose is the umbrella over there?
questions.explanation: B says あれは {先生|せんせい}のです: "That one over there is the teacher's." The umbrella A is holding (これ) is B's: わたしのです.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "name"?
questions.explanation: 名 (な, メイ) is "name", as in {名前|なまえ}: an evening shape over a mouth. 多 (many) has two of the evening shape and no mouth, 外 is "outside" and 右 is "right".

questions.stem: How do you say 300?
questions.explanation: After さん, ひゃく is voiced to びゃく: さんびゃく. さんひゃく ignores the sound change, ぴゃく is the change after ろく and はち (ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく), and み is a native reading of three.

questions.stem: How do you say 800?
questions.explanation: はち shrinks to はっ and ひゃく hardens to ぴゃく: はっぴゃく. はちひゃく has no sound change; びゃく comes only after さん (さんびゃく).

questions.stem: How do you say 3,000?
questions.explanation: After さん, せん is voiced to ぜん: さんぜん. さんせん misses the change, and さんびゃく is 300.

questions.stem: How do you say 10,000?
questions.explanation: Japanese counts in ten-thousands, and まん always needs a number: いちまん. じゅうせん (ten thousands) isn't used, まん alone is incomplete, and せんまん is ten million.

questions.stem: Match each number to its reading.
questions.explanation: These are the sound changes to learn: さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん, はっせん. はちひゃく and さんせん are the regular forms that Japanese doesn't use.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm eight years old."?
questions.explanation: Before さい, はち shrinks to はっ: はっさい. はちさい misses the change, やっつ is eight things, and はっせん is 8,000.

questions.stem: Which word is the special word for "twenty years old"?
questions.explanation: はたち is twenty years old. ふたつ is two things, にさい two years old, and とお ten things.

questions.stem: How is 4{円|えん} (4 yen) read?
questions.explanation: 4 yen is よえん, one of the small surprises of Japanese numbers. With bigger numbers 4 is regular: 40{円|えん} is よんじゅうえん, 400{円|えん} よんひゃくえん. し is avoided in prices.

questions.stem: You want to know the price of something you're holding. What do you ask?
choices: これは いくつですか。
これは いくらですか。
これは {何|なん}さいですか。
これは {何|なん}ばんですか。
questions.explanation: いくら asks "how much (money)". いくつ asks "how many", {何|なん}さい asks an age, and {何|なん}ばん asks "what number".

questions.stem: Which is the more polite way to ask an adult's age?
questions.explanation: おいくつですか is the softer, more polite question. {何|なん}さいですか is fine with children and peers. いくら asks a price and {何|なん}ばん a number.

questions.stem: How is 百 read in "コーヒーは 百{円|えん}です。"?
questions.explanation: 百 is ひゃく, a hundred: ひゃくえん. せん is 千 and まん 万. びゃく appears only after さん (さんびゃく).

questions.stem: Which kanji means "thousand"?
questions.explanation: 千 (セン) is thousand: 十 with a slanted stroke on top. 十 is ten, 万 ten thousand, and 午 (noon, a later lesson) looks like 千 with an extra line.

questions.stem: How is 三千円 read?
questions.explanation: 三千 is さんぜん (voiced after さん) and 円 is えん: さんぜんえん, 3,000 yen. さんびゃくえん would be 三百円, 300 yen.

questions.stem: When you read a phone number aloud, what do you say for each hyphen (as in 090-1234-5678)?
questions.explanation: Phone numbers are read digit by digit with の for each hyphen: ゼロきゅうゼロの いちにさんよんの … と, は and も are other particles with other jobs.

questions.stem: Type how you say 600 in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: 600 is ろっぴゃく: ろく shrinks to ろっ and ひゃく hardens to ぴゃく. Type roppyaku.

questions.stem: Type how you say 1,500{円|えん} (1,500 yen) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: 1,000 is just せん (no いち), then ごひゃく, then えん: せんごひゃくえん.

questions.stem: Listen. How much is it?

audio.text: 三百五十円です。

questions.explanation: さんびゃくごじゅうえん: 300 + 50 = 350 yen. 3,500 would be さんぜんごひゃくえん, and 530 ごひゃくさんじゅうえん.

questions.stem: Listen. How much is it?

audio.text: 八千円です。

questions.explanation: You heard はっせんえん: 8,000 yen. 800 would be はっぴゃくえん and 80,000 はちまんえん.

questions.stem: Listen. How old is the speaker?

audio.text: じゅうきゅうさいです。

questions.explanation: じゅうきゅうさい is 10 + 9 = 19. Nine would be きゅうさい, ten じゅっさい, and ninety きゅうじゅっさい.

questions.stem: Read the menu: "うどん 330{円|えん}　カレー 420{円|えん}　コーヒー 100{円|えん}". Which costs よんひゃくにじゅうえん?
questions.explanation: よんひゃくにじゅうえん is 400 + 20 = 420 yen, the カレー (curry). うどん is さんびゃくさんじゅうえん and コーヒー ひゃくえん.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: おちゃ ___ ください。 (Tea, please.)
questions.explanation: The thing you ask for is the object of ください, marked by を (read "o"). は would make おちゃ the topic, か ends a question, and の links two nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Three apples, please."?
choices: みっつ りんごを ください。
りんごを みっつ ください。
りんごを さん ください。
りんごを みつ ください。
questions.explanation: The pattern is thing を number ください, with the つ counter: りんごを みっつ ください. The number doesn't go before the noun, plain さん isn't used for counting things, and みつ (with no small っ) means honey.

questions.stem: How do you say "two (things)" with the つ counter?
questions.explanation: The native counting words are a separate set: ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ… Two things is ふたつ. につ and にっつ mix in the number に, which doesn't combine with つ.

questions.stem: How do you say "ten (things)" in the native set?
questions.explanation: Ten is とお, with no つ: it's the one exception in the set. とおつ adds a つ that isn't there, and じゅう doesn't combine with つ.

questions.stem: A shop assistant asks how many eggs you want: "たまごは ___ですか。"
questions.explanation: いくつ is "how many (things)". いくら is "how much (money)", {何|なん}さい "how old", and どれ "which one".

questions.stem: Which question means "How much is it altogether?"
choices: ぜんぶは {何|なん}ですか。
ぜんぶで いくつですか。
ぜんぶで いくらですか。
ぜんぶを ください。
questions.explanation: ぜんぶで means "in total" and いくら asks the price. いくつ would ask "how many altogether", {何|なん}ですか "what is it", and ぜんぶを ください is "I'll take all of it".

questions.stem: You point at several umbrellas. How do you say "The red one, please."?
choices: あかいのは ください。
あかいを ください。
あかいの ください を。
あかいのを ください。
