questions.explanation: の after the color word stands for the thing: あかいの, "the red one", then を ください. A color word like あかい can't take を by itself, を comes before ください, and は doesn't go with ください.

questions.stem: What does "{白|しろ}い かばん" mean?
questions.explanation: {白|しろ}い is white. Black is くろい, big is {大|おお}きい and red is あかい.

questions.stem: How is 店 read in "あの 店は {大|おお}きいです。"?
questions.explanation: Standing alone, 店 is read with its kun'yomi みせ (shop). テン is its on'yomi, used in longer words such as てんいん; たな is a shelf, いえ a house.

questions.stem: How is 小さい read?
questions.explanation: 小さい is ちいさい (small): the kun'yomi ちい + the okurigana さい. ショウ is the on'yomi, used in compounds; こ and お are short kun'yomi used in some names and words, such as {小川|おがわ}.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to write おおきい (big)?
questions.explanation: 大 carries the meaning and is read おお; the okurigana きい follows: 大きい. 大い leaves out part of the okurigana, 大おきい repeats the お, and 多 (many) is a different kanji.

questions.stem: Which word is "nine (things)"?
questions.explanation: Nine things is ここのつ, four beats. きゅう doesn't combine with つ, くつ means shoes, and ここつ drops a beat.

questions.stem: Type the word for "four (things)" in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: Four things is よっつ, with a small っ: type yottsu. It's the native set ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ, よっつ.

questions.stem: Complete the order: おにぎりを ___ ください。 (Two rice balls, please.)
questions.explanation: Two things is ふたつ, and it goes between を and ください: おにぎりを ふたつ ください.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the customer want?

audio.text: りんごを五つください。

questions.explanation: You heard りんごを いつつ ください: five apples. Four is よっつ, six むっつ, and eggs would be たまご.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the total?

audio.text: ぜんぶで六百八十円です。

questions.explanation: ろっぴゃくはちじゅうえん is 600 + 80 = 680 yen. 860 would start with はっぴゃく, and 6,800 with ろくせん.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: あかいのをください。

choices: あおいのを ください。
あかいのを ください。
あかいのは いくらですか。
くろいのを ください。
questions.explanation: "Akai no o kudasai", the red one, please. あおい (blue) starts with "ao", くろい (black) with "ku", and the third choice is a price question.

questions.stem: Read: "てんいん: いらっしゃいませ。 きゃく: すみません、この パンを {三|みっ}つ ください。それから、ぎゅうにゅうも {一|ひと}つ ください。 てんいん: はい。ぜんぶで 520{円|えん}です。" (きゃく = customer) What did the customer buy?
choices: one bread roll and three milks
three bread rolls and one milk
questions.explanation: The customer asks for パンを みっつ (three bread rolls) and then ぎゅうにゅうも ひとつ: も means "also", so one milk too.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: おちゃ is tea (usually green), ぎゅうにゅう milk, たまご egg, りんご apple and パン bread. A rice ball is おにぎり.

questions.stem: Which word is normally said with the polite お in front?
questions.explanation: Money is almost always お{金|かね}. Loanwords such as ペン and ジュース never take お, and かばん is used without it.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: へやに ねこが ___。 (There's a cat in the room.)
questions.explanation: A cat moves by itself, so it takes います. あります is for things and plants, です links a topic to a description, and ありません is "there isn't".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "There's a book on the desk."?
choices: つくえの {上|うえ}に {本|ほん}が います。
{本|ほん}の {上|うえ}に つくえが あります。
つくえの {上|うえ}で {本|ほん}が あります。
つくえの {上|うえ}に {本|ほん}が あります。
questions.explanation: Place (つくえの {上|うえ}) に, thing ({本|ほん}) が, あります. The second choice puts the desk on the book, で marks where an action happens (not where something is), and a book takes あります, not います.

questions.stem: Choose the particle: へやに だれ ___ いますか。 (Who is in the room?)
questions.explanation: A question word can't be the topic, so it takes が, the subject particle. は after だれ is wrong, を marks an object, and だれも with a positive verb isn't a question.

questions.stem: How do you ask "Where are the keys?"
choices: かぎは どこに いますか。
かぎは どこに ありますか。
どこは かぎに ありますか。
かぎの どこに ありますか。
questions.explanation: The keys are already known, so they're the topic with は; the place is どこに; keys take あります. いますか is for people and animals, どこは puts は on a question word, and の doesn't join かぎ to どこ.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "under the chair"?
questions.explanation: The thing comes first, then の, then the location word: いすの {下|した}, "the chair's underneath". {下|した}の いす means "the chair below", and に or を can't link the two nouns.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "between the window and the door"?
choices: まどの ドアの あいだ
まどや ドアの あいだ
まどと ドアの あいだ
あいだの まどと ドア
questions.explanation: あいだ needs two things joined by と: まどと ドアの あいだ. や suggests "and other things", まどの ドア is "the window's door", and the location word goes last.

questions.stem: On the desk there are a pen, a notebook and other things too. Choose the particle: つくえの {上|うえ}に ペン ___ ノートが あります。
questions.explanation: や lists examples and leaves room for more ("a pen, a notebook and so on"). と would mean exactly a pen and a notebook, の would make it "the pen's notebook", and も means "also".

questions.stem: How is 右 read in "ドアの 右に まどが あります。"?
questions.explanation: 右 is みぎ, right: there's a window to the right of the door. Left is ひだり (左, which looks similar), up is うえ (上), outside そと (外).

questions.stem: How is 外 read in "いぬは 外に います。"?
questions.explanation: Standing alone, 外 is そと (outside): the dog is outside. ガイ is its on'yomi, as in {外国人|がいこくじん}; なか is inside (中) and した below (下).

questions.stem: Which kanji means "left"?
questions.explanation: 左 (ひだり) is left; it has エ under the hand shape. 右 (みぎ, right) has 口 instead. 友 (friend) shares the top, and 大 is big.

questions.stem: What does "{店|みせ}の {前|まえ}に {人|ひと}が います。" mean?
choices: There are people inside the shop.
There are people behind the shop.
The shop is in front of the people.
There are people in front of the shop.
questions.explanation: {店|みせ}の {前|まえ} is "in front of the shop", and {人|ひと}が います "there are people". Behind would be {後|うし}ろ and inside {中|なか}.

questions.stem: What does となり mean in "{大学|だいがく}の となりに {店|みせ}が あります。"?
questions.explanation: となり is "next to, next door": there's a shop next to the university. Behind is {後|うし}ろ, between あいだ, and "far" isn't a location word in this lesson.

questions.stem: Type the word for "inside" (kana or kanji): ___
questions.explanation: Inside is {中|なか}: かばんの {中|なか}に, in the bag. Outside is {外|そと}.

questions.stem: Type あります or います to complete the sentence: {大学|だいがく}に {先生|せんせい}が ___。
questions.explanation: A teacher is a person, so the verb is います: The teacher is at the university / There's a teacher at the university.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the sentence mean?

audio.text: いすの下にねこがいます。

choices: There's a dog under the chair.
There's a cat on the chair.
There's a cat under the chair.
There's a cat under the desk.
questions.explanation: いすの {下|した}に ねこが います: under (した) the chair (いす) there's a cat (ねこ). On would be {上|うえ}, dog いぬ, desk つくえ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: かばんの中にさいふがあります。

choices: かばんの {中|なか}に かぎが あります。
かばんの {外|そと}に さいふが あります。
さいふの {中|なか}に かばんが あります。
かばんの {中|なか}に さいふが あります。
questions.explanation: "There's a wallet in the bag." You heard なか (inside), not そと, the bag came first, and the thing was さいふ (wallet), not かぎ (key).

questions.stem: Listen. What is the question?

audio.text: へやにだれがいますか。

questions.explanation: だれが いますか asks "who is there?". "What" would be {何|なに}が ありますか, "where" どこ, and "whose" だれの.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしの へやに つくえと ベッドが あります。つくえの {上|うえ}に パソコンが あります。ベッドの {下|した}に ねこが います。" Where is the cat?
questions.explanation: ベッドの {下|した}に ねこが います: the cat is under the bed. The computer (パソコン) is on the desk.

questions.stem: You're telling a friend something new: "There's a dog in the park." Which is the natural sentence?
choices: こうえんに いぬが います。
こうえんに いぬは います。
こうえんに いぬが あります。
こうえんで いぬが います。
questions.explanation: New information takes が, a dog takes います, and existence takes に: こうえんに いぬが います. は would treat the dog as already known, あります is for things, and で marks where an action happens.

questions.stem: Match each location word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: {上|うえ} on, {下|した} under, {前|まえ} in front, {後|うし}ろ behind, となり next to. Between is あいだ and outside {外|そと}.

questions.stem: In the name {山本|やまもと} ゆき, which part is the family name?
choices: Neither: it's a given name and a title
questions.explanation: Japanese names put the family name (みょうじ) first: {山本|やまもと} is the family name and ゆき the given name.

questions.stem: Which suffix would a shop or bank use to address a customer very politely?
questions.explanation: さま is more respectful than さん and is used for customers, in formal letters and when calling names in waiting rooms. くん and ちゃん are for juniors and children, and no suffix is only for close friends and family.

questions.stem: What's wrong with calling a teacher "{山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}さん"?
choices: {先生|せんせい} is only for doctors
さん must come before {先生|せんせい}
{先生|せんせい} already replaces さん, so the title is doubled
questions.explanation: {先生|せんせい} works as the title by itself: {山本|やまもと}{先生|せんせい}. Adding さん doubles it. {先生|せんせい} is used for teachers, doctors and some other experts.

questions.stem: A teacher calls a young boy in her class by his given name. Which is most likely?
questions.explanation: くん is used for boys and juniors. さま is far too formal, and {先生|せんせい} and {社長|しゃちょう} are titles for teachers and company presidents. (Many schools now use さん for all pupils, which would also be fine.)

questions.stem: Why do Japanese speakers usually avoid あなた with someone whose name they know?
choices: It is a rude word in all situations
It sounds distant or too direct; the name is used instead
It can only be used to children
questions.explanation: あなた isn't rude in itself (you'll see it on forms and in songs), but said to someone you know it sounds distant or confrontational. The name, a title or a role is used instead.

questions.stem: What is みょうじ?
questions.explanation: みょうじ is the family name, which comes first. A seal is はんこ and a business card めいし.

questions.stem: A delivery driver says: "ここに はんこか サインを おねがいします。" What does the driver want?
questions.explanation: はんこ is a personal seal, サイン a signature, and か between two nouns means "or": stamp or sign here, please.

questions.stem: Which kind of seal is registered at the city office and used for the most important contracts?
questions.explanation: じついん is the registered seal for big contracts such as buying a house or a car. みとめいん is for everyday use, ぎんこういん is registered with a bank, and めいし is a business card.

questions.stem: Since 2020, how do Japanese government documents in English write Japanese names?
choices: Family name first, often in capitals: YAMAMOTO Yuki
questions.explanation: The government decided in 2019 to keep the Japanese order in its English documents from 2020, family name first, often capitalized to make it clear. Many others still write given name first, so both orders are common.

questions.stem: Which suffix can you put after your own name?
questions.explanation: Name suffixes show respect or closeness towards someone else, so none goes with your own name: わたしは エマです.

questions.stem: Listen. Who is most likely speaking?

audio.text: 山本さま、どうぞ。

choices: a receptionist calling Ms Yamamoto in a waiting room
a teacher calling a boy in class
questions.explanation: {山本|やまもと}さま、どうぞ is "Ms Yamamoto, please (come in)". さま is used by staff for customers and patients; nobody uses it about themselves, and it's far too formal for friends or pupils.

questions.stem: In a school or university club, what does a junior member call a senior member?
questions.explanation: Juniors call seniors せんぱい, alone or after the family name. ちゃん and くん are for younger people or close friends, and あなた is avoided.

questions.stem: Why do many people avoid reading 4 as し?
choices: し sounds like the word for "death"
し is only used in writing
questions.explanation: し (4) sounds the same as the word for death, and く (9) like the word for suffering, so よん and きゅう are preferred, especially where luck matters.

questions.stem: What is the police emergency number in Japan, and how is it said?
choices: 119, ひゃくじゅうきゅうばん
questions.explanation: The police number is 110, said ひゃくとおばん with the native とお for ten. 119 is fire and ambulance, and 911 is the number in North America, not Japan.

questions.stem: A price tag says "ぜいこみ 1,100{円|えん}（ぜいぬき 1,000{円|えん}）". How much do you pay?
questions.explanation: ぜいこみ means tax included: that's what you pay. ぜいぬき, 1,000 yen, is the price before the 10% tax.

questions.stem: How is 3かい (third floor) most commonly read?
questions.explanation: After さん, かい usually voices to がい: さんがい (さんかい is also heard). み is a native reading of three used with the つ counter, not with かい.

questions.stem: In a Japanese building, which floor is at street level?
questions.explanation: The ground floor is 1かい, as in American English. ちか1かい is the first basement floor, and there's no floor 0.

questions.stem: How do you say 1,000,000 in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Japanese counts in ten-thousands: 1,000,000 is 100 × 10,000, ひゃくまん. じゅうまん is 100,000.

questions.stem: Which number can be read as よろしく in a number pun (ごろあわせ)?
questions.explanation: 4649 is よ (4), ろ (6), し (4), く (9): よろしく. 1122 is いい ふうふ, the "good married couple" date.

questions.stem: On a tally board, what does one complete {正|せい} stand for?
questions.explanation: {正|せい} has five strokes, drawn one at a time as you count, so a finished one means 5.

questions.stem: Which number is thought lucky partly because its kanji widens towards the bottom?
questions.explanation: {八|はち} (8) opens out at the bottom like a road to a prosperous future. 4 and 9 are the unlucky ones.

questions.stem: What is the consumption tax on food bought to take away?
questions.explanation: Food and drink to take away (except alcohol) has the reduced rate of 8%. Most other things, including eating in at a restaurant, are taxed at 10%.

questions.stem: Listen. Which service is this number for?

audio.text: ひゃくじゅうきゅうばん

questions.explanation:
ひゃくじゅうきゅうばん is 119, the number for fire and ambulance. The police is ひゃくとおばん,
110.

questions.stem: When Japanese people count on their fingers, how do they usually start?
choices: From an open hand, folding the thumb in for 1
From a fist, raising the index finger for 1
From a fist, raising the thumb for 1
By touching each finger with the other hand
questions.explanation: The usual way starts with an open palm and folds the thumb in for 1, then the index finger and so on to a fist at 5. When showing a number to someone else, people raise fingers instead.

questions.stem: How is 4時 (four o'clock) read?
questions.explanation: Four o'clock is よじ, one of the three irregular hours. よん is the usual "four", but with 時 it shortens to よ; しじ is avoided, and there is no small っ.

questions.stem: How is 9時 (nine o'clock) read?
questions.explanation: Nine o'clock is くじ, with two short beats. きゅう is the usual "nine", but not with 時; くうじ stretches the vowel, and きゅじ isn't a word.

questions.stem: How is 6分 (six minutes) read?
questions.explanation: After 6 the counter becomes ぷん and ろく shrinks to ろっ: ろっぷん, four beats. ろくふん is the most common mistake; ろくぷん and ろっふん change only one of the two parts.

questions.stem: Type the reading of 10分 (ten minutes) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: 10分 is じゅっぷん (also heard as じっぷん): じゅう shrinks to じゅっ and ふん becomes ぷん. Type it as juppun.

questions.stem: Which means "half past three"?
questions.explanation: {半|はん} follows the hour: {3時半|さんじはん}. はんさんじ puts it in front, さんじさんぷん is 3:03, and さんぷんはん would be "three and a half minutes".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "It's 2 p.m."?
questions.explanation: {午後|ごご} (p.m.) comes before the time: {午後|ごご} {2時|にじ}. Putting it after is English order; {午前|ごぜん} is a.m., and {2分|にふん} is two minutes, not two o'clock.

questions.stem: "{9時|くじ} {5分前|ごふんまえ}です。" What time is it?
questions.explanation: 〜{前|まえ} after a time means "before": five minutes before nine, 8:55. 9:05 would be {9時5分|くじごふん}, or {9時5分|くじごふん}すぎ.

questions.stem: What does ごろ add in "{3時|さんじ}ごろです。"?
questions.explanation: ごろ after a time is "about": It's about three. Exactly would be ちょうど (before the time), until is まで, and just after is すぎ.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{店|みせ}は {10時|じゅうじ} ___ {9時|くじ}までです。" (The shop is open from ten to nine.)
questions.explanation: から is "from" and まで "until": {10時|じゅうじ}から {9時|くじ}まで. まで is already used for the closing time, に marks the time of an action, and ごろ means "about".

questions.stem: Read the sign: "さくらカフェ　{午前|ごぜん} {7時|しちじ}から {午後|ごご} {6時|ろくじ}まで　ランチ：{11時|じゅういちじ}から {2時|にじ}まで". Can you have lunch there at 3 p.m.?
choices: Yes, the café is open until 6
questions.explanation: Lunch (ランチ) runs from {11時|じゅういちじ}から {2時|にじ}まで, 11 to 2. The café itself is open until 6 p.m., so it's open at 3, but lunch is over.

questions.stem: Listen. What time is it?

audio.text: 7時半です。

questions.explanation: You heard しちじはん: 7 o'clock and a half. いちじ (1 o'clock) sounds similar, which is why some people say ななじ; よじ is 4 o'clock.

questions.stem: Listen. What time is it?

audio.text: 4時10分です。

questions.explanation: よじ じゅっぷん: four o'clock and ten minutes. The hour always comes first, so 10:04 would be じゅうじ よんぷん; くじ would be nine.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: ろっぷん

questions.explanation: ろっぷん, six minutes: type roppun. The small っ is the short pause before ぷ.

questions.stem: Match each reading to its time.
questions.explanation: よじ is 4, くじ is 9 and しちじ is 7, the three irregular hours; いちじ is 1. 8:00 would be はちじ and 6:00 ろくじ.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "half"?
questions.explanation: 半 (はん) is half, the one with a line straight through the middle. 分 is minute, 午 is noon (as in 午前, 午後) and 今 is now.

questions.stem: How is 今 read in "今 {何時|なんじ}ですか。"?
questions.explanation: On its own, 今 is いま, "now". こん is its reading in words like 今週 (こんしゅう), きょう is the special reading of 今日 (two kanji), and まえ is 前.

questions.stem: How is 午後 read?
questions.explanation: 午後 is ごご, p.m. ごぜん is 午前 (a.m.). Both kanji here are short ゴ, so no long vowel, and あと is the reading of 後 on its own, not in this word.

questions.stem: A stranger asks: "すみません、{今|いま} {何時|なんじ}ですか。" What is the best answer?
choices: いいえ、{今|いま}じゃありません。
{5時|ごじ}{20分|にじゅっぷん}です。
questions.explanation: The question asks the time, so answer with the time + です: 5:20. はい/いいえ answer yes-or-no questions; {5時|ごじ}からです says "from five", which answers "from what time?".

questions.stem: Which sentence says "It's about 8 a.m."?
choices: ごろ {午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}です。
{午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}ごろです。
{午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}までです。
{8時|はちじ} {午前|ごぜん}ごろです。
questions.explanation: {午前|ごぜん} goes before the time and ごろ after it: {午前|ごぜん} {8時|はちじ}ごろ. ごろ can't go first, まで means "until", and {午前|ごぜん} can't follow the hour.

questions.stem: Write "It's 9:20." in hiragana (nine o'clock, twenty minutes, です): ___
accept: くじにじゅっぷんです
questions.explanation: くじ にじゅっぷんです: くじ for nine (not きゅうじ) and にじゅっぷん for twenty minutes, with the small っ and ぷん. にじっぷん is also accepted.

questions.stem: What is the ます form of {飲|の}む (to drink)?
questions.explanation: {飲|の}む is a group 1 verb: the last kana む moves to the い row, み, then ます: {飲|の}みます. Adding ます to the dictionary form ({飲|の}むます) is the classic beginner mistake; め is the え row, and り belongs to verbs ending in る.

questions.stem: What is the ます form of おきる (to get up)?
questions.explanation: おきる is a group 2 verb (い-row sound + る): drop る and add ます, おきます. おきります treats it like group 1; the other two change the stem.

questions.stem: What is the ます form of かえる (to go home)?
questions.explanation: かえる looks like a group 2 verb, but it's group 1: る becomes り, かえります. かえます is the trap; かいます is the ます form of a different verb (かう, buy).

questions.stem: Which form means "I didn't eat"?
questions.explanation: 〜ませんでした is the past negative: {食|た}べませんでした. With か it becomes a question ("didn't you eat?"), {食|た}べました is "I ate", and {食|た}べません is "I don't eat / won't eat".

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "うち ___ ばんごはんを {食|た}べます。" (I eat dinner at home.)
questions.explanation: The place where an action happens takes で. に marks where something is (うちに います), を is already on the object ばんごはん, and へ is for a destination.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{7時|しちじ} ___ おきます。" (I get up at seven.)
questions.explanation: A clock time takes に: {7時|しちじ}に. で marks a place or means, を an object (おきる has none), and と is "with".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: きのうに テレビを {見|み}ました。
きのう テレビで {見|み}ました。
きのう テレビを {見|み}ました。
きのう テレビを {見|み}ます。
questions.explanation: きのう is relative to today, so it takes no に. The thing watched takes を, not で, and "yesterday" needs the past form ました, not ます.

questions.stem: Complete: "けさ {何|なに}も ___。" (I didn't eat anything this morning.)
questions.explanation: {何|なに}も ("nothing") always goes with a negative verb, here the past negative because of けさ (this morning). The other three are positive, so they don't fit with {何|なに}も.

questions.stem: What does "{時々|ときどき} {新聞|しんぶん}を {読|よ}みます。" mean?
choices: I read the newspaper at the time.
questions.explanation: {時々|ときどき} is "sometimes" and {新聞|しんぶん} is newspaper. Always would be いつも; the verb is positive, so "don't" is wrong.

questions.stem: How is 見 read in "テレビを 見ます。"?
questions.explanation: 見ます is みます, from 見る (みる). けん is the on'yomi, used in compound words; め is the reading of 目 (eye), and き is 来 in 来ます.

questions.stem: Which kanji goes in "コーヒーを □みます。" (I drink coffee.)?
questions.explanation: 飲 is drink: 飲みます (のみます). 食 is eat (食べます), 見 is see (見ます) and 行 is go (行きます).

questions.stem: Which of these is a group 2 (る) verb?
questions.explanation: ねる drops る: ねます. のむ and はたらく end in other kana, so they're group 1. かえる ends in える but is one of the group 1 exceptions (かえります).

questions.stem: Type the ます form of する (to do): ___
questions.explanation: する is irregular (group 3): します. Every する verb follows it, so べんきょうする becomes べんきょうします.

questions.stem: Write "I didn't do anything." in Japanese (polite): ___
accept: なにもしませんでした
questions.explanation: {何|なに}も しませんでした: {何|なに}も (nothing) with the past negative of する. {何|なに}も replaces を, so there's no を after it.

questions.stem: Listen. What did the speaker do?

audio.text: きのう えいがを 見ました。

questions.explanation: きのう (yesterday) + {見|み}ました (watched): "I watched a movie yesterday." The negative would be {見|み}ませんでした, and the future would use あした with {見|み}ます.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: 毎日 6時に おきます。

choices: I get up at six every day.
I go to bed at six every day.
I got up at six today.
I get up at seven every day.
questions.explanation: まいにち ろくじに おきます: every day, at six, get up. Going to bed would be ねます, the past would be おきました, and seven is しちじ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: コーヒーを 飲みませんでした。

choices: コーヒーを {飲|の}みました。
コーヒーを {飲|の}みません。
コーヒーを {飲|の}みませんか。
コーヒーを {飲|の}みませんでした。
questions.explanation: You heard the whole ending ませんでした: "I didn't drink coffee." ました is the positive past, ません the non-past negative, and ませんか an invitation.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしは {毎日|まいにち} {6時半|ろくじはん}に おきます。あさごはんは {食|た}べません。コーヒーを {飲|の}みます。それから、{会社|かいしゃ}で はたらきます。" What does the writer do in the morning?
choices: drinks coffee but has no breakfast
gets up at 6 and goes back to bed
questions.explanation: あさごはんは {食|た}べません says no breakfast, and コーヒーを {飲|の}みます says coffee. Then (それから) the writer works at the company. Nothing says they go back to bed.

questions.stem: Match each dictionary form to its ます form.
questions.explanation: たべる (group 2) drops る; のむ (group 1) changes む to み; する and くる are irregular: します, きます. かえる is group 1, so かえります. くります and かえます are the wrong guesses.

questions.stem: "コーヒーを {飲|の}みますか。" — "いいえ、___" (No, I don't.)
questions.explanation: Japanese answers by repeating the verb: いいえ、{飲|の}みません。 English uses "do", but しません would mean "I don't do (it)". ちがいます means "that's wrong", and {飲|の}みました is "I drank".

questions.stem: How is 来 read in "{友|とも}だちが 来ます。"?
questions.explanation: In the ます form, 来る is read き: 来ます (きます). く is its reading in the dictionary form 来る, and らい is the on'yomi in words like 来週. こ belongs to forms you'll learn later.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{電車|でんしゃ} ___ {行|い}きます。" (I'll go by train.)
questions.explanation: The means of transport takes で: {電車|でんしゃ}で. に and へ would make the train the destination ("go to the train"), and を marks an object.

questions.stem: Which sentence says "I walk to the station."?
choices: {駅|えき}まで あるいて {行|い}きます。
{駅|えき}まで あるいてで {行|い}きます。
{駅|えき}を あるいて {行|い}きます。
あるいて {駅|えき}で {行|い}きます。
questions.explanation: あるいて already means "on foot", so it takes no で. まで (as far as) or へ marks the station as the goal; を would mean walking along it, and で would make the station the place of the action.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{友|とも}だち ___ {行|い}きます。" (I'm going with a friend.)
questions.explanation: と after a person means "with". で marks means or place, を an object, and も would make it "my friend is going too".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: いつに {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きますか。
いつ {日本|にほん}で {行|い}きますか。
いつ {日本|にほん}を {行|い}きますか。
いつ {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きますか。
questions.explanation: いつ (when) takes no に, and the destination takes へ (or に). で would make Japan the place of the action, and を would make it the object.

questions.stem: You're at home, talking on the phone to a friend who is having a party at her place tomorrow. How do you say "I'll come to the party"?
choices: あした パーティーに {来|き}ます。
あした パーティーに {行|い}きます。
あした パーティーに かえります。
あした パーティーで {来|き}ます。
questions.explanation: Japanese chooses the verb from where you are now: you'll move away from your place, so it's {行|い}きます, even though English says "come". かえります is for going back home, and で doesn't mark a destination.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "バス ___ のります。" (I get on the bus.)
questions.explanation: The vehicle you get on takes に: バスに のります. を goes with おりる (get off), で would mean "by bus" with a verb of movement, and と is "with".

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "つぎの {駅|えき}で {電車|でんしゃ} ___ おります。" (I get off the train at the next station.)
questions.explanation: The vehicle you leave takes を with おりる. に goes with のる (get on), and で is already on the station where it happens.

questions.stem: How is 駅 read?
questions.explanation: 駅 is えき, station. みち is 道 (road), くるま is 車 (car), and でん is the reading of 電 in 電車.

questions.stem: How is 車 read in "車で {来|き}ました。"?
questions.explanation: On its own, 車 is くるま, car: "I came by car". しゃ is its reading inside compounds like 電車 (でんしゃ, train), and みち is 道.

questions.stem: What is a {電車|でんしゃ}?
questions.explanation: {電車|でんしゃ} is "electric car", the everyday word for a train. A car is {車|くるま}, a telephone is {電話|でんわ}, and a station is {駅|えき}.

questions.stem: Type the Japanese for "alone, by myself": ___
questions.explanation: ひとりで ({一人|ひとり}で), "as one person". Type hitoride. It answers だれと {行|い}きますか (who are you going with?) when you're going alone.

questions.stem: Write the past of {来|く}る in the polite form ("came"): ___
questions.explanation: {来|く}る is irregular: {来|き}ます, {来|き}ました, with the kanji read き. くりました and くました don't exist.

questions.stem: Listen. How did the speaker come?

audio.text: バスで 来ました。

questions.explanation: バスで {来|き}ました: "I came by bus". Taxi would be タクシー, on foot あるいて, and train {電車|でんしゃ}.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: あした 友だちと 行きます。

choices: I went with a friend yesterday.
I'm going with a friend tomorrow.
questions.explanation: あした (tomorrow) + {友|とも}だちと (with a friend) + {行|い}きます (go). Alone would be {一人|ひとり}で, yesterday きのう with {行|い}きました, and "is coming" would use {来|き}ます.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: としょかん

questions.explanation: としょかん, library: to-sho-ka-n. しょ is one beat (し + small ょ), typed sho, and the final ん is nn or n.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしは {毎日|まいにち} じてんしゃで {駅|えき}へ {行|い}きます。{駅|えき}から {会社|かいしゃ}まで ちかてつで {行|い}きます。{金曜日|きんようび}は {会社|かいしゃ}の {友|とも}だちと タクシーで かえります。" How does the writer get from the station to work?
questions.explanation: {駅|えき}から {会社|かいしゃ}まで ちかてつで: from the station to the office by subway. The bicycle is for getting to the station, and the taxi is only for going home on Fridays.

questions.stem: Match each place to its meaning.
questions.explanation: ぎんこう bank, ゆうびんきょく post office, としょかん library, くうこう airport, こうえん park. A station is {駅|えき} and a cinema えいがかん.

questions.stem: "どうやって {来|き}ましたか。" — What is a good answer?
choices: ちかてつで {来|き}ました。
questions.explanation: どうやって asks "how, by what means", so the answer gives the means with で. {9時|くじ}に answers いつ, {友|とも}だちと answers だれと, and はい answers a yes-or-no question.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses かえる naturally?
choices: あした デパートに かえります。
{9時|くじ}に うちに かえります。
あした えいがかんに かえります。
{友|とも}だちの うちに かえります。
questions.explanation: かえる means going back to where you belong: home, your own country or office. You don't "return" to a department store, a cinema or a friend's house; use {行|い}きます there.

questions.stem: How is 1日 read when it means "the 1st" of a month?
questions.explanation: The 1st is ついたち, a word of its own. いちにち is "one day" as a length of time, and the other two aren't used.

questions.stem: How is 20日 (the 20th) read?
questions.explanation: The 20th is irregular: はつか, three short beats. にじゅうにち follows the regular pattern, but it isn't used for the 20th.

questions.stem: How is 4月 (April) read?
questions.explanation: April is しがつ. With hours 4 is よ (よじ), but with months it's し; よんがつ and よがつ are common mistakes.

questions.stem: Which reading means "the 8th" (of a month)?
questions.explanation: The 8th is ようか, with a long よう. よっか, with a small っ, is the 4th; はちにち isn't used, and やっか isn't a date.

questions.stem: Which day is 火曜日?
questions.explanation: 火 (fire) is Tuesday, かようび. Wednesday is 水 (water), Thursday 木 (wood) and Friday 金 (gold, metal).

questions.stem: How is 土曜日 (Saturday) read?
questions.explanation: 土曜日 is どようび, with a short ど. どうようび adds a long vowel, つち is the kun'yomi of 土 on its own (earth), and とようび isn't voiced.

questions.stem: How is 今年 (this year) read?
questions.explanation: 今年 has a special reading, ことし, learned as a whole like 今日 (きょう). The other three put together the kanji's separate readings, which doesn't work for this word.

questions.stem: How is "Tuesday, 3 November 2026" written in Japanese?
choices: {2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}{11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}（{火|か}）
{3日|みっか}{11月|じゅういちがつ}{2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}（{火|か}）
（{火|か}）{11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}{2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}
{11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}{2026年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}（{火|か}）
questions.explanation: Japanese dates go from the biggest unit to the smallest: year, month, day, then the day of the week in brackets. The others follow English or American order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: {来週|らいしゅう} {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きます。
{来週|らいしゅう}に {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きます。
{来週|らいしゅう}で {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きます。
{来週|らいしゅう}を {日本|にほん}へ {行|い}きます。
questions.explanation: {来週|らいしゅう} (next week) is relative to now, so it takes no particle. に is for clock times, days of the week and dates; で and を don't mark time at all.

questions.stem: How is 毎月 (every month) usually read?
questions.explanation: 毎月 is usually まいつき, with the native reading つき. まいげつ exists but is rare and formal; まいがつ isn't a word, and まいにち is 毎日 (every day).

questions.stem: Type the reading of 10日 (the 10th) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: とおか, spelled with お (type tooka). とうか is a misspelling, and じゅうにち isn't used for the 10th.

questions.stem: Type the reading of 9月 (September) in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: September is くがつ, with く as in くじ (9 o'clock). きゅうがつ is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Listen. Which date did you hear?

audio.text: 7月8日です。

questions.explanation: しちがつ ようか: July (7) the 8th. よっか would be the 4th, しがつ is April, and Japanese puts the month first, so it isn't August 7.

questions.stem: Listen. Which day did you hear?

audio.text: 水曜日

questions.explanation: すいようび is Wednesday ({水|すい}, water). Thursday is もくようび, Tuesday かようび and Sunday にちようび.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: むいか

questions.explanation: むいか, the 6th (type muika). It's one of the old native date words, not ろくにち.

questions.stem: Match each day to its meaning.
questions.explanation: 月 (moon) Monday, 水 (water) Wednesday, 木 (wood) Thursday, 金 (gold) Friday, 日 (sun) Sunday. Tuesday is 火曜日 and Saturday 土曜日.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしの たんじょうびは {5月|ごがつ}{24日|にじゅうよっか}です。{今年|ことし}は {日曜日|にちようび}です。{友|とも}だちと カラオケに {行|い}きます。{来年|らいねん}は {日本|にほん}で パーティーを します。" Which is true?
choices: Next year the party is at karaoke.
This year the birthday falls on a Sunday.
Last year the writer was in Japan.
questions.explanation: {今年|ことし}は {日曜日|にちようび}です: this year it's a Sunday. にじゅうよっか is the 24th, not the 4th; next year there will be a party in Japan (not karaoke), and the text says nothing about last year.

questions.stem: "たんじょうびは いつですか。" — What is a good answer?
choices: {5時|ごじ}{20分|にじゅっぷん}です。
はい、たんじょうびです。
questions.explanation: いつ asks "when"; a birthday is a date: {5月|ごがつ}{20日|はつか}です (May 20th). 5:20 is a time of day, {5日|いつか}ぐらい is "about five days", a length of time, and はい answers a yes-or-no question.

questions.stem: What does {来月|らいげつ} mean?
questions.explanation: {来|らい} is "next": {来月|らいげつ}. Last month is {先月|せんげつ}, this month {今月|こんげつ}, and every month {毎月|まいつき}.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "week"?
questions.explanation: 週 (シュウ) is week, as in 今週, 来週. 曜 is in 曜日 (day of the week), 毎 is every, and 道 (road) shares the moving-along part with 週 but means road.

questions.stem: How do you politely invite someone: "Would you like to see a movie with me?"
choices: いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ます。
いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ませんか。
いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ませんでした。
いっしょに えいがを {見|み}ましたか。
questions.explanation: 〜ませんか ("won't you…?") is the polite invitation. {見|み}ます just states a plan, and the last two are about the past.

questions.stem: "{土曜日|どようび}に テニスを しませんか。" — "いいですね。___" (Sounds good. Let's play.)
questions.explanation: 〜ましょう (let's) accepts the invitation. しません refuses it rather bluntly, しましょうか asks "shall we?" back, and しませんか repeats the invitation.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{何時|なんじ}に {会|あ}い ___。" (What time shall we meet?)
questions.explanation: With a question word, 〜ましょうか asks the other person to help decide: "What time shall we meet?" ましょう has no question, ませんか with {何時|なんじ} doesn't make sense, and ました is the past.

questions.stem: A colleague invites you to dinner on Saturday, but you can't go. What is the most natural polite answer?
choices: いいえ、{土曜日|どようび}です。
すみません、{土曜日|どようび}は ちょっと…。
はい、{行|い}きませんでした。
questions.explanation: A trailing ちょっと… with an apology is the usual polite refusal. A flat いいえ、{行|い}きません sounds cold; the other two don't make sense as answers.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{土曜日|どようび}は ひまです ___、{日曜日|にちようび}は いそがしいです。"
questions.explanation: が after です joins two clauses: "I'm free on Saturday, but busy on Sunday." でも starts a new sentence instead; を and と don't join clauses.

questions.stem: Which uses でも correctly?
choices: テニスは しませんでも、サッカーは します。
テニスは しません。でも、サッカーは します。
でも テニスは しません サッカーは します。
テニスは でも しません。
questions.explanation: でも ("but") starts a new sentence, after the 。 of the first one. Inside one sentence use が: テニスは しませんが、サッカーは します。

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: "{駅|えき}で {友|とも}だち ___ {会|あ}います。" (I'm meeting a friend at the station.)
questions.explanation: {会|あ}う takes に (or と) for the person you meet, not を as in English "meet someone". で is already on the station, and へ marks a destination.

questions.stem: How is 休み read in "{今日|きょう}は 休みです。"?
questions.explanation: 休み is やすみ, a day off: "I'm off today." キュウ is the on'yomi, used in compounds; やすむ is the verb (to rest), not the noun.

questions.stem: How is 会社 (company) read?
questions.explanation: 会社 is かいしゃ, with the on'yomi of both kanji. あ is the reading of 会 in the verb 会う, not in this word.

questions.stem: What does "ざんねんですが、あしたは アルバイトが あります。" mean?
choices: Great, I have a day off tomorrow.
I'm sorry, I had work yesterday.
Unfortunately, I have my part-time job tomorrow.
questions.explanation: ざんねんですが is "it's a pity, but": a polite way to turn something down, followed by the reason. アルバイトが あります is "I have my part-time job"; あした is tomorrow, not yesterday.

questions.stem: Make an invitation from する: "Won't you (do it with me)?" ___
questions.explanation: Replace ます with ませんか: します → しませんか. A plain しません is "I don't"; the か turns it into a gentle invitation.

questions.stem: Write "Let's meet." in Japanese (use {会|あ}う): ___
questions.explanation: {会|あ}う is group 1: {会|あ}います → {会|あ}いましょう. Type aimashou.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker doing?

audio.text: いっしょに テニスを しませんか。

questions.explanation: いっしょに (together) + しませんか is an invitation: "Would you like to play tennis with me?" Without いっしょに and in another context, しませんか could be a negative question, but here it invites.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker mean?

audio.text: すみません、日曜日は ちょっと…。

choices: They want to meet for a short time on Sunday.
questions.explanation: "Sorry, Sunday is a bit…" trailing off after ちょっと is a polite no. ちょっと literally means "a little", but here it isn't about time or amount.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: 駅で 会いましょう。

choices: {駅|えき}で {会|あ}いましょうか。
questions.explanation: You heard 〜ましょう with no か at the end: "Let's meet at the station." ましょうか would end in "ka", ませんか has "sen", and ました is the past.

questions.stem: Read the message: "けんさんへ　{日曜日|にちようび}に こうえんで しゃしんを とりませんか。{10時|じゅうじ}に {駅|えき}の {北口|きたぐち}で {会|あ}いましょう。ひるごはんは わたしが つくります。まりより" What is Mari suggesting?
choices: taking photos in the park on Sunday
having lunch at the station on Sunday
meeting at the park at 10 on Saturday
cooking dinner together at Ken's house
questions.explanation: しゃしんを とりませんか is an invitation to take photos, at the park, on Sunday. They meet at the station's north exit at 10, and Mari will make lunch herself.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to what it does.
questions.explanation: 〜ませんか invites, 〜ましょう suggests or accepts ("let's"), 〜ましょうか asks the other person to decide or offers help, and a trailing ちょっと… turns something down. "I did" would be 〜ました, "I didn't" 〜ませんでした.

questions.stem: What does しゅうまつ mean?
questions.explanation: しゅうまつ is the weekend: "end of the week". Every week is {毎週|まいしゅう}, and last week {先週|せんしゅう}.

questions.stem: Your friends are trying to fit everyone in a photo. How do you offer, "Shall I take a photo?"
choices: しゃしんを とりませんか。
しゃしんを とりましょうか。
しゃしんを とりました。
しゃしんを とりません。
questions.explanation: 〜ましょうか without a question word offers to do something: "Shall I take a photo?" とりませんか would invite them to take photos with you; the other two are statements.

questions.stem: What is the ましょう form of あそぶ (to hang out)?
questions.explanation: あそぶ is group 1: ぶ moves to the い row, び, then ましょう: あそびましょう. The ます stem is the same for all the endings: あそびます, あそびませんか.

questions.stem: How do you use an IC card such as Suica at the ticket gates?
choices: Touch it only when you go in.
Touch it on the reader when you go in and again when you go out.
Touch it only when you go out.
Show it to the staff at the window.
questions.explanation: The fare is worked out from where you entered and where you leave, so you touch in and touch out. If the balance is too low, the exit gate closes and you use the fare adjustment machine.

questions.stem: A screen says "とうきょう行き". How is 行き read here, and what does it mean?
choices: いく, going to go (to Tokyo)
questions.explanation: In railway use 行き is read ゆき (also いき) and means "bound for". The snow word ゆき sounds the same but is a different word with a different kanji.

questions.stem: You want to get off at a small station. Which train should you take to be sure it stops there?
questions.explanation: かくえきていしゃ (also ふつう) stops at every station. かいそく (rapid), きゅうこう (express) and とっきゅう (limited express) skip stations, so check the stop list first.

questions.stem: Fill in the blanks: "しぶや ___ ちかてつ ___ のりかえます。" (At Shibuya I change to the subway.)
questions.explanation: The station where the change happens takes で (place of an action) and the train you change to takes に, as with のる.

questions.stem: You want to leave the station. Which sign do you follow?
questions.explanation: 出口 (でぐち) is "exit". 入口 (いりぐち) is the entrance; 東口 and 北口 are the east and north exits, useful only if you know which side you need.

questions.stem: Your friend says to meet at the 西口. Which exit is that?
questions.explanation: 西 (にし) is west, so 西口 (にしぐち) is the west exit. East is 東, south 南, north 北.

questions.stem: What does "3ばんせん" on a sign tell you?
questions.explanation: 〜ばんせん numbers the tracks at a station, so 3ばんせん is platform 3. Lines are named with 〜せん, and exits with 〜ぐち.

questions.stem: A timetable shows: 8 | 04 12 20 28 36 44 52. It's {8時|はちじ}{30分|さんじゅっぷん}. When is the next train?
questions.explanation: The row for hour 8 lists the minutes of each departure. After 8:30 the next one is 36: 8:36. 8:28 has already left.

questions.stem: Which is good manners on a crowded commuter train in Japan?
choices: setting your phone to silent and not making calls
eating a full meal at your seat
keeping a large backpack on your back
getting on before other passengers get off
questions.explanation: Phones go on マナーモード and calls wait until you're off the train. Meals are for long- distance trains, backpacks come off and go in front or on the rack, and people get off first.

questions.stem: What is しゅうでん?
choices: the first train of the day
a train that stops at every station
the last train of the day
questions.explanation: しゅうでん is the last train, around midnight in big cities. The first train is しはつ, a local is かくえきていしゃ, and a change of trains is のりかえ.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker doing?

audio.text: しんじゅくで のりかえます。

questions.explanation: のりかえます is "change trains", and しんじゅくで gives the station. Getting off would be おります, and meeting {会|あ}います.

questions.stem: You're on a platform and want to check the train. How do you ask "Does this train stop at Ueno?"
choices: この {電車|でんしゃ}は うえので とまりますか。
この {電車|でんしゃ}を うえのに とまりますか。
この {電車|でんしゃ}は うえのへ のりますか。
この {電車|でんしゃ}は うえのに とまりますか。
questions.explanation: とまる (stop) takes に for the place where the train stops. で would mark a place of action, the train is the topic (は), not an object (を), and のります is "get on".

questions.stem: Reiwa began in 2019. Which Reiwa year is 2026?
choices: れいわ {26年|にじゅうろくねん}
questions.explanation: 2019 was Reiwa 1 (がんねん), so subtract 2018: 2026 − 2018 = 8. Subtracting 2019 gives 7, the usual off-by-one mistake.

questions.stem: How is 元年 read, and what does it mean?
choices: もとねん, the original year
がんねん, New Year's Day
がんねん, the first year of an era
questions.explanation: 元年 is がんねん, the first year of an era, used instead of "year 1". 元 is read げん in 元気, but がん here. New Year's Day is 元日 (がんじつ).

questions.stem: Heisei began in 1989 (Heisei 1). Which Western year was へいせい {12年|じゅうにねん}?
questions.explanation: For Heisei, add 1988: 1988 + 12 = 2000. Adding 1989 gives 2001, again off by one.

questions.stem: A Japanese form says 3/11. What date is that?
questions.explanation: Japanese dates always go month before day (after the year), so 3/11 is the 11th of March. There's no day-first order as in British English.

questions.stem: When is Golden Week?
questions.explanation: Golden Week is the cluster of holidays from {4月|しがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち} to {5月|ごがつ}{5日|いつか}. Mid-August is おぼん, and late December to early January is the New Year break.

questions.stem: When do people start saying "あけまして おめでとう ございます"?
questions.explanation: It means "Happy New Year" (literally, congratulations on the year opening), so it's said only once the New Year has begun. Before that, people say よい おとしを.

questions.stem: What is a しゅくじつ?
questions.explanation: しゅくじつ is a national holiday; Japan has sixteen. A weekday is へいじつ, a birthday たんじょうび, and the summer vacation なつやすみ.

questions.stem: On which date is {子|こ}どもの{日|ひ} (Children's Day)?
choices: {11月|じゅういちがつ}{3日|みっか}
questions.explanation: Children's Day is May 5th (いつか), the last day of Golden Week. November 3rd is Culture Day and January 1st is New Year's Day; March 3rd is a girls' festival day, not a national holiday.

questions.stem: How is 日 read in holiday names such as 山の日 (Mountain Day)?
questions.explanation: 〜の日 uses the native reading ひ: やまのひ. にち is in 日曜日, び in 曜日, and か in dates like 2日 (ふつか).

questions.stem: In which month does the Japanese school and business year start?
questions.explanation: New pupils, students and employees start in {4月|しがつ}, April. January is only the start of the calendar year, and September is the start in many other countries.

questions.stem: A shop notice: "{12月|じゅうにがつ}{29日|にじゅうくにち}から {1月|いちがつ}{3日|みっか}まで {休|やす}みです。{1月|いちがつ}{4日|よっか}から {午前|ごぜん} {10時|じゅうじ}に あきます。" Can you shop there on January 2nd?
choices: Yes, but only in the morning.
No, it closes for good on December 29th.
questions.explanation: {休|やす}みです with から … まで: closed from December 29th to January 3rd. It opens again (あきます) on January 4th at 10 a.m.

questions.stem: Listen. When would you say this?

audio.text: あけまして おめでとう ございます。

choices: at the start of Golden Week
in the first days of the New Year
questions.explanation: あけまして おめでとう ございます is the New Year greeting, used from January 1st. A birthday gets おたんじょうび おめでとう ございます, and on New Year's Eve you say よい おとしを.

questions.stem: Which is the polite negative of {高|たか}い (expensive)?
choices: {高|たか}くないじゃないです
questions.explanation: Drop the final い and add くないです: {高|たか}くないです. じゃないです is for nouns and な-adjectives, and the い must go before く is added, so {高|たか}いくないです is wrong too.

questions.stem: What is the negative of いい (good)?
questions.explanation: いい is irregular: its other forms come from the older word よい, so the negative is よくないです. いくないです is a very common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: この{本|ほん}はあまり___。 (This book isn't very expensive.)
questions.explanation: あまり means "not very" only together with a negative, so the adjective must be negative: あまり{高|たか}くないです. あまり{高|たか}いです is a typical English-speaker mistake.

questions.stem: Which phrase correctly means "a new car"?
questions.explanation: An い-adjective goes straight before a noun with nothing in between: {新|あたら}しい{車|くるま}. の joins two nouns and な belongs to な-adjectives.

questions.stem: How is the kanji read in "この{店|みせ}は安いです。"?
questions.explanation: 安い is やすい, cheap. The kanji's on reading アン is used in compounds, never with the okurigana い. たかい (expensive) is written 高い.

questions.stem: What does 古い mean?
questions.explanation: 古い (ふるい) means old, for things. "New" is 新しい, "long" is 長い and "cheap" is 安い.

questions.stem: Which kanji is used to write ながい (long)?
questions.explanation: ながい is written 長い. 高 is たか(い), 新 is あたら(しい) and 安 is やす(い).

questions.stem: What is the opposite of ひろい (spacious)?
questions.explanation: ひろい (spacious, wide) and せまい (cramped, narrow) are a pair. みじかい is the opposite of {長|なが}い, かるい of おもい and ちかい of とおい.

questions.stem: Type the polite negative of おいしい, ending in ないです: ___
questions.explanation: Drop the final い and add くないです: おいしい → おいしくないです.

questions.stem: Type in Japanese: "This room is spacious." (この, へや, ひろい) ___
accept: このへやはひろいです
questions.explanation: この + へや, the topic particle は, then the adjective with です: このへやはひろいです。 Remember to type は as "ha".

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: この本は高くないです。

questions.explanation: The speaker says この{本|ほん}は{高|たか}くないです: {高|たか}くない is the negative of {高|たか}い, "isn't expensive". "Cheap" would be {安|やす}い.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: とてもおもしろいです。

questions.explanation: とてもおもしろいです: とても (very) + おもしろい (interesting). "Not very interesting" would need あまり and a negative: あまりおもしろくないです.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear: ___

audio.text: ながい

questions.explanation: The word is ながい (長い), long. Its opposite is みじかい.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its opposite.
questions.explanation: {大|おお}きい/{小|ちい}さい (big/small), {新|あたら}しい/{古|ふる}い (new/old), {長|なが}い/みじかい (long/short), おもい/かるい (heavy/light). ひくい is the opposite of {高|たか}い in height.

questions.stem: What does "{駅|えき}からとおいです。" mean?
choices: It's in front of the station.
questions.explanation: とおい is far, and から marks the starting point: far from the station. "Near the station" is {駅|えき}にちかいです.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしの{日本語|にほんご}のクラスは{毎週|まいしゅう}{月曜日|げつようび}です。{先生|せんせい}はとてもおもしろいです。でも、テストはむずかしいです。クラスの{本|ほん}はあまり{高|たか}くないです。" Which is true?
choices: The class book isn't very expensive.
questions.explanation: クラスの{本|ほん}はあまり{高|たか}くないです: the class book isn't very expensive. The teacher is おもしろい (interesting, fun), the tests are むずかしい (difficult), and the class is on {月曜日|げつようび}, Monday.

questions.stem: A: {日本語|にほんご}のじゅぎょうはどうですか。 B: ___
questions.explanation: どうですか asks "How is it?", so the answer is an adjective: たのしいです (it's fun). どう is a question word and can't be used in the answer; はい and いいえ answer yes-or-no questions.

questions.stem: Which sentence is wrong?
choices: このかばんはおもくないです。
この{店|みせ}はよくないです。
このへやはあかるいです。
このパンはおいしいじゃないです。
questions.explanation: おいしい is an い-adjective, so its negative is おいしくないです, not おいしいじゃないです. The others are correct: おもくない, よくない (from いい) and あかるいです.

questions.stem: Choose the word: このテストは___むずかしくないです。 (This test isn't difficult at all.)
questions.explanation: ぜんぜん + negative means "not at all". とても (very) goes with affirmatives: とてもむずかしいです.

questions.stem: Why can Japanese be read without spaces between words?
choices: Every word is a single kanji
The mix of kanji, hiragana and katakana shows where words and endings begin
All particles are written in katakana
Japanese words are all one syllable long
questions.explanation: Kanji usually start a content word, hiragana after them is an ending or a particle, and katakana words stand out, so readers can see the chunks. Particles are hiragana, not katakana, and many words have several kanji or none.

questions.stem: Which is the polite negative of しずか (quiet)?
choices: しずかなじゃないです
questions.explanation: な-adjectives don't change; the negative goes on です, just as with nouns: しずかじゃないです. くないです is only for い-adjectives, and な is used only before a noun.

questions.stem: Which is the polite negative of きれい (pretty, clean)?
questions.explanation: きれい looks like an い-adjective, but it's a な-adjective (its い is part of the long え sound), so: きれいじゃないです. きれいくないです is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: ゆうめい___ {人|ひと} (a famous person)
questions.explanation: Before a noun a な-adjective takes な: ゆうめいな{人|ひと}. ゆうめい is a な-adjective even though it ends in い. の joins two nouns.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: わたしはコーヒー___すきです。
questions.explanation: With すき, the thing you like takes が: コーヒーがすきです. It isn't an object of a verb, so を is wrong here.

questions.stem: You want to say you're good at math without sounding boastful. Which is best?
choices: すうがくが{上手|じょうず}です。
すうがくが{下手|へた}です。
すうがくがとくいです。
すうがくがきらいです。
questions.explanation: とくい means "my strong point" and is fine about yourself. {上手|じょうず} is praise, which sounds like bragging about yourself; {下手|へた} means bad at, and きらい means you dislike it.

questions.stem: A: {日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}ですね。 B: ___
choices: はい、{上手|じょうず}です。
{上手|じょうず}じゃないですか。
questions.explanation: The usual reply to praise is modest: いいえ、まだまだです (Oh no, I've still got a long way to go). Agreeing that you're {上手|じょうず} sounds boastful, and どういたしまして answers thanks, not praise.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: たなかさんは___ {人|ひと}ですか。 — しんせつな{人|ひと}です。
questions.explanation: どんな + noun asks "what kind of…": どんな{人|ひと}, what kind of person. どう stands on its own (どうですか) and can't go before a noun; どれ means "which one".

questions.stem: Which of these is a な-adjective?
questions.explanation: ゆうめい (famous) is a な-adjective: ゆうめいな{店|みせ}, ゆうめいじゃないです. The others are い-adjectives: {大|おお}きくない, おいしくない, たのしくない.

questions.stem: How is 元気 read in "お元気ですか。"?
questions.explanation: 元気 is げんき. 元 is read ゲン here (its kun reading もと is used in other words), and 気 is キ. てんき is 天気, weather.

questions.stem: How is the word read in "この{店|みせ}は人気があります。"?
questions.explanation: 人気 here is にんき, popularity: 人気があります = is popular. 人 is read ニン in this word, not ひと or ジン, and 気 is キ.

questions.stem: What does "このへやはきれいじゃないです。" mean?
questions.explanation: きれいじゃないです is the negative of きれい (pretty, clean). "Isn't quiet" would be しずかじゃないです, and "I don't like it" uses すき: すきじゃないです.

questions.stem: Type "a quiet town" in Japanese (しずか + まち): ___
questions.explanation: A な-adjective takes な before a noun: しずかなまち.

questions.stem: Type the polite negative of べんり (convenient), ending in じゃないです: ___
questions.explanation: べんり is a な-adjective, so the negative goes on です: べんりじゃないです.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: ねこがすきです。

questions.explanation: ねこがすきです: ねこ (cat) + が + すき (liked). "I love cats" would be だいすきです, and "I don't like" すきじゃないです.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: りょうりがへたです。

questions.explanation: りょうりが{下手|へた}です: {下手|へた} means bad at. "Good at" would be {上手|じょうず} or とくい; "like" is すき.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: にぎやかなまちです。

choices: にぎやかなまちですか。
にぎやかじゃないです。
questions.explanation: The speaker says にぎやかなまちです, "It's a lively town". しずか is the opposite, quiet; ですか would make it a question.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: {上手|じょうず} is skilled (praise for others), {下手|へた} unskilled, すき liked, きらい disliked and ひま free. "Busy" is いそがしい, an い-adjective.

questions.stem: Read: "エマ：けんさんは、どんなスポーツがすきですか。 けん：テニスがすきです。でも、{下手|へた}です。 エマ：わたしはテニスがにがてです。" Which is true?
choices: Ken likes tennis but isn't good at it.
questions.explanation: Ken says テニスがすきです。でも、{下手|へた}です: he likes tennis, but he's bad at it. Emma says tennis is にがて for her, not her thing.

questions.stem: Which sentence is wrong?
choices: {元気|げんき}な{子|こ}どもです。
questions.explanation: ゆうめい is a な-adjective, so its negative is ゆうめいじゃないです. The others are correct: しずかな and {元気|げんき}な before a noun, and べんりじゃないです.

questions.stem: Which is the gentlest way to say you don't like natto?
choices: なっとうがきらいです。
なっとうはだいきらいです。
なっとうはあまりすきじゃないです。
なっとうはまずいです。
questions.explanation: あまりすきじゃないです ("I don't really like it") is the soft, polite choice. きらい and だいきらい are strong, and まずい says the food tastes bad, which is blunt.

questions.stem: Which is the polite past of さむい (cold)?
questions.explanation: For an い-adjective the past goes into the adjective: drop い and add かったです. さむいでした is the classic mistake: でした is only for nouns and な-adjectives.

questions.stem: What is the polite past of いい (good)?
questions.explanation: いい is irregular and uses よ for all its other forms: よかったです (was good). The other choices keep いい or put the past on です.

questions.stem: Which is the polite past of しずか (quiet)?
choices: しずかくなかったです
questions.explanation: しずか is a な-adjective, so です changes: しずかでした. かった belongs to い-adjectives, and な appears only before a noun.

questions.stem: Which is the polite past negative of たのしい (fun)?
choices: たのしくなかったです
たのしいじゃなかったです
questions.explanation: Make the negative たのしくない, then treat its い like any い-adjective: たのしくなかったです. たのしくないでした is wrong because the past is never put on です after an い-adjective.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: きのうは___。 (It rained yesterday.)
questions.explanation: {雨|あめ} is a noun, so the past is {雨|あめ}でした. かった is for い-adjectives, and {雨|あめ}です is present, not past.

questions.stem: A: りょこうはどうでしたか。 B: ___
choices: とてもたのしいでした。
とてもたのしかったです。
questions.explanation: どうでしたか asks "How was it?"; answer with a past adjective: たのしかったです. たのしいでした is the common mistake, and どう can't be used in the answer.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: ___ {水|みず}をください。 (cold water)
questions.explanation: Things you touch or drink are つめたい when cold. さむい is for the weather or air and how you feel, so さむい{水|みず} sounds odd. すずしい is pleasantly cool weather.

questions.stem: How is the word read in "{今日|きょう}はいい天気ですね。"?
questions.explanation: 天気 is てんき, weather. でんき is a different word (electricity, 電気). 天 is テン and 気 is キ here.

questions.stem: How is the kanji read in "きのうは雨でした。"?
questions.explanation: 雨 on its own is あめ, rain. ウ is its on reading, used only in compounds. ゆき (snow) and くも (cloud) are written in kana in this course.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "river"?
questions.explanation: 川 (かわ) is a picture of flowing water. 山 is mountain, 花 is flower and 天 is sky, heaven.

questions.stem: How is the kanji read in "きれいな花ですね。"?
questions.explanation: 花 on its own is はな, flower. カ is its on reading in compounds; き is 木 (tree).

questions.stem: Type the polite past of あつい (hot): ___
questions.explanation: Drop い and add かったです: あつい → あつかったです.

questions.stem: Type the polite past of きれい (beautiful): ___
questions.explanation: きれい is a な-adjective, so です becomes でした: きれいでした. Not きれいかったです.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: きのうはさむかったです。

questions.explanation: きのうはさむかったです: きのう (yesterday) + さむかった, the past of さむい. "Wasn't cold" would be さむくなかったです.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: あまりよくなかったです。

questions.explanation: あまりよくなかったです: あまり + the past negative of いい. "Isn't very good" (present) would be あまりよくないです.

questions.stem: Listen and type the word you hear: ___

audio.text: ふゆ

questions.explanation: The word is ふゆ, winter.

questions.stem: Match each season to its meaning.
questions.explanation: はる spring, なつ summer, あき autumn, ふゆ winter. The rainy season is つゆ.

questions.stem: Read: "{山|やま}のホテルにいます。きのうは{雨|あめ}でした。さむかったです。{今日|きょう}ははれです。{山|やま}がとてもきれいです。" What was the weather like yesterday?
questions.explanation: きのうは{雨|あめ}でした。さむかったです: it rained and it was cold. Today (きょう) is はれ, sunny.

questions.stem: Which sentence is wrong?
questions.explanation: おいしい is an い-adjective, so its past is おいしかったです; でした can't follow it. The others are correct.

questions.stem: Which correctly says "The weather was nice."?
choices: いい{天気|てんき}かったです。
いい{天気|てんき}でした。
いい{天気|てんき}よかったです。
よかった{天気|てんき}です。
questions.explanation: いい{天気|てんき} (nice weather) is a noun phrase, so the past goes on です: いい{天気|てんき}でした. You could also say {天気|てんき}がよかったです, but かった never attaches to a noun.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: {電車|でんしゃ}はバス___はやいです。 (The train is faster than the bus.)
questions.explanation: より means "than" and follows the thing being compared against: バスより, than the bus. ほう needs の before it and が after it (バスのほうが), and から means "from".

questions.stem: Fill the gap: コーヒーとおちゃと、___がすきですか。
questions.explanation: For a choice between exactly two things, ask with どちら (which of the two). どれ is for three or more, {何|なに} asks "what", and どこ "where".

questions.stem: A: {電車|でんしゃ}とバスと、どちらがはやいですか。 B: ___
choices: {電車|でんしゃ}のほうがはやいです。
{電車|でんしゃ}ほうがはやいです。
{電車|でんしゃ}はより、はやいです。
questions.explanation: Answer a どちら question with Nのほうが〜です: {電車|でんしゃ}のほうがはやいです. After a noun, ほう needs の. はい doesn't answer a which-question, and より must follow the thing compared against.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: くだものの{中|なか}で、___がいちばんすきですか。 (What's your favourite fruit?)
questions.explanation: For a kind of thing chosen from a whole category (fruit), ask {何|なに}がいちばん…. どちら is only for two things, だれ asks about people, and どう means "how".

questions.stem: Fill the gap: クラスの{中|なか}で、___がいちばんせが{高|たか}いですか。 (Who is tallest in the class?)
questions.explanation: The answer is a person, so the question word is だれ (who). {何|なに} is for things, どこ for places and いつ for times.

questions.stem: What does "あにはわたしよりせが{高|たか}いです。" mean?
choices: I'm taller than my older brother.
My brother and I are the same height.
My older brother is the tallest.
My older brother is taller than me.
questions.explanation: In AはBより〜, A is the one that is more so: あに (my older brother) is taller than わたし. より follows the one who is less tall. "The tallest" would need いちばん.

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural Japanese?
choices: このまちは{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです。
{多|おお}い{人|ひと}が{来|き}ました。
このまちは{多|おお}い{人|ひと}です。
{人|ひと}は{多|おお}いのまちです。
questions.explanation: {多|おお}い is normally used at the end of a sentence with が: {人|ひと}が{多|おお}いです (there are lots of people). Before a noun, say たくさんの{人|ひと}, not {多|おお}い{人|ひと}.

questions.stem: How is the word read in "少しさむいです。"?
questions.explanation: 少し is すこし, a little. The same kanji is すく in 少ない (すくない, few); ショウ is its on reading, for compounds.

questions.stem: How is the word read in "白いシャツ"?
questions.explanation: 白い is しろい, white. くろい is black and あかい red; ハク is the on reading of 白, used in compounds, not with い.

questions.stem: Which kanji means "many"?
questions.explanation: 多 (おお-い) means many. 少 means few or a little, 白 is white, and 名 is name.

questions.stem: Type the Japanese word for "both (of the two)": ___
questions.explanation: どちらも: どちら (which of two) + も (also, too): both. どちらもすきです = I like both.

questions.stem: Complete with one word: コーヒーの___がいいです。 (Coffee would be better.)
questions.explanation: Nのほうが〜です: "N is more ~", here "coffee is better".

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: バスより電車のほうがはやいです。

choices: The train is faster than the bus.
The bus is faster than the train.
The train and the bus are both fast.
questions.explanation: バスより{電車|でんしゃ}のほうがはやいです: より follows the bus (the slower one), and のほうが marks the train as the faster one.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: なつがいちばんすきです。

choices: I like summer more than winter.
questions.explanation: なつがいちばんすきです: いちばん + すき = like best. "More than winter" would need より: ふゆよりなつのほうがすきです.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: どちらもおいしいです。

questions.explanation: どちらもおいしいです: どちらも (both) + おいしい. A question would end in か, and "more delicious" would need のほうが.

questions.stem: Which phrase correctly means "a green bag"?
questions.explanation: みどり (green) is a noun, not an adjective, so it joins a noun with の: みどりのかばん. Colours like {白|しろ}い and あかい are い-adjectives and need no の.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its meaning.
questions.explanation: はやい fast or early, おそい slow or late, つよい strong, よわい weak, あまい sweet. Spicy is からい.

questions.stem: Read: "さとうさんとたなかさんとエマさんの{中|なか}で、エマさんがいちばんせが{高|たか}いです。さとうさんはたなかさんよりせが{高|たか}いです。" Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: エマさん is the tallest of the three, and さとうさん is taller than たなかさん, so たなかさん is the shortest.

questions.stem: Which sentence is wrong?
choices: この{中|なか}で、どれがいちばん{安|やす}いですか。
{何|なに}はいちばんおいしいですか。
{山|やま}と{川|かわ}と、どちらがすきですか。
questions.explanation: A question word is never followed by は; it takes が: {何|なに}がいちばんおいしいですか. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: コーヒーを___ください。 (A little coffee, please.)
questions.explanation: {少|すこ}し means "a little" and works like an adverb before the verb. {少|すく}ない (few) is an adjective used at the end of a sentence: {人|ひと}が{少|すく}ないです.

questions.stem: You tell your teacher about your father. Which word do you use?
questions.explanation: About your own family to someone outside it, use the modest word {父|ちち}. お{父|とう}さん is for someone else's father (or for calling your own father to his face). おとうとさん is someone else's younger brother, and そふ is your grandfather.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: たなかさんの___は{先生|せんせい}です。 (Mr Tanaka's mother is a teacher.)
questions.explanation: Someone else's mother is お{母|かあ}さん. {母|はは} is only for your own mother. あね is your own older sister, and おばさん is an aunt.

questions.stem: How do you say "four people"?
questions.explanation: Four people is よにん ({四人|よにん}). よんにん is a common mistake, and しにん is avoided (it sounds like "dead person"). 〜つ isn't used for people.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: いもうとが___います。 (I have two younger sisters.)
questions.explanation: One and two people are irregular: ひとり, ふたり. ふたつ counts things, not people, and 〜じん means nationality.

questions.stem: Fill the gap: あにが{一人|ひとり}___。 (I have one older brother.)
questions.explanation: People take います, not あります. The number needs no particle, so there's no が after {一人|ひとり}.

questions.stem: How do you say "My older sister is married."?
choices: あねはけっこんします。
おねえさんはけっこんです。
あねはけっこんでした。
あねはけっこんしています。
questions.explanation: Being married is けっこんしています. けっこんします means "will get married". And for your own sister, use あね, not おねえさん.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "My younger brother is tall."?
choices: おとうとはせが{高|たか}いです。
おとうとは{高|たか}いです。
おとうとはせが{長|なが}いです。
おとうとさんはせが{高|たか}いです。
questions.explanation: Height is described with せが{高|たか}い: おとうとはせが{高|たか}いです. Without せが, {高|たか}い about a person sounds odd, and {長|なが}い is for length, not height. おとうとさん is someone else's brother.

questions.stem: How is the kanji read in "父は{会社|かいしゃ}いんです。"?
questions.explanation: On its own, 父 is ちち (my father). It's read とう only inside お父さん. はは is 母 (mother).

questions.stem: How is 母 read in the word お母さん?
questions.explanation: In お母さん (おかあさん) 母 is read かあ. On its own it's はは, and ボ is its on reading in compounds.

questions.stem: How is 女の子 read?
questions.explanation: 女の子 is おんなのこ, girl. おんなのひと is 女の人 (woman), and おとこのこ is 男の子 (boy).

questions.stem: Which kanji means "man"?
questions.explanation: 男 (おとこ) is man: a field on top and a sign for strength below. 女 is woman, 子 child and 父 father.

questions.stem: Type the word for "my older brother" (talking about your own family): ___
questions.explanation: Your own older brother is あに. Someone else's is おにいさん.

questions.stem: Type "three people" in Japanese: ___
questions.explanation: From three on, people are counted with 〜にん: さんにん ({三人|さんにん}).

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: あにが二人います。

questions.explanation: あにが{二人|ふたり}います: あに (my older brother) + {二人|ふたり} (two people). Younger brothers would be おとうと, older sisters あね.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker ask?

audio.text: ごかぞくはなんにんですか。

choices: How many people are in your family?
questions.explanation: ごかぞくは{何人|なんにん}ですか: {何人|なんにん} asks "how many people". ご in ごかぞく shows it's the listener's family.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear: ___

audio.text: よにん

questions.explanation: You heard よにん, four people.

questions.stem: Match each word for your own family to the word for someone else's.
questions.explanation: {父|ちち}/お{父|とう}さん (father), {母|はは}/お{母|かあ}さん (mother), あに/おにいさん (older brother), いもうと/いもうとさん (younger sister). おとうとさん goes with おとうと.

questions.stem: Read: "わたしのかぞくは{五人|ごにん}です。{父|ちち}と{母|はは}とあねとおとうととわたしです。あねは{二十|にじゅう}さいです。けっこんしています。おとうとは{十|じゅっ}さいです。" Which is true?
choices: The writer has two older sisters.
The writer's younger brother is twenty.
There are four people in the family.
The writer's older sister is married.
questions.explanation: あねは…けっこんしています: the older sister is married. There are five people (including the writer), one older sister (twenty) and one younger brother (ten).

questions.stem: You're talking politely to your boss. Which sentence is NOT appropriate?
choices: うちのお{母|かあ}さんは{元気|げんき}です。
{父|ちち}は{六十|ろくじゅう}さいです。
あにが{一人|ひとり}います。
いもうとは{学生|がくせい}です。
questions.explanation: Talking to someone outside the family, call your own mother {母|はは}: {母|はは}は{元気|げんき}です. お{母|かあ}さん about your own mother sounds childish in a polite conversation. The other sentences use the modest words correctly.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "a young teacher"?
choices: {新|あたら}しい{先生|せんせい}
questions.explanation: わかい is young, for people. {新|あたら}しい{先生|せんせい} means a new teacher (newly arrived), not a young one, and {古|ふる}い is never used for people's age.

questions.stem: When is つゆ, the rainy season, in most of Japan?
choices: From June to mid or late July
questions.explanation: つゆ begins around June and ends in mid or late July in most of the country; Okinawa's comes earlier and Hokkaido has almost none.

questions.stem: What is {花見|はなみ}?
choices: Going to look at the cherry blossoms, often as a picnic
questions.explanation: {花見|はなみ} ("flower viewing") is a spring picnic under the cherry blossoms. Fireworks are {花火|はなび}, and the autumn leaves are もみじ.

questions.stem: How is the word read in "花火はきれいでした。"?
questions.explanation: 花火 is はなび: はな + ひ (fire), with ひ voiced to び. はなみ is 花見, flower viewing.

questions.stem: What kind of weather is むしあつい?
questions.explanation: むしあつい is the sticky heat of a Japanese summer: hot and humid. Cool weather is すずしい.

questions.stem: What are もみじ?
questions.explanation: もみじ is the Japanese maple and its red autumn leaves. Cherry blossoms are さくら, festivals まつり and typhoons たいふう.

questions.stem: In a weather forecast, what does はれのちくもり mean?
choices: Sunny in some places, cloudy in others
questions.explanation: のち means "later, then", so はれのちくもり is sunny first and cloudy later. "Occasional" would be ときどき.

questions.stem: Read: "あしたは{午前|ごぜん}はくもり、{午後|ごご}は{雨|あめ}でしょう。さいこうきおんは{十五|じゅうご}どです。" What will tomorrow afternoon be like?
questions.explanation: {午後|ごご}は{雨|あめ}でしょう: the afternoon will probably be rainy. It will be cloudy in the morning ({午前|ごぜん}). The high is 15 degrees.

questions.stem: A: さむいですね。 B: ___
questions.explanation: Weather lines with ね invite agreement, and ええ、ほんとうに (Yes, really) is the natural reply. いいえ、さむいです contradicts itself, and どういたしまして answers thanks.

questions.stem: Where in Japan does it snow most heavily in winter?
choices: On the Sea of Japan side and in the mountains
On the Pacific side, around Tokyo
questions.explanation: Heavy snow falls on the side facing the Sea of Japan and in the mountains. The Pacific side, including Tokyo, has mostly dry, sunny winters.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: いい天気ですね。

questions.explanation: いい{天気|てんき}ですね: ね asks for agreement, "isn't it?". A question would end in か, and the past would be いい{天気|てんき}でした.

questions.stem: Listen to part of a forecast. What will the weather be?

audio.text: くもりときどき雨でしょう。

questions.explanation: くもりときどき{雨|あめ}: ときどき means "sometimes", so it's cloudy with occasional rain. "Then later" would be のち.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: さくら cherry blossom, もみじ red autumn leaves, たいふう typhoon, つゆ rainy season. Fireworks are {花火|はなび}.

questions.stem: Talking to a colleague about your own grandmother, which word do you use?
questions.explanation: Your own grandmother, to people outside the family, is そぼ. おばあさん is someone else's grandmother, おばさん is an aunt, and そふ is your grandfather.

questions.stem: Which word means "grandfather" (someone else's)?
questions.explanation: おじいさん, with a long い, is grandfather. おじさん (short) is uncle, おじ is your own uncle and そふ your own grandfather.

questions.stem: Which word means someone else's wife?
questions.explanation: Someone else's wife is おくさん. つま is your own wife, おっと your own husband, and そぼ your grandmother.

questions.stem: A stranger walks you all the way to the station to help you. Which word best describes what they did?
questions.explanation: しんせつ is kind in the sense of helpful to others, exactly this. まじめ is earnest or hard-working, くらい gloomy, and かっこいい cool or good-looking.

questions.stem: What is the polite negative of かっこいい (cool)?
choices: かっこいいじゃないです
questions.explanation: かっこいい ends in いい, so it follows いい: かっこよくないです. かっこいくない is the same mistake as いくない.

questions.stem: What does a small child usually call her older sister?
questions.explanation: Inside the family, older siblings are called by their role, often with ちゃん: おねえちゃん. あね is the modest word used about her to outsiders, and いもうと means younger sister.

questions.stem: Why might a woman call her husband お{父|とう}さん at home?
choices: It is the formal word for husband
She names him from the children's point of view
questions.explanation: Families often name people from the youngest member's point of view: to the children he is お{父|とう}さん, so the parents use the word too. The formal word for someone else's husband is ごしゅじん.

questions.stem: What does あかるい{人|ひと} mean?
questions.explanation: あかるい literally means bright; about a person it means cheerful and outgoing. A quiet person is しずかな{人|ひと}.

questions.stem: What does まじめ usually mean when said about someone in Japan?
questions.explanation: まじめ means earnest, serious, hard-working, and it is usually a compliment. Only まじめすぎる (too serious) is a criticism.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say about the person?

audio.text: めがねをかけています。

questions.explanation: めがねをかけています means "wears glasses" (めがね = glasses). Tall would be せが{高|たか}い, long hair かみが{長|なが}い.

questions.stem: Listen. Which word did you hear?

audio.text: おばあさん

questions.explanation: You heard おばあさん, with a long あ: grandmother. おばさん (short) is aunt, おばあちゃん is the warmer family form.

questions.stem: You're an adult, and a child calls you おばさん. Why might this make you uneasy?
choices: It only means "aunt", so it's confusing
It is only used for men
Used for a stranger, it can suggest you look middle-aged
questions.explanation: For strangers, おばさん and おじさん mean "middle-aged woman" and "middle-aged man", so some adults feel it makes them sound old. Shop staff avoid them and say おきゃくさま.

questions.stem: What is the て form of {書|か}く (to write)?
questions.explanation: Group 1 verbs ending in く change く to いて: {書|か}く → {書|か}いて. {書|か}きて adds て to the ます stem, which only works for group 2 verbs; って is for う, つ and る.

questions.stem: What is the て form of {読|よ}む (to read)?
questions.explanation: む, ぶ and ぬ become んで, with a voiced で: {読|よ}んで. {読|よ}んて has the right sound change but the wrong ending; after ん it is always で.

questions.stem: What is the て form of {行|い}く (to go)?
questions.explanation: {行|い}く is the one exception to the く → いて rule: its て form is {行|い}って. {行|い}いて is what the rule would predict, which is exactly why it's the tempting mistake.

questions.stem: Type the て form of まつ (to wait): ___
questions.explanation: まつ is group 1 and ends in つ; う, つ and る all become って: まって. まちて (ます stem + て) is the group 2 pattern and doesn't work here.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs is group 1, even though it ends in -eる?
questions.explanation: かえる (to go home) is group 1: its ます form is かえります, with り, and its て form is かえって. {食|た}べる, おしえる and あける are ordinary group 2 verbs ({食|た}べます, おしえます, あけます).

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Please wait a moment"?
choices: ちょっとまちますください。
ちょっとまつください。
ちょっとまってください。
questions.explanation: A request is the て form + ください: まってください. ください never follows the dictionary form (まつ) or the ます form (まちます). まってます is a casual "I'm waiting", not a request.

questions.stem: Type the て form of する (to do): ___
questions.explanation: する is irregular (group 3): its て form is して, and every する verb follows it (べんきょうして, でんわして).

questions.stem: Match each verb to its て form.
questions.explanation: す → して, ぶ → んで, ぐ → いで, う → って. The ぐ ending keeps the voicing: いそいで, not いそいて; ぶ verbs never take the ます stem + て (よびて).

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker asking you to do?

audio.text: 名前を書いてください

questions.explanation: {名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてください: please write your name. {書|か}いて (kaite) is from {書|か}く, to write; "read" would be {読|よ}んで and "say" {言|い}って.

questions.stem: Listen. Which sentence did you hear?

audio.text: もういちど言ってください

choices: もういちど{書|か}いてください。
もういちど{言|い}ってください。
もういちど{来|き}てください。
もういちど{聞|き}いてください。
questions.explanation: "Mou ichido itte kudasai": please say it once more. {言|い}って is from {言|い}う; {聞|き}いて would be "kiite", {書|か}いて "kaite" and {来|き}て "kite". ({行|い}って, from {行|い}く, sounds exactly the same as {言|い}って; only context tells them apart.)

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear, in hiragana: ___

audio.text: まってください

questions.explanation: "Matte kudasai", please wait: まってください. Don't forget the small っ, a one-beat pause.

questions.stem: You want a stranger to take your photo. Which is the most polite way to ask?
choices: しゃしんをとりますか。
すみません、しゃしんをとってくださいませんか。
しゃしんをとってください。
すみません、しゃしんをとってもいいですか。
questions.explanation: For a favour from a stranger, すみません + 〜てくださいませんか is the kindest. 〜てください is fine but more direct. とりますか only asks whether they take photos, and 〜てもいいですか asks permission for yourself to take one.

questions.stem: How is the word in this sentence read? {父|ちち}は{毎日|まいにち}新聞を{読|よ}みます。
questions.explanation: 新聞 is しんぶん, newspaper. 聞 is read き(く) on its own as a verb, but in this word it takes its on reading ブン. モン is another on reading, used in other words.

questions.stem: What does the kanji 話 mean?
questions.explanation: 話 is talk or speak: {話|はな}す, {話|はなし}, {電話|でんわ}. Write is 書, read is 読 and listen is 聞. 話 and 読 have 言 (say) on the left; 話 adds a tongue.

questions.stem: Which kanji is used to write いう (to say)?
questions.explanation: いう is written 言う. 語 is language (lesson 18), 読 read and 話 talk: all three contain 言 on the left, which is why they look alike.

questions.stem: How is the verb read? {先生|せんせい}に聞いてください。
questions.explanation: 聞いて is きいて, from 聞く (to ask, listen). The verb uses the kun reading き; ブン is for words like {新聞|しんぶん}. かいて is {書|か}いて (write).

questions.stem: Type the て form of かえる (to go home), in hiragana: ___
questions.explanation: かえる (to go home) is a group 1 verb even though it ends in -eる (ます form かえります), so る → って: かえって. かえて would be the て form of the group 2 verb かえる "to change".

questions.stem: You forgot your pen and want your classmate's for a moment. What do you say?
choices: ペンをかしてくださいませんか。
ペンをかりてくださいませんか。
questions.explanation: You ask the other person to lend: かして (from かす). かりてください would ask them to borrow something, the wrong direction. かしますか / かりますか only ask about their habits.

questions.stem:
Read the note. What should Ken do first?
けんさんへ　としょかんへ{行|い}って、この{本|ほん}をかえしてください。それから、{六時|ろくじ}に{電話|でんわ}してください。ゆき
choices: Return a book at the library
Borrow a book from the library
questions.explanation: The first request is としょかんへ{行|い}って、この{本|ほん}をかえしてください: go to the library and return this book. The phone call at six comes after それから (then). かえす means give back, not borrow (かりる).

questions.stem: Type the て form of {来|く}る (to come): ___
questions.explanation: {来|く}る is irregular: its て form is きて ({来|き}て), with the same vowel as the ます form {来|き}ます. くて is a common mistake.

questions.stem: What does あねはけっこんしています mean?
choices: My sister is getting married right now.
My sister wants to get married.
questions.explanation: けっこんする happens in a moment, so 〜ています gives the resulting state: she got married and still is. It is not "is getting married", the tempting English reading.

questions.stem: Someone asks: あの{人|ひと}をしっていますか。 You don't know the person. What do you answer?
choices: いいえ、しっていません。
いいえ、しりませんでした。
questions.explanation: "I know" is しっています, but "I don't know" is しりません. しっていません is the classic learner's error. しりませんでした is "I didn't know", used when you've just learned something.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: くろいズボンを___います。
questions.explanation: Trousers go on the legs, so they take はく: はいています. きる is for the top half or the whole body, かぶる for hats and かける for glasses.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: {子|こ}どもはぼうしを___います。
questions.explanation: Hats take かぶる: ぼうしをかぶっています. かぶる is group 1 (かぶります), so its て form is かぶって.

questions.stem: Choose the verb: たなかさんはめがねを___います。
questions.explanation: Glasses take かける: めがねをかけています. Hats are かぶる, shoes and trousers はく, shirts and coats きる.

questions.stem: Fill in the verb in the ている form (she is wearing a coat): コートを___。
